0.title: 2 Corinthians: Strength in Weakness
0.overview:
Second Corinthians is the most autobiographical of Paul's letters and, by many measures, the most emotionally raw document in the New Testament. Where Romans is a theological treatise and Galatians a polemical defence of the gospel, 2 Corinthians is a window into the interior life of an apostle under siege — attacked by opponents, misunderstood by the very church he founded, exhausted by suffering, and yet mysteriously sustained by a grace he cannot fully explain. It is the letter in which Paul most fully exposes the paradox at the heart of the Christian life: strength made perfect in weakness, treasure carried in jars of clay, life produced through death.

The letter was written from Macedonia, probably in AD 55–56, after a painful sequence of events: a “painful visit” to Corinth that went badly (2:1), a severe letter that followed (2:3–4; 7:8), anxiety about how the Corinthians would respond, and then the relief of Titus's report that most had repented (7:6–7). Paul writes in the aftermath of that partial reconciliation, addressing a church that has largely come back to him — but not entirely, since a group of opponents (often called the “super-apostles” or “false apostles”) still commands a following and challenges his authority.

How many letters did Paul write to Corinth? At least four. An early letter, now lost, warned against associating with the sexually immoral (1 Cor 5:9); then came 1 Corinthians; then a painful visit (2:1); then a letter written with many tears (2:4; 7:8); and then this one. Many scholars think chapters 10–13 are part of that tearful letter, or a later one, because the tone changes so sharply at chapter 10. But no manuscript ever divides the letter; the tearful letter was written to grieve them over an offence, which chapters 10–13 never mention; and the change of tone is explained by Paul turning from the repentant majority (chapters 1–9) to the false apostles still at work. The more likely reading is that 2 Corinthians is one letter, and the tearful letter is lost.

The letter falls into three broad movements. Chapters 1–7 address the ministry of suffering and reconciliation: Paul defends the authenticity of his apostleship by pointing to suffering as its credential, not its disqualification, and unfolds a breathtaking theology of the new covenant ministry. Chapters 8–9 address the collection for the Jerusalem church — a sustained theology of generosity rooted in the self-giving of Christ. Chapters 10–13, which contain the “fool's speech,” are Paul's sharp and ironic defence of his apostleship against the super-apostles, climaxing in the account of his thorn in the flesh and the word that defines the entire letter: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

The letter's central theological contribution is its theology of weakness and glory. Paul's opponents measured apostleship by rhetorical skill, impressive presence, and spiritual fireworks. Paul measures it by the cross: authentic ministry looks like dying and rising, like carrying in the body the death of Jesus so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested. This is not merely Paul's personal psychological coping; it is a fundamental claim about how the kingdom of God advances — through the cruciform shape of those who carry it.

1.title: The God of All Comfort and the Yes of Christ
1.overview:
Corinth was a rich, proud, commercial city on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, refounded by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony in 44 BC and full of ambitious freedmen on the way up. Status, eloquence and success mattered enormously there. After Paul founded the church (Acts 18) and wrote 1 Corinthians, things went badly: he made a short “painful visit” in which someone in the church publicly opposed him (2:1–5), then wrote a severe letter “with many tears” (2:4), and changed his plan to visit again. Meanwhile visiting preachers, impressive speakers with letters of recommendation, were telling the church that Paul was weak, unreliable and second-rate. 2 Corinthians is Paul’s reply, written from Macedonia once Titus brought news that most of the church had repented (7:5–7).

Chapter 1 sets the theme of the whole letter: God’s power shows up in weakness. Paul blesses the God of all comfort for carrying him through a crushing affliction, then answers the charge that his changed travel plans prove him fickle.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God of All Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens by naming himself an apostle by God’s will, the very point his critics dispute. Then, instead of complaining about a terrible year, he praises God for comfort in it: comfort that equips him to strengthen others, and a rescue from near death in Asia that taught him to rely on the God who raises the dead.
verseByVerse.theology:
The title “Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (v. 3) is carefully built. “Mercies” echoes the Hebrew compassion related to the word for womb, and “comfort” shares its root with the Helper, the Holy Spirit (John 14:16). Every genuine comfort, whatever hands deliver it, is finally God’s own.

In vv. 4–7 suffering and comfort are bound together in ministry. Those comforted in their own trouble have something to give that ease cannot supply. This does not make suffering good in itself; it means God wastes nothing.
verseByVerse.examples:
A pastor who has come through a severe depression returns to ministry and finds that his care for depressed people has changed. He is not applying techniques; he is giving what he has received, and his people sense it.

And v. 11 puts the same dynamic in reverse. A member who has never taught or led prays through the week for a missionary she has met once. Her praying is a shoulder under the load, and she should hear how God answered, because the thanksgiving was the point of the rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians is Paul’s most personal letter, written with relief, love and warning after a painful visit, a severe letter and an attack on his authority. It asks what true Christian ministry looks like, and answers: like the cross, strength in weakness and comfort in suffering. Chapter 1 blesses the God of all comfort, who comforts Paul so that he can comfort others and rescued him in Asia to teach him to rely on the God who raises the dead (vv. 3–11). Then, charged with fickleness, Paul answers that all God’s promises find their Yes in Christ, that God has sealed his people with the Spirit, and that he stayed away only to spare them (vv. 12–24).

The setting. Paul wrote from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, about a year after 1 Corinthians. Between the two letters: a second, painful visit (2:1; 13:2), where someone attacked him publicly (2:5–8; 7:12); a severe, tearful letter, now lost, sent by Titus (2:3–4; 7:8); an anxious wait in Troas; and at last Titus in Macedonia with good news (2:12–13; 7:5–7). Chapters 10–13 deal with false apostles who had arrived in Corinth.

By the will of God. Every letter Paul wrote begins by naming himself, and here the words compress the thesis of the whole letter. The letter is read aloud to people not united about the man who wrote it; some have been told, persuasively, by teachers with better credentials and a better manner, that Paul is unimpressive, inconsistent, possibly a fraud. And the first thing they hear is where his commission came from: not from a committee, not from Jerusalem, not from the Corinthians, who might therefore withdraw it, but from the will of God.

Authority his critics cannot reach. That is not vanity. If his standing came from the Corinthians’ approval, their disapproval would end it, so Paul puts his authority where his critics cannot reach it (Galatians 1:1). Anyone who has served in a church for long has felt the ground move: the elder quietly criticised, the pastor who learns that a group has been meeting to discuss him. The temptation is to build a case and reclaim the room. But if God put you where you are, the room’s good opinion was never what was holding you up.

Sent by the Sent One. Apostle means one sent, and the sender matters more than the messenger. Paul was sent by the risen Christ himself (Acts 26:16–18), and Christ was the Sent One before him, the apostle and high priest of our confession (Hebrews 3:1), sent not in splendour but in weakness. The authority Paul carries is borrowed from a Lord who was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God (13:4), and a messenger of that Lord should not be surprised to look unimpressive.

And Timothy our brother. Not my assistant. Timothy had helped to found the church in Corinth (Acts 18:5) and been sent back to it (1 Corinthians 4:17), and is here given a name that levels rather than ranks. The man defending his own apostolic authority does not use it to raise himself above the young man beside him.

The church of God. The possessive is startling. This is the congregation that had split into factions, tolerated incest, sued one another in pagan courts, got drunk at the Lord’s Supper and quarrelled over spiritual gifts. It is the church of God. It belongs to him. It is at Corinth the way a ship is at anchor: located there, not owned there. Whatever a congregation is like on a bad Sunday, its title deed is not in the hands of the people who spoil it. He does not wait for a church to deserve his name before he writes it on the door.

The whole of Achaia. The Roman province of southern Greece: Athens, Cenchreae (Romans 16:1), and the scattered believers in between. Paul knew that his most personal, most wounded words would be read out well beyond Corinth.

Grace to you and peace. Grace is God giving what was not earned; peace is what grace produces when it lands: the war over, the relationship restored. And they come from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, out of one source; only God gives grace, so the Son is named beside the Father as its giver without a word of explanation. Paul opens a letter soaked in tears by wishing on his critics the two things he most needs himself.

Should I leave a church that has hurt me, or that is in a mess? Not simply because it is a mess. Every church is made of sinners, and Paul did not abandon Corinth when it divided, misjudged him and listened to his rivals; he wrote, prayed, wept and waited. Ordinary failures, poor leadership, hurt feelings and disagreements over secondary matters are reasons to work and pray for repair, not to walk away. But there are real reasons to leave: where the gospel itself is denied, where open sin is defended and never disciplined, or where abuse is covered up and victims are silenced. Abuse must never be tolerated, and no one is bound to sit under it. If you go, go honestly, without slander, and join another faithful church rather than none.

In everyday life. Think of the person in your congregation with whom things are strained. Before you rehearse your case against them, say this sentence about them to God: they belong to you, not to me. Then wish them, in prayer and if possible in person, grace and peace.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, after a painful visit to Corinth and a severe letter written “with many tears.” Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the God. Paul has just come through a burden beyond his strength, and the first thing out of his mouth is not a complaint but a blessing. Blessed (eulogētos) is the opening of Jewish prayer, barukh attah Adonai, blessed are you, Lord (Ephesians 1:3; 1 Peter 1:3), and Paul fills it with the name of Jesus: no comfort in this chapter is not finally the Father’s comfort reaching us through him.

In the flow. In most letters Paul follows the greeting by thanking God for his readers (1 Corinthians 1:4). Here he blesses God for what God has done for him in affliction, and lays down the theme the whole letter will defend: God’s comfort comes through suffering, not around it, and his power shows itself in weakness (4:7–12; 12:9–10).

The Father of mercies. The Greek is oiktirmoi, mercies, compassions, behind the Hebrew rahamim, from the word for a womb. It is the word for what a mother feels when her child is hurt: the movement toward the pain before any decision has been made. As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Psalm 103:13). Compassion is not something God occasionally does. It is something God fathers.

And God of all comfort. The word is paraklēsis, and it or its verb appears ten times in five verses. English has weakened it into a warm drink and a soft chair. The Greek means to be summoned to someone’s side: what a defence counsel does in court, what a friend does on the edge of your bed at two in the morning, strengthening as well as consoling. Its cousin is paraklētos, the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit (John 14:16). Comfort in this sense does not remove the trouble. It puts someone beside you in it, and the someone is God (Isaiah 40:1).

All. Not the God of some comfort, or of religious comfort, or of the comfort that arrives once the crisis is over. Every real consolation you have received, the friend who said the right thing, the sleep that finally came, the verse that surfaced in a sleepless hour, the hand on your shoulder outside the ward, came out of his treasury. Those were not distractions from God while you waited for him to act. They were God acting.

Of our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul names the Father of mercies as the Father of Jesus, and that is where the mercies were seen. When Jesus met a widow following her only son’s body out of Nain, he had compassion on her and said to her, Do not weep (Luke 7:13): the womb-deep pity of God, walking in human flesh to a funeral. And the God of all comfort proved his name finally not by sparing his Son but by giving him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Paul is not thanking God for suffering. He is blessing the God he found inside it, and he found him there because the Son had gone into suffering first. These titles are not from a textbook. They are from the field, and from a cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God removes all suffering. It means he comforts us in it. Nor does it mean that every comfortable feeling is from God: the comfort of a lie, of a drink, of a sin that numbs the pain for an evening, is counterfeit. God’s comfort always leaves you nearer to him and more truthful about your life, not further away.

What if I do not feel comforted? Then you are not alone, and you have not been passed over. Comfort in this chapter is not first a feeling but a presence: God summoned to your side. Feelings of consolation often come late, sometimes long after the worst is over, and Paul is writing from the far side. In the meantime, go where God has promised to meet you: his word read and heard, the prayers of others, the Lord’s Supper, the friend who will sit with you without fixing anything. Tell God plainly that you do not feel him; the Psalms do it constantly (Psalm 13:1; 88). The God of all comfort is not offended by the honesty. He is the one who prompted it.

For worship. Blessed be he. Not because the affliction was light, for it was not. But because when the strength ran out there was Someone already alongside, whose compassion is not a decision but a nature, and whose consolation has no visible floor. He has never once been found to be less than his names.

parallels.desc: I, I am he who comforts you

verseByVerse.quote: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who comforts us in all our affliction. Here is the sentence that governs the letter, and its key words are so that. Affliction is thlipsis, from a verb meaning to press or crush: the pressure of a weight. And God comforts us in affliction, not only by taking us out of it.

So that we may be able. God comforts us; that comfort makes us able; and what we give away is the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God, the same substance, handed on, like water in a bucket line. The God at the head of the line has more. He could have consoled each of his children privately and left it there. Instead he has built his family so that his comfort travels from hand to hand, and the weakest believer who has been held by him becomes a carrier of his consolation to another.

The first link in the chain. The chain does not begin with Paul. It begins with the one old Simeon was waiting for when he looked for the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), and Luke’s word there is Paul’s word, paraklēsis. Christ is the comfort of God in person, and he walked the very road this verse describes: because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). He was afflicted, and so he is able. Every comfort handed along a line of believers was first drawn from him, which is why Paul says in the next breath that comfort overflows through Christ (v. 5). We comfort others as people comforted by a Saviour who suffered.

All and any. God comforts us in all our affliction so that we can comfort those in any affliction. The comfort received in one kind of trouble is transferable to another. The woman who was carried through a bereavement is not disqualified from sitting with the man losing his business, because what she has to give is not a technique specific to grief. It is God. That answers a common objection: I have never been through what she is going through. The qualification is not that you have suffered the same thing. It is that you have been comforted by God, and the currency you hand over is his, not yours. You are not being asked to be wise. You are being asked to be there, with what you were given.

Comforted by God. Think of the hardest stretch you have lived through. Who got the benefit of it? God comforted you not merely so that you would feel better but so that you would be able, and that ability may be sitting unused while somebody two rows behind you on Sunday is going through it now. If you are still too bruised to give anything, that is no failure: a bucket is filled before it is passed, and God is not in a hurry with you.

Nothing wasted. There is a hard implication in the other direction too. If comfort is given to be passed on, then some of what God allows into your life is allowed for someone else’s sake; Paul says it outright in verse 6. That does not make you a training exercise for somebody else’s benefit, for God loves you for your own sake. It means that nothing in it will be wasted: not the sleepless nights, not the questions you could not answer, not even the months you handled it badly. God is not merely repairing you. He is equipping you. Paul’s opponents looked at a beaten, imprisoned, shipwrecked man and concluded that God was plainly not blessing his ministry. Paul looks at the same evidence and sees not the damage to his ministry but the making of it (12:9).

What do I actually say to someone who is suffering? Often less than you think. Go, and stay; presence is most of it. Say that you are sorry and that you are praying, and then pray, sometimes with them if they welcome it. Listen more than you speak, and do not rush to explain why it happened or to tell them it will be all right; Job’s friends did best in the week they said nothing (Job 2:13). Offer specific help rather than a general “let me know”: a meal on Thursday, a lift to the hospital, an hour with the children. When the moment is right, share briefly what God was to you in your own dark place, and point them to his promises rather than to your story. Then keep coming back after everyone else has stopped.

parallels.desc: as one whom his mother comforts

verseByVerse.quote: For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s sufferings. Literally, the sufferings of Christ overflow to us. In what sense does a Christian share in the sufferings of Christ? Did the cross leave something outstanding?

The atonement is finished. The New Testament is emphatic that the atoning work of Christ is finished and unrepeatable: a single sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12, 14); It is finished (John 19:30). Nothing you suffer adds a gram to the payment for your sin. When Paul speaks of filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Colossians 1:24), he is not topping up the atonement but saying that the Messiah’s sufferings spill over into the age of the church through the people who carry his message (1 Peter 4:13). The cross was an event that happened once and is never to be repeated as a payment. But it is also a shape, and the Lord who bore it has bent the whole life of his people into conformity with it, so that dying and rising is not an interruption of the Christian life but its rhythm.

Why are you persecuting me? The risen Christ said to Saul not my followers but me (Acts 9:4): the Head feels what happens to the body. Our pain does not complete his; his life has been so joined to ours that our pain is drawn inside his. (See Acts 22:7–8 for the fuller answer.)

Comfort too. Two things follow, and both are what a suffering believer needs in the middle of the night. First, the measure is exact. The word rendered share abundantly is used on both sides of the sentence: the sufferings overflow, and so does the comfort, at the same rate. That is not a promise that the pain will be small. It is a promise that it will never outrun the supply. If the flood rises, so does the boat. Second, the channel is named: through Christ. The comfort is not dispatched from a distance by a God who has only heard about suffering. It comes through the one who was in it: whose friends fell asleep while he prayed, who was misrepresented at his trial, deserted by those closest to him, and who cried out that God had forsaken him. There is no experience of yours that he learned about second-hand. He goes first into every dark place his people are asked to enter, and he comes out.

Which sufferings count? Not every hardship is in the first place a sharing in Christ’s sufferings; Paul is speaking chiefly of what comes upon a person for the sake of Christ and his gospel. But do not draw that line too tightly. Paul is not building a hierarchy of holy pain. He is telling a church that despises weakness that the sufferings of their apostle are not evidence against him. They are the family likeness. And every trouble borne in faith by someone joined to Christ is borne in fellowship with him, who is touched with the feeling of our weakness (Hebrews 4:15).

Should a Christian go looking for suffering? No. Paul never sought pain for its own sake, and he used lawful means to escape danger: he was lowered over a wall in a basket (11:33) and appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25). Suffering is not a merit badge, and inflicting it on yourself has no value before God (Colossians 2:23). What Paul did refuse was to avoid suffering at the cost of faithfulness. Do not court it; do not dodge it by denying Christ. When it comes because you belong to him, receive it as fellowship with him, and expect his comfort to overflow in proportion.

For worship. The risen Lord sits at the Father’s right hand in glory, and still he will not hold his people’s pain at arm’s length. His suffering for sin is finished, and nothing can be added to it. His sympathy is not finished, and nothing can wear it out.

verseByVerse.quote: If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For your comfort and salvation. The Corinthians were sitting in relative comfort, comparing their apostle unfavourably with more impressive teachers. Paul was in Asia being crushed to the point of despair. And his reading of the situation is that the crushing was on their account.

How can that be? The verse gives two ways. The first is the one we have already met: what he receives in affliction he hands on. He is being taken through it so that he will have something real to give them, which is why the sentence works just as well the other way round: and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort. Both halves of his experience are theirs. His bad years are their supply. The second is nearer the surface than we notice. A watching church learns what the gospel can carry by seeing what it carries a man through. Doctrine held under no pressure teaches nothing. When the Corinthians heard that Paul had been beyond his strength and had not let go of Christ, they were being handed evidence about the strength of the one he was holding. Paul’s sufferings also brought them the gospel in the first place, for he preached it at Corinth through opposition and fear (Acts 18:6–10; 1 Corinthians 2:3).

The shape of the Servant. The shape of this sentence belongs first to Christ, afflicted for the comfort and salvation of others in a sense no apostle shares: upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace (Isaiah 53:5). Paul’s sufferings save no one. But his life has been bent into the same shape on a smaller scale: death is at work in us, but life in you (4:12). A servant of the Crucified ends up living for others because his Master died for them.

Patiently endure. The comfort is not received by studying Paul’s hardships from a safe distance, but where the same pressure bears on you. The word is hypomonē, steadfast endurance: not gritted teeth and not resignation, but staying put under a weight instead of crawling out from under it. God’s comfort is not found by the man who has arranged his life to avoid all pressure. It is found by the one who stayed.

The same sufferings. Most believers will never be flogged for the gospel. They will be passed over at work for being honest, or lose a friendship over what they believe, or carry a chronic illness for thirty years. Paul does not put his trials in one category and their smaller griefs in another: whatever is borne under the pressure of belonging to Christ draws on the same comfort. Manuscripts arrange the clauses of verses 6–7 a little differently, so the KJV’s order differs from modern Bibles; the meaning is the same.

Is it wrong to pray for my suffering to end? No. Paul himself asked three times for his thorn to be removed (12:8), and Jesus prayed, if it be possible, let this cup pass. Asking for relief is not a failure of faith; it is a child speaking to his Father. What Paul adds is that while the answer is not yet, the suffering is not empty. Pray for healing, for rescue, for the trouble to lift; and pray too that while it lasts it will do its work, in you and in those who are watching you.

In everyday life. Somebody is watching how you carry the illness, the loss, the long wait. You do not have to perform cheerfulness. But let them see where you go with it: that you still pray, still come to worship, still say that God is good while the tears are real.

verseByVerse.quote: Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our hope for you is unshaken. Paul now says what he expects suffering to produce in them, and the word he reaches for is bebaia: firm, secured, the word used of a legally binding contract or an anchor that holds. His hope for this church is not a wish. It is a settled expectation.

Who he is talking about. This is the congregation of 1 Corinthians: lawsuits, incest, drunkenness at the Lord’s table, factions. Since then, a visit too painful to repeat and a letter written in anguish. If any pastor ever had grounds for giving up on a church, it is this one. And his hope for them is unshaken, not because he has revised his opinion of their behaviour.

Share in our comfort. His confidence is not in their track record but in the pattern of how God deals with his people: he never takes anyone into the affliction without taking them through to the consolation. Paul is sure of them because he is sure of God. Share is koinōnoi, partners: no clean line between the man in the pulpit and the people in the seats.

Into the fellowship of his Son. In his first letter, before a word about their scandals, Paul told them God will sustain you to the end, because God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship (koinōnia) of his Son (1 Corinthians 1:8–9). Both apostle and church are joined to Christ, and his sufferings and consolation now run through all of them. Paul’s hope does not rest on Corinth. It rests on the Son into whose life Corinth has been called.

Who have you written off? That is a lesson for anyone who has given up on someone. Hope that rests on a person’s performance is shaken every time they fail, which is why such hope for other people is so often worn out by the second or third disappointment. Hope that rests on God’s character survives the failures, because it was never resting on the record in the first place. The question is not whether they deserve better. It is whether the God who has not finished with you has finished with them.

What if the comfort has not come and it has been a long time? Then hold to the tense Paul uses: you will share. It is a certainty about the future, not a description of how you feel tonight. Some comfort comes quickly; some comes in small portions that only add up in hindsight; and some of God’s comfort is kept for the morning of the resurrection, when he will wipe away every tear. Meanwhile do not suffer in secret. Tell a pastor or a trusted friend, let the church carry you, and keep putting yourself where God speaks. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning (Psalm 30:5). The night has an end, and the one who promised it is faithful.

For worship. Hope for the worst of us is anchored where none of us can reach to loosen it: Jesus has gone ahead as a forerunner behind the curtain (Hebrews 6:19–20). He has never yet brought a child of his into affliction and left him there, and his word is not may but will: you will share in the comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The affliction in Asia. The church has needed this sentence badly and expected it least. The apostle who sang hymns at midnight with his back opened by rods (Acts 16:22–25) says plainly that he came to the point of despairing of life itself. Asia is the Roman province around Ephesus, and brothers includes the sisters of the church.

Beyond our strength. Burdened is bareō, weighed down. Utterly is kath’ hyperbolēn, beyond all proportion; beyond our strength is hyper dynamin, past the limit of what he could carry. God let his apostle be given more than he could handle in his own strength.

That we despaired of life itself. The verb is exaporeomai: utterly at a loss, no exit visible in any direction. He could see no way he was coming out of it alive, and he stopped expecting to.

What was it? He does not tell us. The riot in Ephesus recorded in Acts 19:23–41 is the usual guess; some think of a near-fatal illness, others of an imprisonment or a plot we have no record of. The silence is frustrating and it may be a mercy, because a named crisis would let the reader file it under somebody else’s category. As it stands, whatever is crushing you fits the gap.

Oxygen for the despairing. For some readers this verse is oxygen. There are Christians who have come to a place where they no longer wanted to be alive, and who have carried on top of that darkness the private conviction that a real believer could never get there. They have heard that despair is unbelief, and concluded that whatever they have disqualifies them. This verse takes that conclusion away. The man who despaired of life itself is the man who wrote Romans 8. He was not backslidden when it happened; he was in the middle of one of the most fruitful ministries the church has known. And he was not ashamed of it afterwards. He wrote it down, to a church that already thought him too weak, knowing they would read it aloud.

The saints have been here. Elijah asked to die (1 Kings 19:4). Jeremiah cursed the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14). The psalmist ended a psalm with darkness as his closest friend (Psalm 88:18), and God put it in the hymnbook. The Bible does not hand us a faith that floats above the water. It hands us a faith that has been to the bottom. God let his apostle go down to the very bottom, and then had him write it in Scripture, so that no believer who goes down there would ever think he was the first.

Loud cries and tears. The deepest place in this company belongs to Christ. In Gethsemane his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Mark 14:34), and he offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard (Hebrews 5:7). The answer came on the third day. A believer crushed beyond his strength is on a road the Saviour has already walked, prayed on and come out of alive.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul lost his faith. It means he lost hope in himself. And it does not contradict 1 Corinthians 10:13. That verse is about temptation to sin: God will never put you in a place where obedience is impossible and sinning is your only option. It is not a promise that you will never be given more suffering than you can carry. Paul says here that he was. The point of that weight is the next verse.

Is depression a sign of weak faith, and should a Christian get help? Darkness of mind is not in itself a sign of weak faith; Paul, Elijah and the psalmists knew it. Sometimes it has spiritual causes that need dealing with, such as unconfessed sin or bitterness, but often it has causes in the body, in grief, in exhaustion or in trauma. Seek help, as you would for any illness. Tell your pastor and a trusted friend. See your doctor, and do not be ashamed of medicine or counselling; using means is not distrusting God, any more than Paul’s advice to Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach was (1 Timothy 5:23). And if you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today and contact emergency help now. You are not a burden to God’s people. You are one of them.

In everyday life. If you are the one who is well, look around. Somebody in your church may be carrying a weight like this with a smile on Sunday. Ask them how they actually are, and wait for the answer.
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not say what the danger in Asia was; it may have been the riot at Ephesus, severe illness or another threat.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence of death. The sentence (apokrima) was used in official documents for a ruling given in answer to a petition. This is not a mood. It is a man who has heard the judgment read out and knows the appeal has failed.

Not on ourselves. Then the word that turns the letter: but that was to. Paul is not saying his suffering was light, or that every affliction comes with an explanation attached, and he is not handing us a sentence to say breezily at a funeral. He is saying, looking back, that the crushing was not random. It was aimed, and the target was his self-reliance.

The end of himself. Paul had the training, the languages, the stamina, the intellect. A man with resources will keep using them and never discover what God can do at the point where they are gone. There was no way to teach Paul otherwise except to take him past the end of himself.

Where does your confidence rest? Not the answer you would give in a Bible study: the answer your body gives at three in the morning. When the letter arrives, what do you reach for first? The savings, the contacts, the plan, the argument you have rehearsed? There is nothing wrong with any of those, and God gave them. But if you have never once been past the end of them, then you do not yet know from experience whether the God you profess actually holds. Paul knows. It cost him everything he had to find out.

But on God who raises the dead. Look at the name he gives God at the moment of extremity: not the God who prevents death, nor the God who explains it, but God who raises the dead. If the verdict has been passed and cannot be appealed, what you need is not a rescuer who gets you off the charge but a God whose power operates on the far side of the sentence. Abraham trusted him when his own body was as good as dead, believing in the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17), and he reasoned that God was able even to raise Isaac from the dead (Hebrews 11:19). Paul is not comforting himself that he will probably survive. Whether he survives or not, the God he serves has already emptied one tomb and has committed himself to emptying the rest (1 Corinthians 15:20). Death is not the place where his power stops. It is the place where it was displayed.

The sentence carried out. Paul felt that he had received the sentence of death. Christ received it in fact: he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and the stone was rolled across a grave with the case closed. Then the God who raises the dead raised him. For those in Christ the worst verdict has already been executed on their Substitute, so the death they still face is no longer a sentence but a doorway.

Does God send my suffering, or only allow it? Scripture speaks of God as truly sovereign over our troubles, not a bystander who reacts to them. Nothing reaches his child by accident; even what others mean for evil, God means for good (Genesis 50:20), and he works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Yet he is never the author of sin, and the cruelty of people or of Satan remains theirs, not his. Scripture holds both together without explaining every case. For the sufferer the comfort is this: what is happening to you is not meaningless and not out of control. It is in the hands of a Father whose purpose for you is to bring you to rely on him, and finally to raise you from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will deliver us. The same verb three times: he delivered, he will deliver, he will deliver again. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, put the middle verb in the present (and doth deliver); the earliest have the future, as most modern Bibles do. The word is rhyomai: to drag someone clear, as a man pulls a child out from under a falling wall.

Memory and hope wired together. Because God did it, God will do it: the past tense is evidence. We have astonishingly short memories for mercy. We can be delivered in March and be certain by August that God has abandoned us, because we never wrote March down (Psalm 78:11).

The deliverance behind every deliverance. The deepest memory a Christian has is not his own: Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10), the same verb, and the God who did not spare his own Son will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32). If God has pulled you out from under the greatest weight of all, his judgment against your sin, he will not leave you under the smaller ones. Every deliverance in a believer’s life is a small rehearsal of the final one, when the God who raised Jesus will raise us also (4:14).

What about the times he does not deliver? The harder question must not be dodged, because a reader will hit it within seconds. Paul, writing this, had perhaps a decade left before a Roman sword ended his life. That, at least, is how the early church remembered his death under Nero. The deliverance he is so sure of did not, in the end, keep him out of Nero’s hands. The answer is in the title he used one verse earlier. The God he is trusting is God who raises the dead, and a God like that has a wider definition of rescue than we do. Paul says as much to Timothy at the end, writing from prison: the Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom (2 Timothy 4:18). He did not mean he expected to be released. He meant that the sword would be the last thing that ever happened to him, and that on the far side of it he would be safe. Deliverance is not always deliverance from; sometimes it is deliverance through. Not one child of God has ever failed to arrive.

On him we have set our hope. The perfect tense: a decision made that is still standing, a stake driven into the ground. Between verse 8 and verse 10 nothing in Paul’s circumstances has changed. What has changed is what he is looking at.

How do I build this kind of memory? Keep a record. Write down, in a notebook or at the back of your Bible, the specific things God has carried you through and the prayers he has answered, with dates. Tell them to your children and to younger believers; Israel was commanded to do exactly this (Psalm 78:4). Sing hymns and psalms that rehearse God’s past faithfulness, because they train the memory. And when a new trouble comes, read the record before you decide what God is like. The facts on that page are part of your evidence, and they are admissible.

verseByVerse.quote: You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also must help us by prayer. The verb is synypourgeō, to join in helping: several people getting their shoulders under the same load. Paul treats the prayers of ordinary Corinthian believers as genuine labour applied to his actual survival. Somewhere in Corinth there was a believer with no gift anyone could name, no money, no standing, who had never travelled further than the harbour. Paul’s sentence puts that person’s shoulder under an apostle’s survival in Asia. The work of the church is done by people whose names are not recorded, and the God who keeps the record has never once mislaid one of them.

If God has decided, what does prayer change? It is the question every thinking Christian asks and seldom hears answered. If God had already decided to deliver Paul, what did the praying change? And if the praying changed it, is God being steered by us? The answer Scripture gives is not that God is persuadable but that he is generous. He ordains the end and he ordains the means to it, and he has chosen to make the prayers of his people one of the means. A father who could carry the box himself asks the four-year-old to take the other end, and the child really is carrying it. Nothing is being pretended. The father has arranged a world in which the child’s effort genuinely bears weight, because he wants the child in the work and not merely watching it. So here: the deliverance was God’s from first to last, and it came through the prayers of many, and both halves of that sentence are true.

So that many will give thanks. Paul does not say so that I will be delivered but so that many will give thanks. He wants the prayer list long because he wants the choir large. And the blessing is charisma, a gift of grace: even the answer to prayer is grace, not wages, and the raw material of praise.

Behind the prayers of many. These prayers are not lonely voices sent up from a harbour town in the hope of being heard. They rise to the Father through a Son who always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Before Peter fell, Jesus told him that he had prayed for him, that his faith might not fail (Luke 22:32), and the same Lord carries Paul’s name before the Father now. The prayers of the Corinthians are joined to his, and that is why they bear weight at all. Even the thanksgiving Paul longs for will rise through him, for it is through Christ that the church says its Amen to God (1:20).

Does it matter how many people pray? Yes, but not because God is out-voted. The number matters because Paul wants many to share in the work and many to share in the thanks. God hears the single prayer of a lonely believer as surely as the prayer of a thousand (James 5:16–18). But he has made us a body, and he loves to answer in a way that draws many into the asking and many into the praise. So do ask others to pray for you; it is not weakness or self-importance. And when you are asked, pray, and later ask how it turned out.

In everyday life. Tell people what to pray for, and then tell them what happened; a congregation that never hears the outcomes is being robbed of the best half. Pray today for a missionary or pastor in difficulty, by name; then find out how God answers, and give thanks aloud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–24 — The Yes of God in Christ and Paul’s Changed Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul defends his integrity against the charge that his changed travel plans prove him unreliable. He grounds his own word in God’s faithfulness, in whom every promise is Yes in Christ, and explains that he stayed away to spare them, not to dominate them.
verseByVerse.theology:
“All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (v. 20) is a key to reading the Old Testament: every promise, to Abraham, to Moses, to David and through the prophets, is fulfilled in Christ. Not every Old Testament text is directly about Jesus, but the whole line of God’s promise reaches its destination in him.

Verses 21–22 show the Trinity at work in assurance: the Father establishes, the anointing (chrisas, from the same root as Christos) is shared with Christ, and the Spirit is given as seal and down payment of the full inheritance (Ephesians 1:14).
verseByVerse.examples: A church member accuses her pastor of inconsistency when he changes a plan he had announced. He can do what Paul does: show plainly that the change came from care for those affected. Integrity is not never changing a plan; it is an honest motive behind every decision, including the changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand— just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our boast. The tone changes. Paul turns to what his critics have been saying: that there is a hidden Paul behind the written one. His answer begins with boast, a word that will turn into open, painful irony in chapters 10 to 12. When a minister’s integrity is being publicly dismantled, silence is not humility; it leaves the people he serves with no ground to stand on. So he speaks, carefully.

The testimony of our conscience. Not the verdict of the Corinthians, which is divided, and not his self-assessment, which proves nothing (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Conscience watches what we do when nobody is looking, and Paul’s is not accusing him.

Simplicity and godly sincerity. Simplicity is haplotēs: singleness, being one thing rather than two; its opposite is the man in the pulpit and the different man in the car afterwards. Many early manuscripts read holiness here instead, as the ESV notes, and the sense is close. Godly sincerity is eilikrineia, purity of motive, a word the ancients liked to explain as judged by sunlight. Hold my ministry to the light, Paul says; it will bear inspection.

Not by earthly wisdom. Not by cleverness or self-interest, but by God’s grace. He is boasting about something he received.

What you read and understand. Here is the specific accusation answered. Some said Paul’s letters had hidden meanings. What the letter says on the surface is what he means underneath, with no code and no second layer for the initiated. Anyone who has had to decode a message from a colleague, a relative or a leader knows what a rare and restful thing this is. Plain speech is a form of love, because it refuses to make the other person guess.

On the day of our Lord Jesus. They understand him only partially now; but on that day the misunderstanding will be finished on both sides, and each will boast of the other, glad before Christ for what God did through him (Philippians 2:16; 1 Thessalonians 2:19–20), all of it praise to the Lord who did it.

Treated as impostors. The charge against Paul was first laid against his Lord: that impostor (Matthew 27:63), though no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22). He was the one wholly single man, and he went to the cross misjudged and left the verdict with God, who gave it on the third day. The simplicity Paul claims is the grace of the one sincere man, given to his servant.

When you cannot clear your name. Some people will go to their graves with the wrong idea of you. Paul puts the date of the hearing in the future and leaves it there (1 Corinthians 4:5). Until then the need to be thought well of can rule a heart as surely as money can. The only cure is a verdict that matters more, and in Christ the Judge has already given it: there is now no condemnation for those who are in him (Romans 8:1).

What is conscience, and can it be wrong? Conscience is the inner sense, given by God, that judges our own actions as right or wrong (Romans 2:15). It is a real witness, and going against it is sin (Romans 14:23). But it is not infallible. It can be too tender, condemning what God allows, or too dull, excusing what God forbids, and it can be seared by repeated sin (1 Timothy 4:2). So a conscience must be taught by Scripture and kept clean by confession. A clear conscience does not make you right; only God’s word decides that. But a guilty conscience should never be ignored: take it to Christ, whose blood purifies the conscience (Hebrews 9:14), and put right what can be put right.

In everyday life. Can you say with Paul that your conscience is clear in your dealings? None of us is wholly single-hearted; only Christ was, and his perfect obedience, not ours, is counted to us before God (Philippians 3:9). So think without fear of one place where you have been one person in public and another in private: the email with a barb in it, the reason you gave that was not the real reason. Confess it to the one whose blood cleanses the conscience, and put it right today, plainly.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wanted to come to you first. Now the actual grievance, almost too small for so much self-defence: Paul had announced a travel plan (1 Corinthians 16:5–7), changed it to a double visit, and then changed it again.

A second experience of grace. Corinth twice, on the way north to Macedonia and again on the way back. He calls it a second grace: an apostle’s visit was not an inspection but a gift, and the gift was Christ (Romans 15:29). What was at stake was never his diary but the grace of Christ coming to them through him.

On my way to Macedonia. Then Judea with the collection; by the time of this letter the double visit has not happened at all.

A small brick for a large case. His opponents were building a case about his character, and a broken travel plan was the most available brick. A small verifiable failure is seized on because it can be made to stand for a large unverifiable one: he changed his plans, so he is unreliable, so his gospel cannot be trusted either.

Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Two questions, both expecting the answer no. Vacillating translates elaphria, lightness: the flightiness of a man whose word weighs nothing.

Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time? According to the flesh does not mean sinful appetite here. It means deciding as a man does whose only guide is his own convenience: for selfish reasons, to suit myself. The doubled Yes, yes and No, no is the picture of a man saying both at once to different audiences, agreeing with whoever is in the room, with no real commitment.

Is it a failure of integrity to change your mind? Clearly not, or Paul is condemned by his own defence. Scripture nowhere requires that a plan once announced must be carried out regardless of what has happened since. What it requires is that the reason be honest. The sin is not the changed plan; it is the changed plan made for self-serving reasons and then dressed up as principle. Paul will tell them in verse 23 exactly why he stayed away, and the reason turns out to be mercy toward them, the very people now complaining. So when a commitment has to be dropped, do not ask, can I justify this?, since almost anything can be justified given a few minutes. Ask instead: if the person affected could see my actual reasoning, would it look like care for them or convenience for me? That is the line between Paul and the man he is accused of being.

Explaining to people who have not earned it. He could have dismissed the accusation as beneath him; an apostle does not owe the Corinthians his itinerary. Instead he explains himself, at length, to people who have not earned the explanation. That is what pastoral love looks like when it is inconvenient.

What about a promise that has become costly to keep? Then, as far as it is lawful, keep it. Scripture praises the one who swears to his own hurt and does not change (Psalm 15:4). Inconvenience, a better offer or a change of mood are not reasons to break your word. A promise may be set aside only if keeping it would mean sinning, if the other person releases you, or if circumstances genuinely make it impossible. In those cases, go to the person, explain honestly and early, apologise for what it costs them, and make it up to them where you can. Do not let them find out by your silence.

For worship. There was one journey whose plan never changed. The Son set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and nothing turned him aside. His Yes to the Father, and to us, held all the way to the tomb, and he is patient with servants who must explain themselves, because he is making them people whose word can be trusted.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had changed his travel plans, and some at Corinth accused him of being unreliable.

verseByVerse.quote: As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not Yes and No. One of the most audacious turns in Paul’s letters: he is defending a change of travel plans, and within two sentences he is describing the character of the eternal Son of God. That is not evasion. If Paul’s word cannot be trusted, the people who heard the gospel from him will soon wonder whether the gospel can be trusted either. So he stakes the answer on something larger, with what amounts to an oath: as surely as God is faithful.

Silvanus and Timothy and I. Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth when the church was founded (Acts 18:5). Three named men preached, so this is not one man’s word, and the message they preached was Christ himself. He is God’s definitive Yes, and the Greek tense says that it has become Yes and stays Yes.

All the promises. All of them. Not most, not only the obviously messianic ones. Every commitment God has ever made to his people has arrived at its destination in Jesus Christ.

The outstanding balance. Set that against the Old Testament. God promised Abraham a land, a seed and a blessing for every nation, and centuries later his descendants were a small, conquered people. He promised David a son whose throne would never end, and the throne of David ended with a blinded king led away in chains to Babylon (2 Kings 25:7). He promised through the prophets a new covenant, a cleansed heart, a shepherd, a servant pierced for transgressions. Anyone who closes the Old Testament sees an enormous outstanding balance.

Settled in one Person. Paul says the account was settled in one Person: the seed, the throne, the covenant, the shepherd, the servant, every one says Yes in Jesus Christ. Every altar, every sacrifice, every prophecy, every unfinished story in the Hebrew Scriptures was reaching toward someone. God has spoken his final Yes, and it has a face and a name. For an ordinary believer this is great news: you do not receive God’s promises one at a time, by earning each or finding the right verse. You receive Christ, and in him you receive them all (Galatians 3:16, 29).

Our Amen to God. Amen is a Hebrew word meaning it is firm, it is so, said in worship to affirm what God has said. God says Yes; the church says Amen. He makes the commitment; we countersign it. And even the countersigning is through him, as people joined to Christ (Ephesians 1:3), for his glory.

Does this mean I can claim any promise in the Bible, health or wealth, for myself? The promises find their Yes in him: they come to us through union with Christ and on his terms. The great promises of the gospel, forgiveness, the Spirit, adoption, the resurrection, are certain for every believer. Promises given to particular people in particular settings, such as the land to Israel or long life to the obedient, are not blank cheques for health and prosperity now. The promise that is ours in every case is that all things work together for good for those who love God (Romans 8:28), and he decides what that good is.

What if a promise seems unfulfilled in my life? Then read the promise carefully, and read the calendar of God. Some promises are already fully yours in Christ, such as forgiveness and adoption, whatever you feel. Some are being kept now, slowly, such as your growth in holiness. And some are kept in full only when Christ returns: no more tears, a resurrection body, the new creation. The saints of Hebrews 11 died not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). An unfinished promise is not a broken one. God’s Yes in Christ has already been spoken; the rest is delivery.

For worship. Every promise God made was costly to keep. To speak his Yes to us, the Father did not let the cup pass from his Son in Gethsemane, and the Son drank it to the bottom. That is how firm the Yes is: it was sealed in the blood of the Yes himself, and it will never be withdrawn.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth. “Amen” means “it is true, so be it.”

verseByVerse.quote: And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God who establishes us. The obvious question follows: how does an ordinary believer know that the Yes includes him? These two verses are among the clearest statements of Christian assurance in the New Testament. Every verb has God as its subject and believers as its object, and with you puts Paul and his critics inside the same sentence, held by the same hands.

Establishes. The verb is bebaioō, the root of the unshaken hope of verse 7, used in business papers for confirming a contract so that it will stand up in court. It is present tense: something God is doing continually, in Christ, whose standing before the Father is counted as yours. Your place is being actively maintained, today, by someone other than you.

And has anointed us. Oil was poured on a prophet, a priest or a king to mark him out for God’s work. The word is chrisas, the root of Christos, the Anointed One: we share the anointing of the one we are named after. Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38), and from him the Spirit flows to everyone joined to him (1 John 2:20). There is no second-class member of the body of Christ.

His seal on us. A seal marked ownership, and guaranteed that the contents had not been tampered with in transit. The Holy Spirit in a believer is God’s stamp saying this one is mine, and his guarantee that what he has sent will arrive intact (Ephesians 1:13–14; 4:30). Here too Christ goes first: on him God the Father has set his seal (John 6:27).

A guarantee. The word is arrabōn, a commercial term: the down payment, the first instalment of an agreed price, which binds the payer to hand over the rest (5:5; Ephesians 1:14); in modern Greek it means an engagement. Whatever you have known of God, the moments when Scripture came alive, the peace that arrived from nowhere, the homesickness for a country you have never seen, is the deposit, the same currency as the rest, paid early. What awaits you is that, without the interruptions, for ever. The Father has signed the contract, the Son has paid the price, and the Spirit has been given as the deposit and the ring. He has never lost one whom he sealed.

Where Christians differ: assurance of salvation. Some Christians teach that believers cannot be sure of their final salvation in this life, and many Arminians (who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted and lost) teach that a true believer may finally fall away; they are moved by the Bible’s solemn warnings, which every Christian must take seriously. This commentary’s view: God himself establishes, anoints, seals and gives the Spirit as a guarantee. These are God’s acts, not ours, and they make the outcome certain. Believers can have a well-founded assurance, resting on God’s promises, the inner witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16), and the evidence of his work in their lives (Westminster Confession 18.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2).

The weakest witness in the room. When assurance is thin, we ask, do I feel saved?, which is asking the weakest witness in the room. Ask instead: has God established, anointed, sealed and paid a deposit on someone he intends to abandon? The security of a Christian does not rest on the strength of his grip on God. It rests on four actions of God, Father, Son and Spirit, taken while he was still at his worst.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every believer always feels assured. Assurance can be weakened by sin or trial, and a true believer may wait long and struggle hard before he has it. But God’s seal does not break. Nor does it mean that a person who lives in settled, unrepentant sin may comfort himself with the seal; the Spirit who seals is the Holy Spirit, and his presence shows itself in a growing hatred of sin.

When are we sealed: at baptism, or in a second experience? The seal is the Holy Spirit himself, given to every believer when he first trusts Christ: in him you also, when you heard the word of truth and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). It is not a later blessing reserved for some Christians, and it is not conferred by the water of baptism. Baptism, which this commentary holds is for believers because in the New Testament it follows faith (Acts 2:41; 8:12), is the public sign that declares the Spirit’s work already done; many of our paedobaptist brothers (who baptise the infants of believers) call the sacraments seals as well, and we share with them the conviction that the sign does not save without faith. If you trust Christ, you have been sealed.

What about “anointed” leaders and special anointings today? The New Testament never divides Christians into the anointed and the ordinary. Every believer has the anointing of the Spirit (1 John 2:20). So be wary of anyone who claims a special anointing that places him beyond question or correction. God does gift and call particular men to preach and lead, and they deserve honour, but their teaching is tested by Scripture like everyone else’s (Acts 17:11). The anointing that matters is the one every humble believer already has.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership. The word for “guarantee” was used in business for a first instalment or deposit, pledging that the full payment will follow.

verseByVerse.quote: But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I call God to witness. At last the real reason: not weakness, not indifference, but mercy. He introduces it with an oath, inviting divine scrutiny on his own motives. The Corinthians could not see inside him; God could (Hebrews 4:13). Only a man with nothing to hide calls that God as witness against himself.

But did Jesus not say, Do not take an oath at all (Matthew 5:34)? He was condemning the casual and evasive swearing of his day, oaths used to make some promises binding and leave others loose; that is why he goes on, Let what you say be simply Yes or No (Matthew 5:37). He was not forbidding a solemn, truthful appeal to God. Paul makes such appeals (Romans 1:9; Galatians 1:20), God himself swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), and Jesus answered when put under oath (Matthew 26:63–64). A Christian may take an oath in court or make marriage vows; what he may not do is need an oath to be believed.

To spare you. A visit would have meant discipline exercised in person on a church only half repentant, coming with a rod (1 Corinthians 4:21). So he stayed away to give them time to repent, and wrote instead (2:1–4). The man accused of being unreliable had been protecting the very people filing the complaint, and could not say so at the time without making it worse.

The slower road. It is often easier to confront than to wait: confrontation feels decisive, and it discharges the tension in the person doing it. Paul chose the slower, more humiliating road. Anyone who has held back a hard conversation for the other person’s sake, and been thought cowardly for it, is standing where Paul stood.

Not that we lord it over your faith. Talk of sparing them could sound like a man describing the punishment he graciously withheld, so he corrects it at once. Lord it over is kyrieuō: to rule as master, the word Jesus used of the kings of the Gentiles when he said it would not be so among his disciples (Luke 22:25–26; 1 Peter 5:3). Paul has apostolic authority, and he will use it in chapter 13. But it does not extend to standing between a believer and God.

The thing Paul refuses. This needs saying plainly, because ignoring it has done great damage. There are churches where a leader’s approval functions as the measure of a member’s standing with God, where questions are treated as rebellion, where major life decisions require clearance, where people are told that to leave is to leave the Lord. Every one of those is the thing Paul refuses here. A minister who makes himself the gatekeeper of another Christian’s relationship with God has taken a place that is not his.

The meekness and gentleness of Christ. Paul’s restraint is a likeness: he appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (10:1), the one Lord with every right to rule their faith, who came as one who serves (Luke 22:27) and would not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20). An under-shepherd who domineers is not merely harsh. He misrepresents the Chief Shepherd to his own sheep.

For your joy. What is offered instead is startling. Work with is synergoi, fellow workers: on the same side of the table, and the goal is not compliance but gladness. Ministers are helpers of believers’ joy. Any authority in the church that produces fear rather than joy has misunderstood its own job description.

You stand firm. And the reason he gives is generous. This is the church of the factions and the lawsuits, the one that has been listening to men who despise him. And his verdict on them is that they are standing. Their faith rests on God, not on Paul. Not because they are impressive, but because they are held: the Master is able to make him stand (Romans 14:4). Paul planted, he wrote and he wept, and the one who keeps them upright is Christ, the only Lord of the conscience, who has never yet let a believer fall out of his hand.

Where Christians differ: church authority over conscience. Some churches claim authority to bind believers’ consciences in matters beyond Scripture. This commentary’s view: Church leaders have real authority to teach Scripture and to discipline, but no authority to rule over faith or bind the conscience beyond what God’s word requires. God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster Confession 20.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2). Leaders serve believers’ joy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church leaders have no authority. Paul used his authority. It means authority serves, not dominates. Believers are still told to obey their leaders and submit to them, so that their work may be a joy and not a groan (Hebrews 13:17).

How do I tell faithful leadership from lording it? Faithful leaders point you to Scripture and let it bind your conscience, not their preferences. They welcome questions, explain their decisions, and can be corrected. They care about your joy in Christ more than your loyalty to them. They exercise discipline for open sin according to the word, not for disagreement with them. Lording it looks different: control over personal decisions the Bible leaves free, punishment of questions, secrecy, isolation from family and other churches, fear. And where there is abuse of any kind, it must never be tolerated or covered up. Speak to other elders or leaders outside the situation, report crimes to the authorities, and know that leaving such a church is not leaving Christ.

In everyday life. If you have any authority over others, as a parent, an employer, an elder, ask whether the people under you are more joyful in Christ because of you or more afraid of you. Ask one of them, and listen. And pray for your pastors, that they will lead as helpers of your joy.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia:<sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,<sup>4</sup>who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.<sup>5</sup>For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.<sup>6</sup>If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.<sup>7</sup>Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.<sup>8</sup>For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.<sup>9</sup>Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.<sup>10</sup>He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.<sup>11</sup>You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.<sup>12</sup>For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you.<sup>13</sup>For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand—<sup>14</sup>just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.<sup>15</sup>Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace.<sup>16</sup>I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea.<sup>17</sup>Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?<sup>18</sup>As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No.<sup>19</sup>For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes.<sup>20</sup>For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.<sup>21</sup>And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us,<sup>22</sup>and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.<sup>23</sup>But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth.<sup>24</sup>Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.

2.title: Forgiveness, the Aroma of Christ, and the Triumph of God
2.overview:
Paul continues to explain why he did not come back to Corinth. After the “painful visit”, in which one man publicly wronged him, he wrote a tearful letter instead. The church has now disciplined the man, and Paul’s concern turns to the opposite danger: they must forgive and restore him, or Satan will take advantage.

Then Paul tells of his anxiety at Troas and, before finishing the story (it resumes at 7:5), bursts into thanks for the God who leads his servants in Christ’s triumphal procession and spreads through them the fragrance of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Severe Letter and Forgiveness of the Offender
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why he wrote a severe letter instead of making another painful visit, and urges the church, now that it has disciplined the offender, to forgive, comfort and openly welcome him back.
verseByVerse.theology: Church discipline has a defined goal: restoration, not condemnation (Matthew 18:15–20; Galatians 6:1; 1 Corinthians 5). Once it has done its work, withholding forgiveness becomes a sin of its own, one Satan is glad to see, because it divides the church and tells the world that the gospel of forgiveness does not apply inside its walls.
verseByVerse.examples: A church elder removed from office after a moral failure has spent two years in genuine repentance. A vocal minority insists that any restoration betrays those he hurt. This passage does not minimise the hurt (v. 5), but it insists that discipline aims at restoration, and that refusing to forgive when repentance is genuine is not faithfulness; it is a gift to the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 2 finishes Paul’s explanation of his changed plans and opens the great theme of the letter, the nature of gospel ministry. A chapter that begins with tears over a tearful letter and a disciplined man ends with the whole world smelling of Christ’s victory.

Another painful visit. The word another carries a whole episode in it. Somewhere between 1 Corinthians and this letter, Paul went to Corinth and it went so badly that he cannot bring himself to describe it and will not risk repeating it. “Painful” is lypē, grief, sorrow. Acts says nothing about this visit; we know of it only from the scar tissue it left in these chapters.

Piecing the story together. The story is pieced together from hints (2:5; 7:12; 13:2). It seems that on the painful visit someone in the congregation opposed and humiliated him publicly, and the church did not defend him. He went back, wrote a letter out of tears calling them to deal with the man, and waited in agony for news. So the changed plans of chapter 1 were not avoidance of trouble: a second confrontation, before they had had time to respond, would have destroyed something.

For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained? This is a disarming sentence, because what it exposes is that the apostle needs them. His argument is simply this: you are my joy. There is no reserve supply. If I come and wound you, I have wounded the only people who can make me glad, and I will go home emptier than I came. A man who did not care could confront them and feel nothing. Paul cannot confront them without paying for it himself, because the people he would have to hurt are the people his happiness depends on. Love makes the pastor’s happiness depend on his people’s well-being.

The joy set before him. Paul’s gladness hangs on his people, and in that he is a small likeness of his Lord. Christ has freely bound his own joy to a people. He is the shepherd who lays the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing and calls his friends to rejoice with him (Luke 15:5–6), and for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). So his correction is never cold; it comes from one who sympathises with their weakness (Hebrews 4:15). A pastor whose happiness depends on his flock is not weak. He is wearing his Master’s heart.

Will this cost me anything? There is a searching question in this for anyone who has to speak hard truth to another person: a parent, an elder, a friend, a manager. Not, am I right? Usually you are, and being right is the cheapest part of it. Ask instead: will this cost me anything? If a rebuke costs the person delivering it nothing, something has gone wrong upstream. It has become an exercise of position rather than an act of love, and the one receiving it can always tell the difference. Real correction is expensive at both ends. That is why so little of it is done well, and why the little that is done well is remembered for a lifetime by the person who received it.

Should a hard conversation be in person or in writing? Usually in person, where tone can be heard, questions asked and misunderstandings corrected on the spot; Jesus’ pattern begins with going to your brother (Matthew 18:15). But Paul shows there are times when writing is wiser: when a meeting would inflame things, when the other person needs time to think before responding, or when you need to choose your words with great care.
