Whichever you choose, never use writing to hide, to fire a parting shot, or to say what you would not say to the person’s face. Write as if you were sitting across the table, and re-read it the next morning before you send it.
verseByVerse.note: This painful visit is not recorded in Acts; it came between 1 and 2 Corinthians.

verseByVerse.quote: And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I wrote as I did. Here is the severe letter, written instead of a visit so that when he came things would already be resolved. Paul refers here and in 7:8 to a letter written between 1 and 2 Corinthians, dealing with the man who had wronged him. Some suggest it survives as chapters 10 to 13, but those chapters never mention the offender, and 1 Corinthians does not fit a letter written with many tears. The straightforward reading is that it is lost. God preserved every word the church would need, not every word Paul wrote.

The joy of you all. He expected the letter to work, because he believed that what made him glad and what made them glad were finally the same thing. They are not a minister and his clients with separate interests to be negotiated, but one body, and when it goes right the joy is shared whole by each.

Out of much affliction. Now look at the cost: much affliction, anguish of heart, many tears. Anguish is synochē, a pressing together, the walls closing in. He wrote it the way you write something late at night after four attempts, with your hands shaking.

The abundant love. He says plainly what the aim was, and that sentence should be printed above every difficult conversation in the church. The letter caused pain; he does not deny it and will admit as much in chapter 7. But pain was not the purpose. Love was the purpose, and the pain was the route it had to take. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6).

He wept over it. Paul’s tears have a precedent. When Jesus drew near and saw Jerusalem, he wept over it (Luke 19:41), and his sternest words against its leaders ended in a lament: how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing (Matthew 23:37). The hardest things the Son of God ever said were said by a heart breaking for those who heard them. That is the only ink in which a Christian rebuke should be written.

Anger or love? That question gives an unusually clear test for anyone about to say a hard thing. Rebuke that comes out of anger wants the other person to feel what you feel. Rebuke that comes out of love wants the other person to be restored, and would gladly skip the whole episode if there were another way. The two can use identical words. They are not remotely the same act, and the tears are usually where the difference shows. Anyone who has ever been afraid to send the message, and has sent it anyway, and has then lain awake, knows exactly where Paul was standing. He is not writing as a man for whom this comes easily. He is writing as a man who did the hard thing and then had to live through the silence afterwards.

What if my loving rebuke is rejected? Then you have still done what love required, and the outcome is in God’s hands. Paul did not know, as he wrote, how the letter would be received; he had to wait for Titus. Give it time, keep praying, and do not repeat the rebuke louder or recruit others against the person. Keep the door open, and treat them kindly in the meantime. If the matter is serious sin in the church, Jesus gives further steps involving others (Matthew 18:16–17). But many rebukes do their work slowly, and the person who angrily rejected your words in March may come back to them in September.
verseByVerse.note: This severe letter is probably lost; some think it is part of 2 Corinthians 10–13.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if anyone has caused pain. Paul is the injured party: on the most likely reading, the man had humiliated him in front of the church. Yet in the one sentence where he could press his own case, he does two remarkable things, and he tactfully avoids naming the man at all.

Who was this man? The older tradition took him to be the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 for living with his father’s wife, and pointed to the punishment by the majority (v. 6) and to Paul’s hope there that he would be saved (1 Corinthians 5:5). The more likely reading is that he was someone who had publicly opposed or insulted Paul during the painful visit. Paul speaks of the wrong as done against himself (v. 10; 7:12), not as sexual sin, and he is far gentler here than he was over the incest. Either way the lesson is the same: discipline aims at restoration, and when a man repents, the church must forgive and welcome him back (vv. 7–8).

In the flow. Verses 1–4 gave the reason for the tearful letter; now Paul turns to the man it was about. The whole passage from 1:23 answers the charge that Paul is fickle and harsh by showing a wounded apostle working for the restoration of the man who wounded him (compare 7:12).

He has caused it not to me. The first remarkable thing is that he refuses to make it personal. That is not literally true and everyone knew so; Paul is declining to stand in the centre of the picture. Once it becomes a quarrel between two men, the congregation divides into supporters and the whole thing is lost. The injured leader who insists on his own injury turns a sin into a faction.

Not to put it too severely. The second is the restraint. He could have said far more; the man had earned it. With the whole province about to hear the letter read out, he chooses to understate. That is a wounded man refusing to use his platform to settle a score.

Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter. Paul’s refusal to stand at the centre of his own injury has a deeper source. The one most wronged in all history was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Jesus did not use his trial to settle scores; he let the worst thing ever done against him become the cure for the people who did it. A wounded leader who steps out of the way so that a church can heal is not weak. He is being like his Lord.

No private sins. But the restraint is not indifference. The pain, he says, was caused to all of you. There is no such thing as a private sin in the body of Christ. We think of sin as a personal debt; Paul thinks of it the way a doctor thinks of an infection in a limb: what is done in one member is felt in all (1 Corinthians 12:26; Joshua 7:1). This is why a congregation can become subtly cold or joyless and nobody can point to a cause.

Whom did it touch? Test it against your own experience. Recall the last time you were harsh at home, or dishonest at work, or nursed a grudge through a Sunday morning. Whom did it touch? The honest answer is never only me. There was a wife who found you difficult that evening, a colleague who learned something about how things are done, a child who was watching. Sin is never contained where it is committed, and this is one of the reasons the New Testament takes church discipline seriously at all: it is not the policing of private morals but the care of a shared body. And it is the reason forgiveness, when it comes in the next verses, has to be shared too. If the whole body was wounded, the whole body must do the healing.

When someone wrongs me, should I keep it private or tell the church? Begin privately. Most personal wrongs should be covered by love and never mentioned again (1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 19:11). If a wrong is too serious to overlook, go to the person alone first (Matthew 18:15), and only if he will not listen involve one or two others, and then the church. Do not talk about it to everyone else in the meantime; that is gossip, and it turns a sin into a faction, exactly what Paul refuses to do here. The exception is crime and abuse: those must be reported to the proper authorities and the church leaders, and a victim is never required to confront an abuser alone.
verseByVerse.note: The offender is unnamed; he is most likely not the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 but someone who had publicly opposed Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough, so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This punishment is enough. Two words carry this passage, and both cut against the way churches usually behave. The first is enough. “Punishment” is epitimia, a rebuke or penalty: church discipline, carried out by the majority acting together. Paul is not asking whether the man has suffered as much as he deserved; asked honestly, that would never be answered yes about anyone, including the people asking. He is asking whether the discipline has done its work. It has. So it stops.

Hard to start, harder to end. Discipline is difficult to start and far more difficult to end. Once a person has been put outside, a settled respectability attaches to keeping him there; those who want him back can be made to look soft on sin, and no one is ever criticised for being too rigorous. A church that cannot say this punishment is enough has not understood what discipline was for. God himself is the God who says enough. He did not merely permit the prodigal to return; he ran, and embraced him, and put a ring on his hand (Luke 15:20–22).

Turn to forgive and comfort him. Rather turn is a change of direction, required of the same people who administered the discipline: the majority who excluded him must now go and get him. Forgiveness here is a shared act, as public as the discipline was. Forgive is charizomai, to show grace; comfort is parakaleō, the comfort of chapter 1. The man is to be walked back in, not merely permitted to return. Someone has to sit next to him (Galatians 6:1).

Overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. The second word is overwhelmed, katapinō: to swallow down, used of the Egyptians drowned in the sea and of death swallowed up in victory (Hebrews 11:29; 1 Corinthians 15:54). Paul pictures a man going under, and what is swallowing him is not his sin but his sorrow. We are alert to the man who repents too little. Paul is alert to the man who has repented and cannot get up, sinking under a guilt that has already been dealt with, by the Son who swallowed up the sorrow that would have swallowed us.

Breakfast on a beach. The Lord himself shows the church how this is done. Judas was sorry, genuinely and violently sorry, and his sorrow drove him to his death (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, and the risen Jesus did not leave him to sink. He cooked him breakfast by the lake, asked him three times whether he loved him, as if once for each denial, and gave him work to do: Feed my sheep (John 21:9–17). That is forgiving and comforting in its fullest form, and a church that restores the repentant is doing for one sinner what Christ did for Peter, and for every one of us.

If you are the one who is sinking. Hear the verse aimed at you. There is a sorrow that God uses and a sorrow that Satan uses, and they can feel identical from the inside. The difference is where they end. One drives you to Christ and leaves you lighter. The other drives you in circles round your own failure and leaves you heavier every time (7:10). Paul is so concerned about the second that he writes to an entire province to stop it happening to one man.

What is church discipline, and when is it used? Church discipline is the loving correction of a church member by the church, following Christ’s instructions (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5). Most of it is quiet and private: a brother going to a brother. Formal discipline, up to removal from membership and the Lord’s Table, is for serious, public or persistent sin where the person refuses to repent after patient appeals. Its aims are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church and the honour of Christ, never revenge or the protection of a leader’s reputation. And as this verse shows, the moment of genuine repentance is the moment the church turns, wholeheartedly, to forgive.

How can a church tell the repentance is real? Not by a perfect performance, but by fruit: the person owns the sin plainly without blaming others, grieves over the harm done, puts right what can be put right, accepts accountability, and turns from the sin over time (Luke 3:8; 2 Corinthians 7:11). The church should be careful but not suspicious, and should never demand a level of grief that would crush. Where trust has to be rebuilt, as after serious sin, the forgiveness is still full and immediate; the rebuilding of trust follows over time.

In everyday life. Is there someone who has repented whom you still keep at a distance, still mention in a certain tone, still watch for the next failure? Forgive and comfort them, as Christ has you, with something concrete this week: a call, an invitation, a word of welcome. And if you are the one who cannot stop sinking, tell a pastor or trusted friend that you need help believing you are forgiven. That help is exactly what this verse commands the church to give.

verseByVerse.quote: So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I beg you. The verb is parakaleō once more, here in its urgent sense: I plead with you. An apostle with authority to command is pleading instead, because some things cannot be commanded into existence. You can order a church to readmit a man; you cannot order it to love him, and a readmission without love would be a worse cruelty than exclusion.

Reaffirm. The word is kyroō, a legal term: to ratify, to make officially and publicly binding, as a will is confirmed or a treaty ratified. Paul is asking not only for warmer feelings but for a public act, as public as the discipline was.

Forgiveness made public. We have made forgiveness an interior condition, done in the heart, alone, which the other person may never learn about. Paul makes it public. Somebody has to stand up and say, in front of the people who watched him fall, that this man is ours and we love him. A restoration that is never announced is not believed. The man will come back into the room and read every face, carrying his disgrace like a coat he cannot take off, and the whispering will move underground. A public sin healed in private is not healed.

Not ashamed to call them brothers. The public love Paul asks for is an echo of Christ’s. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners in full view of those who despised them (Luke 15:1–2), and he has promised that everyone who acknowledges him before men he will also acknowledge before his Father in heaven (Matthew 10:32). He is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The sinner Christ restores is not slipped back in through a side door, and a church that reaffirms its love out loud is only saying on earth what its Lord has already said in heaven.

What was done for Paul. Paul is begging for what was done for him. Saul of Tarsus was not quietly tolerated by the church he had hunted: Barnabas brought him to the apostles and vouched for him out loud (Acts 9:27).

Should a restored person go straight back into leadership? Not necessarily. Forgiveness restores a person to the fellowship and the Lord’s Table at once and completely. Restoration to an office of trust is a separate question, governed by the qualifications God gives for leaders, who must be above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2). After serious sin that may take a long time, or may not be wise at all. And where the sin was abuse of any kind, the person must not be placed again in a position of trust over the vulnerable, however sincere the repentance; protecting the weak is itself an act of love. None of this withdraws forgiveness. It is simply wisdom about trust.

For worship. Our forgiveness was never a private, unannounced arrangement. God ratified it in public: at the cross, in the empty tomb, in baptism, at the Lord’s Table week by week, so that his children would never have to wonder. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: For this is why I wrote, that I might test you and know whether you are obedient in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That I might test you. A modern reader may flinch: was the severe letter a loyalty test, a manufactured crisis to see whether the Corinthians would jump when he said so? That would contradict 1:24, where he disowned lording it over their faith, so it cannot be what he means.

What is being tested. The word, dokimē, means proving something genuine, as metal is assayed, not as a student is trapped. What is being proved is not their loyalty to him but whether a church that has received the gospel will act on it when acting is costly. They had to confront a man many of them liked. Now they have to forgive a man some are still angry with, and the second is harder than the first.

Obedient in everything. The phrase in everything is the whole issue. Half-obedience is the standing temptation of religious people: we assemble a personal edition of the Christian life from the commands we find agreeable and let the others lapse, one avoided verse at a time. Half-obedience rarely feels like rebellion; it feels like being busy, or reasonable, or not quite ready. They passed the first test by disciplining the offender. Now obedience means forgiving him.

Obedient to the point of death. There has been one Son who passed this test entirely. Jesus never assembled a personal edition of his Father’s will; he became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8), and his obedience included the very command this church now faces: he forgave those who had wronged him. That obedience in everything is counted to everyone who trusts him, so the half-obedient who come to him are not cast off. It is also the source of their growth, because the Spirit of the obedient Son is at work in them, making the commands they had treated as optional their own.

Always working on them. Paul says the letter was written not to punish the offender but to prove the church: the offender was the occasion, the congregation the concern. God works the same way. A trial is not only a thing that happens to us but a thing being worked in us: the tested genuineness of your faith, more precious than gold that perishes (1 Peter 1:7). He is not merely getting you through the trial. He is proving something in you, and he intends to show it to you on the day Christ is revealed.

Does obeying in everything mean obeying my pastor in everything? No. Paul’s authority as an apostle was unique, and his commands are now in Scripture, which binds every Christian. Your pastors and elders are to be respected and followed as they teach and apply God’s word (Hebrews 13:17), and you should not resist them lightly. But they cannot command what Scripture does not, and you must not obey them if they tell you to sin; we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Obedience in everything means obedience to Christ in every area of life, including the hard and costly ones like forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Paul binds himself to their decision, though the man had wronged him more than any of them. He does not reserve the right to hold on privately to an injury the church has released.

In the presence of Christ. Paul plays down his own hurt: if I have forgiven anything. Then a phrase lifts the matter off the ground: in the presence of Christ, literally in his face, under his gaze. Forgiveness in the church is not a social convenience or an agreement to move on. It is transacted in front of the Lord, by his authority, in imitation of what he has already done: as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive (Colossians 3:13). It is the same face in which the glory of God shines into our hearts (4:6).

Does forgiving mean feeling differently? No. It means deciding, before Christ, not to hold the debt against the person any longer: not to raise it, not to punish with it, not to run it again in your mind at two in the morning. Feelings usually follow that decision, sometimes slowly, sometimes years later. They are the fruit, not the entry fee. If the old anger rises again, forgive again; that is not failure but the ordinary work of a forgiving heart.

Does forgiving mean restoring trust? Not automatically. Forgiveness is released freely, because that is how it was given to us. Trust is rebuilt over time and by evidence, and it is not unloving to say so. A forgiven embezzler need not be handed the accounts. But look at the direction Paul is pushing this church: they are drifting toward too little restoration, not too much, and he is pushing back hard.

Does it mean pretending nothing happened? No. Paul says what happened in this very paragraph. Forgiveness that requires everyone to lie about the past is not forgiveness; it is suppression, and it always leaks.

What if the person has not repented? Then you are still to forgive in your heart, letting go of bitterness and revenge and leaving judgment to God (Mark 11:25; Romans 12:19), and you are to stand ready to be reconciled the moment he turns. But full reconciliation, the restored relationship, waits on repentance: if your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3). God himself forgives the repentant. So you need not pretend the wrong is resolved, or put yourself back in harm’s way. You can be free of hatred and still wait, praying, for the person to come home.

Not outwitted by Satan. Then the reason, and it is startling. The word is pleonekteō: to get the better of someone in a transaction, to cheat a man out of what should have been his. An unforgiving church has been swindled: it thought it was defending righteousness and has been robbed. Satan uses unforgiveness to divide churches, crush repentant sinners and make discipline harsh, and harsh, unending discipline plays into his hands as much as none at all.

His designs. Noēmata: schemes, thought-out plans (Ephesians 6:11). See what Paul names as one of the enemy’s chief instruments in a church: not persecution, heresy or immorality, but a congregation that will not forgive a repentant man. Forgiveness is the church displaying in public the one thing it exists to announce, and a body that will not do inside its doors what it proclaims at them has made the announcement unbelievable. And the face in which forgiveness is transacted is the face of the one who forgave us first, at the cost of his own blood. He prayed for those who were driving in the nails.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Satan is behind every problem. It means he exploits our sins, including the sin of unforgiveness. He is real and he is clever, but he is a defeated enemy, and his schemes are known to those who read God’s word.

In everyday life. Unforgiveness gives Satan a foothold (Ephesians 4:26–27). Name the person you are still holding something against, and say to God, in the presence of Christ, that you release the debt. You cannot manufacture this, but the Spirit of the Christ who forgave you can do it in you. Shut that door in the enemy’s face today.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul resumes the story of his journey, from the open door at Troas to Macedonia, and breaks into thanks for the ministry God has given him: a captive in Christ’s victory parade, spreading a fragrance that means life to some and death to others, and speaking sincerely as one sent by God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Paul surprisingly pictures himself not as the general in a Roman triumph but as a captive in Christ’s train. Yet to belong wholly to Christ is not degradation but the highest dignity, the same paradox as Paul’s title “servant of Christ” (doulos Christou).

The double effect of the gospel, life to some and death to others, echoes Isaiah 8:14 (the stone of stumbling) and Luke 2:34. When the gospel is refused, the gospel has not failed; the human heart has been revealed.
verseByVerse.examples: A missionary returns from years in a largely unresponsive field and struggles with a sense of failure: few converts, much opposition. His task was to be the aroma of Christ; the effect, life or death, belongs to God. Faithfulness is measured by the fragrance, not by the response.

verseByVerse.quote: When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord, my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Troas. Two verses of travel narrative contain one of the most honest admissions in the New Testament. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast near ancient Troy. Paul had sent Titus to Corinth with the severe letter and arranged, it seems, to meet him there and hear how it had been received. He arrives. Titus is not there.

A door was opened. It is the phrase Paul uses elsewhere for a genuine, God-given opportunity (1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3). Preaching is bearing fruit. It is exactly what he lives for.

My spirit was not at rest. And he cannot do it. Not at rest is built on anesis: the relief of a strap being let out. He had none. He could not concentrate for worrying about a letter and a church and a friend who had not arrived.

On to Macedonia. So he closed an open door to look for Titus, who at last met him with good news (7:5–7). He could have left this out. Instead he tells a church that already thinks him weak that he was so anxious he walked away from fruitful work.

Who opens and no one will shut. We are often taught that an opportunity is the will of God by definition. Paul walked away from one and does not apologise, because of whose door it was. The risen Christ has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut (Revelation 3:7), and Luke records a church at Troas later, gathering to break bread (Acts 20:6–12). Christ is not so short of workers that his gospel collapses when one exhausted man goes to find his friend. He holds the keys, which leaves his servants free to love particular people.

Is anxiety a sin? The anxiety is in the Bible, unrebuked. Paul wrote do not be anxious about anything (Philippians 4:6), and here he is, anxious, and God did not delete it from the record. That should be handled carefully by anyone who has been told that all their worry is simply sin to be repented of and dropped. What Philippians forbids is anxiety left to run: worry that is never brought anywhere, that distrusts God and will not be turned into prayer. What we see here is a man whose distress drove him across a sea to find out how his people were. His agitation had a direction, and the direction was love. Look too at what it was about: not his own reputation, not his safety, not his finances. He could not settle because he did not know how the church was. Paul elsewhere calls it his daily pressure, the anxiety for all the churches (11:28).

What do I do with anxiety for someone I love? Bring it to God, specifically and repeatedly; that is what Philippians 4:6 commands, with thanksgiving. Then do what love can rightly do: Paul went to find Titus. Write, call, visit, ask. Where nothing can be done, keep praying and entrust the person to the God who loves them more than you do. Talk to a friend who will pray with you. And if anxiety becomes constant and disabling, seek help from your pastor and your doctor; that is not a lack of faith. Love without news is hard to bear, and God does not despise the sleepless.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast of Asia. Titus was a trusted Gentile co-worker, sent to Corinth with the severe letter.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God. Paul has just said he was too distressed to preach, and the sentence bursts into thanksgiving as he remembers how God answered his anxiety (7:6). Between here and the end of the Titus story in chapter 7 stands his most sustained account of Christian ministry, and it begins with a parade.

Triumphal procession. A Roman triumph was the highest honour the state could confer. The general rode in a chariot; his troops followed; the spoils were carried past; and behind them came the prisoners in chains, some to be sold, some to be executed at the procession’s end. The verb thriambeuō, with an object as here, most naturally means leading someone as a captive, not as a fellow victor. Paul has put himself in the chains.

The conquered one. That is not false modesty; it is the argument of the letter in one image. His critics saw the beatings and imprisonments and called him defeated. Paul says: quite so. I am the conquered one, taken on the Damascus road by a Lord I was fighting. To be Christ’s captive is to have your resistance defeated and to be owned: you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The chains are the grip of a Lord who will not let go of what he has won (John 10:28). The verb appears once more, where Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The victory was won at the cross, and Paul is one of its spoils, and there is no higher position available to a human being than to be a trophy of Jesus Christ.

The fragrance of the knowledge of him. Then the incense. Ancient writers describe incense burning along a triumph’s route, so the city smelled of the victory and the smell clung to everyone in the procession. Through Paul’s preaching the knowledge of Christ spreads like that. A fragrance cannot be argued with; it arrives before the speech does.

Always. Not only when the church is flourishing and the preacher in good voice. Anxious, sleepless and criticised, Paul was still being led in triumph. The parade did not pause while he struggled; he was in it the whole time and could not see it. The procession is not ours and its outcome was never in doubt. Christ went into the one territory nobody had ever come back from, and came out of it in the morning with the keys, and he has been leading his captives home ever since: through prisons, through hospital wards, through the years nothing seemed to be happening. Not one of the chained is ashamed of the chains.

How do I spread the fragrance of Christ in an ordinary week? Mostly by being near Christ, because a fragrance is caught before it is given. Spend time with him in his word and in prayer, and you will carry something of him into the room. Then live in a way that smells of him: honesty when a lie would be easier, kindness to people who cannot repay you, joy that does not depend on circumstances, patience in suffering. And speak of him. The fragrance in this verse is the knowledge of him, and that needs words: what he has done, who he is, why you trust him. Life without words is a scent with no name; words without life are a label on an empty bottle.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman triumph was a victory parade through the city; captives were led in chains, and incense was burned along the route.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The aroma of Christ to God. The word is euōdia, the word used of sacrifices pleasing to God (Genesis 8:21; Ephesians 5:2). Before gospel ministry is anything to the world, it is an offering to God, and it pleases him whatever the results. When a Christian speaks of Christ to an empty room or a hostile face, the Father receives it first, and to him it smells of his Son, in whom he delights (Matthew 3:17). Faithful witness is first an act of worship.

Being saved and perishing. The same smell means opposite things depending on who breathes it (compare 1 Corinthians 1:18). In a Roman triumph, to the soldiers the incense was the smell of home and reward; to the prisoners walking toward execution, the identical smell was the smell of their last hour.

From death to death, from life to life. So with the gospel. The same word about the same Christ produces life in one hearer and hardening in another; the message has not failed. To those perishing it smells of death, a crucified man and their own judgment; to those being saved it is the scent of life. Simeon said of the infant Jesus that he was appointed for the fall and rising of many (Luke 2:34). The sun that softens the wax bakes the clay; the difference is not in the sun.

A weight lifted. This lifts a weight off Christians who talk about Jesus and watch nothing happen. If someone you love has gone colder rather than warmer, you have not necessarily done it badly. Your part was the fragrance; the response was never in your gift. And the tenses are a mercy: being saved and perishing are processes under way, not finished verdicts. Saul of Tarsus was as far down the second road as anyone can travel, and was stopped in the middle of it.

Who is sufficient for these things? Then the question, and it is a real one, not a rhetorical flourish. “Sufficient” is hikanos: adequate, competent, equal to the task. Paul has just said that when he opens his mouth about Jesus, eternal outcomes are in motion. Who is adequate to carry that? Certainly not the man writing: he has told us in one chapter that he despaired of life and could not preach for anxiety. The honest answer to his question is: nobody, in himself. He does not answer it here. He leaves it hanging for six verses and then says our sufficiency is from God (3:5). That is the only answer there is, and it is enough. The people God uses are not the ones who feel equal to it. They are the ones who have stopped pretending they are, and have therefore started drawing on somebody else’s adequacy.

Does God want some people to perish? God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11), and the gospel is offered sincerely to everyone. Scripture also teaches that God has chosen a people for salvation and that he is sovereign over who believes (Acts 13:48). Both are true, and Scripture does not ask us to resolve them before we preach. Those who perish are never victims of a God who refused them; they are responsible for rejecting the light they were given (John 3:19). Those who are saved can only give thanks that grace opened their eyes. Neither truth is a reason to stop offering Christ to anyone.

Should I keep speaking of Christ to someone who resists? Usually yes, with wisdom. Keep praying for them, keep loving them, and keep the door open. Jesus also told his disciples not to throw pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), so there is a time to stop pressing someone who mocks, and let your life and your prayers do the speaking for a while. Do not nag or argue for the sake of winning. But do not conclude from coldness that God has finished with them. Many believers today were once hard and scornful hearers, and somebody kept carrying the fragrance into their lives.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peddlers of God’s word. Paul names the alternative to his ministry with a deliberately insulting word. Kapēleuō is what a kapēlos does: a huckster at a market stall, notorious not for selling as such but for adulterating: watering the wine, weighting the scales. Plato uses the word for those who hawked teaching the same way.

Selling by diluting. So the charge is not simply that these men made money from the gospel, but that they altered the product to move it. Like so many points at the rival teachers in Corinth. And the coin a peddler most wants is not always money. Often it is approval: the warmth of the crowd, the invitation back, the dread of being thought narrow. The heart that needs to be liked will water the wine as surely as the heart that needs to be paid, and only someone who already has God’s approval in Christ is free to stop trimming (Galatians 1:10).

How to recognise a peddled gospel. Watch what happens to the hard parts. Wrath, judgment, repentance, the cost of following: a peddled gospel lets them evaporate, until what is left is a message about your best life, with Jesus attached. Watch where the money flows and who is accountable for it; promises of health and wealth in return for giving are the oldest version of the stall. Paul refused support from Corinth so that nobody could say this of him (chapters 11–12).

Men of sincerity. Against the peddler he sets three phrases. Sincerity is eilikrineia, purity of motive, nothing mixed in. Commissioned by God means sent, not self-appointed: the message is not his to adjust because it is not his.

In the sight of God we speak in Christ. Every preacher, teacher, parent and friend who speaks about God speaks with God listening: present in the room, hearing every sentence as it is formed, including the ones shaped to be liked. He weighs the motives of the heart (Proverbs 16:2; 1 Corinthians 4:5). And to speak in Christ is to speak as someone joined to him by faith (Galatians 2:20). Paul is not a salesman standing outside his product. He speaks from inside the one he proclaims.

Do you want to go away as well? The Lord himself refused to peddle. When he taught that he was the bread of life and that his flesh must be eaten, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:66). He did not chase them with a softer version. He turned to the Twelve and asked whether they wanted to go away as well, and Peter’s answer is the reason no faithful preacher may water the wine: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life (John 6:67–68). The message is Christ’s own, and only unmixed is it life. To speak in Christ is to speak as he spoke, without trimming the hard sayings to keep the crowd.

In the flow. The question of verse 16 gets its quiet answer here: only the man whose message and commission both come from God is sufficient (3:5). To claim this raises at once the charge Paul meets in 3:1, that he is commending himself, and from there to 7:4 he describes what true gospel ministry is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should never be paid. Paul taught that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and the labourer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:18). It means they must never preach for money, or change the message to please people.

Is it wrong to make the message attractive? No, provided you change the manner and never the message. Paul became all things to all people, adapting his approach to Jews and Gentiles (1 Corinthians 9:22), and he spoke differently in a synagogue and in Athens (Acts 17). Clear language, good illustrations, warmth, even humour can all serve the truth. The line is crossed when the content is altered to make it sell: when sin is renamed, judgment is dropped, the cross is softened, or Christ is offered as a means to something else. A good cook may serve the bread warm. He may not put sawdust in it.

In everyday life. Before your next conversation about faith, ask which part of the truth you are most tempted to leave out with this person, and why. Then ask God for the courage and the kindness to say it.

For worship. The peddler waters his wine. God calls everyone who thirsts to come and buy wine and milk without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1), and in his Son he gives the thing itself, undiluted, at his own expense. And every faithful word about Christ he hears with delight, and it will not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).
verseByVerse.note: A peddler was a street trader known for watering down his wine to increase profits.

Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ,<sup>11</sup>so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.<sup>12</sup>When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord,<sup>13</sup>my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. 3.title: Letters of Recommendation, the New Covenant, and the Unveiled Face
3.overview: The visiting teachers in Corinth carried letters of recommendation and probably claimed the authority of Moses. Paul answers both claims. He needs no letter: the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts, as God promised the new covenant would do. Then, through the story of Moses’ shining face in Exodus 34, he compares the two covenants: the old came with a real but fading glory; the ministry of the Spirit has a glory that lasts, and in it every believer, with unveiled face, is being changed into the likeness of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Ministers of the New Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s rivals came with letters of recommendation. Paul needs none: the Corinthian church is his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts. His adequacy comes from God, who has made him a servant of the new covenant, in which the Spirit gives the life the law on stone could not.
verseByVerse.theology: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (v. 6) is often misunderstood. In context, “the letter” is the law of Moses written on stone: a command from outside that demands what it cannot enable and exposes sin it cannot remove. The Spirit gives life by doing what the letter could not, writing the law on the heart, as Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 promised.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation prides itself on doctrinal correctness. Its members can explain every article of their confession, but their life together is cold. The letter and Spirit contrast is not a criticism of doctrine or of Scripture; it names the difference between knowing the truth from the outside and being changed by it from within. The new covenant minister aims not only to fill heads but to be the one through whom the Spirit writes on hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 3 is one of the Bible’s great chapters on the old covenant and the new. It climbs from a dispute about paperwork, rival teachers with letters of recommendation, to the summit of the Christian life: ordinary people looking at Christ and slowly becoming like him.

Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Paul has just said that he speaks as a man commissioned by God, in the sight of God. He hears at once how that could be taken, and he says so: is this Paul recommending himself again? The question is not paranoid. It is what his opponents had been saying. The word again tells us the charge was already in circulation: that his letters were a long exercise in self-promotion, that a man who really had God’s authority would not need to keep asserting it. His defence in chapters 1 and 2 might look like exactly that, and he anticipates the charge.

Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you? Behind the second question lies a real first-century practice. Travel was dangerous, communication slow, and a stranger arriving in a city claiming to teach in the name of Christ could be anyone. So churches wrote letters of recommendation for those they sent. Luke records one: when Apollos wanted to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him (Acts 18:27). Paul himself commends Phoebe to the Romans in exactly this way (Romans 16:1–2), and sent men with letters to carry the collection (1 Corinthians 16:3). There is nothing wrong with the practice and Paul does not attack it.

The credential as currency. What he attacks is what it had become in Corinth. His rivals had arrived with impressive documents, perhaps from Jerusalem, and wanted letters from Corinth too: the endorsement of a well-known church to carry to the next town. The credential had become a currency, and it has not gone away: the conference platform, the endorsement on a book jacket, the size of a following. None of these is wrong in itself. The question is whether the credential is describing something real or standing in for it.

When is it right to speak about your own ministry? There is a genuine tension here that Paul does not dodge. He is about to spend much of the letter defending himself, and he knows it; he calls it foolishness when he gets there (11:1). The answer this chapter gives is that it is legitimate when the people you serve are being taken from you, and illegitimate when your own standing is what is at stake. Paul is not protecting a career. He is protecting a church from teachers who will damage it, and the only thing standing between them is his credibility. A man who defends himself for his own sake is building a reputation; a man who defends himself because his people are in danger is doing something else entirely, and the difference is usually visible in whether he enjoys it. Paul plainly does not. And his answer, when it comes in the next verse, is not another document. It is them: the Corinthians themselves are his letter.

By what authority? Paul’s refusal to wave paper has a pattern behind it. When the chief priests demanded to know by what authority Jesus acted (Matthew 21:23), he produced no document from Jerusalem or anywhere else. He pointed to his works: the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me (John 5:36). The blind saw, the lame walked, the poor heard good news (Matthew 11:4–5), and at last a tomb stood empty. The Lord of the church carried no letters, because his life was the credential. His servant Paul can do no better than follow him and point to what Christ has done in people.

Should churches still check references and credentials? Yes. The early church did, and it is simple wisdom and love. A church should know who is teaching its people and working with its children: it should ask for references from a man’s previous church, test his doctrine against Scripture, and carry out proper safeguarding checks. Leaders should be tested before they serve (1 Timothy 3:10). What Paul warns against is letting paper replace life: being impressed by titles, platforms and endorsements while failing to ask whether a man’s teaching is true and his life is godly. Check the credentials, and then look for the fruit.
verseByVerse.note: Letters of recommendation were common for travellers; Paul’s rivals at Corinth came with them.

verseByVerse.quote: You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves are our letter. Asked for his credentials, Paul points at the people asking. The document is the congregation itself: former idolaters, reformed swindlers, slaves and freedmen who a few years earlier had never heard the name of Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:9–11; 9:2). It is not filed; it walks around Corinth doing business, and the whole city can read it.

Written on our hearts. Some manuscripts read your hearts, but our is well supported and fits the warmth of the letter (7:3). Criticised and dismissed by these people, Paul says they are written on his heart. Yet the letter is also known and read by all. A church is a public document, whether it means to be or not.

A letter from Christ. In verse 2 they are Paul’s letter; here they are Christ’s, and Paul is only the courier. Every faithful minister discovers that he is the postman, not the author.

Not with ink. Then two contrasts that echo the Old Testament. Ink sits on a surface and can be scraped off parchment. The Spirit wrote on their lives: he changed what they love and want, so that the idolater now loves the living God and the thief works so that he has something to give (Ephesians 4:28; Ezekiel 36:27).

Tablets of human hearts. Now the reference is unmistakable. Stone tablets were what Moses carried down Sinai, written with the finger of God (Exodus 24:12; 31:18). And centuries later God had promised through Jeremiah, to a nation that had comprehensively failed to keep what was on them: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Ezekiel put it more bluntly still: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh, and I will put my Spirit within you (Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26–27).

A promise fulfilled in a Greek port. Paul’s claim is enormous. What the prophets promised has happened, and the evidence is sitting in a difficult church in a Greek port. It has happened because of Christ: the covenant that writes on hearts is the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20), and the Spirit who writes is the Spirit he poured out from the Father’s right hand (Acts 2:33). Jeremiah saw the pen; Paul has met the hand that holds it.

What has been written on you? Stone can be inscribed and remain stone; that is the whole tragedy of the old covenant. So what has actually been written on you? Not what you can recite: the law on stone could be recited perfectly by people it never changed. The test is whether anything has moved inward: whether you have come to want what you used to merely comply with. That shift is not something a person performs on himself. It is what the Spirit of the living God does with a heart, and it is the only credential any church has ever really had.

What if my life does not look much like a letter from Christ? Then look more carefully, and more honestly, in both directions. The letter is still being written, and the Spirit writes slowly; Paul calls the Corinthians Christ’s letter while they are still full of faults. Ask what has changed since you came to Christ, not whether you are finished: a sin you now hate, a person you now love, a hunger for God’s word you once lacked. Those are his handwriting. And if you honestly find nothing at all, do not despair or pretend. Go to Christ now, ask him for the new heart he promised, and keep coming to him in his word and among his people. He has never refused anyone who asked.

For worship. Ink can be scraped off; nothing scrapes away what Christ has written. He paid for the page with his blood and sealed it by his Spirit for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30). The first tablets lay smashed at the foot of the mountain (Exodus 32:19); the letter written on a heart of flesh will be finished on the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

parallels.desc: tablets of stone, written with the finger of God
a heart of flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Confidence through Christ. Paul guards his claim from being heard as self-assurance. The confidence is real, pepoithēsis, settled trust, but it is anchored through Christ and faces toward God: not confidence in himself measured against his rivals, but in what God has done, standing before God’s own scrutiny.

Not sufficient in ourselves. Not merely insufficient for the big things, but for claiming anything as from himself. This answers 2:16: who is sufficient for these things? Nobody, in himself.

But our sufficiency is from God. The word running through both verses is hikanos and its noun hikanotēs: adequate, competent, up to the job. It is a word with a history. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, one of the names of God is rendered by this very word, the Sufficient One, translating Shaddai (Ruth 1:20–21). God does not merely have sufficiency. He is it. And the word recalls a line of men who knew they lacked it. When God met Moses at the bush and told him to go to Pharaoh, Moses said, Who am I that I should go? (Exodus 3:11). When God called Jeremiah, he said, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth (Jeremiah 1:6). When Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple he said, Woe is me! For I am lost (Isaiah 6:5). Every one of them was right. Not one of them was adequate. God’s answer in each case was never to argue the point; it was to supply what was missing. He has never once called a servant and then left him to supply his own strength.

Which sentence do you live in? There is a question here, and it cuts both ways. Ask yourself which of these two sentences you actually live in: I can do this, or, I cannot do this and it is going to be done anyway. The first sounds like faith and is usually self-reliance in good clothes. The second sounds like defeat and is where God does most of his work. There is real comfort here for anyone who has backed away from something because they did not feel up to it: the class they were asked to teach, the parent they have to care for, the marriage they no longer know how to mend. The feeling of inadequacy is not a verdict. It is accurate. Paul felt it and said so in writing. What he learned is that adequacy was never the entry requirement, because it was never going to be supplied from inside him.

Through Christ. The confidence runs through Christ, the one man who ever stood before God with nothing to hide. And he lived the very dependence Paul describes: the Son, who is himself God, took a true human nature and in it said that the Son can do nothing of his own accord (John 5:19), living on the Father’s word and the Spirit’s power (Luke 4:14). Then he went to the cross so that sinners could have confidence to enter the holy places by his blood (Hebrews 10:19).

So do I still need to prepare, study and train? Yes. God’s sufficiency does not replace means; it works through them. Paul studied the Scriptures, asked for his books and parchments in prison (2 Timothy 4:13), and told Timothy to do his best to be a worker who rightly handles the word of truth. Prepare the lesson, learn the skills, take advice, practise. But do all of it leaning on God rather than on the preparation. Pray before you study and while you study, and when you have done everything you can, go in knowing that the change in people’s hearts will still be his gift, not your achievement. Hard work and dependence are not rivals; they are the two hands of faithful service.

verseByVerse.quote: who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ministers of a new covenant. Paul has been made sufficient to be a minister of a new covenant, not a better teacher of the old one: something the prophets promised and never saw (Jeremiah 31:31–34). A covenant is a binding relationship God establishes by his word, with promises he pledges to keep, sealed by sacrifice, in which he is their God and they are his people. The night before he died the Lord lifted the cup and said that this cup is the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20). It was inaugurated not with tablets on a mountain but with a body given and blood poured out.

Not of the letter but of the Spirit. This sentence has often been used to mean that careful attention to the text of Scripture is deadening while a spiritual impression is where the life is. The context rules that out. The letter is set against a new covenant, and the next verse defines it: the ministry of death carved in letters on stone. The letter is the law of Moses, standing outside a person and telling him what to do. The Spirit is the life-giver who writes God’s law on hearts.

For the letter kills. Not because it is bad: the law is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). It kills because it can tell you the standard with perfect accuracy, cannot give you the least power to meet it, and pronounces death on those who fail (Galatians 3:10). It describes the disease with total precision and hands you no medicine, and a diagnosis with no cure is a death sentence read aloud.

But the Spirit gives life. And the Spirit gives life by doing the one thing the stone could never do: regenerating a dead heart, and writing the command inside it, so that obedience comes out rather than being demanded in (John 6:63; Romans 8:2, 11). The letter could kill; it took the death of the Lawgiver’s Son to make anything alive. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation now breathes on dead hearts, and they live.

Where Christians differ: the letter and the spirit. Since Origen, the third-century teacher, some have read this verse as a principle of interpretation: the literal meaning of Scripture kills, but the spiritual or allegorical meaning gives life. This commentary’s view: Paul is not speaking about methods of reading Scripture, but about two covenants: the law written on stone, which condemns, and the Spirit’s new covenant work, which gives life. The Reformers rightly insisted on the plain, literal-grammatical meaning of Scripture, read in the light of Christ. The law is not abolished as God’s moral standard for believers; but it cannot justify or give life. Only the Spirit, through the gospel, does that.

Backwards. Ignoring the words of Scripture is not walking in the Spirit; the Spirit inspired them. The real warning is aimed at the person who knows the Bible thoroughly, keeps the rules scrupulously, and has never been changed by any of it. Life under the letter can be conducted with a well-marked Bible.

Then how should I read the Bible? For its plain, intended meaning, which is what the Reformers meant by reading it literally. Ask what the human author meant his first readers to understand, paying attention to the kind of writing it is: history read as history, poetry as poetry, parable as parable, prophecy with its images. Read each passage in its context and let clearer passages explain harder ones. Then follow it to Christ, as the apostles did, because the whole Bible is about him (Luke 24:27). Do not hunt for secret meanings no ordinary reader could find. And read prayerfully, asking the Spirit who wrote it to give you understanding and a heart to obey; he works through the words, never around them.

In everyday life. When you obey God this week, is it a wall you keep running into, or a direction you want to go? If it feels like the wall, do not throw away the commandments; ask the Spirit to write them on your heart, and look again at the Christ who kept them all for you.
verseByVerse.note: The “letter” is the law written on stone, which could condemn but not give life.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–18 — The Fading Glory and the Surpassing Glory; the Unveiled Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul compares the two covenants through the story of Moses’ shining face. The law came with real glory, but that ministry brought condemnation and was temporary; the ministry of the Spirit, which brings righteousness and lasts, is far more glorious. The veil over Moses’ face becomes a picture of the veil over hearts that read him without Christ, removed whenever anyone turns to the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Paul reads the story of Moses’ veil (v. 13) in the light of its fulfilment in Christ: the whole Mosaic arrangement was temporary and pointed beyond itself.

Verse 18 is a key text for the Reformed teaching that sanctification is the Spirit’s work through the word. Beholding (katoptrizomenoi) is the means: the word presents Christ, and the Spirit makes the believer like the one he beholds.
verseByVerse.examples: An older believer meets with a young Christian worn out by the effort of holiness: striving, measuring, failing, striving again. She encourages him to meditate slowly on passages that show the character and glory of Christ, and to rest in what he sees before rushing to apply it. Months later he notices his desires changing, not through more effort but through beholding.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ministry of death. Paul now runs an argument three times in five verses: if the lesser thing had that much glory, think what the greater must have. Applied to the law God gave at Sinai, the ministry of death sounds close to blasphemy. But for sinners its result was condemnation. The commandment is good; what it does to a sinner is fatal, because it can only tell him what he has failed to be.

Such glory. Moses has been forty days on the mountain. He comes down carrying the tablets, and he does not know that his face is shining (Exodus 34:29–35). Aaron and the people see him and are afraid to come near. The light is not his; it is residue. He has been standing in the presence of God and has come away carrying some of it on his skin, the way a man who has been near a fire comes back smelling of smoke. And it was so bright that they could not look at him. This is what holiness looks like when it touches a human face. Even the reflected edge of his glory was more than they could bear. That is Paul’s whole point: such was the glory of the covenant that kills. The old covenant really was glorious, because it came from God.

Which was being brought to an end. The verb is katargeō: to set aside, to bring to an end. The shine was fading even while they were too frightened to look at it, a picture of the old covenant itself (Hebrews 8:13). Exodus does not say in so many words that it faded; Paul draws it from the veil, and interpreters still discuss how he reads the passage. Real glory, and temporary. Centuries later three men watched another face on another mountain, and his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2), and that light was not residue from a visit. It was his own, coming out. Moses was there to see it, and this time the glory belonged to the man in the middle. The light Moses carried for a season, Christ is for ever.

Will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory? So the question answers itself. If a fading light on one man’s face after forty days on a mountain was more than a nation could look at, what is the weight of the ministry that does not condemn but makes righteous, that does not sit on the skin but is written on the heart, and that does not fade?

The death the stone pronounced. How can a ministry of death give way to one of life without God cancelling his own sentence? Only because the sentence was carried out. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The death the tablets pronounced on every lawbreaker fell on the one man who had kept every word on them. So the new ministry is not the old one softened: the law’s demand has been met in Christ’s life and its penalty paid in his death, and the Spirit can now write on hearts the law that once could only condemn them.

Does this mean the Ten Commandments are obsolete? No. What is being brought to an end is the old covenant as a ministry: the arrangement under which the law stood outside a person, written on stone, and condemned him. The law itself is holy, and its moral demands still show believers how to love God and neighbour. Paul says we uphold the law (Romans 3:31) and sums up its second table (the commandments about how we treat our neighbour) in the command to love (Romans 13:8–10). Some Christians hold that the whole law of Moses has given way to the law of Christ, though the moral teaching it contains is repeated and deepened in the New Testament. Most in the Reformed tradition hold that the moral law summarised in the Ten Commandments still binds, now written on the heart by the Spirit (v. 3). On the fourth commandment Christians differ: the Westminster and 1689 Baptist confessions keep it as the Christian Sabbath, moved to the Lord’s Day; others hold that the Sabbath, like the ceremonial law, is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), while the first day remains the day of worship. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). The confessional view (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8) is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both sides honour the Lord’s Day, and both should do so without judging the other.

Short-changed? There is something here for the Christian who reads the Old Testament and feels quietly short-changed. The fire on the mountain, the sea opening, the pillar of cloud, the shining face: it can seem that they got the spectacle and we got the routine of an ordinary Tuesday. Paul says the comparison is real and runs entirely the other way. They had a glory nobody could look at, and it was on its way out. You have a glory that does not fade, in a covenant that cannot be broken, administered by the Spirit of God living inside ordinary people. The reason it looks less impressive is that it has moved inside, where the work needed doing.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

verseByVerse.quote: For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ministry of righteousness. Three verses press the comparison from three directions: what the two ministries do, how they compare side by side, and how long each lasts. One is the ministry of condemnation, the other of righteousness, both courtroom words. The law brings a verdict of guilty, accurately. The gospel brings a verdict of righteous to the same defendant: justification, the Judge’s acquittal of the guilty, for Christ’s righteousness put to their account and received by faith alone (5:21; Romans 3:21–22; 4:5). That is the whole distance between Sinai and Calvary in two nouns.

No glory at all. Verse 10 is not a contradiction. It is what happens when a lamp left burning meets the sunrise: the lamp was never a fraud, but in the new light there is nothing left for it to do.

What is permanent. In verse 11 the decisive difference: one was being brought to an end, the other is permanent (menō, abiding). The old arrangement was scaffolding: good, necessary work, put up around a building that was coming.

Why still read the Old Testament? This matters practically for how a Christian reads the first three-quarters of his Bible. It would be easy to conclude from this passage that the Old Testament has been superseded and can be quietly shelved. Paul, who is about to say that the Israelites read Moses with a veil on, is not saying that. He quotes the Old Testament constantly, including in this very argument; his point is not that the old covenant was wrong but that it was never meant to be the end. The scaffolding does not become rubbish when the building appears. It becomes the thing that shows you how the building went up.

Everything else fades. There is a warning in the fading aimed at us. Health fades, beauty fades fast, careers end, and twenty years of achievement are summarised in one line at a funeral. None of these is worthless; the shine on Moses’ face was real. They are simply all being brought to an end, and the question is whether you have anything that is not.

What does the ministry of righteousness mean for me? It means that the verdict over your life, if you trust Christ, is righteous, and that it was given as a gift, not earned. God counts the perfect righteousness of Christ as yours and your sin as his: for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (5:21). You do not stand before God on your record, good or bad, but on Christ’s. This is why a believer can come to God on his worst day with confidence, and why his best days add nothing to his acceptance. The new covenant does not lower God’s standard. It meets it, in Christ, for you.

If the old covenant was fading all along, did God change his mind? No. The old covenant was never a first plan that failed. God promised a new covenant through Jeremiah while the old one was still in force (Jeremiah 31:31–34), and Paul says the law was a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24). A guardian is not a mistake; he is appointed for a season, with the end in view. God’s purpose from the beginning was to bless the nations through Abraham’s offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16). What changed was the stage of the plan, never the God who made it (Malachi 3:6).

For worship. The covenant remains because its Mediator remains. Moses came down shining for a while and then died outside the land. The Son went up to a cross and down into a grave, and rose to a life that cannot end; he holds his priesthood permanently (Hebrews 7:24). He is the Lord our righteousness (Jeremiah 23:6), and his glory has no evening.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are very bold. The boldness does not come from temperament (he was too anxious to preach at Troas) or from success. Since we have such a hope: it is a conclusion drawn from a glory that does not fade. The word is parrēsia, freedom of speech, the citizen’s right to speak openly and frankly. Paul has nothing to manage and nothing to hide, so he can say it all.

Not like Moses. Exodus 34:33–35 tells of the people’s fear of Moses’ shining face, and that he wore a veil after speaking to them, removing it when he went in to speak with the LORD. The outcome is the telos, the end: Moses veiled his face so that they would not watch the glory dying away. The veil was a sign that the old covenant was temporary, and became a symbol that Israel could not see its full meaning, which pointed to Christ.

Is Paul rewriting Exodus? No, and it is worth seeing what he is actually doing. Exodus records what happened; Paul is reading it in the light of what it turned out to mean. The narrative records the veil without explaining it, and Paul, standing on the far side of the cross, sees the significance the veil carried in the whole arrangement: an old covenant whose glory was never permanent, and whose end was screened from the people living under it. This is not allegory imposed on the text. It is the same instinct the Lord himself modelled on the Emmaus road, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets to interpret what was said about himself (Luke 24:27).

The end behind the veil. What was the end the veil concealed? Paul uses the same word in Romans: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4). The fading glory on one man’s face was a covenant pointing past itself to a face whose glory would not fade. Paul is not guarding a light that is running down. He is announcing what the old covenant was moving towards: Jesus Christ, crucified and risen.

Managing an impression. Moses covers something that is fading, and the people deal with a screen rather than a face. That is a common condition of religious life. The love has cooled, the prayers have dried up, and rather than say so, we put on the veil. We answer fine and keep the vocabulary, the attendance, the tone of voice; and nobody can see a fading glory through a cloth, so nobody asks. Paul’s alternative is not to shine harder but the open face of a man whose glory is not his own and is therefore not running out, who has no reason to cover anything, including his weakness.

Does boldness mean I must tell everyone all my struggles? No. Openness is not the same as broadcasting. Paul chose what to tell, to whom and why, and he wrote of his weaknesses to help the church, not to draw attention to himself. What boldness rules out is the managed mask: pretending to God and to the people closest to you that all is well when it is not. Have at least one or two mature believers to whom you can say the truth about your soul (James 5:16). Be honest with God always; he sees through every veil anyway. And in public, be open about the gospel and about your need of it, without performing either strength or weakness.

For worship. The one who gave us a glory that cannot fade had nothing to hide either. He spoke openly to the world, and in secret said nothing (John 18:20); and on the cross the whole city saw him, exposed, so that our shame could be covered and our faces uncovered for ever.

parallels.desc: he put a veil over his face

verseByVerse.quote: But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But their minds were hardened. The veil moves from Moses’ face to the reader’s heart. The Scriptures Paul’s own people revere are read every Sabbath by minds hardened to what they are for. “Hardened” is pōroō: made callous, dulled (Romans 11:7).

Two things to say first. This passage has been misused with terrible consequences. First, Paul writes as a Jew, a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), with great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his kinsmen (Romans 9:2–3). This is not contempt but grief. Second, the hardening is not final: within a sentence the veil is removed whenever a person turns, and Paul is the proof that it happens to the hardest cases.

That same veil remains. The old covenant here means the Scriptures, especially the law, read in the synagogue; this is the only place in the New Testament where the phrase appears. The veil is not over the text; it is over the heart. The words are read accurately and honoured, and what they point at is not seen (John 5:39). The problem was never a lack of Bible.

Only through Christ. Christ is the key to the Old Testament. And the veil is not removed by debate. Paul could out-argue any man in a synagogue, and he does not say the answer is a better case. That is worth knowing if you pray for a relative who knows all the answers and remains cold: you are not up against a shortage of information. Think what did happen to Paul on the Damascus road. He did not lose an argument. He was struck blind, and then something like scales fell from his eyes (Acts 9:18): the veil removed by the one person who can remove it, in a man who had been furiously certain he was reading Moses correctly. Christ is the light of the Scriptures, and he has never yet failed to be seen by the one he chose to open.

Whenever Moses is read. Moses means the books of Moses, read each Sabbath (Acts 15:21), and Moses himself was writing about Christ: if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me (John 5:46). The Passover lamb, the bronze serpent, the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15): the veil does not hide a stranger. It hides the one the reader is waiting for.

Closer to home. Christian readers can do the same: read the Bible through on a plan, know the outline of every book, and miss the person the whole library was assembled to present. Reading Scripture without seeing Christ in it is not a Jewish failing but a human one, and any of us can do it in English.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish people are worse than others. Every unbeliever has a veil over the heart (4:3–4). And it does not mean the Old Testament is obscure in itself. It is clear to those who see Christ in it. Nor does it ever justify contempt or hostility toward Jewish people, which the church has too often shown, to its shame.

Will the veil ever be lifted from Israel as a people? Christians who share the same gospel read Romans 11 differently. Many believe Paul promises a future large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in and all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). Others understand all Israel to mean the full number of God’s elect, Jews and Gentiles together, gathered throughout this age. Both agree that the hardening is partial, that Jewish people are coming to Christ now, and that there is only one way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike: faith in Jesus the Messiah. Both should lead us to pray, with Paul, for our Jewish neighbours and to share the gospel with them gladly.

In everyday life. Pray for Jewish friends and all who read the Scriptures without seeing Christ. And next time you read the Old Testament, ask before you close it: where is this pointing to Christ?
verseByVerse.note: “Moses” here means the books of Moses, read aloud each Sabbath in the synagogue.

verseByVerse.quote: But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when one turns to the Lord. One short sentence, the hinge of the chapter, reaching back into Exodus 34: whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil (Exodus 34:34). The covering was for the crowd. In the presence of God it came off.

The Lord Moses met. Paul has just said whom that turning now reaches: only through Christ is the veil taken away (v. 14). The LORD before whom Moses stood unveiled has come near with a human face: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9). Moses had to go into the tent to take off the veil. Now the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and to turn to Jesus is to stand where Moses stood.

Turns. The word is epistrephō, turning round: a change of direction, not only of opinion, repentance and faith together. It does not say the veil is removed when a person understands enough or has cleaned himself up first. It says when one turns.

The veil is removed. The verb is periaireō: taken away completely, all round. In Exodus it is Moses who takes the veil off; Paul’s form of the verb could mean the same, but most translations rightly read it as passive, the veil is removed, because verse 14 has just said that only through Christ is it taken away. Nobody pulls the covering off his own heart, any more than a blind man cures himself by deciding to see. Something is done to him. Then the Scriptures become clear, and the glory of Christ is seen. This is the whole difference between religion and the gospel: one tells a man to lift the veil, the other tells him that when he turns he will find it has been taken.
