And even the turning is God’s gift: God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ (4:6). The turning is not the achievement that earns the sight; it is the moment the sight is given.

Open at both ends. If the Bible has gone flat, if God has become an idea you defend rather than a person you know, the instruction is not try harder to feel it. It is turn: face the other way, and speak to him. Paul attaches no conditions, not even that you have not wasted the last ten years. The sentence is open at both ends.

If the Bible feels veiled to me after years as a Christian, am I not saved? Not necessarily. Believers go through dry seasons, and Scripture can feel flat because of tiredness, grief, unconfessed sin, distraction or simply the way we read. The question is not whether you feel the glory today but whether you are turned toward Christ, trusting him and wanting him. If you are, keep turning. Confess what needs confessing. Read more slowly, and pray before you read: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Read with others, and sit under faithful preaching. The veil does not return over a believer’s heart the way it covers an unbeliever’s; but the eyes of a believer can grow dim, and the Lord delights to brighten them.

What can I do for someone who is still veiled? Pray first, because only the Lord removes the veil, and he does it in answer to prayer. Then do what Philip did for the Ethiopian reading Isaiah: open the Scriptures with them and show them Jesus (Acts 8:35). Do not rely on winning arguments, though you should answer honest questions. Invite them to read a Gospel with you. Live in a way that makes Christ attractive. And keep hoping. You cannot lift the veil, but you can stand beside the person while the Lord does.

For worship. There is no antechamber, no preliminary examination, no queue. A man turns and the covering is gone. That is what it cost the Son of God to arrange: the curtain of the temple torn in two from top to bottom on the afternoon he died (Matthew 27:51). Nobody has ever come and been told to wait.
verseByVerse.note: Paul echoes Exodus: whenever Moses went in before the LORD, he removed the veil.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Lord is the Spirit. The Lord in verse 16, in the Exodus passage Paul is expounding, is Yahweh, the LORD. In the new covenant, turning to the Lord means encountering the Spirit, who applies Christ’s work and removes the veil.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord the Spirit? Some (modalists, who hold that Father, Son and Spirit are one person appearing in three ways) take this verse to mean the Son and the Spirit are the same person. This commentary’s view: Paul distinguishes the Spirit and the Lord in the same verse: the Spirit of the Lord. He is saying that the Lord of the Exodus passage is now encountered through the Spirit, who is himself the Lord, fully God. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three distinct persons, one God (2 Corinthians 13:14).

There is freedom. Then the freedom, eleutheria. From the veil first; but the context builds a bigger answer: from the covenant that could only condemn, from bondage to sin and death (Romans 8:2; Galatians 5:1), from the terrible arithmetic of a religion in which everything depends on your performance; and, given verse 13, from the exhausting business of managing the veil. Freedom, above all, of access: a child coming into his Father’s presence.

The Spirit of his Son. Where did that freedom come from? Paul tells the Galatians: God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons; and because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba! Father! (Galatians 4:4–6). The Son went under the law that bound us and paid what it demanded; then the Spirit came to make his freedom ours. The Spirit of the Lord brings freedom because he is the Spirit of the Son who bought it.

Free on the instrument. It is not freedom to do as you please (Galatians 5:13). The heaviest masters are not laws imposed from outside but appetites, resentments and fears chosen freely that cannot now be put down. Christian freedom is like a musician’s: years under a discipline he did not invent let him play what he hears. He is not free from the instrument. He is free on it.

Does the freedom of the Spirit mean worship should be unplanned and spontaneous? No. Paul is speaking of freedom from condemnation and the veil, not of a style of worship. The same Spirit who gives freedom is the God of order, not of confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33, 40), and he is as present in a carefully prepared sermon and a written prayer as in an unplanned one. Nor is freedom measured by dramatic experiences or the kind of gifts that marked the apostles’ day; the Spirit’s presence is seen most surely where Christ is exalted, the word is believed and lives are changed. This commentary holds that the sign gifts which confirmed the apostles’ message (12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4) belonged to that founding generation, though many faithful Christians believe they continue; on either view, the Spirit is known most surely by his witness to Christ. Planned or spontaneous, worship is free when it comes from forgiven hearts that love God and know they are welcome.

In everyday life. If you obey God mainly to keep something bad from happening, his disappointment or withdrawal, something in you is still standing at the foot of Sinai. The commandments have not gone soft; the fear has gone out of them, because the verdict was settled before you began. Obey today as a son, not a hired hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we all, with unveiled face. The chapter has been climbing since verse 7, and here it arrives. We all. On Sinai only Moses went up into the cloud of glory, while the nation stood at the bottom and was warned not to touch the mountain, and he veiled what he brought down. Now the whole congregation is on the mountain. There is no spiritual class in the new covenant who see what ordinary members do not. The tired mother, the apprentice, the man who has never been asked to do anything in church: we all. With unveiled face: the covering has been taken off. Nothing stands between the believer and the glory of God; the face is bare and it is safe for it to be bare, which is more than Moses could say of the people.

Beholding the glory of the Lord. Katoptrizomai can mean gazing as into a mirror or reflecting like one. The context favours gazing: we do not see him yet as he is, but truly, as in a good mirror, in the face of Christ (4:6) revealed in the gospel and Scripture. The posture is looking.

Being transformed. The verb is metamorphoō, used of the Lord’s transfiguration and of the renewing of the mind (Romans 12:2). It is passive, done to us by God, and present: happening now, in ordinary weeks, felt or not. Into the same image: the image of Christ (Romans 8:29).

From one degree of glory to another. Literally, from glory to glory, by stages. Moses’ glory faded; ours increases. This is sanctification, God’s slow, sure work of making a pardoned sinner holy in fact, and it ends in glorification, when Christ will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

We become what we look at. Sanctification in this verse is not first a matter of effort or resolutions, useful as those are, but of gaze. That is why John Owen, near the end of his life, wrote that the great means of holiness is the beholding of the glory of Christ, and why a man can grit his teeth through disciplines for a decade and change very little.

The other direction. The principle cuts the other way too. Look every evening at people who are richer, and you will become discontented without deciding to; feed on outrage and you will become angry. Of idols Scripture says that those who make them become like them (Psalm 115:8). Whatever we keep gazing at with longing, approval, comfort or success, is quietly remaking us. So the question is not, am I trying hard enough? It is, what am I looking at?

From the Lord who is the Spirit. The end of the sentence takes the whole weight off the one doing the looking. The change is not manufactured by the intensity of your concentration. The Spirit is doing it, and he has never abandoned a half-finished work (Philippians 1:6).

In the flow. Verse 18 answers the opening dispute: the Spirit making Paul’s converts like Christ is the letter (3:2–3). It leads into chapter 4, where the glory is seen in the face of Christ (4:6), carried in jars of clay (4:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean transformation is instant or that we become perfect in this life. It means steady growth as we look at Christ. Nor does it make effort pointless: the same apostle tells us to put sin to death and to train ourselves for godliness. But all our effort is the effort of looking, and of removing what blocks the view.

How do I actually behold the glory of the Lord? Mainly through the means God has given. Read the Gospels slowly and often, and ask in each scene what it shows you of Jesus: his holiness, his compassion, his authority, his cross. Sit under preaching that sets Christ before you. Take the Lord’s Supper as a looking at his body given and blood shed. Sing hymns full of him. Meditate on a single verse about him through the day. And pray that the Spirit would show you his glory as you look; beholding is not mere reading, but reading with the eyes of faith, asking to see him.

Why do I not feel that I am changing? Because growth is slow and mostly invisible from the inside, like a child’s height measured against the door frame only once a year. The verb is present and passive: it is being done to you, gradually, whether you feel it or not. Look back over years, not days. Ask others who know you well. Often the clearest sign is that you see your sin more clearly than before, which feels like going backwards but is the light growing. Keep looking at Christ, and leave the measuring to the one who is doing the work.

In everyday life. Add up the hours honestly: what is in front of your eyes most in an ordinary week, and where is Christ put before you long enough for anything to happen? Change one habit that keeps your gaze elsewhere, trusting the Spirit who dwells in you to do the changing (Romans 8:11).

For worship. In people who mostly cannot see it happening, the Spirit is painting the face of Jesus on the faces of sinners. The day is coming when the mirror is taken away, and we shall see him as he is, and being like him will be a fact (1 John 3:2). Moses’ face shone for a season and faded. Ours, in him, will shine for ever.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?<sup>2</sup>You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all.<sup>3</sup>And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.<sup>4</sup>Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God.<sup>5</sup>Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,<sup>6</sup>who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.<sup>7</sup>Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end,<sup>8</sup>will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?<sup>9</sup>For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory.<sup>10</sup>Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it.<sup>11</sup>For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.<sup>12</sup>Since we have such a hope, we are very bold,<sup>13</sup>not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.<sup>14</sup>But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away.<sup>15</sup>Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.<sup>16</sup>But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.<sup>17</sup>Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.<sup>18</sup>And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.

4.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
4.overview:
Paul has described the surpassing glory of the new covenant ministry. Now he faces the obvious objection: if the ministry is so glorious, why is the minister so unimpressive, so beaten up, so weak? Corinth, which admired polish and success, was embarrassed by an apostle who looked like a failure.

Paul answers that the treasure, the glory of God in the face of Christ, is carried in clay jars so that the power is plainly God’s. He does not lose heart, because the God who raised Jesus is renewing him inwardly while his body wears out, and his troubles are preparing an eternal weight of glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Light Shining in Darkness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because his ministry is a gift of mercy, Paul does not give up, and he relies on open truth rather than tricks. If some cannot see the gospel, Satan has blinded them; where anyone sees, it is because the God who first commanded light has shone into the heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ is “the image of God” (v. 4; Colossians 1:15): not merely like God or a representative of God, but the true visible representation of the invisible God, so that to see him is to see the Father (John 14:9). God’s glory is found not in visions or mystical experiences but in the face of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen (v. 6).

Verse 6 echoes Genesis 1:3: conversion is a creative act of God, like the first creation. So, as the Reformers taught, the new birth comes first and produces faith; faith does not produce the new birth.
verseByVerse.examples: A campus minister explains the gospel to a sharp philosophy student who has engaged every argument and remains unconvinced. The problem may be a blindness no argument can cure. He should not stop reasoning, for Paul commends the truth to the conscience, but he should add steady prayer that the God who speaks light into darkness will do it here.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 4 shows what glorious new-covenant ministry looks like in practice: treasure in a clay jar. It is a chapter about a cracked pot, and from the first verse to the last it is really about the face it carries.

By the mercy of God. The therefore reaches back to the whole of chapter 3: the covenant that does not fade, the veil removed, the glory that transforms. Everything here about weakness and wasting away is said by a man who has just described what he has been given: this ministry, and by the mercy of God. He never once speaks of it as an achievement.

We do not lose heart. The verb is enkakeō: to grow weary and give up, to run out of nerve, to quit. He will say it again in verse 16, and everything between is his answer to why he has not stopped. Losing heart is one of the commonest and least discussed conditions in the Christian life. It is not usually a crisis of doctrine. It is the slow arrival of a Tuesday on which you cannot see the point of continuing: the class you have taught for years with nothing to show, the marriage you have prayed about since the children were small, the neighbour who is politely unmovable. Nobody announces that they have lost heart. They simply do slightly less, and then a little less than that.

Mercy, not willpower. Paul’s guard against it is not willpower but the sentence he has just written: this ministry came by mercy. A man carrying something he earned has to defend it, and will eventually be too tired to. The commission rests on the mercy that gave it, not on the strength of the one who holds it, and mercy does not get tired.

A display of patience. That mercy has a name and a face. Paul tells Timothy what happened on the road to Damascus: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost, and I received mercy for this reason, that in me Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience (1 Timothy 1:15–16). The risen Lord met the man who was hunting his people and gave him a commission. The one who showed him mercy when he was an enemy will hardly withdraw it now that he is a servant (Romans 5:10).

Underhanded ways. A striking list of things he has ruled out. Disgraceful, underhanded ways are literally the hidden things of shame: whatever a man would not want brought into the light. Perhaps the rival teachers had accused Paul of hidden motives; he answers by naming what he has refused. Cunning is panourgia, readiness to do anything, the word Paul himself will use of the serpent in Eden (11:3). And tamper with God’s word is doloō, a term from the trade in wine and precious metals: to adulterate, to dilute, to alloy. It is close kin to the word in 2:17 for peddling God’s word: the trader who waters the wine to stretch his profit.

What does tampering actually look like? Rarely a denial. Usually a dilution: the doctrine kept but drained of force, the demand quoted but never pressed, the warning read out in a tone that says nobody here need worry. It also runs the other way: the verse hardened past what it says, used to control people. In both directions the operator has decided he knows better than the text what the text should do.

The open statement of the truth. Against all of it Paul sets one method, phanerōsis, a bringing into the light: say it plainly, in public, and let it do its own work on the conscience, before God, who sees all. No technique, no leverage, no management of what people are allowed to know. It is a slower way to build, and the only way anything gets built that will still be standing when the builder is gone.

Losing heart: does it mean I am not a real Christian? No. Paul would not need to say we do not lose heart unless losing heart were a real danger for real believers. Elijah sat under a broom tree and asked to die (1 Kings 19:4); the psalmist told his own soul to hope in God because it was not doing so on its own (Psalm 42:5). Discouragement is a temptation, not a verdict on your standing. The remedy Paul shows is not to feel stronger but to look again at what you were given and who gave it: the ministry, the calling, the salvation itself came by mercy, and mercy is not withdrawn because you are tired. Rest, tell a trusted believer, keep coming to the means of grace (God’s word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people), and do the next small faithful thing.

How do I commend the truth to someone’s conscience without pressure? Say what is true, plainly, and say it as one who will stand before God for how you said it. Do not exaggerate to make it more appealing, and do not hide the hard parts to make it more acceptable: sin, judgment, the cost of following Christ. Do not use guilt, flattery or a social debt (I helped you, so you owe me a hearing). Give people time; invite questions; let them see you live it. Then leave the result with God. The conscience is God’s territory, and he is the one who makes the truth land.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If our gospel is veiled. The obvious objection follows: if Paul states the truth openly, why do intelligent, decent people hear Christ clearly presented and remain unmoved? Some in Corinth were evidently calling his gospel obscure. His answer is not that the message needs improving. The problem is in the hearers, those on the road to destruction (2:15), and there is a third party in the room.

The god of this world. The phrase must not be heard as though the universe had two gods. There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6). Satan is a creature, on a leash, with a date. The title means he is the god people actually serve: the power this age treats as ultimate, worshipped in a thousand forms that never carry his name. Jesus called him the ruler of this world and said in the same breath that he would be cast out (John 12:31; Ephesians 2:2).

Has blinded the minds. His method is specific. Not persuaded, not argued: blinded. The verb is a single decisive act. He does not need to make people believe something false about Christ; it is enough that they cannot see him at all. Unbelief is not merely an intellectual position. It is spiritual blindness, and it works like this: a person can understand the words of the gospel, even explain them back to you, and still see nothing glorious in Christ: the facts register, but the beauty does not. That is why the same sermon can move one hearer to tears and leave the one beside him bored, and why Paul says elsewhere that the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Corinthians 2:14).

Where Christians differ: the god of this world. Some ancient heretics (Marcion and the Gnostics) took this to mean the God of the Old Testament, a lesser, evil god. This commentary’s view: The god of this age is Satan, who is called god because unbelievers serve him and he holds sway over the present evil age. His power is real but limited and temporary, under God’s sovereign control (Job 1:12), and already defeated at the cross (Colossians 2:15). There is one true God, who made the world and rules it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean unbelievers are innocent victims. Paul calls them unbelievers, and this blindness is never against a person’s will; it confirms a direction already chosen (John 3:19). Nor does it license writing anyone off. The man writing this was as blind as anyone, on the Damascus road with letters to the synagogues (Acts 9:1–2).

You are up against a blindfold. If you have explained the gospel to someone you love, patiently and well, and nothing has happened, you have not necessarily failed. You are up against a blindfold, and blindfolds are not removed by better reasoning. That is why the Paul who reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath (Acts 18:4) also asked churches to pray for him.

The image of God. Look at what the blindfold is designed to prevent. Three phrases are stacked up, each joined to the next by of: the light, of the gospel, of the glory of Christ. Each opens into the next, and they arrive at a person. The image of God is eikōn, the true visible representation: not a rough likeness or a good approximation. Paul says the same to the Colossians: he is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). And the Lord himself put it beyond argument to a disciple who wanted a vision of the Father: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). The invisible God has made himself visible in one place only, and that place is a Galilean carpenter who was executed outside a city wall. That is the light the enemy is working so hard to keep from human eyes, and it is worth asking why he should trouble himself so greatly over one face, unless there really is nothing else to see. The image of the invisible God has stood in the full glare of hell’s hatred and come out risen, and every blindfold in the world is held in place only until he says otherwise.

Does calling unbelievers blind make Christians proud? Only if Christians claimed to see because they were cleverer or better, and Paul claims the opposite. He was the blind man, the zealous, learned, religious one who was sure he saw clearly (Philippians 3:4–6), and he could see only because light came from outside him (v. 6). A man led out of a dark cellar by the hand is not boasting when he calls back to those still inside that there is a door and a light beyond it. The claim humbles the religious and the irreligious alike: the moral man cannot see by his morality any more than the sceptic by his scepticism. Everyone who sees Christ was shown him.

Does “perishing” mean my friend is beyond hope? No. Perishing describes the road a person is on now, not a sentence we can read off his life. You cannot know who God has chosen, and Paul did not know either; he simply kept preaching, because some who are blind today will see tomorrow. Every Christian was once on the perishing road (Ephesians 2:1–3). The word should make you urgent, not resigned. The only point at which anyone is beyond hope is death in unbelief, and while your friend is breathing, the God who once said, Let light shine out of darkness, can still speak.

How should I actually pray for someone who is blinded? Pray to God, not at the devil: ask the Father to do what Paul says he does (v. 6), to shine into this heart. Pray specifically, by name, for the one thing that matters most: that they would see the glory of Christ, not merely that their circumstances would improve or their objections be answered. Ask God to send them other believers, and to give you a clear word at the right time. And pray with confidence rather than nervousness, because you are not asking God to do something unusual. Opening blind eyes is what Jesus came to do (Luke 4:18).
verseByVerse.note: “The god of this world” is Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what we proclaim is not ourselves. One sentence settles what a Christian minister is for. His rivals were promoting their experiences, gifts and success. Nobody sets out to preach himself. It happens by increments: the illustration that makes the speaker look perceptive, the discovery that a certain kind of story gets a certain response. The message stays orthodox. The subject quietly changes.

In the flow. If the light the enemy hides is Christ’s glory (v. 4), the preacher’s task is not to stand in front of it. This is Paul’s answer to rivals who commended themselves (3:1; 10:12): the contest was never about him.

But Jesus Christ as Lord. The earliest Christian confession (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), two words in Greek, and in time it cost lives, because Christians died for refusing to say Caesar is Lord. To say Jesus is Lord was to say the emperor was not. It is a claim about who is actually in charge, of the world and of the hearer.

Your servants. The word is doulos: a slave, with no independent agenda. The apostle who has spent three chapters defending his authority defines his relationship to the people questioning him as slavery to them, the opposite of lording it over their faith (1:24). The shape of that service was set by a Lord who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45), and who on the last night took a towel and washed the feet of the men who were about to abandon him (John 13:4–5). He is Lord of all, and he knelt.

For Jesus’ sake. He is not their slave because the customer is always right; he has just refused to trim the message for them. His Master sends him to serve them, and that keeps his service from becoming flattery. A man who serves people for their sake alone will end up telling them what they want. A man who serves them for Christ’s sake will tell them the truth and stay.

I am no preacher, so does verse 5 apply to me? Yes. Every Christian speaks about Christ to someone: a child at bedtime, a friend over coffee, a home group, a post online. The same drift threatens all of us. Testimony can become a story about how interesting my journey has been; helping in church can become a way of being needed and noticed; online the temptation is built into the format. The question is the same for you as for Paul: when people have listened to you, are they thinking more about Jesus or more about you? Tell your story, but tell it so that he is the one who acts in it. Paul calls himself and his companions your servants for Jesus’ sake, and that title fits every believer who opens his mouth about Christ.

In everyday life. When you catch yourself back in the centre, as all of us do, the Servant who never sought his own glory (John 8:50) stands in your place before God; turn back to him without despair. And look for the menial way to serve someone this week for Christ’s sake, done because your Master would have done it.

verseByVerse.quote: For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let light shine out of darkness. Verse 4 said the mind is blinded; this verse says what God does about it, reaching back to the first page of the Bible (with an echo of Isaiah 9:2). Darkness was over the face of the deep. There was nothing to strike a light from and nobody to strike it. And God said, Let there be light, and there was light (Genesis 1:3). Paul says that is what conversion is.

Has shone in our hearts. Conversion is a new creation (5:17). Paul is surely thinking of his own, when a light from heaven flashed around him on the road (Acts 9:3). But he says our hearts: every believer has had God shine into him. The parallel decides how a person thinks about his own salvation and about everyone he is praying for. The darkness in Genesis did not cooperate. It did not reach toward the light, or make itself receptive, or take a first small step and get helped the rest of the way. It could not, and it was not asked to. Light arrived because God spoke, and the moment he spoke there was no darkness left to consult.

Where Christians differ: how does conversion happen? Many Christians, in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, hold that God first gives every person enabling grace, so that they are able to believe, and that new birth follows faith; others believe that God offers light, and humans by their own will choose to open their eyes. They point to the many calls to believe and to John 1:12, where receiving Christ comes before becoming God’s children. But the next verse says those children were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:13), and John says that everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God (1 John 5:1). This commentary’s view: The picture is creation. As darkness did not cooperate with God in creating light, the blinded heart does not cooperate in its own illumination. God shines in; the result is sight and faith. This is regeneration, God’s sovereign work, effectual because it never fails of its purpose (Ephesians 2:4–5; Westminster Confession 10.1–2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1–2). It is not a piece of theological machinery imposed on the text; it is what this verse says. A blinded mind cannot decide to see. But when God says let light shine into a particular human heart, that heart will believe, as certainly as the deep filled with light on the first day. The person then believes freely and gladly, because he now sees. Christians who see it otherwise love the same Saviour and are right that faith is a real human act; the question between us is only which comes first.

What regeneration is. Regeneration means new birth: God raising to life a heart that was dead towards him, so that it can see and believe. Jesus told Nicodemus that unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God, and that this birth is the Spirit’s work, like the wind, which blows where it wishes (John 3:3–8). Faith is the first breath of the new life, not its cause.

Two anxieties removed. First, your own standing: if God lit the light in you, the flickering you worry about is not evidence against you, because you are not keeping it burning. Second, the person you have given up on: nothing in their hardness is a problem for a God whose speciality is speaking into a void.

The knowledge of the glory of God. God’s glory has been given a location, and it is a human face. Moses asked to see that glory and was told, “You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20); he was shown only the back of God going past. What Moses was refused has been given to ordinary believers.

In the face of Jesus Christ. And it is a face that was spat on, that had a crown of thorns pressed above it, that was set toward Jerusalem and would not turn away. There is the glory of God: not in the fire on Sinai, not in the whirlwind, but in the face of a man dying for his enemies. Glory is God’s worth made visible: his holiness, power and love shining out. To see it in the face of Christ is to watch Jesus in the Gospels, touching a leper, weeping at a grave, silent before Pilate, and to realise that you are not looking at a good man who points to God; you are looking at what God himself is like (John 1:14, 18). Whoever has once seen it never quite recovers, and there is nothing else in the universe that repays looking at in the same way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conversion is always sudden or dramatic, as Paul’s was. The light may dawn gradually, like a morning rather than a lightning flash, and many who were raised in Christian homes cannot name the day. But it is always God’s work.

If God must shine first, why should I tell anyone the gospel? Because the gospel is the light God shines. Verse 4 calls it the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, and verse 6 is what happens when God makes that same gospel break through. He does not usually shine into hearts apart from the message; he shines through it, when it is spoken (Romans 10:14–17). So your words are the lamp he uses, and his sovereignty is the reason to speak with hope rather than a reason to stay quiet. You cannot open a single eye, but you can hold up the light, and God has promised that his word will not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

How do I know God has shone in my heart? Not chiefly by remembering a moment, but by what you see now. Does Christ look glorious to you, not just true but beautiful and necessary? Do you trust him, rather than yourself, for your acceptance with God? Do you want to know him more, and hate the sin that dims the view? Blind eyes do not see glory at all; they find Jesus dull or irrelevant. If he is precious to you, even when your sight seems dim, that is light, and you did not make it.

For worship. What faith sees now in a gospel, his people will one day see with their own eyes: they will see his face (Revelation 22:4), and the city’s lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). The face that was spat on will be the light of a whole new creation, and no one will ever look away.

parallels.desc: let there be light

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Treasure in Jars of Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The treasure of the gospel is carried in fragile, ordinary containers, so that the power is clearly God’s. Paul’s life is a series of near-defeats that never become defeats, and he carries Jesus’ dying so that Jesus’ life may be seen and others may live. Like the psalmist, he believes and therefore speaks, sure of the resurrection, and all of it serves the increase of thanks to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The four contrasts in vv. 8–9 are the pattern of the cross applied to the messengers of the cross. A share in Jesus’ dying is at work in Paul’s ministry (v. 10), and through it resurrection life reaches the churches.

Verse 13 quotes Psalm 116:10 in the Greek Old Testament, the psalm of a man who faced death and was delivered. The minister speaks in the face of death because he believes, with the same spirit of faith as the psalmist, and the resurrection of Jesus (v. 14) grounds his confidence.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor steps down after a serious diagnosis and is replaced by a younger, more energetic man. He feels that his frailty disqualifies him, but the jar of clay is the very condition in which God’s power is plainly seen. The question is not whether the jar is strong but whether the treasure is still in it, and a cracked jar lets the light out.

verseByVerse.quote: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jars of clay. The sentence on which the whole letter turns is built from the most ordinary object in the ancient world. Jars of clay, ostrakina skeuē, were cheap, unglazed containers for oil, grain, water and refuse, cracked, chipped and thrown out without a thought. Valuables were sometimes hidden in them where nobody would look twice; the Dead Sea Scrolls survived in them. The jars are human bodies and lives: weak, mortal, made of dust (Genesis 2:7).

This treasure. Into that he puts this treasure: the light of the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Christ, the most valuable thing in existence in the container you would use once and discard.

In the flow. This answers the charge under the whole letter, that Paul was too weak to be a real apostle (10:10), and prepares for 12:9: my power is made perfect in weakness. The Corinthians wanted a minister who looked like the treasure. God gave them one who looked like the jar, so that they would see the treasure.

The surpassing power belongs to God. It is not an accident, and Paul says so. The mismatch is the point. If the apostle had been physically imposing, magnetic, healthy, wealthy and universally admired, then when people came to Christ under his preaching the question of where the power came from would be permanently ambiguous. Some would credit God; many would credit Paul; and Paul himself, being human, would eventually have credited Paul. The cheap jar removes the ambiguity. Nobody looks at a cracked storage pot and concludes that the light is coming from the pottery.

Your weakness is the design. If you think your weakness disqualifies you, the health that limits you, the temperament that dreads the door, the education you did not get, the failure everybody remembers, this verse is aimed at you. Your fragility is not an obstacle God is working around. It is the design.

A warning folded into the comfort. A church or a Christian can work very hard at not looking like a clay pot: the polished presentation, the projected confidence. The trouble is that it succeeds. People are impressed, and being impressed is not the same as seeing God. The gospel travels furthest through people who are visibly unequal to carrying it.

Should I then make a show of my weaknesses, or stop trying to do things well? Neither. Displaying your weakness can become another way of drawing attention to yourself, a clay pot that wants to be admired for being so honestly cracked. And Scripture commends work done heartily, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23); preparing well, practising, and taking care are not pride. The point is where you put your confidence and whom you want people to see. Do your best, be honest about your limits when it helps others, never hide behind a polished image, and then give God the credit openly for whatever good comes of it.

For worship. The treasure itself once came in earthenware. The Son of God took flesh of our dust, a manger, a working man’s hands, and at last an instrument of execution used on slaves, and he was himself the jar that was broken on the cross, so that the light would pour out over the world. He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God (13:4), and that power is now at work in his cracked servants.
verseByVerse.note: Clay jars were cheap, fragile, everyday containers.

verseByVerse.quote: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afflicted, but not crushed. Four pairs, each a real blow and then a limit. Thlibō is the pressing weight of affliction; stenochōreō means squeezed into a corner. The pressure is real, but there is always still room to move. Not comfort. Room.

Perplexed, but not driven to despair. The same verb, intensified: aporoumenoi all’ ouk exaporoumenoi, at a loss, but not at an utter loss. Yet exaporeomai is the word of 1:8, where he despaired of life itself. So he is not claiming a believer never goes under; he describes the normal condition, not a guarantee against dark seasons.

Persecuted, but not forsaken. Men hunt him; God does not abandon him: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

The Lord stood by me. Who keeps the floor in place? In Corinth itself, when opposition was fierce, the Lord Jesus spoke to him one night in a vision: Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you (Acts 18:9–10). Years later, abandoned by everyone at his trial in Rome, he wrote: the Lord stood by me and strengthened me (2 Timothy 4:16–17). The but not in each pair is not a law of nature or a quality in Paul. It is the risen Christ keeping his word, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). The jar is struck; the hand that holds it does not let go.

Struck down, but not destroyed. A man knocked to the ground, like a wrestler thrown. He goes down; the finishing blow does not come.

Where Christians differ: suffering and the prosperity gospel. Some teach that faith brings health, wealth and success, and that suffering shows weak faith. This commentary’s view: Paul himself was constantly afflicted, perplexed, persecuted and struck down. Suffering is normal in the Christian life (Acts 14:22; 2 Timothy 3:12). God’s promise is not to remove suffering but to sustain us in it and bring us through. The prosperity gospel contradicts the cross and the apostles’ experience.

What it does not mean. Misreading this list has hurt people. It does not say a Christian will be spared affliction; all four blows land. It does not say he will feel calm, or never feel crushed. It says something narrower and more durable: in every case there is a floor, and the floor holds.

But what about Christians who are killed for their faith? Were they not destroyed? No, and this is exactly Paul’s point. He himself, as the early church remembered, would be executed. The body can be killed, but the believer cannot be destroyed, because his life is hidden with Christ and the God who raised Jesus will raise him (v. 14). Jesus said not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28). The martyr is struck down in the most final way this world has, and the floor still holds: he goes straight into the presence of the Lord (Philippians 1:23), and his body waits for the resurrection. Destroyed would mean lost, cut off from God; that is the one thing that cannot happen to those who are his (Romans 8:38–39).

In everyday life. Write the four pairs out with your own circumstances in the first half: pressed by this, but not crushed. Do not falsify the first half. Then read the second half aloud as a statement about God, not your strength. When a fellow believer is in the first half, do not hurry them to the second; sit with them in it.

For worship. Paul is describing his life in the pattern of his Lord’s. Christ was afflicted in Gethsemane, persecuted from Bethlehem onwards, struck down at Calvary, and in his case the last blow fell. He was forsaken; he said so out loud in the dark. The one place the sequence ran all the way to the end, it ran to the end for us, and came back out on the third day. Every but not in this list was bought at a cross where there was no but not at all.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: “perplexed” (aporoumenoi) but not “driven to despair” (exaporoumenoi) — at a loss, but not utterly at a loss.

verseByVerse.quote: always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Carrying the death of Jesus. The four blows amount to the death of Jesus carried about in a body. The word is nekrōsis, the process rather than the event: death at work. Paul does not re-enact Calvary; his sufferings for the gospel are an ongoing dying, a share in Jesus’ sufferings (Philippians 3:10), and always, as the settled condition of his life. He carried his cross through the streets before any of his people carried anything. The dying at work in them is his dying, and it is going the same way his did: through a Friday nobody could explain, to a morning nobody expected.

The life of Jesus. Then the purpose: the risen life of Jesus made visible in Paul’s survival, endurance and joy. Here is the mechanism at the heart of the letter. The dying is not the price paid for the ministry but the channel through which it flows: resurrection life becomes visible exactly where a person is being emptied out.

Where people actually see it. So it is nearly always the wrong question to ask only why God has not removed the difficulty. Watch where people actually see the life of Jesus. Not in the Christian whose life has gone well; there is nothing to explain there, and the world explains it easily. They see it in the man who lost the job and did not become bitter. In the widow who still sings. In the couple who buried a child and are still in church, still kind, still able to sit with someone else who is grieving. Something is showing through, and it is not personality, because personality does not survive that.

Given over to death. Being given over is paradidōmi, handed over, the verb used of Christ, delivered up for our trespasses (Romans 4:25), and the passive has God behind it. That is not a sentence to toss at a person in fresh pain, but it is what Paul lives on: he is not the victim of circumstance but in the hands of a God doing something deliberate, who is not careless with what it costs.

Our mortal flesh. Not in some spiritual compartment, but in the body that gets tired, ill and old: where the dying is most obvious, the life is to be displayed.

Is every hardship the dying of Jesus, or only persecution? Paul’s first meaning is suffering that comes because of Jesus: the beatings, the dangers, the costs of the gospel. But the principle reaches further. Illness, loss and weariness are part of the outer self wasting away (v. 16), and when a believer carries them in union with Christ, trusting him and refusing bitterness, they become the place where his life is seen. What does not qualify is suffering we bring on ourselves by sin or folly (1 Peter 4:15). Even then, confessed and borne humbly, God can use it; but it is not suffering for his sake.

Does God cause my suffering, then? God is sovereign over all of it, and he is never the author of evil. The person who wrongs you is responsible for the wrong; the illness is part of a fallen world. Yet nothing reaches you that your Father has not permitted and does not intend to use for your good and his glory (Romans 8:28; Genesis 50:20). That is why Paul can say he is being handed over and not merely knocked about. It is not a philosophy to answer every why. It is a refuge: the hands that hold the situation are the hands that were pierced for you.

verseByVerse.quote: So death is at work in us, but life in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death in us, life in you. The two halves are held apart deliberately: the apostles absorb death and the church receives life. The beatings that took the skin off his back were part of the price of the gospel reaching Corinth at all. Like Christ, whose death brought life to others, the minister spends himself so that others may live. The verb is energeitai, from which we get energy: death is busy in Paul, and so, in Corinth, is life.

No invoice. They had questioned his credentials and compared him unfavourably with better speakers. He tells them that death is working in him so that life can work in them, without a trace of self-pity or invoice. There is no after all I have done for you. It is simply how the kingdom moves, and he is glad to be where he is. He did not invent the arrangement. There was a death at work in one man on one afternoon, and the life it produced runs out to every believer who has ever lived and will not be exhausted when the last of them is raised. Christ went all the way down, into death and the grave, so that a people beyond counting might come up into life.

Ground that was bought. The principle is far wider than apostles. Nearly everything good in your life cost somebody else something: parents who went without, missionaries buried in the country they went to, believers burned so the Bible could be read in English, whoever prayed for you for years and died before it worked. You are standing on ground that was bought.

Whose life is your death producing? That turns the question round. It is a hard question because most of us have arranged our lives to keep the cost low. But if the pattern of the kingdom is that death here produces life there, then a life that costs nothing is producing correspondingly little, and no amount of activity disguises that. The people whose ministry outlives them are almost always the ones who were spent. And if illness, age or weakness leaves you little to give, hear this as no accusation: the widow’s two small coins were counted the largest gift (Mark 12:43–44), and a life spent in prayer for others is spent.

Does Paul’s suffering, or my pastor’s, pay for anything? No, not in the way Christ’s death does. Only Christ’s death atones for sin; his sacrifice was once for all and nothing can be added to it (Hebrews 10:14). Paul’s suffering brought the Corinthians life because it was the cost of bringing them the message about the One whose death saves. He travelled, was beaten, stayed, wrote and wept, and through all that the gospel reached them. The minister’s sacrifice is the delivery, never the payment. That is why Paul can be content with it: he is not trying to save anyone by his pain, only to get the news of Christ to them at any cost.

How do I spend myself for others without burning out? Paul was spent, but he was not driven. He did not lose heart because he drew daily on a renewal not his own (v. 16), and he lived in prayer and in the Scriptures. Being spent for others is not the same as never saying no, never resting, or carrying burdens God has given to others. Jesus himself withdrew to pray (Luke 5:16). Give yourself gladly where God has placed you, accept help, share the load with the church, and remember that the life you are passing on is Christ’s, not yours to manufacture.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke.” Death is at work in Paul; so why does he keep talking? Because he believes, and because of what he knows about the end. The quotation is from Psalm 116 (Psalm 115:1 in the Greek numbering). It is the song of a man who had been at the edge, “The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me” (Psalm 116:3), who called on the Lord and was heard. In the Greek version Paul used, the line runs: I believed, and so I spoke. The Hebrew is harder to render (some translate it I believed, even when I spoke), but either way the psalmist’s faith found its voice in trouble. The psalmist was in mortal danger and he opened his mouth about God anyway.

The same spirit of faith. Not the same opinions but the same disposition, the same inability to keep quiet: the faith of the Old Testament saint and of the Christian are one thing, worked by the same Spirit.

We also speak. Speech is not an extra for the more confident sort of believer. It is faith surfacing. Most Christians carry a low-grade guilt about not speaking of Christ more, and the usual remedy is a course on how to do it. But silence is often not a technique problem but a sight problem: we have stopped seeing him clearly enough to have anything pressing to say. Nobody needs to be taught how to talk about something they cannot get over.

He who raised the Lord Jesus. Then the second reason, the ground under everything: not hoping but knowing. If death is at work in him and there is nothing on the other side, he is simply being consumed. If there is a resurrection, he is being invested. Death did its worst to the Son, and God undid it on the third day, and the same power stands under every believer who is being worn down for his sake.

With Jesus. Look closely at the preposition. Paul does not only say that God will raise us as he raised Jesus, as though the two were separate events of the same kind. He says God will raise us with Jesus. (Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read by Jesus; the earliest read with Jesus, as most modern Bibles do.) Our resurrection is tied to his. Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20): the first sheaf of a harvest that is already his. Jesus said it to his disciples with the cross only hours away: because I live, you also will live (John 14:19). The believer’s grave is not a separate problem God must solve later. It was answered on the first Easter morning, because the one who rose there rose as the head of his people.

Into his presence. The verb is paristēmi, to present, to stand someone before another. Then the phrase that shows what he is really looking forward to: not bring us home, not even raise us in glory, but with you. After the humiliating visit, the letters and the men who despised him, what he pictures is arriving in the presence of God with these very people beside him, raised together, and the thought gives him pleasure. That is what resurrection hope does to a quarrel. It puts everyone concerned in the same room, standing in front of the same face, and makes the present disagreement look exactly as large as it is going to look then.

I am shy and tongue-tied. Do I have to speak like Paul? You do not have to speak like Paul, but you will want to speak of what you believe, and you can. Speaking of Christ is not only preaching or knocking on doors. It is saying, when a colleague asks how you cope, that you pray and why; offering to pray for a friend; telling your children what God has done for you; inviting someone to church; giving a book with a brief word. Start where faith is already surfacing: what has Christ been to you this week? Say that, simply, to one person. The Spirit who gave the psalmist his voice is the same Spirit in you.

Will we know one another in the resurrection? Yes. Paul expects to be presented with the Corinthians, which means he expects to recognise them and be glad of them. Our Lord spoke of sitting at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11), and Paul comforts the Thessalonians by saying they will be with their departed loved ones and with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). We will be changed, but not into strangers. Every redeemed relationship will be healed and made what it should have been, and the centre of it all will be the face of Christ.

In everyday life. Think of the believer you find hardest to love. Picture the two of you standing together, raised, before the face of Christ. Let that picture shape what you say to them, and about them, this week.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes the Greek form of the psalm.

parallels.desc: I believed, even when I spoke

verseByVerse.quote: For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is all for your sake. The afflictions, the perplexity, the daily dying: all of it is aimed at them. He has said this three times in four chapters (1:6; 4:12; and here), so that they are in no doubt whom the suffering is for.

A chain with three links. Each link produces the next. First, grace extends to more and more people, spreading outward: the suffering of one man is how the gospel gets to the next town. Second, gratitude multiplies with it, because a person given something he could not earn will say so. Third, the terminus: the glory of God. Ministry serves people, and people’s thanksgiving serves God’s glory.

For your sake he became poor. Paul’s all for your sake has a pattern above it, and he names it later in this letter: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (8:9). Everything Paul suffers for the Corinthians is a small echo of what Christ did for them first. And the chain ends where Christ’s own humbling ends. Because he became obedient to the point of death, every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:8–11).

A larger question than what God is teaching me. The usual Christian question in hardship is what is God teaching me? It is a good question, but smaller than this verse. Paul asks how many mouths will end up thanking God because of it. The illness that has made you dependent has given several people the chance to serve, and some are praying for the first time in years. The redundancy that humiliated you is being watched by your children. You may never see the accounting; Paul could not see most of his either.

Is it not selfish of God to want his own glory? It would be selfish in us, because we are not the greatest good and our seeking glory robs others. But God is the greatest good there is. For him to seek anything less than his own glory would be to point us away from the only thing that can satisfy us. When God draws out our thanks, he is drawing us into joy in himself, which is what we were made for; that is why the Westminster Shorter Catechism puts glorifying God and enjoying him in the same answer. His glory and our happiness are not rivals. Thanksgiving is the moment they become one thing.

For worship. The thanks that began with a handful of Corinthians will end in the sound John heard: every creature in heaven and on earth crying, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:11–13). Every grace that went out from the cross comes back as thanksgiving, and the song has one subject.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — The Outer and Inner; the Seen and Unseen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So Paul does not lose heart. His body is wearing out, but his inner life is renewed daily, his troubles are light beside the glory they are preparing, and he keeps his attention on what is unseen and eternal.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between seen and unseen (v. 18) is not the Greek idea that matter is bad and spirit good, or that the body is a prison the soul escapes. It concerns time: what is visible now (the suffering, the wasting body, the opposition) is temporary; what is invisible now (the renewed inner person, the weight of glory) is permanent. The resurrection of the body (5:1–5; 1 Corinthians 15) will make the invisible visible.
verseByVerse.examples: An elderly woman in a nursing home, her body failing, tells her pastor that she has never felt closer to God. This verse names it: the outer self is wasting away while the inner self is renewed day by day, and the decline itself loosens the grip of the seen and turns her gaze to the unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we do not lose heart. The phrase from verse 1 returns as his conclusion, and he says in the same breath that he is falling apart.

Our outer self. The outer self is the body and visible earthly life, subject to ageing, sickness and suffering. The verb, diaphtheirō, means destroyed by degrees, and it is happening now: the eyes worse than they were, the strength that does not come back after a hard week. Christian faith does not require anyone to pretend otherwise. The jar is cracking.

Renewed day by day. Set against it is a second process. The inner self, the heart and spirit united to Christ, is being renewed (anakainoō, passive and continuous), not restored to what it was but made new (Colossians 3:10), day by day, in the same increments as the decline. One process is visible to everybody. The other is invisible, and it is the one that will last.

The verse for a hospital chair. Anyone who has sat with an elderly believer knows it: a body plainly failing and something else plainly not. A hymn surfaces from sixty years ago, or the person says simply that they are not afraid, and you leave having received rather than given.

The mind too. This belongs as much to the mind as to the body. Depression and long mental illness are part of the outer self that is wasting away, and not losing heart is not a feeling to be produced on demand. It is a direction to face, even when the feelings will not follow. Jeremiah cursed the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14); the writer of Psalm 88 ended it in darkness (Psalm 88:18); Paul himself says he despaired of life itself (1:8). None of them was rejected for it. A believer in that darkness should seek help, from the church and from doctors, and know that the inner renewal goes on even when it cannot be felt.

What the renewal runs on. The renewal is not automatic; plenty of people grow old and merely become more themselves. It happens in people who are looking at something: who count the affliction light beside glory and fix their gaze on what is unseen.

Renewed after his image. The new self is renewed after the image of its creator (Colossians 3:10), and Christ is the image of God (v. 4): the daily renewal is Christ being formed in his people (Galatians 4:19). The body that is wearing out is not carrying an empty soul towards death but a likeness of the risen Lord that grows a little clearer every day, and that cannot be buried.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body does not matter, or that the real you is only a soul trapped in a shell. The body will be raised (v. 14). It means its present decay is not the whole story.

What exactly is the inner self, and how is it renewed? The inner self is you as God sees you from within: your heart, mind and will, joined to Christ by the Spirit. It is not a separate person, and it is not something you can see in a mirror. It is renewed as the Spirit applies Christ to you through the means God has appointed: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of believers, and obedience in ordinary things. None of these is magic, and none is optional for someone who wants to be renewed. They are simply where God has promised to meet his people, day by day.

verseByVerse.quote: For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light momentary affliction. Beside the man who wrote it, the sentence is almost outrageous. Paul had been flogged five times with thirty-nine lashes, beaten with rods three times, stoned and left for dead, shipwrecked three times (11:23–27). He had recently despaired of life itself. And he calls it light and momentary, not because it was easy, but because of what it is compared with.

Nobody may say this for him. A man may say this sentence about his own troubles; nobody may say it about another’s. Handled carelessly it becomes a cruel verse: cheer up, it is only light and momentary, said to a woman who has buried a child. Paul is not minimising anything. He has spent four chapters refusing to minimise it.

Weighing, not minimising. Both words are comparative. Put a real weight on a scale with nothing opposite and it is heavy. Put the glory on the other side and the same weight rises. The affliction has not changed; something has been added to the other pan.

For the joy set before him. Paul learned this way of weighing from his Lord. Jesus, for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God (Hebrews 12:2). He set the cross on one side and the joy of a redeemed people and the Father’s glory on the other, and went forward. And his people do not weigh alone: we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). The affliction is light because it is shared with Christ, and the glory is heavy because it is his glory, given to those who are his.

Is preparing for us. The verb is katergazomai, to produce as a result. The suffering is not merely followed by glory; it is doing something. Nothing is being wasted.

An eternal weight of glory. Behind weight lies the Hebrew kabod, glory, from a root meaning heavy, and Paul may be playing on it: glory is substance, the sheer solidity of God. So he sets light affliction against heavy glory, momentary against eternal. What is coming is heavier than what is happening. Paul could call his own load light because Someone had carried the full weight of what we deserved, and found it anything but light. Christ bore the wrath that would have crushed us, so that the only weight left for his people at the end is the weight of glory.

Beyond all comparison. The phrase is built by piling one intensifier on another, literally according to excess unto excess (compare Romans 8:18). He has run out of Greek. It is the expression that gave him the utterly of 1:8, where he was pushed far past his strength; here he doubles it at the other end of the scale. He is not saying the glory will be worth it, as though it were a fair exchange narrowly won. He is saying the two things cannot be put on the same scale at all: that the heaviest grief a human being can carry will one day be found to have been the lighter object in the comparison, and that we do not currently have the vocabulary to say why.

My trouble has lasted decades. How can it be momentary? Measured against your life, it is not momentary, and Paul does not ask you to pretend it is. Many of his own troubles lasted for years, and the thorn in 12:7 was never removed. Momentary is measured against eternity. Thirty years of pain, set beside ten thousand years of glory and then ten thousand more, becomes what Paul calls it, without ceasing to be real. You are not asked to feel it as light today. You are invited to believe that God will one day show you it was, and to let that hope hold you up while it is still heavy.

Will those who suffer more receive more glory? Scripture does speak of reward, and of God’s noticing what was borne for his sake (Matthew 5:11–12; Romans 8:17). But the reward is grace, not wages: no one will stand in glory because he suffered enough to deserve it, and the believer who suffered little is not second class. What the verse promises every believer is that nothing endured in faith is wasted. Leave the measuring to God. He will be generous beyond anything we can imagine, and nobody in heaven will be envious.

In everyday life. Put your present troubles on the scales, every one, in full weight. On the other side write what God has promised: to be with him, the face of Christ, a body that will not fail, no more tears. Do not argue with your feelings; look at both columns, and ask God to let the second grow heavier in your sight.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew the word for “glory” comes from a root meaning “heavy” — glory has weight.

verseByVerse.quote: as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not to the things that are seen. The as states the condition: the renewal and the weighing happen in people whose eyes are pointed somewhere. Skopeō means to fix attention on, to take aim at (our word scope): a man sighting down a line, not glancing.

The things that are unseen. God, Christ at his right hand, the resurrection, the world to come (Hebrews 11:1, 27; 12:2). But how do you look at something you cannot see? Not by mysticism, and not by pretending. Paul has already told us where the unseen is made visible. The glory of God is in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6), and it is beheld in the gospel (3:18). You look at the unseen by looking at what God has said about it, until it becomes as real to you as the things in the room. That is what faith actually is in practice: not a feeling, but attention paid to the invisible on the authority of God’s word about it.

Transient and eternal. Transient is proskaira: for a season, on a timer. We call the visible real and the invisible abstract; Paul says the opposite. The mortgage, the diagnosis, the argument at work have an expiry date. The unseen things, which feel thin, are the ones with no end.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring present responsibilities, nor that matter is bad and spirit good. Paul goes straight on to the resurrection of the body (5:1–5). The present arrangement is temporary, and what is now invisible will one day be the most solid thing there is.

Will fixing my eyes on heaven make me careless about this life? The opposite. The people who have done most good in this world have often been those most sure of the next, because they had nothing to lose and nothing to prove. Abraham looked for a city with foundations, and so could live as a generous stranger (Hebrews 11:10). A believer who knows his treasure is safe can give money away, forgive debts, serve the unthankful, care for creation and work hard at an ordinary job, all without anxiety, because none of it has to be his heaven. It is the man who looks only at the seen who must cling to it.

For worship. Behind everything that can be seen is a glory with a face. Of the Son the Father says: they will perish, but you remain; you are the same, and your years will have no end (Hebrews 1:10–12). The jar is cracking; the treasure is not.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart.<sup>2</sup>But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.<sup>3</sup>And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing.<sup>4</sup>In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.<sup>5</sup>For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.<sup>6</sup>For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.<sup>7</sup>But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.<sup>8</sup>We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair;<sup>9</sup>persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;<sup>10</sup>always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies.<sup>11</sup>For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.<sup>12</sup>So death is at work in us, but life in you.<sup>13</sup>Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak,<sup>14</sup>knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.<sup>15</sup>For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.<sup>16</sup>So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.<sup>17</sup>For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,<sup>18</sup>as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

5.title: The Heavenly Dwelling, the Judgment Seat, and the Ministry of Reconciliation
5.overview:
Paul has just said that his outer self is wasting away. Now he explains why death does not frighten him: the body is a tent that will come down, God has a permanent building ready, and the Spirit is the down payment. So he would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord, and either way his aim is to please Christ, before whose judgment seat all must appear.

What drives his ministry is the love of Christ, who died for all so that the living should live for him. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God has reconciled us to himself through Christ and made Paul an ambassador with a plea: be reconciled to God. The chapter ends with the great exchange: the sinless Christ made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Heavenly Dwelling and the Judgment Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why death does not frighten Paul: the tent will come down, but God has a permanent dwelling ready, guaranteed by the Spirit, and to leave the body is to be at home with the Lord. Meanwhile Paul’s ambition is to please Christ, before whose judgment seat everyone will give account of their life in the body.
verseByVerse.theology: At the judgment seat of Christ (v. 10) Scripture keeps two things apart. Justification settles the believer’s standing for ever, by grace through faith in Christ: there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The judgment seat assesses the believer’s life and works (1 Corinthians 3:10–15; Revelation 22:12). There, salvation is not at stake; stewardship is. Holding both protects the gospel of grace and keeps real accountability for how a Christian lives.
verseByVerse.examples: A Christian professional excuses a string of ethical compromises at work by telling himself that grace covers everything. He is right about grace, but he is using it as a licence rather than a motive. For Paul, knowing it moved him to persuade others (v. 11): for the justified believer it is a spur, not a threat.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 5 carries on from the unseen, eternal glory of 4:18 and climbs to the heart of the gospel: from a tent coming down, to a Judge on his seat, to a King pleading with rebels, to the Son made sin in their place.

A tent. Paul has said his outer self is wasting away; now he says what happens when the wasting finishes, with two buildings. He is a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) and knows what a tent is worth: it goes up in a morning and comes down in an afternoon, and one season it is not worth mending (compare 2 Peter 1:13–14). That is the body, and he does not despise it. A tent is a good shelter for the journey. It is simply not a house.

Destroyed. The word is katalyō: taken down, dismantled, as a tent when the camp moves. Death is not gentle, but a dismantling is not the end when a house is already standing.

A building from God. Each phrase answers the tent: from God, not made with hands (Hebrews 9:11); a building, with foundations; eternal. And it is not a location instead of a body, for Paul does not want to be unclothed. Most take it to be the resurrection body he had described to this church, sown in weakness and raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–54): not escape from embodiment but a permanent body in place of a temporary one.

Destroyed, and built again in three days. The sentence opens with we know, not we hope, and the ground of that knowledge is Jesus. Paul’s two key words, destroyed and not made with hands, are the very words of the charge brought against Jesus at his trial: that he had said he would destroy the temple made with hands and in three days build another, not made with hands (Mark 14:58). John tells us he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). It came true. His body was taken down on a cross, laid in a tomb, and raised on the third day, never to be dismantled again. What God did for the body of his Son he has pledged to do for everyone joined to him: Christ’s risen body is the firstfruits and the pattern of every building from God (1 Corinthians 15:20; Philippians 3:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we receive the resurrection body at death. Paul speaks of being unclothed between death and resurrection (vv. 3–4), and places the new body at the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52). We have expresses certainty: the body is prepared and waiting, so sure it can be spoken of as present. Meanwhile the believer’s soul is at home with the Lord (v. 8), without the body but not without Christ.

Does it matter what happens to my body after I die? Not to God’s power: he will raise his people whether they were buried, lost at sea or burned, because the resurrection depends on him and not on what is left. But the body matters to God, and Christians have long buried their dead as a sign of that hope, laying the body down like a seed (1 Corinthians 15:36–38) and treating it with honour. Families may differ on practical choices, and none of them can hinder the resurrection. What matters is that we speak of the body as Scripture does: not a shell to be discarded, but a tent that God will replace with a house.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, a tentmaker by trade, pictures the present body as a tent — temporary — and the resurrection body as a permanent building.

parallels.desc: houses of clay

verseByVerse.quote: For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We groan. Much Christian talk about death is bright in a way this verse is not. The word stenazō is a deep, inarticulate sound: the noise a person makes under a weight, not a complaint formed into words.
