He uses it in Romans 8 of believers who groan inwardly as they wait for the redemption of their bodies, alongside a whole creation groaning as in the pains of childbirth (Romans 8:22–23). It is the sound of something that knows it was made for more than this. So Christian hope does not require pretending to be comfortable. Anyone who has been ill for a long time, or has watched someone they love become someone they have to care for, knows the groan. It is not unbelief. It is the correct response to a tent in a storm.

Longing to put on. The groaning is not for release or the end of consciousness. Paul mixes his pictures: the house has become a garment, and he longs to have it on.

Not found naked. To be naked is to be without a body: a self exposed, with no dwelling. In much Greek thought that was the goal; Plato could speak of the body as the soul’s prison. Paul calls bodilessness nakedness and shrinks from it. (Some manuscripts read taking it off instead of putting it on, as the ESV margin notes; the point is not affected.)

A correction we still need. Christians can easily absorb the Greek idea. Asked what happens at death, many answer that the soul goes to heaven, and stop there. That is real and it is precious; Paul will soon say that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (v. 8). But it is not the end. It is the interval. The Christian hope is a body: a real one, on a real new earth, standing up out of a grave. God made us to be embodied and called it very good. Human beings are not souls temporarily inconvenienced by flesh. The body is not the problem; death is the problem, and the answer to death is not escape from the body but the resurrection of it.

Clothed in the likeness of the man of heaven. What will be put on? Paul has already told this church: just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven (1 Corinthians 15:49). The heavenly dwelling is cut to the pattern of the risen Jesus, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The Son did not lay his body aside after Easter (Luke 24:39); a true man sits on the throne of heaven now. If the Lord of glory keeps his body for ever, his people will not be left without theirs. Our groan, at bottom, is a longing to look like him.

What it does not mean. The soul without the body is not unhappy: being with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). But it is incomplete until the resurrection.

What will the heavenly dwelling we long to put on be like? It will be like Christ’s risen body (Philippians 3:21). It will be truly you, recognisable, as the risen Jesus was known by his friends and even ate with them (Luke 24:39–43). It will be physical, not ghostly. But it will be imperishable, glorious, powerful and fully suited to the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44): no more decay, disease, disability or death, no more tiredness that sleep cannot cure. Scripture does not answer every curious question, such as age or appearance, but it says enough: the body you will have is the one God always meant you to have, and it will never be taken down. That is why the groaning of this verse is not despair: it is the ache of someone who has seen the house and is waiting for the keys.

verseByVerse.quote: For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Burdened. The word is bareō, weighed down, the root used of the affliction in Asia (1:8).

Further clothed. Then he corrects a misunderstanding. To want to be unclothed is to want to be finished. To want to be further clothed, ependyomai, is to want a garment drawn on over what is already worn: Paul would prefer to be alive at Christ’s return and have the resurrection body put on without dying (1 Corinthians 15:51–53). He longs not for the end of his existence but for the mortal thing to be covered by something so much more alive that mortality disappears inside it.

Swallowed up by life. The verb is katapinō, to swallow whole, the word of Isaiah’s promise that God will swallow up death forever (Isaiah 25:8; 1 Corinthians 15:54). Every funeral has the shape of death swallowing a person. Paul reverses it. Life is the mouth. A candle blown out is unclothed; a candle carried outside at sunrise is swallowed up by life, nothing taken away, so much more light that the flame is no longer needed.

Life has a name. The life that swallows mortality is a Person. I am the resurrection and the life, Jesus said beside a friend’s grave (John 11:25), and death could not keep its hold on him (Acts 2:24); he abolished death and brought life and immortality to light (2 Timothy 1:10). Death opened its mouth for him on Friday and found on Sunday that it had swallowed something it could not keep down. What happened to the Head in a garden tomb will happen to his body: thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:57).

Is it wrong to wish I could just stop? No; Paul was carrying that weight when he wrote this, and Elijah and Job carried it too. If you have ever caught yourself wanting simply to stop, the tiredness that is deeper than sleep, the private wish to be finished, this verse does not condemn you. What it does is take the desire and correct its aim. What you actually want is not to be switched off. It is to be so thoroughly alive that everything currently wearing you out is swallowed and gone. But if the wish begins to turn into thoughts of ending your own life, tell someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor. That darkness lies to you, and God has given you people and help for exactly this.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prepared by God. Katergazomai: to fashion for a purpose. The homesickness is not temperament or wishful thinking; it was made. There is a restlessness no arrangement of circumstances satisfies: get the house, the health, the family, and a thin ache remains. We treat it as a fault to be fixed by one more thing. Paul says God fitted it deliberately, and it corresponds to something real.

The Spirit as a guarantee. Then the evidence. The word is arrabōn again, met already at 1:22 (and Ephesians 1:14): the down payment that legally commits the payer to hand over the rest. Not a token of goodwill. The first instalment, in the same currency as the balance. The Spirit is the first part of our future life, given now, guaranteeing the rest, and the Spirit who raised Jesus will raise us (Romans 8:11). So the argument runs: you were built for the resurrection body; you can tell, because you groan; and to prove the groaning is not a cruel joke, God has put a deposit in your hands, and the deposit is not a thing but a Person.

Poured out by the risen Christ. Jesus said it was to their advantage that he go away, for otherwise the Helper would not come (John 16:7); exalted at the right hand of God, he has poured him out (Acts 2:33). The guarantee is not an IOU from a distant God but the life of the risen Lord already at work in us. We hold the deposit because Christ holds the whole inheritance, and we are fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17). The Father who fashioned us for glory, the Son who rose as the firstfruits of the new creation, the Spirit who lives in us as the down payment: the whole Trinity is engaged in getting us home. God does not make a down payment on something he means to abandon.

The first instalment. The moments when Scripture came alive, the peace that arrived for no reason, the affection for people you once avoided, the fact that you want God at all: these are the first instalment, given so that you would be unable to settle for less. That is why a Christian who is spiritually alive is often more homesick, not less.

Can that guarantee be lost? No. The one who gave it is God, and he does not default on what he has pledged. Paul says the Spirit is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it (Ephesians 1:14). A believer can grieve the Spirit (Ephesians 4:30), but in the same verse Paul says he was sealed for the day of redemption. And the fear of having lost the Spirit is not evidence that one has; it is usually the evidence of a conscience he is still at work in.

Do I need a special experience to know I have the Spirit? No. Every believer has the Spirit; anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). Scripture does not tie his presence to a dramatic sign, a particular feeling or a gift of tongues. The marks it gives are quieter and surer: you call God Father from the heart (Romans 8:15–16), you confess Jesus as Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), you love his people, you fight your sin, and his fruit, love, joy, peace, patience, slowly grows in you (Galatians 5:22–23). Look for those, not for fireworks.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guarantee” was used for a deposit or first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.quote: So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Always of good courage. Paul has been groaning; now, without contradiction, he takes heart (tharreō), always, not only on good days. The courage does not wait for the groaning to stop. It rests on the Spirit’s guarantee.

At home, and away. The words are endēmeō and ekdēmeō: to live in one’s own country, and to be abroad. After the Damascus road and the third heaven, Paul still calls this life away from the Lord: with Christ by the Spirit, but not yet face to face. Every Christian knows the prayers that feel like speaking into the next room. That is not a defect in your discipleship. It is the address you are currently living at.

By faith, not by sight. This does not mean acting on impressions without evidence. Sight is eidos, the visible thing itself: Paul contrasts faith not with thinking but with seeing Christ face to face (v. 8). The believer walks now on the word of a Lord he has not yet seen (1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Peter 1:8). The verb is walk: daily conduct, one foot in front of the other, a way of moving in the dark on the word of Someone who can see.

Blessed are those who have not seen. Jesus himself drew this line. To Thomas, who would not believe until he had touched the wounds, he said: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20:29). Yet faith is not blind, because it has an object: a crucified and risen Lord whose resurrection body was seen by hundreds of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:5–8), and whose word we hold. We walk on their testimony toward the day when we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Faith is simply what loving Jesus looks like while he is out of sight.

How do I make decisions by faith, not by sight? Not by waiting for a sign or an inner voice. Walking by faith means trusting what God has said and acting on it when you cannot see how it will turn out. So decide in the light of Scripture first: what does God command, forbid or commend here? Then use the wisdom God gives: pray, think carefully, ask mature believers, weigh your circumstances honestly (Proverbs 15:22; James 1:5). Where Scripture leaves you free, choose what seems wisest and most loving, and trust God with the outcome. Faith is not a leap away from reason; it is obedience that does not need to see the end of the road first.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At home with the Lord. The words of verse 6 are swapped round, and they answer the question people ask at a graveside: what happens to a believer at the moment of death?

Immediately at home. Away from the body, and immediately at home with the Lord. There is no gap, no waiting room, no period of unconsciousness. He says the same thing to the Philippians from prison: his desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Philippians 1:23). And the Lord himself said it to a dying criminal who had nothing to offer and no time left: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Today. This is what theologians call the intermediate state: the condition of a believer between dying and the resurrection of the body. It is conscious, it is with Christ, and it is better than here.

Where Christians differ: what happens at death? Some teach soul sleep, an unconscious state until the resurrection; Roman Catholics teach purgatory for most believers. This commentary’s view: To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, immediately and consciously. There is no purgatory and no soul sleep. It is difficult to see how being asleep for centuries could be called far better, or how it could be described as being at home with the Lord at all; the New Testament’s language is of presence, and of presence now. Nor is there an interval of purging for believers who died imperfect. Paul, who knew what he still was, expects to be at home the moment he is away. The reason is not that he had reached a standard. It is verse 21, thirteen verses further on: the exchange has already been made. The souls of believers, made perfect in holiness, are received into heaven, where they behold God’s face in light and glory, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). Those who hold the other views are often earnest believers; the disagreement is over what these texts say, not over whether they love Christ.

Two things at a Christian funeral. Being with Christ without a body is far better, and still not the end (vv. 3–4). So a Christian funeral is two things at once: the person is with the Lord today, and a morning is coming when they will be given back their body.

Home is a Person. Home is where a person stops being a stranger, and for Paul that is wherever Jesus is. The promise to the thief was with me, and Jesus prayed that those the Father had given him would be with him where he is, to see his glory (John 17:24). He wanted us with him before we ever wanted to come.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should seek death. It means they need not fear it. Paul stays, gladly, as long as his Lord has work for him (Philippians 1:24–25).

Can my loved one who has died see me, or can I speak to them? Scripture does not tell us that the dead in Christ watch over us, and it firmly forbids trying to contact the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). The great cloud of witnesses in Hebrews 12:1 are witnesses in the sense of those who testify by their lives of faith, not spectators sent to guard us. So speak to God about them, not to them. Thank him for them; tell him your grief. You have not lost them; you have been separated from them for a while, and they are where you are going.

What if they died with sins they never confessed? A believer is not saved by having confessed every sin, but by Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Every believer dies with sins he did not know about or never named; if forgiveness depended on a complete list, no one would be home. Paul expects to be with the Lord because of what Christ did, not because his accounts with God were tidy at the last moment. If your loved one trusted Christ, the unfinished conversations, the last weak years, the failures you remember, do not keep them out. They are at home.

For worship. The last enemy has been made into a door. It cost the Lord of glory his own descent into the ground to change what death is for his people, and now the worst thing that can happen to a Christian is that he goes home. Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints, because he paid for every one of them himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our aim. Living or dead, the aim does not change. Philotimeomai is a term of ambition: to make something your driving purpose. Paul was an ambitious man. This was his ambition.

The judgment seat. The word is bēma, the raised platform from which a magistrate gave verdicts; Corinth had one where Paul had stood before Gallio (Acts 18:12). Appear is phaneroō: not merely to show up, but to have a life laid open.

The seat belongs to Christ. Paul does not say here the judgment seat of God but of Christ, and that changes everything about it. The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), and has fixed a day on which he will judge the world by the man he has appointed, giving proof of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The One on the seat has lived in a body himself; he knows from the inside what is done in the body, the hunger, the tiredness, the temptation, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Nothing will stay hidden from him, and he has borne his people’s condemnation himself, so none of it will be laid on them (Romans 8:1, 34). He once stood before Pilate’s bēma and was condemned there in our place, and he is not looking for reasons to reject his people; he is looking for every cup of cold water, every unseen act of faithfulness, so that he can praise it.

Done in the body. What he has done, not what he intended. The body is where the Christian life is lived: the hands, the diary, the money, the tongue.

Where Christians differ: judgment of believers. How can believers, who are justified and free from condemnation (Romans 8:1), be judged by their works? This commentary’s view: Believers will not be condemned; their sins are covered by Christ. But their lives will be revealed and evaluated, and their works rewarded according to God’s grace (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Matthew 25:21). Good works do not earn justification, but they are the evidence of true faith, and God graciously rewards them (the Westminster Confession 33.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 32.1). The judgment will also openly vindicate God’s people and show his justice. Both statements are true because two different things are in view. The verdict on whether you belong to Christ is not reopened; it was settled at the cross. What is assessed at the bēma is what you did with the life you were given after that verdict was passed. Paul wrote about this to this same church a letter earlier: the foundation is Christ and cannot be relaid, but what a man builds on it is tested by fire, and some of it burns, though he himself will be saved (1 Corinthians 3:15).

What does good or evil mean for a believer? His sins will not be held against him for condemnation; their penalty was paid at the cross. But his life will be brought into the light, what was done in faith and love and what was not, for the Lord will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the heart (1 Corinthians 4:5). What he receives is not a verdict on his salvation but on his service. Scripture speaks of reward, of commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:5), and of work that survives the fire (1 Corinthians 3:14); some will suffer loss, though they themselves are saved. That loss is real, and it is a reason to live well; but it never touches the believer’s standing in Christ.

Should that frighten a believer? Paul does not seem frightened; he moves straight from it to ambition, not to dread. But he plainly does not treat it as nothing either. The honest position is that a Christian may lose a great deal there, the years spent on things that turned out to be nothing, the gifts unused, the reputation protected instead of spent, and will lose nothing of Christ.

Would a loving God really judge anyone? Yes, and his love is one reason he must. A judge who shrugged at the abuse of a child would not be kind; he would be complicit. Love that does not care about evil is not love, and the people who most long for a day of judgment are usually those the world has wronged (Psalm 96:13; Revelation 6:10). What makes this judgment good news is the Judge. The One on the seat was judged himself in the place of everyone who comes to him, so the day that puts every wrong right is a day his people can look forward to rather than dread.

Is it selfish to want rewards? No, as long as the reward is what Scripture says it is. Jesus himself urged us to lay up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:20), and the chief reward is not a prize separate from God but the joy of his approval: well done, good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of your master (Matthew 25:21). Wanting that is not mercenary; it is love wanting to please the one it loves. And the reward is grace on grace: God crowns in us the works he himself worked in us. No one in heaven will boast in his reward; everyone will cast it at the feet of the Lamb.

In everyday life. Take this week as it actually was: the hours, the conversations, what you gave your attention to. That is what will be looked at, by Someone who loves you and died for the failures in it. Make it your ambition today to please Christ in one specific thing you would otherwise have done carelessly.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat (bema) was the raised platform where a Roman official gave judgment; Paul had stood before one in Corinth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Ministry of Reconciliation and the Great Exchange
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fear of the Lord, and above all the love of Christ, drive Paul’s ministry. One died for all, so all who are his have died with him and now live for him, and whoever is in Christ belongs to the new creation. God has reconciled people to himself through Christ, not counting their sins against them, and Paul is his envoy, pleading with people to receive it. The ground of it all is the exchange of verse 21.
verseByVerse.theology:
In verse 19 the one acting is God. Reconciliation is begun, accomplished and offered by him. The obstacle is sin; the removal is the cross, and verse 21 states its cost.

Made him to be sin does not mean Christ became a sinner. It means God treated him as the sin-bearer, standing in the place of sinners and receiving the judgment sin deserves. So we become the righteousness of God in him, counted righteous because of where we are, which is why the standing cannot be damaged by a bad week.
verseByVerse.examples: An evangelism course teaches that the goal is to persuade people to make a decision for Christ. This passage gives a deeper frame: we implore people, on Christ’s behalf, to receive a peace God has already made. The ambassador does not create the peace; he announces it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the Lord. The judgment seat does not send Paul into anxious self-examination; it sends him out to talk to people. The fear of the Lord is not terror of a God who might turn on you, nor mere respect. It is the awe of a creature who has grasped that the nations are like a drop from a bucket before him (Isaiah 40:15), and that every person will stand before his Son’s seat (v. 10). A man who has felt that does not treat other people’s eternity as a conversational risk. The Lord is holy enough to be feared by angels and kind enough to be loved by sinners, and in the gospel these are not two moods but one glory.

We persuade. Peithō, winning someone over by argument: Paul is not manipulating or merely announcing but reasoning and pleading (Acts 18:4), because he believes what he has said about the bēma. Christian silence about Christ is sometimes more than shyness: we have stopped believing much is at stake.

Known to God. God already sees Paul’s heart completely; he hopes the Corinthians’ consciences will recognise it too. A man who lives now as already laid open before God is best prepared for the day when every life will be.

Cause to boast. Then Paul turns to his critics, delicately (compare 3:1). The Corinthians had nothing to say when Paul was disparaged in front of them. He is arming them, not defending himself.

Face and heart. Literally, boasting in the face rather than the heart. The rival teachers had presence, polish, credentials, visions and delivery; Paul had a wasting body and a speaking manner his critics thought contemptible. We still assess by the face: the platform manner, the confidence, the numbers, the production. And God has said from the beginning how he assesses, in the words spoken to Samuel while he was busy admiring the wrong brother: “For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). The awkward implication is that the most impressive Christian you know may not be the one God is most pleased with, and neither of you can currently tell.

No form or majesty. The fault line between face and heart runs straight through the story of Jesus. Isaiah said of the Servant that he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isaiah 53:2). Judged by the face, Jesus was a builder from Nazareth with no schooling in the law, no platform and no following among the great, and at the end a body so marred it hardly looked human (Isaiah 52:14). Those who boasted in appearance despised him; the Father called him his beloved Son. Paul’s critics were making about the servant the very mistake the world had made about the Master. A church that boasts in the face will always be embarrassed by a crucified Lord, and by the ministers who look most like him.

Should a Christian fear God or not? Both answers in Scripture are true, because there are two kinds of fear. The fear that expects punishment is cast out by God’s perfect love (1 John 4:18): a believer need not dread that God will condemn him, because Christ bore the condemnation. But the fear of the Lord, reverent awe at his holiness, majesty and power, is the beginning of wisdom and never leaves the believer; it grows as we know him better (Proverbs 9:10; Hebrews 12:28–29). A child who adores his father and would not dream of grieving him has the right kind. It is the fear that makes us take sin seriously, take people’s souls seriously, and take God at his word.

In everyday life. Bring to mind one person you see regularly who does not know Christ, and who will stand before his judgment seat. Let that, and the love that sought you first, move you to the next honest step: a question, an invitation, a word about what Christ means to you.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beside ourselves. Existēmi: literally to stand outside oneself, to be out of one’s mind. Festus would later shout it across a courtroom (Acts 26:24), and Jesus’ own family said, “He is out of his mind” (Mark 3:21).

What lay behind it. Perhaps the charge came from his ecstatic experiences (12:1–4), perhaps from the shape of his life: a man of formidable training who crossed provinces on foot, took beatings and refused payment. Paul does not deny it. Whatever in him goes past what people find reasonable is between him and God.

In our right mind. The word is sōphroneō: sober, sane. When he is measured and careful, that is for their sake, so that they can be taught. Either way, his life is not for himself.

The right way round. There is a passion that belongs between you and God and needs no audience: the hours in prayer nobody knows about, the extravagance in giving that would embarrass you if discussed. And there is a sober, patient steadiness that belongs to the people you serve. The failure comes when the two are swapped: intensity performed in public, sobriety kept for private life, where zeal quietly cools (Matthew 6:1–6).

For God and for you, all the way down. Paul’s two halves were the shape of Jesus’ life first. Toward his Father he was extravagant, rising a great while before day to pray (Mark 1:35), consumed by zeal for his Father’s house (John 2:17); toward his disciples he was patient and plain. Both were love, and none was for himself (Romans 15:3). That is why Paul’s next sentence names the reason for his own strange life: the love of Christ controls us.

My family thinks I have gone too far with my faith. What should I do? First, be glad you are in good company: they said it of Paul and of Jesus. Then ask honestly whether there is anything in their complaint you should hear. Are you neglecting them, lecturing them, or making your faith a reason to be unkind? If so, put it right; a sober, loving life is itself for them. But if what they object to is simply that Christ comes first, that you worship, give, pray and will not join in sin, do not argue and do not retreat. Love them more visibly than before, keep your private devotion private, and let the steadiness of your life answer the charge over time (1 Peter 3:1–2, 15–16).

For worship. To the watching world the cross was the maddest thing ever done. Yet the foolishness of God is wiser than men (1 Corinthians 1:25), and that holy extravagance was the sanest act in history. The Lord was counted out of his mind for our sake, and gave himself so completely that nothing is left for us to keep back.

verseByVerse.quote: For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The love of Christ. Here is the engine of Paul’s life. Whose love? The love of Christ can grammatically mean Paul’s love for Christ or Christ’s love for Paul, and the sentence itself decides it. Look at what follows the word because: not a description of Paul’s devotion but of Christ’s death. It is Christ’s love for him, shown at the cross, that is doing the driving. A ministry powered by how much you love Christ will run exactly as far as your affections do, which on a bad week is not far. A ministry powered by how much he loved you has a fixed and finished event underneath it.

Controls. Synechō: to press in from both sides, as a crowd round a man (Luke 8:45). Not a whip driving him but banks around a river: not restricted, but given force.

One has died for all. This is the idea of representation, which runs all through Paul: one person standing for many. Christ died as the representative and substitute of his people, and what happens to the one counts as having happened to those he stands for, as Adam’s act counted for the race that came from him (Romans 5:18–19). So when Christ died, those who are in him died with him, in union with him (Romans 6:3–8; Galatians 2:20). His death counts as theirs. The old self, the old account, the old standing, went into the grave with him. That is true in two ways. The penalty your sins deserved has been paid in his death, so it will never be demanded of you (Romans 8:1). And the person you were, owned by sin and living for yourself, has lost its claim on you, as a master loses his claim on a slave who has died (Romans 6:6–7).

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Two words in that sentence have been argued over for centuries, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise: for all. Some take all here to mean that Christ died for every human being equally, making salvation possible for all, and applied on believing. Others take it to mean all who are in Christ, all his people. Both sides are trying to protect something real: one the sufficiency and freeness of the offer, the other the effectiveness of the cross. This commentary’s view: Paul says the all for whom Christ died have died with him, and live for him. That describes those united to Christ, not every human. Christ died effectively for all his people, of every nation, securing their salvation, not merely making it possible (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). This is definite atonement (sometimes called limited or particular redemption): the teaching that the cross was aimed at, and actually secures, the salvation of a definite people. The gospel is offered sincerely to every person, and Christ’s death is sufficient for all, but it was designed to save his people (the Canons of Dort, a Reformed statement of 1619, 2.3, 8). Many faithful Christians read all here more widely, and they preach the same Saviour; on either reading the offer to every sinner is real. What is beyond argument in this verse is its logic: that his death was for people, in their place, and that it did something to them and not merely for them.

No longer for themselves. The whole Christian ethic in one line, and first a consequence rather than a rule. A man who has died is finished with running his own affairs. The cross ends the old life; the resurrection gives the new one its Master and its power, for the risen Christ lives in his people by his Spirit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s love is limited in its sincerity. His love for his people is infinite. And the gospel call goes to all.

Can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for them? You can tell every person, without hesitation, that Christ died for sinners, that he is a full and sufficient Saviour, that he offers himself freely to them, and that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). That is the gospel the apostles preached to unbelievers: they proclaimed Christ crucified and called all to repent and believe (Acts 2:38; 17:30). Many in the Reformed tradition prefer that wording to Christ died for you, because the personal assurance belongs to the one who believes. But the offer is utterly sincere. No one who comes will find that Christ did not die for him.

So what does living for him look like on a Monday? It looks like asking, in ordinary decisions, what would please the one who died for me, and not only what I want. It reaches the diary (how I use my time), the bank account (where my money goes), the tongue (what I say about others), the body (what I do with it), the home (how I treat the people closest to me), and work (doing it as for him). It does not mean a life with no rest or enjoyment; it means a life whose centre has moved. The test is not dramatic sacrifice but small daily choices where self used to sit on the throne.

For worship. Before the love of Christ pressed in on Paul, it pressed in on Christ himself: it held him to the road to Jerusalem and kept him on the cross when twelve legions of angels were a word away (Matthew 26:53). The Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and a life bought like that cannot go back to belonging to itself.

verseByVerse.quote: From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one according to the flesh. If one died for all, everything must be looked at again, beginning with people. According to the flesh means by the world’s standards: the reflex that files a person within seconds by accent, clothes, job or usefulness. Paul says that reflex has been retired.

Christ according to the flesh. The decisive example is himself. Saul had assessed Jesus by exactly those criteria: an executed provincial, a blasphemer, crucified and therefore cursed. He had been completely confident and completely wrong, and a man who has made that mistake about that person never trusts his own first assessment of anyone again.

A new creation. The Greek is even more abrupt than the English: if anyone in Christ, new creation! There is no verb. And the phrase kainē ktisis, new creation, was not, in Paul’s world, a term for personal improvement. It was the great promise of the prophets about the world itself: behold, I create new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17; Galatians 6:15). Paul takes that cosmic vocabulary and says it has already begun, and where it has begun is inside people. Not just a new person, but part of God’s new creation, the age to come breaking in. Conversion is creation, not renovation.

Behold. The words echo Isaiah 43:18–19, where God tells his people to stop dwelling on the former things, because he is doing a new thing. The old order of sin and death is passing; the new has arrived in Christ. And look at the little word at the centre: behold. It is a word for pointing at something. Paul is not describing an inward process; he is drawing attention to an event that has already happened. The event is Easter. The new creation began on the first day of the week, when Christ rose as the beginning, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), and everyone in him belongs to that morning, in the middle of an old world that does not yet know it has been superseded.

The misheard part. Read as a description of how you feel, this verse is crushing: the temper is still there, the same failure of thirty years. But it does not say if anyone feels new. It says if anyone is in Christ. The newness is first a matter of location, not sensation, true on the authority of God who transferred you.

What it does not mean. Believers still sin and struggle (Galatians 5:17), but their identity is new. What has passed away is the old order: the guilt, the condemnation, the dominion of sin. What remains is the mopping up, a lifetime’s work. But a man does not stop being a citizen because he still has an accent from the old country.

If I am a new creation, do the consequences of my past disappear? The guilt does; not always the consequences. In Christ you are fully forgiven, and God will never hold your past against you. But a debt may still need repaying, a broken trust may take years to rebuild, a prison sentence may still need serving, and a damaged body may not be restored in this life. Zacchaeus, newly saved, repaid what he had taken (Luke 19:8). Face those consequences without despair, because they no longer define you; make right what you can, humbly; and do not let anyone, including yourself, call you by your old name. God does not.

In everyday life. Look at others as people for whom Christ died: the colleague you find dull, the neighbour you have written off, the believer whose background makes you uneasy. Ask what God may be making of them.

parallels.desc: behold, I am doing a new thing

verseByVerse.quote: All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this is from God. Before Paul names what has happened, he says where it came from: all this, the new creation, the death of the one for all, everything from verse 14 onward, is God’s work, from start to finish.

In the flow. Verses 18–21 are the summit of the defence of Paul’s ministry from 2:14 to 7:4. After the ministry of the new covenant (3:6) and of righteousness (3:9), here is its warmest name, the ministry of reconciliation, and it turns at once on the Corinthians: be reconciled to God (5:20), and open your hearts to us (6:13).

Reconciled us to himself. Katallassō is not a religious term but an ordinary one: the ending of a quarrel, enmity turned to friendship, two people who could not be in the same room in the same room again. So the human problem, underneath everything else, is not chiefly ignorance or unhappiness but estrangement. We were God’s enemies (Romans 5:10), and the broken relationship is the one every other was hanging from.

The offended party crossed the room. In every human quarrel the offender has to approach the offended. Here the offended party crossed the room. The barrier was on both sides, our rebellion and God’s just wrath, and Christ removed both. God did not wait for us to come round, or ask us to make the first move; he came in the person of his Son, into the middle of the quarrel, and settled it in his own body.

In Christ God was reconciling. The world means people from every nation, a world in rebellion. This does not mean there was nothing to settle; the cost (v. 21) measures how real the estrangement was. What it rules out is a reluctant God softened by a merciful Son. God himself was in Christ doing it.

Not counting trespasses. Logizomai is an accounting term: entering the item in the ledger. The debts are real, and they are not recorded against the reconciled, because God put them on Christ (v. 21; Romans 4:8). Many carry that ledger inside: words to a parent now dead, a year you would give anything to have back. This says the entry was not made against you: not excused or overlooked, but charged to the Son, on whose cross God cancelled the record of debt (Colossians 2:14).

Entrusting the message. God did the work and then handed the announcement to the very people who had been on the wrong side of the quarrel. The ordinary Christian talking awkwardly to a colleague is carrying something placed in his hands on purpose.

Where Christians differ: is the whole world reconciled? Universalists read this as saying every person is already reconciled. Some other Christians read it as a reconciliation achieved for every person, which each must then accept; Reformed Christians read it as the world of those God actually reconciles in Christ, drawn from every nation. This commentary’s view: If everyone were already reconciled, Paul would not need to plead: be reconciled to God (v. 20). God accomplished reconciliation in Christ for the world of his people from every nation, and it is received by faith. The message goes to all, calling all to receive it, and no one is reconciled who does not come.

What if I have never felt at war with God? Most estrangement does not feel like war. It feels like indifference. A grown son who never calls his father, never thinks of him, and lives entirely on what his father gave him may feel no hostility at all, yet the relationship is broken. That is the human condition Paul describes: living in God’s world, on God’s gifts, without honouring him as God or giving him thanks (Romans 1:21). The respectable moralist is in the same place by another road, keeping God at a distance with good behaviour so that he never has to come to him empty-handed. Either way the quarrel is real, and either way God has crossed the room.

If God has reconciled me, do I have to be reconciled with people? Yes, and the one leads to the other. A person who has been forgiven an unpayable debt cannot keep a ledger against others (Matthew 18:21–35). Jesus told his disciples to leave their gift at the altar and go to be reconciled with a brother first (Matthew 5:23–24). Take the first step, whether you are the offender or the offended, just as God did. Reconciliation is not always fully possible: the other person may refuse, and where there has been abuse, safety comes first and trust must be earned. But forgiveness from the heart, and readiness for peace as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18), are always required.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ambassadors for Christ. An ambassador (presbeuō, used of the emperor’s own envoys) is a sovereign’s personal representative in foreign territory. He carries the message exactly; his authority is borrowed, and absolute while he carries it.

Three things about an ambassador. The message is not yours to adjust. An ambassador who improved on his instructions would be recalled. This is the safeguard against every attempt to make the gospel more agreeable, and also the relief, because you are not responsible for whether it is well received. The authority is not yours either, and that is the encouragement. The dignity of an ambassador has nothing to do with his personal impressiveness. A shy man with a letter from a king has more standing in that room than a magnificent man without one. And the posting is foreign. Christians live in a country that is not theirs, representing a King the locals do not acknowledge. That accounts for a good deal of the strangeness of the Christian life. You were not meant to feel entirely at home here.

As the Father has sent me. The first envoy to this rebel province was the Son, who came and preached peace to those far off and near (Ephesians 2:17). He did not merely carry the terms; he was the terms, and paid for them. Then, risen, he said: As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you (John 20:21). Christ is still the one pleading through his ambassadors.

God making his appeal. Appeal is parakaleō, to beg; implore is deomai, to plead. God does not summon; he appeals. The Almighty, who was in the right throughout, pleads with those who wronged him to accept the peace he has made at his own expense. He holds out his hands all day long to a rebellious people (Isaiah 65:2; Romans 10:21). No one has ever been more patient with his enemies, or more eager to be friends with them.

Be reconciled to God. Notice who is being addressed. This is written to a church. Paul is imploring people who are already in the pews, perhaps because some were drifting. A person can be inside the congregation, holding the doctrine, doing the duties, and never have made peace: to be at church and not at home. If the whole thing has been an arrangement you inherited rather than a quarrel that was ended, then this verse is not about the neighbours. It is addressed to you, and it is not a threat; it is a plea. And the verb be reconciled is passive. Nobody reconciles himself. It has all been done; the only thing left is to stop refusing it. That is what the King is pleading for, through the mouths of his own ambassadors, barely a generation after his Son died to make it possible.

I have been in church all my life. How do I know I have actually been reconciled? Not by your attendance or your family, but by whether you have personally come to Christ. Ask yourself honestly: have I seen my sin as an offence against God, not just a mistake? Have I stopped relying on my good record and trusted Christ alone, his death in my place? Do I now want to belong to him and follow him? If you are unsure, do not wait until you are sure; respond to the plea now. Tell God plainly that you have been at war with him, that you trust his Son’s death for you, and that you give yourself to him. Then speak to your pastor. Whoever comes to Christ is never turned away. And if you have trusted him and still fear this describes you, take heart: the wish to be truly at peace with God is itself the work of his Spirit in you.
verseByVerse.note: An ambassador spoke with the authority of the king who sent him.

verseByVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He made him to be sin. Luther called it the joyous exchange. God is the subject, his Son the object, and the verb is deliberate: God did this. Not that Christ became sinful; the next clause forbids it. God treated him as sin: laid our sins on him and punished sin in him (Isaiah 53:6, 10; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24).

In the flow. In the best manuscripts verse 21 arrives with no linking word, like a foundation stone. It answers verse 20 (on what terms can God plead with rebels?) and verse 19 (God does not count their trespasses because he counted them against his Son). The whole argument of chapters 3 to 5 comes to rest on the cross, and turns at once into an appeal (6:1).

The shape of it in the Old Testament. For over a thousand years the Old Testament taught the shape of it: a hand laid on an animal’s head, guilt transferred, the innocent dying for the guilty. Some take sin here to mean a sin offering, as the word sometimes does in the Greek of Leviticus 4. Either way, he bore our sin: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

Who knew no sin. Said of no other human being (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22): no divided motive, no private version of himself. His enemies watched him for three years and in the end needed false witnesses who could not agree (Mark 14:55–56). Only a sinless one could bear others’ sin.

What being made sin sounds like. And it is this one, with nothing owing, who is made sin. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34) is what being made sin sounds like from the inside, in the one relationship that had never had a shadow across it.

The righteousness of God. Now the exchange completes, and it goes further than we expect. It does not say we might be forgiven, though we are. It does not say we might be treated as though we had not sinned, though we are. It says we become the righteousness of God: the right standing God gives, credited to us (Romans 3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). This is what the Bible calls justification: not God making us good inside, but God the Judge declaring us righteous in his sight, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness counted as ours (Romans 4:5). As Christ was treated as a sinner though he was not, we are treated as righteous though we are not. He got what was ours: the guilt, the charge, the abandonment. We get what was his: the standing, the welcome, the Father’s pleasure. Nothing was averaged; each side received the other’s whole account.

In him. And everything turns on the last two words. This is not a transfer of a substance into the believer, as though righteousness were now a quality you possess and might mislay on a bad week. It is true of you because of where you are: in union with Christ. That is why a Christian at his worst is no less righteous before God than at his best. The righteousness counted is the whole obedience of the One who knew no sin, his perfect life as well as his death (Romans 5:19). Our own obedience, even at its best, is never perfect (James 3:2); for his sake God accepts it anyway. The standing was never generated by the performance, and cannot be damaged by it.

Where Christians differ: imputation. Some deny that our sin was legally credited to Christ and his righteousness legally credited to us, saying instead that we are made righteous only by inner transformation. This commentary’s view: The parallel is exact. Christ was made sin, not by becoming sinful inside, but by having our sin counted to him. So we become righteous, not first by inner change, but by having his righteousness counted to us. This is double imputation (our sin counted to Christ, his righteousness counted to us), the heart of justification by faith alone (the Westminster Confession 11.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1; the Heidelberg Catechism Q. 60). Inner transformation follows in sanctification, but it is not the ground of our acceptance with God. And it shows the cross as penal substitution. Penal substitution means that Christ bore the penalty of our sin (that is the word penal) in our place (that is the word substitution): the punishment God’s justice required fell on him instead of on us (Isaiah 53:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ ever stopped being holy, or that God the Father hated the Son. Christ was beloved even as he bore the Father’s wrath against sin. Indeed, the Son was never more pleasing to the Father than in that act of obedience (Philippians 2:8–9).

How can it be just for God to punish an innocent person in our place? It would be unjust if an unwilling stranger were seized and punished for someone else. But that is not the cross. The Son came willingly, laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). He came as the head of his people, joined to them, as Adam was joined to the race. And he is God himself: the Judge did not lay the penalty on a third party but bore it in his own person. At the cross God is both just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). Justice is not set aside; it is fully satisfied, by God, for us.

If I am counted righteous, does it matter how I live? It matters more than ever, though not as payment. Paul anticipated the question: shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase? By no means (Romans 6:1–2). The same union with Christ that gives you his righteousness also joins you to his death and resurrection, so that sin no longer rules you. Those who are in him become a new creation (v. 17) and live for him who died for them (v. 15). Holiness is not the price of your standing; it is the shape of your new life. You obey because you are accepted, not in order to be accepted.

In everyday life. When your conscience accuses you today, do not answer it with your recent performance, good or bad. Answer it with this verse: my sin was counted to him, and his righteousness is counted to me. Then, freed from earning, go and do the good works God has prepared for you, gladly, in the strength of the Spirit he has given you.

For worship. He was made what he was not, so that we might be made what we could never be. The Holy One went down into the dark of our sin, and the guilty walk out of it clothed in his righteousness. The Father planned it, the Son bore it, the Spirit seals it, and it will be the song of the redeemed: worthy is the Lamb who was slain.

parallels.desc: he was pierced for our transgressions

5.text: <sup>1</sup>For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.<sup>2</sup>For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling,<sup>3</sup>if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.<sup>4</sup>For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.<sup>5</sup>He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.<sup>6</sup>So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord,<sup>7</sup>for we walk by faith, not by sight.<sup>8</sup>Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.<sup>9</sup>So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him.<sup>10</sup>For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.<sup>11</sup>Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience.<sup>12</sup>We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.<sup>13</sup>For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.<sup>14</sup>For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died;<sup>15</sup>and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.<sup>16</sup>From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer.<sup>17</sup>Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.<sup>18</sup>All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation;<sup>19</sup>that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.<sup>20</sup>Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.<sup>21</sup>For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

6.title: The Open Heart, the Catalogue of Hardships, and the Unequal Yoke
6.overview:
Having said that God makes his appeal through his ambassadors, Paul makes it: do not receive God’s grace in vain, for now is the day of salvation. A true servant of God is shown not by successes but by endurance, the fruit of the Spirit and a string of paradoxes: dying yet alive, sorrowful yet always rejoicing, having nothing yet possessing everything. He has opened his heart wide to them; he asks them to open theirs.

Then a sudden, sharp section (6:14–7:1): do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. The church is the temple of the living God, so it must come out from idolatry and impurity, and God will be a Father to his sons and daughters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Open Heart and the Catalogue of Hardships
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace must not come to nothing in them, for the time of favour Isaiah promised has arrived. Paul puts no obstacle in anyone’s way; his credentials are endurance and the fruit of the Spirit; and he asks them to open their hearts as he has opened his.
verseByVerse.theology: The list of hardships (vv. 4–5) is one of several in 2 Corinthians (4:8–9; 11:23–29; 12:10). Together they show the cross applied to ministry: a true apostle is known not by spectacular results or an impressive presence but by sharing the sufferings of Christ. This does not glorify suffering for its own sake: in a world that crucified its King, those who carry the message of the cross will bear its pattern in their bodies.
verseByVerse.examples: A young minister starts a church in a hard part of a city, hoping for rapid growth. After three years he has a small congregation, many failures, and a life that looks more like Paul’s list than his plans. He questions his calling. Here the hardships are marks of a true ministry, not a failed one, and the question is whether he is serving with the character of verses 6–7.

verseByVerse.quote: Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 6 continues the appeal of 5:20, be reconciled to God. Do not receive grace in vain, for now is the day of salvation (vv. 1–2); a ministry that puts no obstacle in anyone’s way, proved by endurance, the fruit of the Spirit and a string of paradoxes (vv. 3–10); an open heart asking for open hearts (vv. 11–13); and a warning against being unequally yoked, for we are the temple of the living God (6:14–7:1). The chapter that begins with the day of salvation ends with the Lord Almighty calling former idolaters his sons and daughters.

Working together with him, then. Having implored them to be reconciled to God, Paul gives the second half of the appeal: having received grace, do not let it lie there. The word is synergeō: to be a fellow worker on the same job (1 Corinthians 3:9).

In vain. The phrase is eis kenon, to emptiness: a gift that arrives and produces nothing. Grace here means everything just given them in Christ: reconciliation, forgiveness and a righteousness not their own (5:18–21). Some in Corinth were drifting after false teachers (11:3–4) and back into unholy living (12:21).

Can grace come to nothing? This raises a question honest readers ask and deserve a straight answer to. Does this passage threaten someone’s salvation? Take it carefully. Paul has just told this church that they are a new creation, sealed and guaranteed by the Spirit; he does not now suggest that God’s work in them might quietly fail. What he is warning against is a life in which the grace received makes no difference: grace treated as a transaction completed rather than a relationship begun. That can describe two different people. It can describe a believer who is wasting years he will not get back. It can also describe someone who has all the appearance of faith and has never actually come. Paul does not sort them here, and neither should we; the warning is addressed to everyone in the room and is meant to be taken personally rather than assigned to somebody else. And if it frightens you, take heart: the person who is anxious that grace should not be wasted on him is not a person on whom grace is lying idle.

In a favorable time. Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8, where God speaks to his Servant, the light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6), and tells him that his cry has been heard and his day of help has come. The New Testament tells us when that cry went up: in the days of his flesh Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard (Hebrews 5:7). The answer came on Easter morning. The promise made to Christ is now handed on to everyone who is in him. Our day of salvation is the overflow of his.

Now. Twice behold, twice now. We all know a version of later: when work settles, when the children are older, when I have got a few things straightened out. Scripture says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15), because a heart that intends to respond eventually is already hardening while it waits.

If God does the work, why does Paul call himself God’s fellow worker? Because God chooses to work through means, and the means are people. Paul is not saying he helps God save anyone: regeneration is God’s work alone (4:6), and no one contributes to his own new birth. But in the ministry of reconciliation, the preaching, praying, pleading and serving, God gives real work to real people and lets them share in it. That is not a burden placed on you; it is an honour. You cannot open one blind eye, but you can carry the message, and God is pleased to call you his co-worker when you do.

What does receiving grace in vain look like in a church member? It looks like years of hearing about forgiveness without ever forgiving anyone. Singing about Christ’s love while nursing the same resentment. Knowing the gospel well and never speaking of it. Receiving comfort and never comforting. Treating Sunday as complete in itself and Monday as unaffected. None of these is a single dramatic fall; each is grace landing on ground that does not let it grow. The remedy is not to try harder in general, but to ask: what has God given me that I am sitting on? Then take one step of obedience in that place today, in the strength of the Spirit he has given you.

For worship. The day of salvation dawned in a synagogue in Nazareth, when Jesus read of the year of the Lord’s favour and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). That today has never ended, held open by the One whose cry was heard. Nobody has been promised the favourable time twice, and nobody who comes within it is turned away.

parallels.desc: in a time of favour I have answered you

verseByVerse.quote: We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,
verseByVerse.commentary:
No obstacle. The word is proskopē: something you strike your foot against. Paul’s concern is not that he might be criticised but that something about him might become the reason a person does not come to Christ.

He was fiercely practical about this. It is why he refused financial support from Corinth, working at a trade so that nobody could say he was in it for money (1 Corinthians 9:12–15), why he had the collection carried by men the churches themselves had chosen (8:20–21), and why he became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22): not to be liked, but to remove every avoidable barrier between a person and the gospel. He learned it from his Master, who ate with tax collectors, touched lepers and welcomed children, removing every barrier but one.

The one stone God laid on purpose. One obstacle must never be removed, and it is Christ himself, the stone of stumbling and rock of offence laid in Zion, in whom whoever believes will not be put to shame (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:7–8). A crucified Messiah is a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23). Paul clears the road so carefully precisely so that this stone, and nothing else, is what a person meets. If people are offended that sin is called sin, or that Christ is the only way, that offence is the gospel doing its work. A gospel adjusted until nobody trips over it has been tampered with (4:2).

Every other stone is ours. Every other obstacle is ours to deal with, and there are more than we like to count: the manner that makes people feel small, the money question never explained, the political opinion nailed to the pulpit as though it were doctrine, the way we speak about people not in the room, the reputation for being unforgiving or slightly dishonest about small things. None of these is the gospel. All of them can be the reason somebody stops listening.

No fault found. The verb, mōmaomai, means to find fault, to ridicule. Not with him: with the ministry. He is protecting the message from being discredited by its messenger, which is the only reason a Christian’s reputation is worth anything at all.

What if I already have been an obstacle to someone? Then go and move the stone. Name what you did, without excuses: I was harsh with you, I was dishonest about that, I mocked what you believe, I never paid you back. Apologise plainly, put right what can be put right, and do not make the apology a sermon. Many unbelievers have never heard a Christian say I was wrong, and a humble confession can do more to open a door than years of argument. Then leave it with God, and keep living in a way that does not lay the stone down again.

verseByVerse.quote: but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Servants of God. His rivals came with letters; Paul offers not letters but a life (3:1). This is the fullest list of hardships in the letter so far (compare 4:8–9 and 11:23–29).

By great endurance. This is the heading over the whole list. The word is hypomonē (1:6): a remaining under, staying put beneath a weight. It is not the ability to avoid trouble but the refusal to walk out from under it. The list then comes in three groups of three.

In afflictions, hardships, calamities. First, three broad words for pressure: thlipseis, pressures; anankai, constraints you cannot get out of; stenochōriai, literally a narrow place, being wedged where there is no room.

Beatings, imprisonments, riots. Second, three things done to him by other people: someone swung the rod, someone turned the key, a crowd decided. Philippi, Lystra and Ephesus all supplied them (Acts 16:22–23; 14:19; 19:29), and in chapter 11 he will give the appalling numbers (11:23–25).

Labors, sleepless nights, hunger. Third, three things he took on for the sake of the work: toil to exhaustion; nights deliberately spent travelling, working, praying and sitting up with people (1 Thessalonians 2:9); and going without food, by choice or because there was nothing.

What is missing from the list. There are no results. No church-planting statistics, no numbers converted, no cities won. No one today would commend his ministry with such a document, and that is Paul’s point, aimed at a church that had begun assessing ministers the way the world assesses anyone. His credential is not what he has achieved but what he has absorbed and not quit.

Faithful, not successful. There is a word here for the person whose service has produced very little that can be counted: the years in a small church that never grew, the praying for a family member across two decades with nothing to show. On this list, none of that is failure. Endurance is the credential, the one thing in Christian service that cannot be faked, borrowed or produced quickly. Faithfulness is commanded; success never is.

Carrying the death of Jesus. Paul has already told this church how to read a list like this: he is always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be shown in his body (4:10). The catalogue is the Master’s shape pressed into the servant. Christ too was handed over, beaten, sleepless in Gethsemane and hungry in the wilderness, and for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). Paul can endure because he belongs to the One who endured first.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering proves a ministry is true. False teachers can suffer too. But true ministry is marked by endurance in suffering, not escape from it.

So how should I judge a pastor or a ministry? Not by size, celebrity, polish or how much you enjoy it. Ask the questions Scripture asks. Does he preach the true gospel plainly, Christ crucified and risen, without trimming it (4:2, 5)? Is his life consistent with what he preaches: honest with money, faithful in marriage, gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of status (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? Does he stay when it is hard, and serve when no one sees? Are people being built up in Christ rather than attached to him? A faithful ministry may be small and unremarkable for years. It will be marked by truth, love and endurance.

verseByVerse.quote: by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;
verseByVerse.commentary:
By purity, knowledge, patience, kindness. The list turns inward: from what has been done to Paul to what has been produced in him. This is the more searching half, because a man can endure a great deal and remain unpleasant. Purity, hagnotēs, is moral cleanness and sincerity of motive, nothing to keep out of sight. Knowledge is the true understanding of God and his gospel; warmth without content is no credential. Patience is makrothymia, long-temperedness: the ability to be wronged by the same person repeatedly and not retaliate. Kindness, chrēstotēs, is love’s practical, unglamorous form. It is possible to be doctrinally impeccable and unkind, and this list forbids it (compare Galatians 5:22).

The Holy Spirit. Then, in the middle of a list of virtues, something that is not a virtue at all. Paul does not explain the intrusion, and the absence of explanation is the point. None of the qualities on either side of him is native to a human being. He is named among them because he is the one producing them.

The portrait behind the list. Read the list again and a face appears. Christ was pure, knew the Father as no one else does (Matthew 11:27), was patient with slow disciples and kind to the despised; insulted, he did not answer with insults (1 Peter 2:23). The Spirit stands in the middle because his work is to form Christ in his people (Galatians 4:19). Paul is describing the likeness of Jesus showing through a servant.

Genuine love. Literally love without hypocrisy, anypokritos (Romans 12:9). The word for hypocrite was the word for a stage actor. There is a way of doing all the right things for people while performing, and everybody can eventually tell.

Truthful speech and power. Truthful speech is the gospel and honest speaking, saying what is so; the power of God is the Spirit working through it, without which the whole list is a moral programme and not a ministry.

Weapons of righteousness. A Roman soldier carried the sword in the right hand and the shield on the left: armament for attack and for defence, and the material of both is righteousness, both right living and the right standing with God that Christ gives as a gift, since he was made sin for us (5:21). Paul fights with nothing he has to make up, only a clean life and a gift he did not earn (compare Ephesians 6:13–17).

Defending yourself with righteousness. When you are misrepresented, the instinct is to defend yourself by the means being used against you: the counter-story, the quiet word to the right person. Paul says the shield in the left hand is righteousness. You defend yourself by continuing to live rightly, and you attack by the same means. It is slower and much harder, and it is the only defence that does not have to be maintained, because a life is more difficult to answer than an argument.

Should I never set the record straight when I am falsely accused? You may, and sometimes you should; Paul spends much of this letter doing exactly that. The difference is in the weapons. Speak the truth plainly, to the people who need to hear it, without exaggeration, without attacking the other person’s character, and without a campaign behind their back. Where wrong has been done that needs addressing, use the proper channels: go to the person first (Matthew 18:15), involve church leaders, and where a crime has been committed, the authorities. Then leave your reputation with God. Your job is to tell the truth and keep living rightly; vindication is his.

For worship. The armour was God’s before it was ours. Isaiah saw the LORD, finding no one to intervene, put on righteousness as a breastplate and come himself to save (Isaiah 59:16–17). In Christ he came, alone, and won with no weapon but righteousness and no shield but his own body. Now he arms the weakest of his people from his own armoury.
verseByVerse.note: Weapons “for the right hand and for the left” are weapons for attack (the sword) and defence (the shield).

verseByVerse.quote: through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honour and dishonour. Now the paradoxes begin, each with the same shape: what people see, then what is actually so. In the same week he may be admired in one town and vilified in the next, for the same work. He is not controlled by reputation.

Governed by opinion. We are governed by these two more than we know. We adjust ourselves, often without noticing, toward whatever produces praise and away from whatever produces criticism, and after twenty years of small adjustments a life has been shaped by other people’s opinions. Paul walks through both without changing direction, which is only possible for a man who is expecting to give his account somewhere else (5:10).

Impostors, yet true. The word, planoi, means deceivers, frauds: people pretending to be what they are not. This was actually being said about him, and his answer is not an argument but a fact.

Unknown, yet well known. To the great men of the empire he was nobody; yet he is known to the churches, and known by God, which is the knowing that counts. For anyone who has spent a life doing something no one notices, the question is never whether you are known; it is only ever by whom.

Behold, we live. The behold is a note of astonishment. By every reasonable assessment he should be dead: the stoning at Lystra (Acts 14:19), the night and day adrift at sea, the affliction in Asia (4:10–11). And here he is, writing.

Punished, not killed. The word is paideuō: disciplined, chastened. Behind it lies a psalm: “The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death” (Psalm 118:18). A Father had been at work in the floggings, and had set the limit himself. It was true of the Servant before it was true of Paul: he was smitten by God and afflicted, and the Father did not give him over to death for ever.

The paradoxes of the Master. Every line was true of Jesus first. He was called that impostor (Matthew 27:63), and he is the truth (John 14:6). He was the carpenter’s son nobody in Rome had heard of, and the One through whom all things were made (John 1:3). He died, and behold, he is alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18). Union with Christ gives a servant his Master’s paradoxes, and his Master’s vindication (Galatians 2:20).

The second half of the sentence. The world’s assessment of a Christian is working with incomplete information: it reads the visible half of the sentence and stops. The second half, in every case, is supplied by a God who has never once mistaken one of his servants for a fraud.

How do I stop living for other people’s opinions? Not by ceasing to care about people, but by caring more about God’s verdict. Watch where approval and criticism steer you: what you post, what you avoid saying, which friends you keep, which convictions you go quiet on. Bring those to God and ask what pleases him. Remember that in Christ you already have the only verdict that finally matters: accepted, beloved, righteous (5:21). Then listen to criticism humbly, because it may be true, without being ruled by it; and receive praise gratefully, without needing it. A person secure in God’s love can afford both.

verseByVerse.quote: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. Three more paradoxes, and they go deeper, because they are about what is true inside. The first is often flattened, as though one cancels the other. Both verbs stand, and the second has always attached to it. Paul is genuinely grieving, over sin, suffering and the lost (Romans 9:2), and genuinely rejoicing in the Lord (Philippians 4:4), in the same hour, about different things.

Two floors in one house. Anyone who has stood at a Christian funeral has seen it. The grief is not reduced; a real person is gone and the loss is exactly as large as it feels. And underneath it, not instead of it, there is something that will not go out, because the person who is being buried is with the Lord, and the God who arranged that is still what he was last week. That is possible because Christian joy was never built on circumstances and therefore is not demolished when they collapse.

Grief is not a failure of faith. Christians are often made to feel that a really trusting person would be at peace by now. That is not in the Bible. Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty (John 11:35). What the gospel promises is not the absence of sorrow but a joy that runs at a level sorrow cannot reach.

Poor, yet making many rich. Near the end of his life Paul’s belongings seem to have been a cloak, some books and the parchments (2 Timothy 4:13), and whole provinces were made rich through him. The pattern is his Lord’s, who though he was rich became poor for our sake (8:9).

Possessing everything. A man with no property, no security and no home says he possesses everything, and he is not being brave. All things are theirs, because they are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23); the God who did not spare his own Son will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32). That is the arithmetic of the kingdom, not consolation for people who have missed out. The One who owns everything gave himself to his people, and everything he owns came with him. He had nowhere to lay his head, and he is heir of all things.
