May a Christian work to improve his circumstances, or should he be content with little? Both, rightly understood. Scripture commends honest, diligent work that provides for your family and lets you give to others (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; Ephesians 4:28; 1 Timothy 5:8). There is nothing unspiritual about a better job or a sound budget. What Scripture forbids is the love of money and the anxious craving for more (1 Timothy 6:6–10), and what it teaches is contentment: Paul learned to be content in plenty and in want (Philippians 4:11–12). Work hard, give generously, hold everything loosely, and never think that what you own is what you are.

In everyday life. If you are grieving, do not hurry yourself out of it; let the sorrow be real, and look for the floor beneath it that grief cannot touch: forgiveness, the Father’s love, the Spirit, a future, a family in the church. Then ask whom you might make rich this week.

verseByVerse.quote: We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spoken freely. The rhetoric stops. This is the only time in the letter he addresses them by name, and it is the sound of a man dropping his voice. Literally, our mouth is open to you: nothing withheld, nothing said behind a hand. A man defending his authority has spent five chapters admitting weakness (1:8; 2:12–13).

Our heart is wide open. The verb is platynō: widened, enlarged, made spacious. There is room in him for all of them; whatever they have done, they have not been shut out.

Restricted in your affections. Then the diagnosis, put with great delicacy. Restricted, stenochōreō, means cramped, confined in a narrow space: the opposite of the widened heart. Affections is splanchna, the inward parts, where Greek located deep feeling; its verb is the one used of the Lord’s compassion when he saw the crowds (Matthew 9:36). It is not that Paul has withdrawn. It is that they have narrowed. There is a cramped place in them where he used to be.

The affection of Christ Jesus. Where did a heart this wide come from? Paul tells the Philippians, with the same word, that he yearns for them all with the affection of Christ Jesus (Philippians 1:8). The open heart is borrowed: Christ’s own compassion, now living in a servant who was taken into that heart when he deserved nothing from it, and whom the love of Christ controls (5:14). The width of Paul’s heart is the width of Christ’s, in a smaller vessel. He stretched out his arms on the cross wide enough to take in the world. If there is a cramped place between us and him, it is never on his side.

A cooled relationship. Nothing is formally wrong; the greetings still happen. But something has closed, and the person outside can feel the reduced room. Paul does not accuse them or demand an explanation. He describes what is true, his heart open, theirs narrow, and leaves it in front of them. The instinct is either to pretend not to notice or to make an accusation that forces a defence, and both close the door further.

In the flow. The defence of his ministry since 2:14 stops, and the father speaks. This plea is picked up again at 7:2, and between the two requests stands the warning against the unequal yoke (6:14–7:1): the hearts closed to Christ’s servant were the hearts in danger of opening to idols.

A narrowed heart. Constriction of heart is a real spiritual condition, not merely a social awkwardness. A narrowed heart cannot receive much, which is why the Corinthians could not take in what Paul was giving them. Suspicion does that; so does resentment held for a long time; so does the quiet decision to protect yourself after being hurt once. It always feels like prudence and it always costs the same thing: the ability to be loved.

But what if my heart closed because I was really wronged? Then your hurt is real, and God takes it seriously. Opening your heart does not mean pretending nothing happened, or putting yourself back in harm’s way. Where there has been abuse or ongoing danger, wisdom and safety come first, and trust is something the other person must rebuild over time. But even then, you can refuse to let bitterness have the room: forgive from the heart before God (Ephesians 4:31–32), stop rehearsing the wrong, pray for the person, and remain willing for peace if they repent. A heart can be open toward God and toward reconciliation while still being careful.

In everyday life. Where has your heart narrowed? There is usually a name attached to the answer, and usually a good reason, and the reason has never yet made anybody less confined. Open it this week by one concrete act toward that person.

verseByVerse.quote: In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Widen your hearts. The whole appeal comes to one request, with not a trace of authority in it. He could have commanded. Instead: widen your hearts also, the same word as verse 11. Make room. Love me back. He is asking to be loved by people who have not been loving him, and asking without leverage, and a request for affection can be refused.

I speak as to children. The parenthesis is affectionate: he is their father in the faith (1 Corinthians 4:14–15), and a father may say things to his children that a colleague could not. It also lets them off the formality of an adult negotiation.

What he is not asking for. Not an apology. Not agreement about the past. Only for room in their affections. We tend to make the reopening of a relationship conditional on settling the history: who was right, who should speak first. Paul, who had the stronger case, sets all of it aside and asks for the one thing that would actually change anything. A heart that has opened usually finds the record matters less than it did.

Do you love me? Paul learned this way of asking from his Lord. On a beach in Galilee the risen Jesus met the disciple who had denied him three times. He did not demand an account of the courtyard or a settlement of the past. He asked one thing, three times: do you love me? (John 21:15–17). The Lord of glory, wronged and in the right, asked his friend for room in his heart, and then gave him work to do. That is the shape of Paul’s request: no leverage, no case, only love asking for love. Every reconciliation in the church is a small copy of the one at the cross, where the offended party made the first move.

Widening is an act. A heart does not enlarge by waiting to feel differently. It is an act: the visit made, the message sent, the refusal to run the grievance through your mind one more time, the choice to think the better explanation of what they did. Paul had watched Stephen die and gone looking for more (Acts 7:58–8:3), and the room made for him in the church of God was not made because he apologised his way in; it was made by the One whose heart was so wide that it took in the man who was hunting him. Nobody who has been received like that can plead a shortage of room.

What if I widen my heart and they still refuse? Then you have done what God asked, and the rest is theirs and his. Paul could not make the Corinthians love him; he could only open his heart and ask. Scripture says, if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18), which admits that sometimes it will not be possible. Keep the door open without forcing it. Do not punish them with coldness, and do not keep score of your efforts. Pray for them. Some relationships are restored years later; some only in heaven. Either way, a heart that stays open is free, and it is like God’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–7:1 — Do Not Be Unequally Yoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to bind themselves in partnerships with unbelievers that compromise their loyalty to Christ. The church is God’s temple, so Paul calls them, from several prophetic promises, to leave idolatry and impurity behind, and God will welcome them as his sons and daughters.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage applies in several settings. First, marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, stated directly elsewhere: only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39). Second, formal religious partnerships, such as joint worship that treats basic differences about God as unimportant. Third, business partnerships that require ethical compromise. The principle is that any binding partnership which requires a believer to pull in the same direction as one opposed to Christ is an unequal yoke. Ordinary friendship, work and life alongside unbelievers are not in view (1 Corinthians 5:9–10).
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is invited to co-host a community prayer service with leaders of several faiths, some of whom deny the Trinity and that Christ is the only Saviour. He must decide whether this is civic engagement, speaking to the community, or a spiritual partnership, worshipping together. This passage suggests the difference matters: showing the church’s care for the community is not the same as implying that every faith pulls the same yoke toward the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unequally yoked. The subject changes so abruptly that some think this paragraph was originally somewhere else. But the connection is there. He has just asked them to widen their hearts toward him; now he tells them there is one direction in which the heart must not be opened. A church that has room for everything has room for nothing in particular.

Already in partnership. Why can a believer not take this yoke? Because he is already in a partnership. God called you into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord (1 Corinthians 1:9), the same koinōnia Paul is about to deny to light and darkness. A Christian is not a free agent shopping for alliances; he is joined to the Christ who bought him, and every binding commitment either pulls with that union or against it.

The picture from the farm. Heterozygeō is to be yoked with a different kind. Behind it stands the old law: you shall not plough with an ox and a donkey together (Deuteronomy 22:10). Two animals of different height, strength and stride, fastened to the same beam, cannot work; the furrow wanders, and both are injured by the harness. It is not that the donkey is wicked. It is that they cannot pull together.

For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? Then five questions, of which these are the first two, each expecting the answer none. Partnership is metochē, sharing; fellowship is koinōnia. They are not really questions. The second answers itself in a way anybody can test. Light and darkness do not negotiate, and they do not blend (John 3:19–21; Ephesians 5:8–11). One of them simply ends where the other begins.

Where Christians differ: what is an unequal yoke? Some apply this only to marriage; others to any contact with unbelievers. This commentary’s view: In context, Paul’s main concern is probably Corinthians joining in pagan temple worship and following false teachers. The principle applies to any binding partnership that pulls a believer away from Christ: most clearly marriage (1 Corinthians 7:39), and also business partnerships or alliances that compromise faith and obedience. It does not forbid friendship, work or ordinary life with unbelievers, which Paul assumes (1 Corinthians 5:10; 10:27).

Precision matters. This verse has been used to justify things Paul explicitly refused. Friendship, employment, neighbourliness, hospitality, business dealings: none of these is forbidden, and a Christian who withdraws from the world cannot carry the message of chapter 5. What is in view is a yoke: a binding of your direction to someone whose direction is opposed to Christ, in a way you cannot easily undo.

Does this apply to dating? Yes, where dating means looking for a husband or wife. If a Christian should not marry an unbeliever, he should not begin a romance that is heading that way; hearts follow where time and affection go. Ordinary friendship with unbelievers is not what Paul forbids, and it is often how they come to Christ.

Is it not narrow-minded to refuse to marry someone because of what he believes? Not when you see what marriage is. It is the closest yoke there is: two lives pulling toward one future, raising children, spending money, facing death together. If Christ is the deepest thing in your life, to marry someone who does not share him is to be one flesh with someone who cannot go with you where you are most truly going. That is not contempt for the other person; it is honesty about both of you. And it is kinder to him than a marriage in which the most important thing must stay unspoken.

What it does not mean. A word must be said straight to the person for whom this is not a decision but a situation. If you are already married to someone who does not believe, this verse is not about you, and no one should be allowed to use it against you. Paul’s instruction in that case could not be plainer: “If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him” (1 Corinthians 7:13), and the reason he gives is hope: “For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7:16). God has used a great many such marriages to save the other half of them.

I knowingly married an unbeliever after I became a Christian. Am I living in sin? You may need to confess that the choice was disobedient, but the marriage itself is real, binding and honourable before God, and staying in it is obedience, not sin. Do not torment yourself by treating every day of it as a fresh offence. Love your spouse well, pray for them, and let your conduct speak more than your words (1 Peter 3:1–2). If the unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, Paul says the believer is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15; the Westminster Confession 24.6). And if there is abuse, seek safety and help from your church at once; God never asks anyone to remain in danger.

In everyday life. Before you enter any binding commitment, ask early, before your heart is already fastened: will this pull me with Christ, or against him? Ask a mature believer to help you answer honestly.

For worship. The Lord who forbids the unequal yoke offers his own: take my yoke upon you, he says, for my yoke is easy and my burden is light (Matthew 11:29–30). He does not ask us to pull alone. He fastens us to himself, the One who walks in step with us, carries the heavier side, and never pulls us off the line.
verseByVerse.note: The picture comes from the law forbidding an ox and a donkey to be yoked together at the plough.

verseByVerse.quote: What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What accord has Christ with Belial? This question is sharper, because Paul now names the opposition. Belial is a Hebrew word, and it is not really a name to begin with. It means worthlessness: something with no profit in it, a thing that yields nothing. The Old Testament uses it as a description: the men of Gibeah who surrounded the house were worthless men, sons of Belial (Judges 19:22). By the time of Paul, Jewish writers, including those of the Dead Sea Scrolls, had turned the word into a title for the chief adversary, Satan. It is the only place the New Testament uses it.

Everything against nothing. He could have written Satan. He chose the word that means worthless. Christ, in whom every promise of God is Yes (1:20), against the one whose entire estate is worth nothing: not two powers of comparable weight dividing the world, but everything, against a name that means nothing.

Accord. The word is symphōnēsis, the one behind our symphony. Christ and Belial do not make a chord, and anything that tries to hold both will be discordant.

Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever? The last question of the pair is put in the plainest terms. The word portion, meris, is a word for an allotted share: the piece of land a family received in Israel, what falls to a person by right. It is about what you have in common at the deepest level. In the deepest things, believers and unbelievers have no common share. Their destinies differ. We have no share with worthlessness because we have been given a share in Christ, who is worth more than the world.

What Paul is not saying. Believers and unbelievers share a world, a workplace, a street, a humanity, and Christians who forget that become insufferable. But at the level of what your life is finally for, there is no shared portion. Two people can share a house and thirty years of affection and still be walking in opposite directions on the one road that goes anywhere.

Does this mean my unbelieving relative has no hope? No. The portion describes where a person stands now, not where God may bring him. Every believer once had no share in Christ; such were some of you, Paul told this church, but you were washed (1 Corinthians 6:11). The difference between you and your relative is not that you are better but that grace reached you. So the verse should make you more prayerful and more tender, not more distant. Keep loving them, keep the gospel in view, and pray that God would give them a share in Christ too.
verseByVerse.note: Belial (“worthlessness”) was a Jewish name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What agreement has the temple of God with idols? The last of the five questions is the one the others were climbing toward. Agreement is synkatathesis, a joint decision, a vote cast together. Idols in God’s temple were the ultimate sacrilege; it was what Manasseh did, and what Ezekiel saw in his vision of the abominations in the temple (2 Kings 21:4–7; Ezekiel 8). The reason a believer cannot be yoked to the darkness is not chiefly a rule about company. It is a fact about what he now is.

The temple of the living God. Corinth had temples: to Apollo, to Aphrodite on the height above the city, to half a dozen others, and what made each a temple was that the god was understood to live there. Paul says the temple is the congregation (1 Corinthians 3:16). Not a building; there was none. God has moved out of architecture and into a group of former idolaters, labourers and freedmen in a Greek port. And the word living matters. The idols had mouths but did not speak (Psalm 115:5); the God who lives among his people sees, speaks, acts and judges. To bring an idol into his house is to insult a holy God who is present and awake.

As God said. The quotation weaves together Leviticus 26:11–12, Ezekiel 37:27 and the covenant refrain, sounded in Jeremiah too, that he will be their God and they shall be his people. Every one of those was given to Israel, about a tabernacle, a temple and a land. Paul says they are fulfilled in the church by the Spirit. This is the heart of the covenant: God living among his people.

Dwelling and walking. Make my dwelling recalls God’s tent set in the middle of the camp, the picture John uses when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). And walk among them: at home, as he walked in the garden in the cool of the day before anything went wrong.

Someone already resident. If you are the place where God lives, what you join yourself to is not a private preference; you are deciding what to bring into his house. It is not that idols are intellectually silly. It is that there is Someone already resident.

What counts as an idol today? Anything you look to for what only God can give: security, identity, worth, comfort, meaning. It is often a good thing made into an ultimate thing: money, career, a relationship, children, reputation, health, a political cause, pleasure, even ministry. A useful test is to ask what you most fear losing, what you daydream about, where your spare money and time go, and what makes you angry when it is threatened. Idols rarely look like statues now. But they still demand sacrifices, and they still cannot save. Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:21).

Is my own body God’s temple too? Yes, though that is not Paul’s main point here. In this verse the temple is the church together, we, plural. Elsewhere he applies the same truth to each believer’s body, in the context of sexual immorality: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, so glorify God in your body (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). So both are true. Care for your body and keep it from sin, not because it is your own, but because it is his house. And treat your church with the same reverence: when believers gather, God is in the midst.

In everyday life. Name the one thing most likely to compete with God for your heart this week, and decide in advance, leaning on the Spirit who lives in his temple, what you will do when it calls.

For worship. The whole Bible is the story of God making a way to live with people who could not survive his presence: a garden lost, a tent with a curtain across it, a temple with a room nobody could enter but the high priest, once a year, with blood. Then a body, the true temple, destroyed and raised again in three days (John 2:19–21). And now an ordinary congregation with the living God at home in the middle of them. He gave his Son to have it, and one day he will make his dwelling with us on a new earth for ever (Revelation 21:3).

parallels.desc: I will walk among you and be your God

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go out from their midst. The quotation continues from Isaiah 52:11, words spoken to the exiles as they left Babylon carrying the vessels of the temple home. Paul applies them to a church inside a pagan city. First, what the words cannot mean, because this verse has done damage in the hands of people who wanted a reason to withdraw.

Not withdrawal. The Lord prayed, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). The Christian is planted in society, as light is planted in a dark room. Every version of the faith that measures holiness by how few outsiders you know has misread this sentence.

The Servant leads the way out. Paul’s quotation comes from the doorway of Isaiah’s fourth Servant Song. The call to go out and touch no unclean thing (Isaiah 52:11) is followed by the promise that the LORD will go before his people and be their rear guard (52:12), and then by the Servant pierced for our transgressions, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (53:5–6). The new exodus is not a march the people manage by their own purity. Only Christ could come out of Babylon clean, and he makes his people clean by bearing their uncleanness. We separate from idols because he first separated us to himself.

Touch no unclean thing. What then is being commanded? This phrase controls the other two. Uncleanness here is moral and spiritual now, rather than ritual. It is not people who are to be avoided but defilement. The exiles leaving Babylon were not told to hate Babylonians; they were told not to carry Babylon home with them.

A line through your own life. So the separation is real, but it is not a line between us and them. It is a line through the middle of your own life, wherever the surrounding culture would make itself at home in the temple of God: what you watch, what you are willing to laugh at, how you get money, what you do with your private hours, the ambitions you have absorbed without examining them. You can live in a Christian bubble and be thoroughly Babylonian inside it, or work in the least Christian environment imaginable and touch nothing unclean.

Where Christians differ: separation. Some interpret separation as withdrawing from all association with the world, or even from other Christians who associate with unbelievers. This commentary’s view: Separation here means refusing to take part in idolatry and sin, not physical withdrawal from the world (John 17:15; 1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Christians are to be in the world but not of it. Separating from other true believers over secondary matters is not what Paul teaches; he calls for separation from false worship and from those who teach a false gospel (Galatians 1:8–9; Romans 16:17).

Then I will welcome you. At the end of the verse, from Ezekiel 20:34, comes the thing that turns a command into gospel. The verb is the word for taking someone in: receiving a guest, gathering someone to yourself. God receives those who come out from idolatry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God only welcomes us after we have cleaned ourselves up. He welcomes sinners, and those he welcomes leave their idols; chapter 5 ended with the righteousness of God given to people who had none. But a life divided between two houses does not feel welcomed, and the way back into the enjoyment of what you already have is to stop carrying Babylon into the room where he lives.

How do I decide what is unclean in entertainment and daily life? Start with what Scripture plainly calls sin, and do not make it entertainment: sexual immorality, cruelty enjoyed for its own sake, mockery of God, greed held up as glory (Ephesians 5:3–12). Then ask honest questions about the rest. Does this make sin attractive to me? Does it leave me colder toward God and people? Would I be comfortable watching it with Christ in the room, because he is? Am I free in this, or does it have a grip on me (1 Corinthians 6:12)? Christians will draw some lines differently in matters of conscience (Romans 14), and should not judge one another for it. But each of us must draw them, and be willing to give something up.

parallels.desc: depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing

verseByVerse.quote: and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
A father to you. The chain of quotations ends with the greatest, from 2 Samuel 7:14. David wanted to build God a house; God turned it round and promised to build David one, and of David’s son he said, I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. It was the charter of the house of David, the sentence that stood behind every king of Judah and finally behind the Messiah himself. Paul hands it to Gentiles in a port city across the Aegean, and to all believers.

Sons and daughters. Paul makes one deliberate alteration. Where 2 Samuel says a son, he writes sons and daughters, echoing Isaiah 43:6. The promise made to one royal heir has become a promise to a family, and the family includes women, equal heirs, in a world where inheritance ran through sons. In Christ, a slave woman in Corinth stands in the sentence that was spoken over the throne of David.

How can that be? Only one way. The Son to whom the promise properly belonged took his inheritance and shared it. He is the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29), and everyone joined to him is inside his standing: adopted (Galatians 4:5–7), in the Roman picture taking a new father, a new name and the full rights of an heir. The believer is not a servant allowed in the kitchen but a child at the table: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1).

The Lord Almighty. Then the title, and the collision is deliberate. Almighty is pantokratōr, ruler of all, often rendering the Lord of hosts. That is the One who has just said he will be your Father. A father who is not almighty can love you and be unable to help; an almighty God who is not a father can help and have no particular interest in doing so. Here is one Person who is both. This is where the argument about yokes has been going: Paul is telling them what they would be trading, and whom they belong to.

What it does not mean. It does not mean adoption is earned by separation. It is God’s gracious gift, which calls us to holy living. Nor is it undone when our separation falls short, as it always does: the Son who was perfectly holy in our place keeps us in the family (Romans 5:19; Hebrews 2:11).

My earthly father was absent or cruel. How can I relate to God as Father? Slowly, honestly, and by letting God define the word rather than your memories. Your father showed you what a father should not be; God shows you what a father is. He is never absent (Hebrews 13:5), never cruel, never fickle; he disciplines only in love and for your good (Hebrews 12:10); he gave his own Son for you. You may need to tell him plainly that the word is hard for you; he will not be offended. Read how Jesus speaks of the Father (Luke 15:11–32; Matthew 6:25–33). Over time, the true Father heals what the false one wounded, and the church can be part of that, as older believers become fathers and mothers in the faith to you.

For worship. The Lord of hosts has taken the promise he made to a king and given it to fishermen and slaves and idolaters who came in late, and he calls them sons and daughters, and he means it. The Son of David, the only Son by right, stood under the Father’s wrath so that we might stand under the Father’s smile. The Ruler of all, who commands the stars by name, bends down to be called Abba by the weakest of his children. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will never be anything less than a Father to us.

parallels.desc: I will be to him a father
bring my sons and my daughters

7.title: Godly Grief and the Joy of Reconciliation
7.overview:
Chapter 7 finishes two things. First, the call to holiness: since God has promised to live among his people and be their Father, they must cleanse themselves from every defilement of body and spirit (7:1). Second, the story Paul broke off at 2:13. In Macedonia he found no rest, until Titus arrived with news that the severe letter had hurt the Corinthians and the hurt had led to repentance.

So Paul sets out the difference between godly grief, which leads to repentance and salvation, and worldly grief, which leads to death, and he names what their godly grief produced. Titus has been refreshed by them, and Paul rejoices that he can have complete confidence in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 7 closes Paul’s long defence of his ministry (2:14–7:4) and returns to the story of Titus. Verse 1 draws the conclusion of chapter 6; Paul asks again for open hearts (vv. 2–4); then he tells how, harassed and afraid in Macedonia, he was comforted when Titus arrived with news that the Corinthians had met his severe letter with grief, longing and zeal (vv. 5–7). Their grief was godly grief, which leads to repentance (vv. 8–12), and Titus’s joy completes Paul’s comfort (vv. 13–16). It is one of Scripture’s best descriptions of true repentance, and under every line is the God of all comfort, keeping his word.

Since we have these promises, beloved. Everything hangs on the first words. These promises are the ones just quoted: I will dwell among them, I will be a father to you (6:16–18). The command that follows is not the condition of the promises but their consequence. Read as “cleanse yourself and then God will come to live in you”, the verse turns holiness into a probation with no end. Read as Paul wrote it, holiness is what a person does because the house is already occupied. God did not wait for the house to be clean before moving in; he moved in and began to clean it, paying for every stain with the blood of his Son.

Every promise is Yes in him. All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ (1:20). God said he would dwell among his people; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and by his Spirit he makes believers his temple (6:16). God said he would have sons and daughters; he sent his Son, so that we might receive adoption as sons (Galatians 4:4–5). The house is occupied because Christ opened the door, at the cost of his own body.

Beloved. Dropped into the middle of a command, one of only two places in this letter he calls them that (12:19). A command to holiness from someone who does not love you is a burden; from a father who does, it is an invitation to become what you already are.

Let us cleanse ourselves. Let us: Paul includes himself; there is no plateau from which an apostle instructs people below him. And ourselves: cleansing is something a Christian actively does, though earlier chapters had God as the subject. Both are true: we do the cleansing, and we do it by the Spirit who lives in the house (Romans 8:13).

Body and spirit. “Defilement” (molysmos) is a stain that clings. Corinth knew defilement of the body well: sexual sin, idol feasts, drunkenness. Defilement of the spirit is the one religious people forget, the sin that leaves no mark on the body: settled contempt, appetite for other people’s failures, the private rehearsal of grievances, false worship held in the mind. A man can keep his body clean and be filthy where nobody can see, and Paul refuses to let the two be separated.

Bringing holiness to completion. “Bringing to completion” (epiteleō) means carrying through to the end: a process with a direction. Nobody is finished, and even our best cleansing is never spotless; God accepts it for the sake of Christ, whose obedience was perfect and is counted as ours (Romans 5:19; 1 Peter 2:5). But a Christian ought to be able to name something he is further on with than five years ago. This is sanctification: not the once-for-all verdict that declares a sinner right with God (justification), but the slow change by which God makes a forgiven person actually holy, more and more like Christ (3:18). And it is done in the fear of God: not the terror of a God who might reject you, but the awe of someone who knows who is living in the house.

Where Christians differ: who does the cleansing? Some say sanctification is entirely God’s work, with believers passive, waiting to be carried along; others speak as though it is entirely up to our effort. This commentary’s view: Paul calls believers to cleanse themselves, yet it is God who sanctifies by his Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Sanctification is God’s work in which we actively cooperate: we work out what God works in (Philippians 2:12–13; the Westminster Confession 13.1, 3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.1, 3). It is never complete in this life; perfect holiness comes at glorification, when we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a Christian who still finds defilement in himself has never been cleansed. The blood of Christ has cleansed his guilt once for all (Hebrews 10:14); what he is doing now is clearing out of the house the things that do not belong in it.

What does cleansing myself actually look like? It looks like taking specific things out of your life, not making general resolutions. Name the defilement plainly before God and confess it (1 John 1:9). Then cut off its supply: the website, the habit, the friendship that always ends in gossip, the late evening alone with nothing to do. Put something in its place, because an empty house soon fills again (Matthew 12:43–45): Scripture read and memorised, prayer, the company of believers, work for others. Tell a trusted Christian friend if the sin is stubborn. And go on doing it. The verb is continuous because the work is.

Does this verse mean I must cut off my unbelieving friends? No. Paul has just been speaking of being unequally yoked (6:14), a binding partnership that pulls you away from Christ, such as marriage to an unbeliever or a venture that demands compromise. He said in his earlier letter that to avoid all contact with unbelievers you would have to leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10), and Jesus was called the friend of sinners. Keep your friendships and keep them for Christ’s sake. What you must cut off is whatever defiles, including any friendship in which you are being drawn into sin rather than drawing your friend toward the Saviour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–16 — Godly Grief, Worldly Grief, and Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks again for a place in their hearts and denies the charges against him, in love, not accusation. Then he takes up the story from chapter 2, God’s comfort through Titus, and the contrast between the two kinds of sorrow and the marks of the true kind.
verseByVerse.theology: Worldly grief can look like repentance: tears, distress, self-accusation. But it is about the cost to oneself, reputation, relationships, comfort, rather than the offence against God. Judas is distraught and even returns the money, yet does not turn to Christ; Peter weeps as bitterly, but turns toward Jesus, and is restored. Where the grief is heading decides where it ends.
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is found to have been dishonest with money for years. He weeps and says how devastated he is: by the damage to his reputation, the pain to his family, the end of his ministry. He never speaks of the harm done to those he took from, or of the offence against God. His fellow elders see real grief, pointed in the wrong direction. Genuine repentance asks different questions: not what have I lost, but against whom have I sinned, and what must I do to put it right?

verseByVerse.quote: Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make room. Paul picks up where he left off at 6:13. “Make room” (chōreō) means to give space: their affection had shrunk into a cramped corner, and he asks for the room back.

Wronged no one. Three denials, answering charges actually being made: no one treated unjustly (adikeō); no one ruined (phtheirō), perhaps answering the charge that his teaching led people astray; no one exploited (pleonekteō), the money charge, that the collection was a scheme, which he will answer again at 12:17–18.

Three flat denials. He gives no explanation and produces no evidence. Some accusations should not be dignified with a long defence, only with a plain contradiction and a life that goes on being what it is (6:3–10).

I do not say this to condemn you. Forced to deny that he is a fraud, his first concern is that they should not feel accused by his denial. Anyone who has suffered a false rumour knows how rare that is: the natural motion, once you finally get to speak, is to make somebody pay. Paul closes that door before it opens.

To die together. Here is the reason he can afford to be generous. This is covenant language, like Ruth’s pledge to Naomi and the bond David and Jonathan swore before the LORD (Ruth 1:16–17; 1 Samuel 20:42): there is no circumstance in which I stop being yours, not if you believe the rumours, not if you never apologise.

Dying first. We would say live and die together; Paul puts dying first. He describes a fellowship that has already been through death: people who died with Christ and now live in him (5:14–15). That is a rebuke to how easily Christian relationships are abandoned, over the music, a comment, an estate. What Paul offers people who have been cool toward him for months is a commitment with no exit clause.

When I am falsely accused, should I defend myself? Sometimes, briefly and plainly, as Paul does here, especially when the accusation damages the gospel or other people rely on your trustworthiness. Say what is true, without heat and without counter-accusation, and then leave it. Do not spend your life chasing every rumour; you will never catch them all, and the effort will sour you. Let your conduct over years answer what words cannot (1 Peter 2:12, 15). Hand the matter to the Lord, who judges justly, as Christ did when he was reviled and did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). And watch your heart: aim to win the accuser back, not to defeat him.

For worship. Only one man has ever been able to make Paul’s three denials without exception. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22), and he was charged with everything. He who alone had the right to condemn came not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17), and he loved his own to the end (John 13:1), before Peter stopped denying him. That is a heart with no exit clause, and nothing in all creation can shut us out of it (Romans 8:38–39).

verseByVerse.quote: I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great boldness. The word is parrēsia: frankness, the freedom to say everything. A guarded heart produces guarded speech; an open one says what it means.

Great pride. Literally, much boasting about you. After the factions, the immorality and the cold year, Paul tells them how he speaks about them when they are not in the room: he brags.

Filled with comfort. The letter’s theme word, now an accomplished fact. Paul, who despaired of life itself (1:8), is filled.

Overflowing with joy. Not after the affliction, and not merely in spite of it: in it. Hyperperisseuomai, to run over the top. His circumstances are no safer; something else has been poured in.

Where joy comes from. Titus arrived with news that people Paul loved had turned the right way. That is what filled him: not health, safety or reputation, but the spiritual good of other people. Joy that hangs on circumstances will be up and down for life; joy fastened to what God is doing in people is tied to something that tends in only one direction.

Overflowing through Christ. As we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (1:5). On the night before the cross Jesus spoke of his own joy and wanted it to be in his disciples, and their joy to be full (John 15:11). That is the joy running over in Macedonia: not Paul’s temperament, but the joy of the crucified and risen Lord, poured into a frightened man by news that sinners Christ died for had come home. There is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10), and Paul, in a Macedonian lodging with fighting outside and fear inside, was let in on that joy. So are we, whenever we rejoice in what God rejoices in.

In the flow. This verse closes the defence that began at 2:14 with a man led in triumph (2:14) now overflowing with joy in affliction, and the next verse takes up the story of Titus broken off at 2:13.

Is it honest to say I am joyful when life is hard? Yes, if the joy is real and you do not pretend the hardship away. Christian joy is not a feeling that everything is fine; it is gladness in God and in his work that sits underneath the grief and is not destroyed by it. Paul elsewhere calls himself sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (6:10), both at once. So you can say truthfully, this is very hard, and I am glad of Christ and of what he is doing. If you cannot feel joy at all just now, do not manufacture it. Ask God for it, look for what he is doing in others, and wait; joy is the Spirit’s fruit, not your performance.

In everyday life. Tell someone today that you are proud of them in the Lord, and be specific about what God has done in them.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
No rest. Paul picks up the story he broke off at 2:13, when he left an open door at Troas to look for Titus. “Bodies” is literally flesh, his frail human self; at 2:13 it was his spirit that had no rest, now the body too.

Fear within. Fighting without we expect. Fear within is the remarkable one: an apostle admitting, to a church that already thinks him weak, that he was frightened. He does not qualify it. The man who wrote that God gave us a spirit not of fear (2 Timothy 1:7) says here that he had fears within, and the Bible puts both sentences in the canon without apology.

But God. Two words turn the sentence, as they turn the story in Ephesians 2:4. Everything before them is the human situation, honestly told. Everything after them is what God does with it.

Who comforts the downcast. The title echoes Isaiah 49:13. Tapeinos means low, brought down. Of all the titles available, Paul reaches for the one that describes what God does for people who are on the floor: I was down there, and this is what he is like when you are.

A troubled soul without sin. The same word is the one Jesus used of himself: I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). Facing the cross he said, Now is my soul troubled (John 12:27), and in Gethsemane he was greatly distressed and sorrowful even to death (Mark 14:33–34). Here is why Paul’s fear within is no proof of unbelief: the sinless Son of God felt the full weight of dread and did not sin. And a downcast believer is never alone at the bottom; our high priest went lower than any of us will go.

The coming of Titus. Not a vision, not a voice: a friend walked in the door. Most of the comfort God gives arrives on two legs, with a face and a name: a visit, a meal on a doorstep, a phone call. The sentence has God as the subject and Titus as the instrument. Pray for a suffering friend, certainly; but the comfort of the downcast usually requires somebody to make the journey.

I struggle with anxiety or depression. Does that mean my faith is weak? Not necessarily. Paul was harassed, sleepless and afraid, and he was not walking in unbelief; Elijah asked to die, and the psalmists were often downcast. Anxiety and low mood have many causes: exhaustion, grief, illness, the chemistry of a body living in a fallen world, as well as sin and unbelief. Bring all of it to the God who comforts the downcast. Tell a trusted friend or your pastor, so that someone can be Titus to you. Use the ordinary means God gives, including rest, food, sleep, and a doctor or counsellor where needed; taking medication is not a failure of faith. And do not measure God’s nearness by how you feel. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).

For worship. The God of the Bible has a particular address, and it is the low place: he dwells in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit (Isaiah 57:15). The Son crossed the distance between heaven and earth, and he did not send explanations ahead of him. He came. Every knock at the door of a downcast believer since is a small echo of that coming.
verseByVerse.note: Paul picks up the story he broke off in 2:13: waiting anxiously for Titus.

verseByVerse.quote: and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Comforted by you. Follow the comfort as it moves. God comforted the Corinthians; the Corinthians comforted Titus; Titus came and comforted Paul. The chain runs exactly as chapter 1 said it would (1:4), and the supply at the head of the line is God. God chose not to be the only one who comforts. He could have done it directly and instantly. He preferred to do it through his people, and in doing so gave every ordinary Christian a share in the work of the God of all comfort. What a Father, who will not keep even his consolations to himself, but makes his children carriers of them.

Not merely a messenger. Titus had been changed by his stay in Corinth, and the state of the man, as much as his news, lifted Paul. People rarely encourage others by transmitting facts; they do it by being visibly people to whom something good has happened.

Longing, mourning, zeal. Each is a mark of a church coming right. Longing: after months of distance, they wanted to see Paul again. Mourning: lament, the grief voiced at a death; they were not merely embarrassed, and a church that mourns an episode, unlike one that merely regrets it, changes. Zeal: heat, eagerness to put things right. The coldness had been replaced not by politeness but by warmth.

What restoration looks like. These are the marks of genuine restoration in a marriage, a family or a friendship too: not merely the end of hostilities, but longing, grief and warmth.

Reconciled first to God. Underneath lies the theme of the whole letter: be reconciled to God (5:20). The Corinthians had turned back to God in repentance, and the warmth came flooding back toward the man who had brought them the gospel. The two travel together: people brought home to the Father through the cross find that the cold walls between them and his servants cannot stand either.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all problems were solved. Chapters 10 to 13 show that some opposition remained. Paul rejoices in real progress without pretending it is the finished article.

What if I have no one to comfort me, or no one comforts me well? Then begin where the chain begins, with God himself, who comforts the downcast directly through his word and Spirit; the Psalms were written for exactly this. Then make yourself known. Most people are not comforted because nobody knows they need it. Ask for help plainly, even if it feels awkward, and give people the chance to be Titus to you. And look for someone to comfort yourself. It sounds backwards, but comfort often arrives on the return journey: the person you visit frequently sends you home lighter than you came.

verseByVerse.quote: For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The severe letter. This is the letter written out of much affliction and many tears (2:3–4), sent between 1 Corinthians and this one and probably carried by Titus.

I do not regret it, though I did regret it. Watch him change his mind twice inside a single line. The letter went off; Paul spent the waiting weeks wishing he had not sent it; now, knowing the outcome, he is glad he did. An apostle admits it, and does not tidy it away.

The stretch afterwards. Anyone who has had to say a hard thing knows the sequence: you agonise, you speak, and then comes the awful silence in which you become certain you were too harsh, or too soft. That stretch is in the Bible. Paul lived in it.

What resolved the regret. Not a better argument with himself but the outcome. During the weeks of regret Paul was wrong, and the letter he wished unwritten was right all along. The regret you feel after a hard conversation is usually only evidence that you love the person and cannot see the end from here.

Only for a while. The grief had a term on it: real, severe and temporary, because it led somewhere. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Proverbs 27:6). The friend’s wound hurts and heals. The flattery feels better and leaves the thing that was killing you exactly where it was.

The Lord who writes hard letters. The risen Christ dictated seven letters to seven churches, and most of them wound, and he gives his reason: those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent (Revelation 3:19). Zeal and repentance are exactly what Paul’s letter produced (7:11). But Paul wished his letter back for a while; Christ has never had to wish back a word, because he sees the end of every wound he gives. And the Lord who reproves his people was pierced for their transgressions (Isaiah 53:5), so that even his hardest word to them is spoken by a Saviour.

If an apostle regretted his letter, was the letter Scripture? We do not have the severe letter, and the church never received it as part of the New Testament. Not everything an apostle wrote was given to the church as Scripture; God preserved what he intended his people to have, and the canon he gave is complete and closed. Paul’s passing regret does not touch the reliability of what we do have. The inspired letter we are reading is the one telling us about the regret, and it tells us honestly, which is part of why we can trust it.

How do I know whether I should say the hard thing at all? Ask a few honest questions before you speak. Is it a real sin or harm, or only a difference of taste? Is it my place, because of my relationship or responsibility? Have I dealt with my own log first (Matthew 7:5)? Do I want this person’s good more than my own relief or vindication? Have I prayed, and if possible taken counsel? If the answers are yes, speak, gently and clearly, and then leave the outcome with God. Your feelings afterwards will not tell you whether you were right; only time and fruit will.

In everyday life. If you still carry the regret of something you had to say, you are not yet in a position to judge; Paul could only write this sentence because Titus came back. Pray for the person, keep the door open, and wait for God’s timing.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grieved into repenting. The grief was never the goal; it was the road. Paul rejoices in its fruit: repentance (metanoia), a turning of the mind that turns the whole life round. Anyone who enjoys the discomfort he causes in the name of correction is not doing what Paul did.

Godly grief. Literally, grief according to God: sorrow shaped by his view of the matter, sorrow that God approves, that sees sin as God sees it. And so that you suffered no loss through us: the letter hurt, but did them only good.

Without regret. The chain runs: godly grief, repentance, salvation. And it is never regretted (ametamelētos). Nobody who has ever come to Christ in genuine sorrow has looked back and wished he had not.

Worldly grief. The difference between the two kinds of grief is not intensity; both hurt and both produce tears. The difference is direction. Godly grief sees the sin as an offence against God first, and moves toward him: against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight (Psalm 51:4). David had wrecked several lives, and he says against you only because he had seen who the offended party ultimately is. Worldly grief is sorrow about consequences: embarrassment, self-pity, the pain of being caught, without turning to God. It is entirely about the self, and it leads to despair, bitterness and death. It has a religious form too: the person who punishes himself with misery, as though enough bad feeling could pay for the sin, when the only payment that counts was made at the cross.

Two men, one night. Scripture gives us both kinds within the same few hours. Judas changed his mind, threw the money back into the temple, and said, I have sinned by betraying innocent blood; and he went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3–5). Remorse, confession, restitution: every visible mark is there, and it ended in death, because it never turned toward anyone. Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, went out and wept bitterly, and was restored over breakfast on a beach (Luke 22:62; John 21:15–19). Judas’s end is a warning about despair that will not turn to Christ; it is not a verdict on every believer who has died by suicide in the darkness of illness, and those who grieve such a loss may leave their loved one with the Lord who knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19).

Godly and worldly grief. Godly grief runs to God; worldly grief runs from him. Godly grief changes behaviour; worldly grief only feels bad. The Westminster Shorter Catechism defines repentance unto life as a saving grace whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, does, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience (Q. 87). At the centre stands the mercy of God in Christ. Grief without hope of mercy never turns anyone; it only drives him into hiding.

Looking on the one they pierced. Zechariah foresaw a day when God’s people would look on him whom they have pierced and mourn, and a fountain would be opened to cleanse them from sin (Zechariah 12:10; 13:1), and John saw it fulfilled at the cross (John 19:37). There sin is seen at its worst and mercy at its fullest, since the same wounds are the fountain. Worldly grief looks at itself and its losses. Godly grief looks at him, hates the sin that pierced him, and runs to the blood that washes it.

Listening to your sorrow. When you are sorry for something, listen to the sentences in your head. If they are mostly about how this looks, what it will cost you and how you will get out of it, that is the sorrow of the world, and it will not save anyone. If they are about God, that you have grieved someone who loves you and need him to deal with it, that is godly grief, and it is already carrying you toward the cross, where every sin it names has been paid for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean repentance earns salvation. It is the fruit of grace and the way into salvation’s blessings. God grants repentance (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25); we do not pay for forgiveness with tears. Nor does it mean that a believer who has felt worldly grief has lost his salvation. Every Christian’s sorrow is mixed. The question is where it is taking you.

What if I do not feel sorry enough? Then you are in good company, because no one’s sorrow is ever as deep as his sin deserves, and we are not forgiven because of the depth of our grief but because of the death of Christ. Paul’s test is direction, not volume. Are you turning to God and away from the sin? Then go on turning. Ask God to show you your sin as he sees it, read the account of the cross slowly, and remember that tenderness grows as you walk with him. Some of the most genuine repentance is quiet and dry-eyed, and some of the loudest is only worldly grief. Do not wait to feel enough before you come.

What about the shame I keep feeling after I have confessed? Distinguish conviction from accusation. The Spirit convicts of a specific sin in order to lead you to Christ, and once you have confessed it he points you to the cross and says it is finished. The accuser keeps a vague cloud of shame hanging over you after the sin has been forgiven, to keep you from God. If the sin is confessed and, as far as possible, put right, then the lingering shame is not godly grief. Answer it with the promise: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

For worship. The deepest difference between Judas and Peter is not in Peter at all. It is in the Lord who had already prayed for him, that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), who turned and looked at him across the courtyard (Luke 22:61), and who came looking for him on the shore. Godly grief is never a payment we offer to win God back. It is the sound of a sinner being found, and the Saviour who finds him does not stand back to measure whether the sorrow is adequate.

parallels.desc: Peter’s tears and Judas’s remorse

verseByVerse.quote: For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What earnestness. Having defined godly grief, Paul shows what it looked like when it landed: seven marks, and they can be laid against a life. Earnestness (spoudē) is literally speed, urgency. Real repentance is in a hurry; it does not put the matter down to be dealt with when convenient.

Eagerness to clear yourselves. The word is apologia, a defence. Not self-justification: they had just admitted they were wrong. It is the desire to put right what they were rightly blamed for, so that the charge no longer stands against them because the thing itself has been dealt with, and to show they did not approve of the wrong.

Indignation, fear, longing, zeal. Indignation is anger at the sin and at themselves for tolerating it; repentance without any heat in it is usually just embarrassment. Fear is a proper seriousness about God, whose name had been dishonoured, and perhaps about an apostle who might come with a rod (1 Corinthians 4:21). Longing is for the restoration of what was broken: sin isolates, and real repentance wants back into the room. Zeal is energy for what is right, where before there had been indifference.

What punishment! “Punishment” (ekdikēsis) means justice carried out, a wrong put right: probably the discipline by the majority of 2:6. They acted, and without this mark apparent repentance changes nothing.

Lay the list beside our usual repentance. We tend to be satisfied with the first minute: an apology, some distress, a request to move on. Paul’s list has urgency, anger, fear, longing, energy and action in it, and the apology is not even mentioned. Walk the seven over your own repentance, not to find whether it was thorough enough to pay, for Christ has paid, but to see where the Spirit still has work to do. And if you are judging whether someone who wronged you has turned, this is a far better instrument than his tone of voice.

Innocent in the matter. “Innocent” (hagnos) means pure, clear. The matter is closed, and the church must treat it so: not a probation, not a permanent asterisk, but a case fully shut.

A case shut at the cross. Paul can close the file because God closes his. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1); it is God who justifies, and Christ Jesus is the one who died and who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34). A repentant believer is clear because every charge against him was answered when Christ was condemned in his place. A church that keeps a forgiven man on probation in its gossip is keeping open a case the Judge of all the earth has shut, at the price of his Son.

If someone has truly repented, must everything go back to how it was? Forgiveness, yes, fully and from the heart; the case is shut and must not be reopened in gossip or held over him. But forgiveness is not the same as restoring every position of trust at once. A treasurer who stole may be forgiven and still not handle the money again for a long while, and perhaps never; an elder who fell may be restored to fellowship long before he is restored to office (1 Timothy 3:2). Real repentance will accept those consequences without resentment; indeed eagerness to put things right is one of Paul’s marks. Where there has been abuse, protecting the vulnerable comes first: the matter must be reported to the authorities where the law requires it, and the abuser kept away from those he harmed. Forgiving him never means returning a victim to danger, and the church must never tolerate abuse under the name of grace.

For worship. Only God can produce a list like this in a church like Corinth. The congregation that had shrugged at sin and gone cold on its founder was suddenly urgent, angry at evil, reverent, longing and zealous, and no committee manufactured it. The Son of God was grieved at sin, burned with zeal for his Father’s house (John 2:17) and longed over Jerusalem. A repentant church is beginning to feel about sin as its Lord feels, which means it is beginning to look like him.

verseByVerse.quote: So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not for the wrongdoer’s sake. Paul did not write mainly to punish the offender, now dealt with and forgiven (2:6–8), nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, very probably Paul himself: he did not write to get himself vindicated.

Who was the one who did the wrong? Some take him to be the man of 1 Corinthians 5, who had his father’s wife, with the father as the one who suffered the wrong. The more likely reading, as at 2:5, is that during the painful visit a member of the church had openly opposed and humiliated Paul himself, and the church had failed to stand with him, so that Paul is the one who suffered the wrong (2:5–11). Nothing in the application depends on the identification.

Revealed to you. Not to Paul or the other churches, but to themselves, in the sight of God. The Corinthians had grown cold and would have said this was simply how things stood. The severe letter did not create their earnestness; it brought it out where they could see it. And the One who lays us open in his sight is the same One who has clothed us in his Son, so that being revealed before God is no longer a terror but, for his people, the discovery of grace.

How God uses tests. God often puts his people into a situation whose purpose is to show them what he has already done in them. God led Israel forty years in the wilderness, testing them to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). God already knew; it was Israel who needed to find out.

The Son who was tested for us. Deuteronomy 8 has a sequel. In the wilderness for forty days, the Son of God answered the tempter from that very chapter: man shall not live by bread alone (Matthew 4:4). Israel’s forty years revealed a heart that failed again and again; Christ’s forty days revealed a heart that never failed once, and he passed the test as our representative. For those in him, a trial is no longer a court that might condemn us. It is the testing of a genuine faith, which will be found to result in praise and glory and honour at the revelation of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 1:7). What the test reveals, he put there.

What Paul assumed about them. He never believed these people had stopped loving him; he believed the affection was buried and wrote a letter to dig it up, which is what a father does.

How do I know what is really in my heart? Partly by watching what comes out when you are tested. Pressure does not create what is in you; it reveals it. Pay attention to how you respond when you are crossed, when you lose something, when a believer is under attack and it would cost you to stand with him. Ask God to search you, as David did (Psalm 139:23–24), and invite honest friends to tell you what they see. And take comfort from this verse as well as warning: tests reveal grace as well as sin. You may find there is more of Christ’s work in you than you dared to think.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore we are comforted. The God of all comfort has done in Paul’s case what he promised, and it took many months, a painful visit, a letter written in tears and a friend’s long journey. God’s comfort is rarely quick. It is always sure.

The joy of Titus. What lifted Paul higher than his own comfort was watching somebody else be happy, the mark of a man who lives for the one who died and was raised for him (5:15). It can be easier to weep with those who weep than to rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15), because another person’s gladness can feel like a comment on our own lack. Paul simply delights in his friend.

Refreshed. “Refreshed” (anapauō) is the word Jesus used when he promised rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28). Titus had gone to Corinth expecting trouble and came away rested. Some churches send their workers away refreshed and some send them away hollow, and the difference is almost never about size or resources.

Not put to shame. Paul had bragged about the Corinthians to Titus when the evidence was thin, and then had to wait to see whether he had made a fool of himself. They proved him right.

Proved true. His word is reliable whether spoken to them or about them, the same yes he defended in chapter 1 (1:18–20). Telling the hard truth to someone’s face and speaking well of him elsewhere are both honesty.

Believing the best goes first. Paul’s confidence went ahead of their performance, and very probably helped produce it. It is the opposite of how difficult people are usually handled: we approach the awkward member expecting the worst, communicate it without a word, and are then proved right. Somebody has to go first in believing the best (1 Corinthians 13:7), and it had been done for Paul first, when Barnabas vouched for him and nobody else would (Acts 9:26–27).

Named before he was a rock. The first time Jesus met Simon, he gave him a new name, Cephas, a rock (John 1:42), long before Simon had shown anything rocklike, with three denials still ahead. Christ speaks of his people by what his grace will make them, and his word makes it so. Paul had to wait anxiously to see whether he would be put to shame; the Lord never waits that way, because what he says of his people he has already undertaken to do.

What is the difference between encouragement and flattery? Encouragement is true, specific and for the other person’s good; flattery is exaggerated, vague and usually for the speaker’s benefit, to be liked or to get something. Encouragement points to what God is doing in someone (1 Thessalonians 1:2–3); flattery puffs up the person himself. Encouragement is said behind someone’s back as readily as to his face; flattery is mostly said to his face. So praise freely, but praise what is real, name it concretely, and give God the glory for it. And do not withhold true praise out of fear it will make someone proud. Paul was not afraid to boast of the Corinthians.

In everyday life. Ask whether you send whoever serves your church most visibly home refreshed or drained, and do one thing that refreshes him: a note, a thank you, a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His affection. Splanchna again, the word of 6:12 where the Corinthians’ affections had gone narrow. Titus’s are enlarged, and growing.

The obedience of you all. Not most of them: all. Whatever divisions ran through that congregation, on this they moved together and obeyed the apostolic instructions they had been given.

Fear and trembling. Not fear of Titus, but Paul’s standard phrase for proper seriousness before God (Philippians 2:12; Ephesians 6:5). They received Titus with reverence, taking his message as from God, and knew that what was happening in that room was not merely a difficult meeting with a visiting delegate.

Receiving the one he sent. Whoever receives the one I send receives me, Jesus said, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me (John 13:20). In receiving Titus, who carried the word of Christ, the Corinthians were receiving Christ, and their obedience was a church bowing again to its Lord. When Christ is received in his word, he brings what only he can give: a cleansed church and a refreshed servant.

The right altitude. Church conflict is often handled as a matter between people, to be managed with tact and procedure, good things that never reach the actual height of it. The Corinthians handled theirs before God, and the outcome was not a settlement but a restored church.

Complete confidence. Literally, I take courage in you in everything. This is the church of the factions, the lawsuits and the drunkenness at the Lord’s table, and the last word of the chapter is confidence. It prepares the way for chapters 8 and 9, where he will ask this same church to give generously.

Confidence in what? Nobody should read that as a verdict on how good they were. Paul is about to spend chapters 10 to 13 dealing with the opposition still active among them; he is not naive. His confidence is of the same kind as the unshaken hope of 1:7, resting not on their record but on what God does with people he has begun with. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

Does this mean I must obey my church leaders without question? No. The Corinthians obeyed the apostolic word Titus brought, the teaching that is now in Scripture, and they received it as from God. Church leaders deserve respect, and we should gladly follow them as they lead us in God’s word (Hebrews 13:17). But no pastor or elder may bind your conscience beyond Scripture (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2), and leaders are themselves under the word and accountable. Fear and trembling is directed toward God. If a leader demands obedience to something Scripture does not teach, or uses his position to control or harm, you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and the church must deal with him.

How can I keep hoping for a church, or a person, that keeps letting me down? By resting your hope where Paul rested his: not on their track record but on God’s faithfulness to finish what he started. Pray for them specifically. Notice and name real progress, as Paul does, instead of only cataloguing failures. Keep speaking the truth where it is still needed, as he will in chapters 10 to 13. And remember how long God has been patient with you. Hope is not pretending things are fine; it is trusting that God has not given up, and so you will not.

For worship. God’s faithfulness to finish is the only ground on which anyone has ever hoped for a difficult church, a difficult family, or himself. The God who took a wrecked relationship, a humiliated apostle and a letter written in tears, and produced longing, mourning, zeal and complete confidence, has not lost his touch. He has never yet been handed a situation past mending. The Saviour who bled for the church will present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27). Every church that has broken our hearts is a church he has not stopped washing.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.<sup>2</sup>Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one.<sup>3</sup>I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.<sup>4</sup>I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.<sup>5</sup>For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within.<sup>6</sup>But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,<sup>7</sup>and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.<sup>8</sup>For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.<sup>9</sup>As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us.<sup>10</sup>For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.<sup>11</sup>For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.<sup>12</sup>So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.<sup>13</sup>Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all.<sup>14</sup>For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.<sup>15</sup>And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling.<sup>16</sup>I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

8.title: The Grace of Giving: Christ Became Poor
8.overview:
Chapters 8 and 9 are about money: the collection Paul was gathering from his Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. When his apostleship was recognised there, the leaders had asked him to “remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). For Paul the collection was more than relief: it was a sign that Jews and Gentiles were one body (Romans 15:25–27). Corinth had started eagerly a year earlier (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), but the quarrel with Paul had stalled it.

In chapter 8 Paul encourages them to finish. He points to the poor Macedonians, who gave beyond their means because they first gave themselves to the Lord, and above all to Christ, who though he was rich became poor for our sake. Giving should be willing and proportionate, and Titus and two trusted brothers will handle the gift above suspicion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Macedonian Example and Christ Who Became Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul holds up the Macedonians, who gave joyfully out of deep poverty, and urges the Corinthians to excel in this grace too: not a command but a test of genuine love, set beside the grace of Christ. They should finish what they began, in proportion to what they have, so that, as with the manna, no one has too much or too little.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 stands with Philippians 2:5–8 and John 1:1–14 as a key text on the incarnation. Though he was rich describes the Son before he became man, possessing all the glory, honour and power of God. He became poor describes the incarnation and above all the cross: without ceasing to be God, the Son took a human nature and the lowly life of a servant, down to a cursed death. That you by his poverty might become rich names the result: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit and the inheritance of the new creation.
verseByVerse.examples: A church board is setting its budget and the share given to work beyond its own walls. One member argues that the church should make sure its own buildings and staff are well funded before giving generously elsewhere. This passage sets before him poor churches begging to give, and the Son of God, who did not secure his own comfort before giving himself for others. Does this budget reflect the grace of verse 9?
