verseByVerse.quote: We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapters 8 and 9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, begun a year earlier and not finished (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), and they are the Bible’s fullest teaching on Christian giving. Chapter 8 turns on one sentence: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (v. 9). The Macedonians gave because they had first given themselves to the Lord (vv. 1–5); the Corinthians are to finish what they began, in proportion to what they have (vv. 6–15); and the money is to be handled honourably by church-appointed men (vv. 16–24). Paul never once says money. He calls it grace, because it is Christ’s grace, moving on.

In the flow. Only now, with the relationship mended (7:16), does Paul raise the collection, which seems to have stalled during the troubles. A church reconciled to God (5:20) and to its apostle is invited to let that grace reach the poor. And because chapters 10 to 13 answer the charge that Paul took advantage of them (12:16–18), his care here over every coin matters for the whole letter.

The grace of God given. Paul is about to ask for money, and he begins as no fundraiser would. He does not describe the need. He describes what God has been doing in Macedonia, northern Greece, with churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. Their giving is described as something God did in them. That word, charis, grace, runs through these two chapters ten times. Giving, in Paul’s mind, is not first a duty discharged. It is a grace received, and then passed on.

A severe test. By every human reckoning the equation does not work. The Macedonian churches had suffered from the start: riots, a jailing, a congregation Paul had to leave by night (Acts 16:19–24; 17:5–10; 1 Thessalonians 2:14).

Extreme poverty. Literally, poverty down to the depths, the beggar’s level. Nothing to spare, and every excuse in the world.

A wealth of generosity. What came out was joy and generosity, both the language of overflow, from people who had nothing to overflow with. “Generosity” is haplotēs: single-heartedness, the open hand that gives without calculating. Poverty makes people tight, and affliction makes them inward; together they produce a closed hand every time, unless something has got in underneath.

Grace, not character. Paul is not holding the Macedonians up as heroes to shame the Corinthians. He is showing what God does in people over there by his Spirit, and can do here. God is the fountain, and every overflow in his people is only his own fullness running over.

Poor, yet making many rich. What got in underneath has a name, and Paul gives it a few sentences later: the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who though he was rich, for your sake became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich (8:9). The Macedonians are a living copy of that sentence. Out of the depths of poverty came a wealth of generosity, which is exactly the shape of the gospel: the one who went down to nothing made multitudes rich. Paul had already described his own ministry the same way, as poor, yet making many rich (6:10). Wherever the grace of Christ truly lands, it reproduces its own pattern. People who have been made rich by his poverty begin, even in their poverty, to make others rich.

Waiting for the right season. We often have a threshold in mind before we become generous: when the mortgage is down, when the children are through school. The Macedonians never reached it. They gave out of the depths, and joy and generosity overflowed together, out of the same well.

Why were the believers in Jerusalem so poor? Several reasons came together. There had been a severe famine in the reign of Claudius, and the church in Antioch had already sent help (Acts 11:27–30). Many Jewish believers lost work, family support and standing when they confessed Jesus, and Hebrews speaks of believers, probably Jewish, whose property was seized (Hebrews 10:34). The church also cared for a large number of widows (Acts 6:1). And the collection meant more than relief. It was a Gentile gift to the mother church of the Jews, a visible sign that Jew and Gentile were one body in Christ: if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings (Romans 15:26–27).
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 8–9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The Macedonian churches — Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea — were poor and persecuted.

verseByVerse.quote: For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beyond their means. Every phrase removes another of the usual explanations. According to their means: proportionately, the normal biblical standard. And beyond their means: literally beyond power, past what they could afford. Paul inserts himself as a witness: as I can testify. He watched it happen.

Of their own accord. “Of their own accord” (authairetoi) means self-chosen. There was no appeal, no target, no pressure from an apostle who wanted the collection to succeed. In fact the pressure ran the other way.

Begging to give. It is the reverse of the usual appeal for money. Paul is not begging them to give; they are begging to be allowed to. It seems he had been reluctant to take a collection from destitute people, and they pressed him until he agreed. And the word they used for what they were asking is charis again, which the ESV renders favour. They regarded being permitted to give as a privilege granted to them.

Taking part. “Taking part” is koinōnia, fellowship, and “relief” is diakonia, ministry. Money given to brothers they would never meet was a way of being in fellowship with them. In many churches the offering is the awkward part of the service; we think of giving as money leaving, and the Macedonians thought of it as being let in on the work God was doing.

What makes people beg to give. Not guilt, which produces a payment and then resentment. Not obligation, which produces a calculation. Only having grasped what he has already been given. The Macedonians had seen the Son of God empty himself for them, and koinōnia is the word John uses for fellowship with the Father and with his Son (1 John 1:3). To give to Christ’s poor brothers was to have something in common with the one who became poor for them.

Does this mean Christians should give beyond what they can afford, even into debt? No. Paul reports what the Macedonians did; he does not command it: I say this not as a command (v. 8). The rule he gives is proportion: acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (v. 12); and I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened (v. 13). The Macedonians’ giving was a work of grace in them, and it is meant to stir us, not to shame anyone into borrowing or neglecting his family (1 Timothy 5:8). Sacrifice, yes, gladly; going without some comfort so that others may have bread is exactly what love does. But a gift paid for with a debt you cannot repay, or with your children’s needs, is not what God asks of you.

For worship. Before the Macedonians begged to give, Someone far greater had freely given everything. No one would take his life from him; he would lay it down himself, by his own authority (John 10:18), and he went to the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). Of their own accord, Paul says of the Macedonians; of his own accord, the Saviour says of himself. Every glad giver in the church is a small likeness of him.

parallels.desc: the widow gave out of her poverty

verseByVerse.quote: and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this, not as we expected. Here is the key to everything the two chapters say about money. Paul was taken by surprise, and when he looks for the reason, he does not find it in their circumstances or temperament.

Themselves first. Before any money moved, they had handed over the people the money belonged to. The financial gift was not the transaction; it was the receipt. Giving begins with consecration, handing yourself over to God to be his and for his use: present your bodies as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1).

He gave himself before he gave anything. The Macedonians’ order is their Lord’s order. When Christ set out to make us rich, he did not send gifts from a safe distance. He came himself. The Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20); he gave himself for our sins (Galatians 1:4). His poverty was not a donation from his surplus but the giving of his own person, down to his body on the cross (8:9). So when people who have received him hand themselves over first and their money second, they are not inventing a spiritual technique. They are answering him in kind: a self given for a self given.

First. The word is an order, not a coincidence, and it explains why teaching about money often produces so little. We address the wallet directly, and the wallet was never the problem. For many of us money is the thing we quietly trust to keep us safe, and the hand will not open until the heart has found a better safety in God. A man who has not given himself to God will find good reasons not to give his money. A man who has given himself has already given everything else; what remains is bookkeeping.

The order is a comfort. Do not ask first, am I giving enough? Ask, have I given myself? The second cannot be answered with money at all, so the person with almost nothing is not at a disadvantage. God had already received what he was after.

Then to us. A second surrender: to Paul, the mission, the church. There is no giving yourself to God in the abstract; it lands on people, usually the nearest inconvenient ones. And Paul calls even that the will of God.

What does it mean to give myself to the Lord? It means acknowledging that you belong to him, body, time, money, gifts and future, because he bought you (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and telling him so. It happens decisively when you first trust Christ, and then it is renewed again and again, often at the points where something specific is being asked of you. In practice it sounds like a prayer: Lord, I am yours, and so is everything I hold; show me what to do with it. Then it shows itself in plain decisions: the budget, the diary, the use of your home, your willingness to serve where you are needed rather than where you are noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We urged Titus. Titus, who had already begun the collection in Corinth, is sent back to finish it. Even with a trusted colleague, Paul asks (parakaleō) rather than orders.

This act of grace. In the Greek simply this grace. God’s grace came down in Christ, and the same word describes it going out again as money to strangers, as comfort moved in chapter 1 and reconciliation in chapter 5.

Complete. “Complete” (epiteleō) is the verb of 7:1, bringing holiness to completion. The Corinthians had started, enthusiastically, a year earlier, and stopped. It is the ordinary shape of religious enthusiasm: the weeks pass, the sum that seemed straightforward in the meeting looks larger at the kitchen table, and the thing quietly lapses. Nobody decides against it.

A graveyard of good intentions. What did you begin and not finish? A commitment made at a conference, a monthly amount you meant to set up, a person you said you would visit.

A person, not a sharper paragraph. Paul’s remedy is not a rebuke but a person. He sends Titus, because good intentions do not need more motivation; they need somebody to come and help finish them.

Is it wrong for churches to ask for money or organise giving? No. Paul organised this collection carefully, gave instructions about setting money aside weekly (1 Corinthians 16:2), and sent men to gather it. Asking is right when it is honest about the need, puts Christ’s grace before the appeal, leaves people free to give willingly (9:7), and handles the money openly. What is wrong is manipulation: guilt, pressure, emotional stunts, promises that God will pay back a hundredfold if you give to this ministry, or appeals that hide where the money goes. Paul asks, explains and trusts. He never squeezes.

For worship. The God we worship finishes. His Son set his face to go to Jerusalem and on the cross cried, It is finished (John 19:30), and the Spirit who began a good work in us will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). We are a people of half-built towers, and we belong to a Lord who has never left anything of his undone.

verseByVerse.quote: But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you excel. Paul names the Corinthian strengths generously before he says what is missing. “Excel” (perisseuō) is overflow; they were not lacking in any gift (1 Corinthians 1:5–7).

Faith, speech, knowledge. These were what the Corinthians prized, and Paul adds their recent earnestness (7:11). He does not sneer at any of it. Some manuscripts read your love for us rather than our love for you; either way the bond between apostle and church is the point.

This grace also. Then the sentence turns. Generosity is placed alongside faith, speech and knowledge as a grace a Christian is expected to grow in. We do not usually think of a person as immature in giving as we might think of him as immature in patience. Paul does, and he puts it in the same sentence as faith.

Advanced in everything but this. It is possible to know your Bible, speak well, be warm toward the congregation, and give exactly what you gave ten years ago on a smaller income. See that you excel is an imperative: make sure of it. Paul does not expect it by drift, and drift is precisely what had happened to the collection.

A rich church learning from a poor one. Gift, eloquence and knowledge do not produce an open hand; if anything they supply better arguments for keeping it shut.

Enriched in him. Yet the Corinthians’ riches were the fruit of Christ’s poverty: in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge (1 Corinthians 1:5). To excel in giving is to let the riches Christ bought for them begin to look like the one who bought them. Every gift they boasted of had been poured out by the same open-handed God who gives generously to all without reproach (James 1:5). He is not a God who excels in power and knowledge and is stingy in mercy.

Is generosity a spiritual gift only some Christians have? Paul does list giving among the gifts in Romans 12:8, and some believers are clearly given an unusual capacity and joy in it, as some are given an unusual gift for mercy or teaching. But here he speaks of generosity as a grace every Christian should excel in, just as every Christian is to show mercy even though some have a special gift of it. So do not excuse yourself because you do not feel gifted. Grow in it the way you grow in any grace: by looking at Christ, by asking God for it, and by practising it until it becomes a joy.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say this not as a command. He is an apostle and could order it. He declines because a commanded gift would prove nothing and change nobody. Christian giving must be willing: not reluctantly or under compulsion (9:7).

How much? This is the natural place to answer the question every reader of these two chapters actually has, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a silence: is a Christian required to give a tenth? The honest answer is that the New Testament nowhere commands the tithe of believers, and Paul is the proof. Here he has two entire chapters on giving, the longest treatment of the subject in the New Testament, written to a church that had stalled and needed a clear standard, and he never names a figure. He had every opportunity and every reason to, and he did not. What he gives instead is harder rather than easier. He gives proportion (according to their means, v. 3), readiness (v. 12), cheerfulness (9:7) and one supreme example (v. 9). A fixed percentage can be paid and forgotten; a proportion has to be thought about again every time the circumstances change, and it will not let you stop at ten if you could give forty. (When Jesus told the Pharisees they ought to tithe, Matthew 23:23, he was speaking to men still under the law of Moses.)

The tenth as a benchmark. None of which makes the tenth useless. Christians who treat it as a floor rather than a ceiling are being sensible, with Abraham and Jacob before the law behind the instinct (Genesis 14:20; 28:22). But it must never become the number that tells a rich man he has done enough or a poor man that he has failed.

Your love genuine. “Prove” (dokimazō) is the assayer’s word: testing metal to see whether it is what it claims to be. Money is one of the most reliable tests of love, because it is hard to fake and it costs exactly what it costs. Few things reveal what a person values as accurately as where the money goes when nobody is watching, which is why the Lord put it so bluntly: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21). He did not merely say the heart directs the treasure. He said the heart follows the treasure, so that where the money goes both shows and shapes what we love. So the invitation is not to be dutiful but to find out whether the love is genuine, and Paul is confident enough to let the test run.

Love that answers his. Paul’s very next word is for, and what follows is the grace of the Lord who became poor (8:9). The love being assayed is love kindled by his: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). His love passed every test, and it was proved where it cost most, at the cross. And here is the deepest reason Paul names no figure. The standard beside the Corinthians is the Son of God going from riches to a manger and a cross, and that can never be matched, only answered, gladly and again and again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving is optional for Christians. It means it must be willing, not forced.

Should my giving go to my local church first? Usually, yes, a regular and substantial part of it. The local church is where you are fed, shepherded and cared for, and Scripture expects those who are taught to share all good things with the one who teaches (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). The weekly setting aside Paul taught was gathered through the churches (1 Corinthians 16:1–2). But this very collection shows that Christian giving also reaches beyond the local congregation, to needy believers elsewhere and to gospel work in other places. A wise pattern is faithful, planned giving to your church, with freedom and joy in giving beyond it as God opens your eyes.

In everyday life. If someone who did not know you read your bank statement, what would they conclude you love? Do not be crushed by the answer; let it lead you to Christ, and then plan next month’s giving deliberately, in proportion, before anything else is spent.

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the grace. Paul has been arguing about a collection, and in one sentence he goes to the incarnation, the ground the two chapters stand on. They know it already; they were told it the day they believed. The supreme motive for Christian giving is not a need but a Saviour.

That though he was rich. The riches are not metaphorical. This is the Son before Bethlehem, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed (John 17:5), in the form of God (Philippians 2:6), through whom and for whom all things were created (Colossians 1:16). He had never in eternity known a moment of want.

He became poor. The verb is decisive and voluntary: he impoverished himself. “Became poor” (ptōcheuō) is built on the word for the beggar, which is not modest means. It is the man with nothing, dependent on what other people put in his hand. And the descent is traceable. He was laid in a manger, born to a family that could afford only the two birds the law allowed the poor to offer (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8). He worked with his hands. As a grown man he said that foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20). He was supported by the means of women who followed him (Luke 8:3). He rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room, and was buried in a borrowed grave. At the very end soldiers divided his clothing, which was all he had, and gambled for the seamless tunic they did not want to tear (John 19:23–24). He died stripped, owning nothing at all.

The real poverty. And beneath the material poverty lies the deeper one. On the cross he was stripped of the thing that had never been taken from him in all eternity: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Matthew 27:46)? That is poverty. That is destitution. The one who had always had the Father’s face bore the Father’s judgment on our sin, and went without the light so that we could stand in it.

That you might become rich. Not so that you might become comfortable. Rich. Forgiven, justified, adopted, indwelt by the Spirit, given a righteousness that is not our own, made heirs of everything, blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places (Ephesians 1:3, 18). Each word carries a gift. To be justified is to be acquitted in God’s court and pronounced righteous, on the ground of Christ’s own righteousness (Romans 4:5). To be adopted is to be taken into God’s family as his sons and daughters, with the right to call him Father and a share in his inheritance (Galatians 4:4–7). All things are yours, he had already told this church (1 Corinthians 3:21). The exchange is exact and it runs in both directions: his poverty for our wealth, as at 5:21 his being made sin was for our becoming the righteousness of God.

Why Paul does not need to command. Look at what was done for you, then at your bank account, and see whether the two can be held in the same mind. Every other line of this chapter hangs from this one: the Macedonians’ overflowing poverty is a copy of it, and the manna, the fairness and the honest couriers are ways of letting the riches he won move toward the poor.

Where Christians differ: what did the Son give up? Some, holding kenotic theories (from the Greek word for emptied in Philippians 2:7), teach that the Son gave up some of his divine attributes, such as omniscience or omnipotence, when he became man. This commentary’s view: The Son did not stop being God or lose any divine attribute. He became poor by taking a human nature and the humble life and death of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine privileges for himself (Philippians 2:6–8). He remained fully God while becoming fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion, change, division or separation (the Chalcedonian Definition of AD 451; the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2). His poverty was not a loss of deity but the addition of humanity and the humiliation he willingly bore in it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s poverty promises believers material wealth. The riches are spiritual and eternal, as the prosperity gospel forgets. Paul himself, who wrote this verse, was often hungry, thirsty and poorly clothed (11:27), and called himself poor, yet making many rich (6:10).

If Christ became poor, is it wrong for a Christian to be wealthy? Not in itself. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and Scripture never treats having money as sin. But wealth is dangerous: it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom (Matthew 19:23), and the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). So Paul tells the rich not to be haughty, not to set their hopes on uncertain riches but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). The question is not how much you have, but whether you hold it as Christ’s, with an open hand, and whether his poverty has made you rich toward others.

For worship. He was rich, and he is rich again, at the Father’s right hand, still the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6). But he did not go back to his riches alone. He went back carrying the people he made rich, heirs of God and fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17). No language of commerce has a word for an exchange like that. Paul has only one: grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My judgment. After the summit of verse 9, Paul comes back to practical business, with counsel, not a command (v. 8).

This benefits you. The advantage is theirs: the settled New Testament view is that a generous person gains most from his own generosity, freed from greed, and the Lord Jesus said, It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35). A closed hand damages the one it belongs to before it damages anyone else.

A year ago. He reminds them what they themselves wanted. The Corinthians were the first to begin (1 Corinthians 16:1–2), and had stalled, very probably during the troubles of chapters 1 to 7. The most powerful motivation is not somebody else’s expectation but our own earlier and better intention, recalled gently: you wanted this; finish it.

Finish doing it. The whole weight is on completion. The desire and the deed are to be the same size: not that you should do great things, but that what you actually do should correspond to what you actually meant. Many of us live with a gap there, the quietest self-deception in the Christian life. We are moved by an appeal and count the feeling itself as our response, though nothing has been given, and after some years a person can have a rich interior life of good desires and very little to show.

The one whose willing became doing. God’s desire and God’s deed have never once been different sizes: he purposed to save a people, and he sent his Son; he promised a Spirit, and he poured him out. And there has been one human life with no gap in it. My food, Jesus said, is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work (John 4:34), and he made the whole journey through Gethsemane to the cross, until he could say, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). Stalled Christians are not mended by a sharper resolution but by union with the one who finished, whose obedience is counted as ours where our own still falls short (Romans 5:19), and whose Spirit now works in us both to will and to work (Philippians 2:13).

Out of what you have. And here is the relief attached to the demand: not out of what you wish you had, not out of what the Macedonians managed, but out of what is actually in your hand. It is within reach of everyone reading it today.

What if I promised a gift I can no longer afford? Then be honest, with God and with whoever you promised. Paul’s own rule is out of what you have, and circumstances genuinely change: a job is lost, an illness comes, a family need arises. Do not quietly let the promise lapse and hope nobody notices; that is the very drift Paul is correcting. Tell the person or church plainly what has changed, give what you now can, and keep the intention alive for when you are able again. Where a vow can still be kept at cost, keep it (Psalm 15:4). Where it cannot be kept without neglecting your family, God does not ask it.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The readiness. This is the verse for anyone who feels his giving is too small to matter. “Readiness” (prothymia) is eagerness, a forward-leaning heart, the order of verse 5 again. Without a willing heart the sum is beside the point in either direction.

It is acceptable. The word means well received: not tolerated, not graciously overlooked, but welcomed.

What a person has. And there is the liberty. The measure is your actual resources: not the giving of the person beside you in the pew, whose circumstances you do not know; not what you could have given had life gone differently; not the figure in the appeal letter. What you have. A great deal of Christian unhappiness about money is comparison, and it runs both ways. The person of modest means feels his gift is negligible beside the one that paid for the roof; the person with more looks at the sacrifice of someone with less and wonders whether he is doing anything at all. This verse dismantles both, because it makes the measure personal and proportional rather than absolute. Underneath, comparison usually has an audience in mind: we want our gift to look respectable to others. The God who sees in secret takes that audience away, and the pressure goes with it.

The widow’s two coins. The Lord watched large sums go into the temple treasury, and then a poor widow put in two small copper coins: out of her poverty she had put in everything she had, all she had to live on (Mark 12:43–44). That is the kindness of a God who sees the heart, who sat opposite the treasury and noticed two copper coins. The largest gift that day was worth less than a penny. And Mark sets the scene days before the cross, where the one watching would himself give everything he had for people with nothing to offer him.

I have almost no money. What can I give? Give what you have, however small, gladly; this verse says it is welcomed. And remember that money is only one of the things God has put in your hand. Give your time, your skills, your home, your prayers, your presence with the lonely and the sick. Peter had no silver or gold, and gave what he had (Acts 3:6). The widow who prays faithfully for missionaries every night is investing in the same work as the rich man who funds them. God does not ask you for what you do not have; he asks you for a willing heart and what is actually in your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eased and burdened. Paul heads off a suspicion before it forms, perhaps because somebody in Corinth had voiced it: he is not proposing that Corinth be squeezed so that Jerusalem can relax.

Fairness. The word is isotēs: equality, an even balance, opening and closing the sentence. The aim is that no believer lacks the necessities while others have plenty. The word will not bear more: Paul is not proposing that all Christians hold the same amount, nor that anyone compel a transfer. Every element of this collection has been voluntary.

At the present time. Abundance is surplus, over and above need, and at the present time makes it a snapshot. Corinth had more; Jerusalem had less. Neither was guaranteed in five years.

Circulation. One day the Corinthians may be in need, and others will help them. So the picture is not redistribution but circulation: a body in which resources move to wherever the lack currently is. The aim is not that everyone should have the same but that no one should be in want.

What came out of Jerusalem first. The circulation had already begun in the other direction. Gentiles in Corinth were rich in Christ because Jewish believers had first carried him to them (Romans 15:27). A church that has received that much has every reason to send back bread.

The radical assumption. Underneath lies the genuinely radical part. Paul takes it for granted that a Gentile church in Greece is responsible for Jewish believers in Judea whom they have never met, will never meet, and who differ from them in language, diet, culture and temperament. There is no natural bond there at all. There is only the one thing they have in common, Christ, and Paul treats it as sufficient. That puts a question to any congregation with a surplus. It is easy to feel that the money raised here should stay here, where the needs are visible. Paul’s categories do not let the question be settled locally. If the church is one body, a need in another part of it is not somebody else’s problem being brought to our attention. It is our need, currently being felt somewhere else.

Where Christians differ: Christian sharing and economics. Some use this passage to support enforced redistribution of wealth by the state. Others ignore it. This commentary’s view: Paul is speaking of voluntary giving within the body of Christ, not compulsory state action (v. 8; 9:7). He does not call for absolute equality of possessions, but for generous sharing so that no believer lacks basic needs. Christians remain owners of their goods as stewards, but are called to deep generosity, especially to fellow believers (Acts 4:32–35; Galatians 6:10; 1 John 3:17). Christians may disagree on public policy, but they cannot neglect personal generosity.

Should I help unbelievers in need, or only fellow Christians? Both, with a particular care for believers. Paul’s rule is: as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). This collection was for the household of faith, and a church that neglects its own poor while giving elsewhere has its order wrong (1 Timothy 5:8, 16). But Jesus’ Samaritan helped a stranger, and God sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). Christians feed the hungry and care for the vulnerable in their neighbourhood because their Father is kind to all, and such mercy often opens a door for the gospel.

In everyday life. Look at what is genuinely over and above your need. Ask your church whether any member is quietly going without, or which believers elsewhere, persecuted or poor, you could help. Then share it, this month, not some day.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written. Paul settles the argument with a sentence about breakfast in a desert. In Exodus 16 God sends bread every morning, with instructions to gather an omer a person and keep none of it till morning (Exodus 16:16, 19): whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack (Exodus 16:18).

Picture the camp. Some men were strong and fast; some were old, or ill, or slowed by small children. They came back with different amounts in their jars, and when it was measured, everyone had exactly enough.

How God provides. This is how God provides for his people: sufficiency for each, without regard to capacity. Nobody starved because he was weak, and nobody got ahead because he was quick, and the church is meant to look like that camp. In Exodus God did it by a miracle; in Corinth, through the offering.

Manna keeps badly. Second, and it is the sharper point, the man who gathered much never actually owned the surplus. It was not his to keep, and if he tried, as some did, it bred worms and stank by morning (Exodus 16:20). Manna was given daily, for use, and it rotted the moment it was treated as property. What you have beyond your need was not given you to store, nor as a reward for gathering faster. It is manna, and manna keeps badly. We think of surplus as margin, security, evidence that things have gone well. Paul, quoting Moses, says the surplus in your jar this morning may have somebody else’s name on it, and that God arranged the imbalance so that his people would become the means of each other’s supply.

The true bread from heaven. Jesus himself read the manna story as pointing to him. Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, the crowd told him, and he answered that his Father gives the true bread from heaven: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:31–35). The wilderness rule finds its fullness there. In Christ no one who gathers little goes without, and no one who gathers much has anything over to boast of. Every believer, quick or slow, strong or frail, receives the same portion: the whole of Christ. That is why the church’s sharing of bread is not a political programme but a family likeness. People who all live on the same bread cannot let one another go hungry.

Is saving for the future, or for retirement, hoarding? Not necessarily. Scripture commends the ant that stores in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8), Joseph who stored grain for the famine, and the person who provides for his household (1 Timothy 5:8); leaving an inheritance is called good (Proverbs 13:22). Hoarding is different. It is keeping more and more out of fear or greed, trusting the stockpile rather than God, while needs around you go unmet. Jesus’ rich fool built bigger barns and was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16–21). So save wisely and modestly for real responsibilities, give generously as you go, and ask regularly whether your savings serve love or have become your security.

For worship. Bread came down six mornings a week for forty years, and the LORD never once failed them. Then the Bread himself came down, and he was not gathered but broken: this is my body, which is given for you (Luke 22:19). The manna could not be stored; he cannot be exhausted, and the whole family of God, the quick and the slow, will sit down at last at the marriage supper of the Lamb with no one lacking.

parallels.desc: whoever gathered much had nothing left over

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Titus and the Brothers; Transparency in Giving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God for Titus’s eagerness and introduces two companions, one well known for his gospel work and chosen by the churches, the other proven in many tests. The arrangement is deliberate: the money must be handled honourably before the Lord and before people. He asks the Corinthians to show these men the love he has boasted of.
verseByVerse.theology: Handling ministry money with open accountability applies to every Christian church and organisation. Paul, who could have relied on his own integrity, insists on several overseers chosen by the churches, because the ministry’s integrity is at stake before the watching world too. Financial scandal has often damaged the gospel’s credibility, and Paul’s precaution (v. 20) is wisdom exercised before any accusation is made.
verseByVerse.examples: A mission agency introduces a rule that larger payments need two signatures, with an independent audit each year reported to all its members. Some staff feel this implies distrust. But the precautions are not about suspecting individuals; they protect the honour of the Lord before people who would use any irregularity to attack the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thanks be to God. The argument about money pauses, and Paul thanks God for a person: not that Titus agreed to go, but that God put the care into his heart, who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

A habit worth having. When someone shows us real kindness we thank them, which is right. Paul thanks God. Think of the friend who kept turning up, the older believer who prayed for you for years. Have you thanked God that they wanted to? That is accuracy about where affection comes from.

The same care, from one heart. Paul yearned for his churches with the affection of Christ Jesus (Philippians 1:8). The same earnest care lived in Paul’s heart and in Titus’s, and both had it from the Lord who gave himself for this very church. Christ’s love for the Corinthians did not stay in heaven; it went to Corinth on his servants’ feet.

Of his own accord. Paul asked him, and Titus accepted; but he was already going anyway, out of his own eagerness. The phrase is the one used of the Macedonians in verse 3, and its reappearance is not accidental. Everything in this chapter that God is doing, he is doing through people who chose it freely and would tell you it was their own idea. Both are said without embarrassment: God put it in his heart, and he is going of his own accord. That is the ordinary pattern of the Christian life. Titus was not moved about like a piece on a board; the eagerness was his. And behind it was Someone who had arranged it, which is why the paragraph opens with thanks rather than congratulation. God’s work in us does not cancel our willing; it creates it.

What Titus was eager about. Not a preaching tour, but organising a collection in a difficult church and handling other people’s money where he could easily be accused. That is the kind of enthusiasm only God puts in a heart.

How do I know whether a desire to serve comes from God? Test it by Scripture first: God never moves anyone to do what his word forbids. Then ask whether it fits the gifts and opportunities God has given you, whether it is aimed at others’ good and Christ’s glory rather than your own name, and whether mature believers who know you confirm it. Titus’s desire matched Paul’s appeal; inward desire and outward call agreed. You do not need a voice or a sign. A good desire, tested by the word and confirmed by the church, is very often God’s way of leading. Act on it, and thank him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The famous brother. Paul does not tell us his name. Some early writers guessed Luke; others suggest Barnabas, Silas or Apollos. There is no way to decide. But the Lord who knows the names of all the stars knows the name of this brother, and on the last day the unnamed brother will hear his own name spoken by the Lord of glory.

Famous for the gospel. One of the best-known preachers around the Aegean spends months as a courier and an auditor, because the money has to be handled properly. Nobody is too senior for the practical work.

Nobody too great for a towel. He learned it from his Master. Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, tied a towel round himself and washed his disciples’ feet, and said, I have given you an example (John 13:3–5, 15). A famous preacher carrying a collection bag for the poor is not stepping down from the gospel into administration. He is preaching it with his feet.

Appointed by the churches. “Appointed” (cheirotoneō) originally meant to elect by show of hands. Several men, chosen by the givers, travel with the gift. Paul, who could honestly have said his own integrity was sufficient, arranges things so that it does not have to be taken on trust.

For the glory of the Lord. A collection for hungry believers, carefully audited and honestly delivered, is done for the glory of the Lord. That is worth saying to everyone who feels that the practical end of church life is the unspiritual end: the treasurer, the person who counts the offering, the one who checks the invoices and is never thanked. Paul puts that work and the glory of God in the same sentence, because a church whose money is handled honestly is telling the truth about its God, and one whose money is handled loosely is telling a lie about him with every receipt.

Does it matter if my service is never noticed or remembered? Not to God, and that is the only audience that finally counts. This brother was famous in his day and is nameless now, and his work still stands in the record of Scripture. Your Father sees in secret and will reward you (Matthew 6:4). Many of the most important people in your church are those you never hear about: the woman who prays, the man who fixes the boiler, the couple who have quietly helped the same struggling family for years. Serve for Christ’s glory, not for recognition, and trust that nothing done for him is forgotten (Hebrews 6:10).
verseByVerse.note: The famous brother is unnamed; some early writers guessed Luke.

verseByVerse.quote: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That no one should blame us. Some did suggest that Paul was crafty and took them in by deceit (12:16–18). So independent, church-appointed men travel with the money. And he takes the precaution before any accusation about this sum, which is the only time such arrangements can be made, since afterwards they always look like a reaction.

In the sight of man. The principle comes from Proverbs 3:4 in the Greek Old Testament. Two audiences, and both are taken seriously. The first is obvious, and it is where Christians usually stop. God sees; my conscience is clear; he knows my motives. All true. And it is weightier than we usually feel, for no creature is hidden from his sight, and all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Hebrews 4:13). And Paul says it is not enough. The second audience is the watching world, which cannot see motives and must judge by arrangements. Here is the point sincere people can miss: it is not sufficient to be honest. Where other people’s money is concerned, you must be visibly, checkably honest, in a way that does not depend on anyone believing you.

When oversight feels like an insult. This cuts against a common and rather pious instinct. A man of genuine integrity finds oversight faintly insulting: the second signature, the audit, the receipts, the rule that he may not authorise his own expenses. It feels like being suspected. Paul, whose integrity nobody should have doubted, built the structure himself and volunteered for it, and he did it precisely because he was trustworthy. It was not about him. The reputation of a ministry is not the private property of the person carrying it. It belongs to the gospel. And money has done great damage to the church’s credibility in ordinary people’s eyes: the ministry whose accounts nobody sees, the appeal that funded a lifestyle, the collapse that made the news and gave many people a reason never to listen again. Such things often start with someone who did not think the precautions applied to him.

Nothing in secret. Jesus could say at his trial, I have spoken openly to the world; I have said nothing in secret (John 18:20), and his enemies had to look for false witnesses (Mark 14:55–56). Openness did not spare him accusation, and it will not spare his servants. What it does is leave the accuser with nothing true to say.

How should I choose a ministry or charity to give to? Look for what Paul built here. Is the money handled by more than one person, with independent oversight and accounts that are open to givers? Is the work faithful to the gospel and doing what it says it does? Are the leaders known, accountable to a church, and living modestly rather than lavishly? Does the appeal tell the truth, without pressure or promises of guaranteed return? Give first to what you know well, your own church and workers it sends, and then to others you have checked. A ministry that bristles at reasonable questions about money has answered them.

In everyday life. Two people count the offering; nobody handles a fund alone; the person who decides the spending is not the person who signs the payment. None of it implies distrust; all of it removes a stumbling block from the road (6:3). If you hold any money that is not your own, ask today whether someone else can see what you do with it.

For worship. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). In the company of his Son on earth, the thief was the man who held the moneybag (John 12:6); the Son never took a coin that was not his, and in the end gave away everything that was. A church that handles money in the light shows the world a God with nothing to hide.

verseByVerse.quote: And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Often tested. A third man, also unnamed, described only as often tested and found earnest: a reputation built slowly, in small situations, over years, in a church culture often impressed by the newly arrived and the obviously able. The reliability was shown before the responsibility was given. One who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10).

More earnest than ever. Titus’s good report has energised this man too. A church that comes right does not merely settle its own trouble; it energises people who have only heard about it.

Partner and fellow worker. “Partner” is koinōnos, a colleague with a stake in the enterprise; “fellow worker” is synergos, one who labours alongside.

Messengers of the churches. Literally apostoloi, sent ones: men formally commissioned as the churches’ delegates. They are not apostles of Christ like the Twelve and Paul, sent by the risen Lord himself, who laid the foundation once for all (Ephesians 2:20); but every church still sends and receives trusted messengers.

The glory of Christ. Then the last phrase, dropped in without explanation, and it is the largest thing in the verse. Of these men, one unnamed, one described only as reliable, both currently employed as couriers of a charitable fund, Paul says that they are the glory of Christ. Not only that they bring glory to Christ, though they do. They are his glory. It is the same astonishing claim as chapter 3, where the Corinthians were a letter from Christ, and chapter 4, where the treasure is in jars of clay. Christ has arranged that his glory in this world should be visible in people: in ordinary, unnamed, tested, faithful people carrying out unglamorous work for churches. He is not ashamed of the arrangement. He chose it. He does not borrow glory from them; he lends his glory to them.

How can an ordinary Christian be the glory of Christ? Because the glory of Christ is seen wherever his character is reproduced, and it is most clearly seen in faithfulness that nobody applauds. When a believer keeps his word, handles money honestly, serves without being noticed and loves a difficult church, people see something of the Lord who did all those things perfectly. We are being transformed into his image from one degree of glory to another (3:18). You do not have to be gifted or famous to display him. You have to be his, and faithful in what he gives you to do.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “messengers” is literally “apostles” — men sent by the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give proof. After twenty-three verses on grace, Christ becoming poor, readiness, proportion and transparency, it comes down to this: when the three men arrive, put something in the bag. That is where the heights were always going.

Proof of your love. Back to verse 8. Love that cannot be demonstrated has not yet been shown to exist. By this we know love, John writes, that he laid down his life for us; and then at once: if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him (1 John 3:16–17)? The road from the cross to the collection bag is one sentence long.

Our boasting. He has told the Macedonians that Corinth would come through (9:2), and told Titus they were a good people (7:14). Now he tells them in writing that his reputation is attached to what they do next. I have vouched for you: that is a form of love, and it makes a demand precisely because it was given before it was earned.

Before the churches. The demonstration is public. The chapter began with Macedonia’s example held up to Corinth and ends with Corinth’s response held up to everyone. That is the ordinary way God spreads generosity, one congregation catching it from another (Hebrews 10:24).

Doesn’t Jesus tell us to give in secret? Yes, and both teachings stand. Jesus forbids giving in order to be seen and praised by others, sounding a trumpet before you like the hypocrites (Matthew 6:1–4). That is about motive: do not give to win applause. But the same Lord says, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father (Matthew 5:16). Paul is not asking the Corinthians to parade individual gifts; the collection was a church’s gift, and its proof was to be seen so that God would be thanked (9:12–13). So keep your own giving quiet, and let your church’s love be visible for God’s glory.

For worship. Every church that has caught generosity from another has caught it, in the end, from a Lord who was rich and became poor for its sake. God gave proof of his love on a cross while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8), before there was anything in us to vouch for. And the Son vouches for us still, confessing as his own before his Father a people who had given him every reason to be ashamed of them (Matthew 10:32), and he is not ashamed.

9.title: Sowing Generously: The Cheerful Giver
9.overview: Paul continues on the collection for Jerusalem. He sends the brothers ahead so that Corinth’s promised gift is ready, and willing, when he arrives. Then he gives the principles of Christian giving: sowing and reaping, a settled decision made in the heart, and the God who supplies enough for every good work. The gift will do far more than meet needs in Jerusalem: it will overflow in thanksgiving to God and bind Jewish and Gentile believers together. The chapter ends with praise for the gift behind every gift: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Sowing and Reaping; the Cheerful Giver; the Inexpressible Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter moves from why the brothers are sent (vv. 1–5), to how to give (vv. 6–11), to what the gift will do (vv. 12–14), and ends in thanks for God’s gift, too great for words (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The sowing and reaping of v. 6 is not a promise of wealth, and the passage corrects that reading itself. The harvest is named in v. 10 as “the harvest of your righteousness”. God supplies “seed to the sower and bread for food”, enough to live on and enough to give again, and it is the seed he multiplies. The giver is kept supplied so that his generosity can continue, and the supreme giver of 8:9 became poor.

Verse 9 quotes Psalm 112:9. The psalm’s portrait of the man who fears the LORD places giving to the poor among his identifying marks: generosity is a feature of godliness, not an extra for generous temperaments.

“God loves a cheerful giver” (v. 7) comes from the Greek Old Testament at Proverbs 22:8, which carries a line the Hebrew text does not, a blessing on the cheerful and generous man. God cares about the heart and manner of the giver, not only the amount.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation uses a pledge campaign with carefully designed giving targets and social dynamics (recognising top givers, publishing goals) that effectively apply social pressure to giving. Many give generously, but the pastor wonders whether the giving is cheerful or compelled. This passage questions not the amount raised but the mechanism: “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (v. 7). The goal is not only generous giving but cheerful givers, people who give because they have been gripped by the inexpressible gift of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 9 continues the appeal for the collection. Paul sends the brothers ahead so that the promised gift will be ready, and willing, when he arrives (vv. 1–5). Then the principles: whoever sows generously reaps generously; each should give as he has decided, for God loves a cheerful giver; and God is able to supply enough for every good work (vv. 6–11). Last, what giving does: it meets needs, overflows in thanksgiving, proves their confession of the gospel and binds Jewish and Gentile believers together. Two chapters of timetables and delegates end in praise for God’s inexpressible gift (vv. 12–15).

In the flow. In Greek the chapter opens with for, tying it to 8:24. Some scholars think it was once a separate note, but as it stands it moves forward, from why to give, to how, to what the gift will do, and ends where chapter 8 began, with the grace of God.

Superfluous. A courtesy everyone recognised, since fourteen more verses follow. But he is not addressing a delinquent church; he takes their willingness for granted and has already staked his reputation on it. “Ministry” is diakonia: the money is a service to the saints.

The least of these my brothers. Who are the saints? Not a charity’s clients, but poor believers in Jerusalem, people made holy in Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2) and so the Lord’s own brothers and sisters. That is why the money is a ministry. The Lord said that what is done for one of the least of these his brothers is done for him (Matthew 25:40), and a bag of coins for hungry saints in Judea is, in the end, a gift placed in his hands.

A circle of encouragement. Macedonia is northern Greece; Achaia the southern province, with Corinth as its capital. In chapter 8 the Macedonian example was held up to stir Corinth; now we learn that Corinth’s example stirred Macedonia in the first place, and Paul has carried the news between them.

Zeal. Zeal proves contagious across provinces. That is a reason for churches to treat news from another congregation as more than a slot in the notices: a church convinced that serious giving is unrealistic will go on believing it if it never hears what a poorer church has just done. Some of the most effective work Paul does in these two chapters is simply carrying news. The heavens declare his glory, and the church does too, one congregation telling another of his grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was manipulating them. He told neither church anything untrue: the Corinthians really had begun eagerly, and the Macedonians really did give beyond their means. He simply would not let two congregations far apart stay ignorant of what God was doing in the other.

Is it healthy for churches to compare themselves with one another? It depends on what the comparison is for. Comparing in order to feel superior, or to compete for reputation, is pride, and Paul condemns it a chapter later (10:12). But telling one church what God is doing in another, so that both thank God and are stirred to love and good works, is exactly what Paul is doing here (Hebrews 10:24). The test is whether the comparison ends in praise of God and fresh obedience, or in boasting and envy. Hear reports of other churches gladly, pray for them, learn from them, and never use them as a weapon.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was southern Greece, including Corinth; Macedonia was to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why the brothers go. The three men of 8:16–24 are sent because Paul has made a claim in public and does not want to be found to have overstated it. That is a plain admission of self-interest, and its plainness is part of the honesty.

To say nothing of you. He names his own embarrassment first and theirs only as an aside; leading with theirs would have applied more pressure.

What he is avoiding. Consider the scene he is preventing. If nothing has been gathered when he walks in with visitors, there will be an appeal on the spot, with witnesses present, and money will be produced. Every coin of it will have been given under social pressure, to avoid a humiliation. It would look like generosity and be nothing of the kind. So Paul builds the timetable to remove the very pressure he could most easily have used. He holds every card, and he arranges not to play them.

Belief and structure. Paul believes the Corinthians will come through, and he sends three men and a timetable, because good intentions need infrastructure. The leader who believes the best about people and gives them nothing to act on has only half believed in them.

Glorified in them before they had finished. On the night before they all ran away, the Lord Jesus said to his Father, I am glorified in them (John 17:10). He spoke of their faithfulness while it was unfinished, and then made sure of it, praying for them, sending his Spirit and keeping them to the end (Philippians 1:6). Paul’s confidence in a church is borrowed from Christ’s confidence in his own.

Is it wrong to make a pledge or promise to give? No. The Corinthians had promised this gift (v. 5), and Paul expected them to keep their word. A pledge freely made, after prayer and with the figures in front of you, can be a wise way to plan and to help a church plan. What is wrong is a pledge squeezed out under pressure, or one made in a moment of feeling without thought. Once you have freely promised, keep it if you can, as you would any promise (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). If circumstances truly change, say so honestly rather than letting it quietly lapse.

verseByVerse.quote: So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessing or exaction. Here is the reason for all the arranging, in two words held deliberately apart. A willing gift is a blessing: eulogia, a good word spoken, and so a benefit freely bestowed.

Not as an exaction. The word is pleonexia: greed, the grasping that takes what is not freely offered (compare 2:11; 7:2). The same sum, in the same bag on the same day, is either a blessing or a shakedown, and the difference is not in the amount but in whether it was freely given.

How compulsion works. The mechanisms that produce compulsion in churches are rarely crude. Nobody is threatened. But there is the giving made visible; the target on a thermometer on the wall; the appeal placed at the emotional peak of a meeting; the pledge card passed along a row where everyone can see; the quiet awareness that the treasurer knows. All of them work, and all of them shift the reason a person gives from what is in his heart to what the room expects. Paul builds the structure that makes freedom possible: notice, time, a decision made at home, and the apostle absent while it is made. He is not making it easier to give; he is making it possible to give freely.

Shaped like the gift it answers. Paul would risk a smaller collection to have a genuine one, because the God who owns everything does not need money on any terms, and because the collection answers a gift that was never extracted. Nobody forced the Son of God to the cross: I have come to do your will, O God (Hebrews 10:7). A gift squeezed out of the Corinthians would have contradicted the gospel it was meant to celebrate. Grace given freely can only be answered freely.

How do I actually plan my giving? Sit down, preferably with your husband or wife, with your income and commitments in front of you, and pray. Decide a proportion of what comes in that you will give regularly, first, before other spending, as the firstfruits rather than the leftovers (Proverbs 3:9). Set it up so that it happens without needing to be remembered. Keep a further amount aside for needs that arise during the year, so that you can respond freely when God puts someone in front of you. Review it whenever your income changes, or at least once a year, and ask whether the proportion should rise. Then give it gladly, and forget about it.

In everyday life. Before you give next, know which sentence you are answering: I want to, or I would look bad if I did not. God is not standing over anybody with a stopwatch. But Paul has gone to considerable trouble to make sure the Corinthians could answer the first, and so can you.

For worship. The first word God spoke over human beings was a blessing (Genesis 1:28), and the Lord Jesus left the earth with lifted hands, blessing his disciples (Luke 24:50–51). The Father has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3), and not one had to be wrung from him. Blessing is simply what he is like.

verseByVerse.quote: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sowing and reaping. Now the principle, a farming proverb Scripture uses often (Proverbs 11:24–25; Galatians 6:7).

Picture the farmer. A farmer walks out in autumn with a bag of seed, and the decision is painful, because the seed is food. His family could eat it. The more he keeps back to eat, the less comes up in the spring, and it never stops being hard, because the eating is now and the harvest is later. What you release is not lost; it is planted.

Bountifully. Literally with blessings, as in verse 5. The harvest is described in the verses that follow: grace, the means to keep giving, righteousness, thanksgiving to God, and the prayers of others (vv. 8–14).

Handle with care. This verse must be handled carefully, because it has been made the foundation of a cruel distortion of Christianity. The prosperity teacher quotes it and stops: sow generously into this ministry and God will return it to you multiplied, and the more you give the wealthier you will become. Money is thereby extracted from poor people by a promise God has not made, using a verse from a passage whose entire concern is that giving must not be extracted. Three things in the passage itself take that reading apart, and none of them requires going outside the chapter. First, look at what Paul actually says the harvest is. Verse 10 calls it the harvest of your righteousness. Verse 11 says you are enriched to be generous. Verse 12 says the yield is thanksgivings to God. The crop, named three times, is righteousness, further generosity and worship. Second, the supply in verse 10 is seed to the sower and bread for food: enough to live on and enough to give again. That is provision for a farmer, not a fortune. Third, and most decisively, the one Paul has just held up as the supreme example of generosity in 8:9 became poor. If sowing bountifully guaranteed material return, the Lord Jesus Christ is the counter-example, and so is Paul, who knew hunger and thirst, often without food (11:27).

The grain that fell into the ground. Jesus took this same farmer’s law and applied it to himself: a grain of wheat kept back stays a single grain; only when it falls into the earth and dies does it yield a harvest (John 12:24), and whoever loves his life loses it (John 12:25). The Son of God was buried like seed in a garden tomb, and the harvest from that one grain is a multitude no one can number. The sowing proverb was never a money trick. It is the shape of the cross, and every gift a Christian lets go of is a small share in the pattern of the one who let go of everything.

Where Christians differ: the prosperity gospel and seed faith. Some teach that if you give money to God, often to a particular ministry, he will return far more money to you, so that giving is an investment for personal wealth. This commentary’s view: Paul does promise that God rewards generosity. But the harvest is mainly spiritual: grace, righteousness, thanksgiving, and the means to be generous again (vv. 8, 10–11). God supplies enough for every good work, not luxury. Giving in order to get is the opposite of the cheerful, self-forgetting generosity Paul describes. Christ became poor to make us rich spiritually (8:9).

Will God reward me for giving? Yes, and you are allowed to want the reward. Jesus himself said your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:4), and told us to lay up treasure in heaven. The rewards are real: joy now, a deeper likeness to Christ, the thanks of those helped, the knowledge that nothing given for him is wasted, and treasure kept for the age to come (Luke 12:33; 1 Timothy 6:18–19). What you must not do is treat God as an investment fund, giving a hundred so that he owes you a thousand. That is not sowing; it is gambling with God’s name on it. Give because he has given, and leave the harvest to him.

A friend of mine follows prosperity teaching. What should I say? Begin with what is true in it: God is generous, he does reward giving, and he cares about our needs. Then open the Bible together at this chapter and ask what the harvest is in verses 8 to 12. Look at 8:9 and ask why, if giving guarantees wealth, Jesus and Paul were poor. Read 1 Timothy 6:5–10, where Paul warns against those who imagine godliness is a means of gain. Be gentle; many who are drawn to this teaching are poor or desperate, and have been exploited. Point them to the riches that cannot be taken away, and help them practically if they have given away what they needed.

parallels.desc: one gives freely, yet grows all the richer

verseByVerse.quote: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he has decided. Each one: there is no exemption for the poor (8:2). As he has decided: proaireō, to determine beforehand. It is a personal, prayerful decision, made in advance, with no fixed amount imposed: planned giving, reached in private with the figures in front of you, before any appeal is heard, as Paul told this church to do weekly (1 Corinthians 16:2).

Not reluctantly. Literally not out of grief, not with a pang: the giving that is done and quietly resented, and the resentment usually surfaces later as a complaint about how the money is spent.

Or under compulsion. Most of the pressure comes from inside: what others will think, what a person in your position ought to be seen to do, or simple guilt.

A cheerful giver. Paul adapts the Greek version of Proverbs 22:8, which says that God blesses a cheerful giver; Paul says he loves him. The word behind cheerful is hilaros. Our word hilarious comes from it, though the Greek means glad rather than comic. It is not sober approval; it is warm, glad-hearted delight. God loves a giver who finds giving a pleasure. That is a genuinely startling thing to be told, because it means God is not primarily after the money. Every beast of the forest is his, the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10). What he loves is a particular kind of person: one for whom letting go has become a joy rather than a loss.

Made by contemplation. That cannot be produced by trying, any more than you can decide to find a person attractive. It comes from looking at Christ, who though he was rich, for our sake became poor (8:9): a manger, a borrowed tomb, and on the cross not even his clothes. Whoever has grasped that knows he cannot out-give him. So if giving is a duty performed with a small inner wince, the answer is not to give more grimly. It is to look at him until the arithmetic changes. Cheerful givers are made by contemplation, as the Spirit changes us while we behold the Lord (3:18), not by resolve.

I don’t feel cheerful about giving. Should I wait until I do? No. Give what you have decided, and ask God to change your heart as you do. Feelings often follow obedience rather than leading it, and many believers have found that gladness came after they began giving regularly, not before. But do not be content with grudging. Bring the reluctance to God honestly; it usually points to fear about the future or love of something else. Meditate on Christ’s giving. And if you are giving out of pressure or guilt that is not from God, a manipulative appeal or a demand nobody has the right to make, you are free to decline it and give where you can give gladly.

For worship. God does not merely approve of cheerful givers; he is one. He gave light and called it good, gave Adam a garden with every tree pleasant to the sight, and gave his Son, to bring many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10). There is no wince anywhere in God’s giving. When he makes us cheerful givers, he is making us like himself.

parallels.desc: from every man whose heart moves him
the Greek Old Testament adds a line about God blessing a cheerful giver

verseByVerse.quote: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is able. Paul now supplies the reason a person can afford to give freely, in a sentence built of totality: all grace, all sufficiency, all things, all times, every good work. The question of capacity is settled, and it is his capacity, not yours. All grace includes the material, since the subject is money, but means every kind of blessing.

All sufficiency. The key word is autarkeia, sufficiency. Among the Stoic philosophers it meant self-sufficiency: the wise man who has trained himself to need nothing from anyone and is therefore untouchable, an admirable and rather cold ideal resting entirely on the individual’s strength. Paul turns the word inside out. The Christian lacks nothing, and his sufficiency does not come from within him at all. It is supplied. He has the freedom the Stoic wanted without the self-reliance the Stoic required. Paul learned it in both directions: I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content (Philippians 4:11), written from prison by a man who had been both well fed and hungry. Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6).

The secret is a person. The contentment had a name: I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13); My grace is sufficient for you (12:9). The all grace of this verse is finally the Lord Jesus himself, giving out of his own fullness, grace upon grace (John 1:16). His supply is never measured by our need but by his riches in glory in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:19). A man who has him can afford to open his hand.

Every good work. Then the purpose clause, left out when this verse is quoted on its own: not so that you may be secure, but so that you may abound in every good work. God gives to us so that he can give through us, as a farmer is kept in seed because there is more sowing to do.

The margin. Everyone has some margin: money, time, a spare room, a skill. The verse says the margin was supplied, and names what for. If it has been quietly reclassified as security, something has gone wrong in the accounting.

What if I give generously and then find I do not have enough? First, look at what God promises: sufficiency for every good work he calls you to, not freedom from all hardship. Paul himself knew both plenty and hunger (Philippians 4:12), and was content in both because Christ strengthened him. Second, God supplies through many means, including the generosity of other believers; that is the very point of 8:14, and you may need to receive as gladly as you once gave. Third, be wise: giving does not mean ignoring debts or your family’s basic needs (1 Timothy 5:8). But many who have given in faith testify that God has not let them down. Tell him your need plainly, and trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written. Paul quotes Psalm 112:9, a portrait of the man who fears the LORD and greatly delights in his commandments: gracious, merciful and righteous, unafraid of bad news. In the middle of the portrait stands this: he has distributed freely, he has given to the poor. Open-handedness is not an optional extra for generous temperaments. It is an identifying feature, listed alongside faith and courage.

Distributed freely. A scattering word, the farmer’s motion of verse 6: arm out, seed flung wide. Not measured allocation, but broadcast. God gives the same way: he scattered his kindness across the whole earth, sending rain on fields that never thanked him. And he gave his Son to the poor, to beggars like us, who had nothing to give back.

His righteousness endures forever. Then the phrase Paul is really after. In the psalm it is the man’s own righteousness: his standing as a God-fearing man, his settled character shown in his giving, and specifically the fact that it does not fade. Its fruit is eternal. And the point Paul draws from it is the contrast running through this whole chapter. The money went out and is gone; nobody can now point to it. What it produced does not go anywhere. The righteousness endures.

What survives. The savings will be spent by somebody. The house will belong to strangers. The estate will be divided and, within two generations, forgotten. The only portion that survives is the portion given away, as the Lord said: lay up treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matthew 6:20).

The portrait’s original. Psalm 111 says the very same words of God: his righteousness endures forever (Psalm 111:3). The righteous man of Psalm 112 reflects the righteous God of Psalm 111, and the psalm describes perfectly only one person: the one who gave to the poor to the point of having nothing, and whose righteousness endures for ever because it is the righteousness of God himself. Every generous believer reflects a little of him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving makes us righteous before God. It means generosity is a mark of the righteous life. Our righteousness before God is Christ’s alone, received by faith (5:21); the generous life is the fruit of it.

Should I give money to people who beg on the street? There is no single rule, and Christians who love the poor differ. Give with open hands and open eyes. Sometimes cash helps; sometimes, where addiction is involved, it feeds the very thing that is destroying someone.
