Often the best gift is food, a hot drink, your time and your name, treating the person as someone made in God’s image. Supporting local churches and ministries that know the people and can help wisely is often the most lasting way to give. Whatever you decide, do not walk past with a hard heart. Look the person in the eye, and remember who became poor for you.

parallels.desc: he has distributed freely; he has given to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seed and bread. This verse decides how verse 6 must be read. The words echo Isaiah 55:10, rain and snow giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater. Seed is given to be put back in the ground; bread is given to be eaten. Every farmer keeps them in separate sacks. Eat the seed and there is no crop next year; sow the bread and the family starves this winter.

A mercy in two directions. So the distinction is a mercy both ways. You are meant to eat: nothing here requires a Christian to give away everything and call the resulting destitution faith. And some of what you have was never meant for consumption. It is seed, and seed kept in the sack does nothing at all.

Multiply your seed. Not multiply your bread. The increase is on the sowing side of the ledger: God makes a generous person more able to give, which is not what most of us would have chosen if asked.

The harvest of your righteousness. The phrase comes from Hosea 10:12: sow for yourselves righteousness, reap steadfast love. Not the harvest of your prosperity or your standard of living, but righteousness: a godly life and its eternal fruit, more like the man of Psalm 112.

The whole offer. So the promise attached to generous giving in this chapter is exactly this: God will keep you supplied, he will enlarge your capacity to give, and he will make you a more righteous man. That is the whole offer. It is enormously generous, and it is not what is advertised on certain kinds of religious television, and the difference has cost poor and desperate people a great deal of money.

A harvest that comes through Jesus Christ. Paul prays that believers will be filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:11). The crop is not grown by willpower; it is Christ’s own life reproduced in his people by the Spirit, as branches bear the fruit of the vine (John 15:5). God is making the giver more like his Son, the one man whose whole life was sown for others.

How do I tell my seed from my bread? Bread is what you and your household genuinely need to live, work and fulfil your responsibilities: food, housing, clothing, transport, care for children and elderly parents, modest provision for the future. Seed is what is over and above that, given to you to sow. The line is not fixed, and godly people draw it differently, but the danger nearly always runs one way: we keep reclassifying seed as bread. A useful check is to ask whether your standard of living has risen with each increase in income while your giving stayed level. If so, some seed has gone into the bread sack. Decide the line in prayer, with your family, and review it regularly.

For worship. He supplies seed to the sower: he fills the bag before the man walks out to the field. The seed you scatter was put in your hand, the bread you eat was put on your table, and the harvest is grown by someone else entirely. Every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights (James 1:17).

parallels.desc: seed to the sower and bread to the eater

verseByVerse.quote: You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enriched. The sentence has a hinge, and everything depends on reading past it. Stop here and it sounds like a prosperity verse: God will make you rich. But for a purpose.

To be generous. It is the third time in four verses Paul attaches the same clause to the same promise (vv. 8, 10, 11). He will not let the promise stand on its own for a single sentence. God’s blessings are given to flow through us, not to stop with us.

A river, not a marsh. Take the picture behind it. A river is enriched by rainfall in the hills. It does not thereby become a lake. It becomes a river with more water going through it, and everything downstream is better for the rain that fell three counties away. Water that stops moving is not a richer river; it is a marsh, and it goes bad. That is the theology of Christian prosperity in one image, and it explains why the New Testament is so unembarrassed about God giving people more. There is nothing wrong with increase. The question is only ever whether it is passing through.

Where the increase went. Where did the increase of the years go? Usually it was absorbed, into a larger house or a better car, without a decision ever being taken, while the giving stayed where it was when the income was half. The guard is the deciding of verse 7, revisited whenever circumstances change.

Enriched in him. Paul has used this phrase to this church before: in every way you were enriched in him (1 Corinthians 1:5). Their riches came through Christ, at his cost: redemption through his blood, according to the riches of his grace (Ephesians 1:7). The first wealth in view is what is already theirs in Christ, and the money is the smallest part of it.

Thanksgiving to God. Follow the chain. God enriches the Corinthians; they give; Paul carries it; Jerusalem receives it, and thanks God. The money makes a complete circuit and returns to its source as worship, and most of it happens where you cannot see it.

Is it wrong for a Christian to enjoy nice things? No. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and gratitude for a good meal, a holiday or a beautiful home honours the giver. Jesus went to feasts and accepted costly perfume. The danger is not enjoyment but absorption: when every increase is spent on ourselves as a matter of course, when comfort becomes something we cannot give up, or when our hope quietly moves from God to our possessions. Enjoy God’s gifts with thanks, hold them loosely, and make sure the river is still flowing out as well as in.

For worship. From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory for ever (Romans 11:36). And the river has a spring: the river of the water of life, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb (Revelation 22:1). We are not the fountain, and we are not the sea. We are the riverbed, and it is a glory to be the place where his goodness passes through.

verseByVerse.quote: For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,
verseByVerse.commentary:
This service. Paul spells out what a collection accomplishes, and the list runs further than anyone would expect. The word for service is leitourgia, from which we get liturgy, used in the Greek Old Testament of the priests’ service in the temple. It makes giving an act of worship. Supplying needs is real, since people in Judea were hungry, and Paul never sneers at the practical. But he says it is the smaller half.

Offered through him. Why may a collection be called priestly service? Because there is a priest. Christ gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2), once for all. What believers bring now is never a payment for sin but a thank offering: spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5). A bag of coins is acceptable not because the sum is large but because it is brought by people who belong to his Son. Yet the God who receives it is the holy God who refused blind and lame offerings (Malachi 1:8, 10). We come gladly, but never casually.

Overflowing. The gift meets needs and multiplies praise: it does not stop when the need is met, but spills over into worship.

Approval. Literally, by the proof (dokimē) of this service: the gift proves the reality of the Corinthians’ faith. To feel the weight of that, remember the deepest fracture in the first-century church, between Jewish believers in Jerusalem and Gentile believers in cities like Corinth. Many Jewish Christians were unsure of a gospel without circumcision spreading among people who had never kept the law. There had been a council about it (Acts 15) and a confrontation between Peter and Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). The suspicion was mutual and serious.

Your confession of the gospel. Now picture what arrives: a bag of money, gathered over a year by Greek believers, most of whom had probably never seen Jerusalem, carried hundreds of miles at real risk, for Jewish Christians they will never meet. It proves that the confession these Gentiles make is not mere words: the gospel has gone in and changed what they do with their money. Submission here means obedience: their lives lining up under what their mouths say. And their confession of the gospel is what every believer says aloud, that Jesus is Lord and that God raised him from the dead (Romans 10:9). The money showed that they meant it. The Jerusalem believers, who might have doubted Paul’s converts, will conclude that God is genuinely at work among the nations, and praise him. Giving is evidence of genuine faith (James 2:15–17).

Contribution. The word is koinōnia: fellowship, sharing. The gift expresses unity with all believers, not only those in Jerusalem.

What argument cannot do. So the collection does what no argument could. Paul had made the case for Gentile inclusion at length, and arguments do not dissolve suspicion. Sacrificial generosity does: it is very hard to go on doubting the faith of people who have gone without so that you could eat. Christ has made Jew and Gentile one, reconciling both to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:16), and the bag of Greek coins carried up to Jerusalem was a small, glittering proof that the wall had really come down. That holds in every division a church knows, between generations, between congregations, between believers wary of one another for reasons half real and half inherited. Suspicion is rarely argued away. It is dissolved by someone being unmistakably and expensively kind.

If my giving proves my faith, how do I know I have given enough to be saved? You never give in order to be saved, and no amount could do it. Christ alone saves, and his gift was complete before you gave a penny (Ephesians 2:8–9). Paul calls the gift proof in the way fruit is proof that a tree is alive: the fruit does not make the tree live; it shows that it does. So if you look at your giving and find it thin, do not try to buy back your assurance with a larger gift. Go back to Christ, rest in what he has done, and ask him to make his grace overflow in you. Generosity grows best in people who are sure they are loved, not in people trying to earn it.

Is giving really part of worship, and should the offering be part of the service? Yes. Paul calls it leitourgia, a word used of priestly service, and elsewhere calls a gift a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Philippians 4:18). Do not neglect to do good and share what you have, says Hebrews, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God (Hebrews 13:16). Whether a church takes an offering during the service or gives by other means is a matter of wisdom, not principle. What matters is that giving is understood as an act of worship offered to God, not a fee for services or a slot between the songs. However you give, give as you pray: to him, with thanks.

In everyday life. Think of believers you find it hard to trust or understand: another tradition, another generation, another church in your town. Do something unmistakably kind for them this week, at some cost to yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They long for you. The last thing the money produces is the most personal. They long for you: the word is a strong one, yearning, an ache of affection. And it belongs to Jewish believers in Jerusalem, directed toward Greek strangers in Corinth. These are the two groups whose relationship had been the great unresolved strain in the early church, and Paul expects the outcome of a collection to be homesickness for one another. And pray for you: the people who received the money will spend themselves on the people who sent it. That is what happens when a gift is received rightly. It creates a debt of love that most naturally repays itself in prayer. On the night before he died Christ prayed for all who would believe, that they may all be one (John 17:21). When believers who have never met long for one another and pray for one another, that prayer of the Son is being answered.

What a sum of money did. It fed the hungry, produced thanksgiving, proved a doubted gospel, bound two suspicious communities together, and set one group praying by name for another. When giving feels like a standing order with nothing visibly happening, remember that most of its effects occur where the giver cannot see them.

The surpassing grace of God. Then the reason for their longing: not your generosity, but the grace of God in you. The Jerusalem believers see straight past the Corinthians to God, and grace in these chapters has a face: the Lord who became poor for their sake (8:9). That is the test that separates the Christian from philanthropy. Philanthropy leaves people impressed with the giver, which is why the names go on the buildings. Grace leaves people looking at God, and the giver is simply out of the way, the position every jar of clay was made to occupy (4:7).

How can I build real bonds with believers in another culture or country? Give to them, and then get to know them. Support a missionary or a church abroad, and ask for their news and prayer requests. Pray for them by name, regularly. Welcome international students and immigrant believers into your home. If you can, visit, to learn rather than to impress. Read about the persecuted church and write to prisoners for Christ. Receive from them too: their prayers, their example, their insight into Scripture. Love grows along the channels where gifts and prayers flow both ways, exactly as Paul hoped it would between Jerusalem and Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thanks be to God. Two chapters of timetables, delegates, audits and proportions end in an exclamation. He breaks off, as though he has looked up from the ledger and seen something.

In the flow. The section that opened with the grace of God given to the Macedonians (8:1) ends with thanks for God’s gift, so that every instruction about money sits inside grace. It is also the last calm word before the storm of chapters 10 to 13.

For his inexpressible gift! The word is anekdiēgētos: indescribable, a gift that cannot be told to the end. Not vague; so definite and so large that language runs out before the description does.

What the gift is. Paul has already named it, and the two chapters have stood on it throughout: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (8:9). The gift is Christ himself, God’s Son, given for us. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son (John 3:16). He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32)? That makes this the proper end of everything Paul has said about generosity. Decide in your heart, give in advance and in proportion, refuse pressure, finish what you started, keep the accounts clean: all useful, and none of it the engine. The engine is that God gave his Son, and that no one has ever got to the end of describing it.

Stop and try. Begin anywhere. The Word who was with God and was God, laid in a manger. The hands that made the world learning a trade. The one who had never been refused anything being refused a bed, a hearing, a friend. Follow it to the garden, and the whipping post, and the nails, and the darkness at noon, and the cry of a Son who had never been out of his Father’s sight. Then the morning, and the stone rolled away, and the wounds still in his hands so that they could be touched. Now add what it purchased: a debt cancelled that could never have been paid; enemies made sons and daughters; the Spirit of God taking up residence in ordinary people; a righteousness that is not ours credited to us as though it were; a resurrection body; a new heaven and a new earth; and, at the end of it, his face. Nobody has ever finished that sentence. The apostles did not, the church has been trying for two thousand years, and the people who see him will spend eternity discovering how much of it they had not yet understood.

How do I thank God for a gift I cannot even describe? Start where Paul does, with plain words: thanks be to God. You do not need eloquence; you need to look at Christ and say thank you, often and specifically. Name one part of the gift each day: his birth, his obedience, his cross, his rising, your forgiveness, your adoption, his Spirit in you, the face you will see. Sing it with the church; the hymns exist because one voice is not enough. Let it shape your life, so that your giving, your forgiving and your patience are thank yous too. And do not be troubled that your thanks always falls short. That is what inexpressible means, and eternity is long enough to go on trying.

For worship. The Father gave the Son. The Son gave himself. The Spirit gives him to us. Every other gift in these two chapters, the Macedonians’ coins, Titus’s eagerness, the prayers of Jerusalem, flows from that one gift as streams from a spring. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing (Revelation 5:12). Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints,<sup>2</sup>for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.<sup>3</sup>But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be.<sup>4</sup>Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.<sup>5</sup>So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.<sup>6</sup>The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.<sup>7</sup>Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.<sup>8</sup>And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.<sup>9</sup>As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”<sup>10</sup>He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.<sup>11</sup>You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.<sup>12</sup>For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God.<sup>13</sup>By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,<sup>14</sup>while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.<sup>15</sup>Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

10.title: Divine Weapons and Boasting in the Lord
10.overview:
With chapter 10 the tone changes sharply. Chapters 1–9 are warm and relieved; chapters 10–13 are a fierce defence against the visiting teachers Paul will call “super-apostles” and “false apostles”. Some scholars think these chapters were a separate letter, but no manuscript divides it, and Paul may simply turn here from the repentant majority to the minority still under the rivals’ influence.

The rivals mocked Paul as bold in letters but feeble in person. He answers in the meekness of Christ, with weapons that are not worldly but divinely powerful; he will be the same man in person as on paper; and he measures himself not by others but by the field God assigned him and the Lord’s commendation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Weapons of Divine Warfare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul appeals in the gentleness of Christ, hoping he will not have to be severe when he comes. He lives in a weak human body, but he does not fight with worldly methods; his weapons are God’s, and they pull down the fortresses of the mind.
verseByVerse.theology: The “weapons of warfare” in v. 4 are the ordinary means of gospel ministry: the word preached, prayer, transformed lives, the power of the Spirit. They are not impressive by worldly standards, but they are divinely powerful: God chooses the weak and foolish things to shame the strong and wise (1 Corinthians 1:27), so that the power is plainly his.
verseByVerse.examples: A church in a university town hires a communications consultant to help them “win the argument” with the secular culture. The consultant advises them to lead with culturally acceptable values rather than with gospel claims. This passage questions the strategy: the weapons that take thoughts captive to Christ are not clever messaging but the gospel itself, prayer and transformed lives.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!— I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapters 10 to 13 answer rival teachers at Corinth, men Paul will call super-apostles and false apostles, who boasted of credentials, eloquence and visions and mocked Paul as weak in person. The tone turns to warning and irony. Paul appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ; his warfare is spiritual, with divine weapons that take every thought captive to obey Christ (vv. 1–6). He will be the same in person as in his letters (vv. 7–11), and he boasts only within the field God assigned him, for only the Lord’s commendation counts (vv. 12–18).

A change of tone. For nine chapters Paul has been warm and relieved; from here to the end he is fighting. Some scholars think chapters 10 to 13 were a separate letter, but no manuscript lacks them or places them elsewhere. Likely he has finished with the majority who have come right, and turns to the minority who have not, and the men working on them.

I, Paul, myself entreat you. The pronouns pile up; some think Paul took the pen himself here. After this the letter is full of I where before it was largely we.

By the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Before a word of combat Paul names the character he intends to fight in. “Meekness” (prautēs) is the Lord’s own word: I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29), strength under control. “Gentleness” (epieikeia) is the forbearance of a ruler who has the right to press a charge and does not insist on its full severity. Put at the head of four chapters of self-defence, it governs how they are read. The gentleness his opponents mocked as weakness is Christ’s.

Humble face to face. Then the taunt, quoted with exasperation: tapeinos, which they meant as timid, brave on paper and small in the room. It lands near home, because almost everyone is bolder at a distance: the complaint made in the car is not made in the meeting, and the strong opinion typed at eleven at night would soften with a face across the table.

Not fierce in person. Paul’s answer is not to become fierce in person. The gentleness they mistook for cowardice was deliberate, and he asks them to make the confrontation unnecessary.

According to the flesh. The charge was that Paul acted by merely human motives and methods: self-interest, manipulation, the calculations of a man protecting his position.

Force with a hand on it. Paul’s restraint, gentle when he has every right to be severe, is what strength under control looks like, and it is why he began with the meekness of Christ. Meekness is not the inability to be forceful. It is force with a hand on it, and the one who models it had more than twelve legions of angels at his disposal and stood silent before Pilate (Matthew 26:53; 27:14). He had every right to come in judgment, and he came in gentleness. And his gentleness was never weakness: it held back the wrath of heaven while he bore it himself on the cross.

How can I be gentle without being a pushover? Gentleness is about how you use your strength, not whether you have convictions. Be clear about what is right and say it plainly; Paul never hides his view. But choose the gentlest means that will do the job, give people time and room to respond, and keep your temper on a lead. Hold your ground on truth and on protecting others, and yield freely on your own preferences and rights. A pushover gives way because he is afraid; a meek man gives way because he chooses to, and stands firm because he must. Ask, in each case: what would the Lord Jesus, who is both lamb and lion, do here?
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 10–13 answer rival teachers at Corinth who belittled Paul.

parallels.desc: Moses was very meek

verseByVerse.quote: For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flesh. He picks up their word and turns it over. Yes, he walks in the flesh, a jar of clay (4:7). But living in a body is not the same as fighting by the body’s rules.

The fortress above the city. Corinth sat beneath the Acrocorinth, a rock rising well over a thousand feet above the city with a fortress on top. When his readers heard the word stronghold, a fortress was not an idea but a fact on the skyline.

Fleshly weapons. Name what fleshly weapons would be: rhetoric, reputation, credentials, charm, political leverage, the ability to out-argue and out-manoeuvre. Precisely the arsenal Paul’s rivals carried, and what he keeps refusing to pick up. His weapons are the open statement of the truth (4:2), a gospel about a crucified man, prayer, righteousness (6:7; Ephesians 6:13–18), and a messenger who is manifestly not the source of the power.

My servants would have been fighting. The Lord Jesus fought this way first. Offered all the kingdoms of the world, he answered with nothing but Scripture (Matthew 4:8–10). Before Pilate he said, If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36). He told Peter to put away the sword and healed the wounded man (Luke 22:51). The King refused every fleshly weapon, conquered by dying, and rose. Paul is fighting the way his Lord fought.

Divine power. The power is God’s, lent to the weapons he ordained. Strongholds were fortified citadels (Proverbs 21:22), and verse 5 explains these: proud arguments and ideas that resist God. What does it look like when one falls? A man who has spent years explaining why God cannot exist hears the gospel of Christ crucified, and the Spirit opens his eyes, so that the wall he built comes down from the inside (4:6; Acts 16:14).

Where Christians differ: what are the strongholds? Some popular teaching takes strongholds to mean territorial demons over cities, to be bound by special prayer, or demonic footholds in a believer’s life to be cast out. Believers who speak this way are usually right to take spiritual evil seriously, and many of them pray with great earnestness; the question is only what this verse means. This commentary’s view: Paul defines the strongholds himself in verse 5: arguments and lofty opinions raised against the knowledge of God. The battle is for minds and hearts, fought with the truth of the gospel. Spiritual forces are real (Ephesians 6:12), but Scripture never teaches us to map or bind territorial spirits. Our weapons are the word, prayer and holy lives.

Does this passage license binding demons or breaking strongholds over cities? No. The strongholds Paul names in the next verse are arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God: false ideas, not demonic territories. The weapons are the truth of the gospel and prayer. Scripture does speak of spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12), but the believer’s part there is to stand, resist and pray, not to name and bind spirits over places. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7). If you want to see a city’s strongholds fall, preach the gospel in it, pray for it, and live holy lives among its people.

Do we actually believe it? The uncomfortable question this puts to the church is whether we actually believe it. It is a great deal easier to reach for the fleshly weapons, because they are visible and they work in the short term: the campaign, the polish, the political alignment, the personality who can hold a room. None is wicked in itself. But a church that has quietly swapped divinely powerful weapons for humanly impressive ones will find it has won some arguments and pulled down no strongholds at all. And the arithmetic runs the other way from what we expect. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27): a message about an executed provincial, carried by unimpressive people. That is not a handicap he graciously works around. It is the chosen instrument, and it has been levelling fortresses for two thousand years.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should use physical force to spread the faith. That is warfare according to the flesh.

Should Christians be involved in politics at all? Yes, as citizens, and many faithful believers serve God well in public life; Joseph and Daniel served pagan governments. Christians may vote, campaign for justice, protect the vulnerable and hold office, and they should do it honestly and with love for their neighbours. What this verse forbids is thinking that the kingdom of God advances by political power, or that the church’s mission is won by getting the right people elected. Laws can restrain evil; only the gospel changes hearts. Believers who differ over policy should not divide over it, and no party should be confused with Christ.

In everyday life. In the next difficulty you face, ask which weapons you are reaching for. If the honest answer is charm, pressure, cleverness or influence, put them down and pick up prayer, the plain truth spoken in love, and patient holiness.

For worship. The fortress on the Acrocorinth has long since fallen to ruins; the weapons Paul carried are still breaking walls, because their power is in the God who said, Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 4:6). He took the cross, the most shameful weapon of the empire, and by it disarmed the powers and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). The gospel of a crucified Saviour has outlasted every empire that despised it, and it will outlast ours.
verseByVerse.note: Strongholds were fortified towers or citadels.

verseByVerse.quote: We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We destroy arguments. Now we are told what the fortress is made of. “Arguments” (logismoi) are reasonings, the constructions the mind builds: intellectual and moral systems that resist God.

Every lofty opinion. Literally a high thing, probably a rampart or tower: pride lifted up against God, like Babel with its top in the heavens (Genesis 11:4). These are not merely mistaken ideas but structures whose function is to keep God at a distance. That explains something puzzling: the reasons a person gives for not believing are often genuinely held and still not the real reason. They are the wall, and the wall was built for a purpose.

Every thought captive. Two military verbs: he pulls down, and he takes prisoners. First the wall comes down, then the occupants are led out. Every thought: there is no province of human thinking with a treaty exempting it.

The knowledge of God has a face. Why captive to Christ? Because the light of the knowledge of the glory of God is in the face of Jesus Christ (4:6), and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). To bring a thought into obedience to Christ is not to make it smaller. It is to bring it to the one person who is the truth (John 14:6). To be his prisoner is to be at last at home in the truth.

Two applications. This verse is usually quoted about the private thought-life, the anxious spiral at three in the morning, the resentment rehearsed for the tenth time. That is legitimate, but it is the second application. Paul is describing his public ministry: the demolition of ideas that stand against the knowledge of God.

A programme for the whole mind. That makes this a vast intellectual programme, the opposite of anti-intellectualism. History, law, art, medicine, economics, the way you read a novel or run a business: all is territory Christ intends to hold, and the Christian mind is not smaller than the unbelieving mind but conquered, and therefore ordered.

Where Christians differ: how should Christians argue for the faith? Apologetics is the reasoned defence of the faith. Some approaches try to meet unbelievers on neutral ground, reasoning from shared premises toward God; others insist that the Christian must argue from Scripture’s view of the world from the start. This commentary’s view: No thought is neutral; all thinking either submits to Christ or rebels against him. Christians should reason carefully and use evidence (Acts 17:2–3; 1 Peter 3:15), but from a standpoint of submission to God’s revelation, not as if human reason were the final judge. The aim is not merely to win arguments, but to bring every thought captive to Christ. Faithful Christians who love Christ equally differ over method here, and the approaches often work together in practice: Paul himself reasoned from shared ground with the Athenians (Acts 17:22–31) without ever treating human reason as the judge of God.

How do I take a thought captive in practice? First, notice the thought for what it is, rather than letting it run unexamined. Then test it against what is true: is it what God says about himself, about Christ and about me? Then replace it, deliberately, with what is true, as Paul says: whatever is true, whatever is honourable, think about these things (Philippians 4:8). Take it to God in prayer, and if it returns, do the same again. An unwanted thought is not itself sin; it becomes sin when it is welcomed and fed. And where anxious or intrusive thoughts will not go, a believer should not be ashamed to seek help from a pastor or a doctor.

I have serious doubts about the faith. Is that rebellion against Christ? Not in itself. Doubt is often a question looking for an answer, and Christ is patient with honest questions; he showed Thomas his hands (John 20:27). Bring your doubts into the light: read, ask, talk to a mature believer, look at the evidence for the resurrection, and keep praying, even if the prayer is, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). The lofty opinion Paul tears down is different: a mind that has decided in advance that God must not be allowed to speak. Watch for that in yourself. Ask whether your doubt wants an answer, or wants an exit.

Is taking every thought captive not simply thought control? No, and the difference is who does the capturing, and how. Thought control is one sinner forcing his views on another by pressure, fear or force, and Paul has just renounced every weapon of that kind (v. 4). Christ captures minds by truth: he shows them what is real, and they bow freely because at last they see. And everyone’s thoughts are already held by something, whether a party, a culture, an appetite or the opinion of the crowd (John 8:34). The only question is which master, and only one of them is himself the truth (John 14:6).

The rampart in your own heart. Most of us have a stronghold: an area where we have built a high wall and decorated it with reasons. The relationship we will not reconsider, the habit with an argument attached, the part of Scripture we have found a way round. Those come down by the same weapons, and to the same Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ready to punish. The siege image runs into its last stage. When an ancient city fell, those who submitted were distinguished from the resistance that fought on. Most of Corinth has come in; a pocket has not, and Paul is ready to exercise church discipline when he comes (13:2, 10). Why would an apostle of the gentle Christ speak of punishment at all? Because the church belongs to a holy God, who disciplines his children for their good, that they may share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). Sin left alone in a congregation is an offence in his house.

When your obedience is complete. But not before. First the church as a whole must return; then Paul can deal with the troublemakers with the church on his side. Acting too early would force people to choose sides and drive the undecided into the wrong camp. All through the letter he has given them room and time (1:23; 2:3).

Patience with a plan. That is not avoidance. Avoidance hopes the problem will dissolve; Paul says plainly in advance that he intends to act, which is itself a mercy. Timing is most of the skill: a confrontation that would split a congregation in March can sometimes be handled almost quietly in September, once the issue is no longer a contest between factions.

Obedience to whom. Paul frames the whole affair not as loyalty to himself but as obedience to Christ, the Lord he is under too (1:24). That keeps discipline from becoming a power struggle, and it is the first thing lost when a leader begins to feel opposition as a personal injury. The question is never whether they are with me, but whether they are obeying Christ.

I gave her time to repent. The risen Christ does the same with his churches. Of a false teacher in Thyatira he says, I gave her time to repent (Revelation 2:20–21). Time first, then judgment: patience that is real, and a warning that is meant. He walks among the lampstands now, never hasty and never careless, and his discipline always aims at complete obedience, freely given, to himself. And the same Lord who will punish every disobedience has already borne the punishment of every disobedience of his people on the cross. His justice and his mercy meet, and neither is ever late.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wants to punish. He wants obedience. Discipline is a last resort. Nor does patience mean delay where someone is in danger; where there is abuse or a threat to the vulnerable, protection cannot wait for a better season.

Does church discipline still happen today, and what is it for? It should, though many churches neglect it. Jesus laid down the steps: go privately, then with one or two others, then tell it to the church, and only if the person still refuses to listen, treat him as an outsider (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul applied it in Corinth (1 Corinthians 5). Its aims are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church, the protection of others and the honour of Christ, never revenge or the leaders’ pride. It is for serious, unrepented sin, handled slowly and humbly, with the door always open to return, as 2:6–8 shows. A church that never disciplines is not kinder; it simply leaves people to their sin.

In everyday life. If you have authority in a home or a church and trouble is brewing, ask God for wisdom about timing before you act. And ask him to make your own obedience complete. In this life it never will be; Christ’s already is, and it is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and his Spirit is at work in you to bring yours on.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul belongs to Christ as much as his rivals, and his authority was given to build up, not tear down. He will be the same in person as in his letters. He refuses to measure himself by comparison, keeps to the field God gave him, and waits for the only approval that counts, the Lord’s.
verseByVerse.theology: The Lord’s commendation (v. 18) is the basis of all true authority in ministry. The super-apostles rested theirs on letters of recommendation (3:1), an impressive presence, skill in speaking, and visions and revelations (12:1). Paul rested his on God’s call (Galatians 1:1), the fruit of his ministry (the changed Corinthians, 3:2), and finally the Lord’s own assessment. This does not make Paul self-certifying; it means his legitimacy is determined at the bar of heaven, not at the bar of human opinion.
verseByVerse.examples: A minister with a large platform cultivates an online presence that constantly showcases his ministry’s results: attendance figures, conversion stories, speaking engagements, endorsements from well-known figures. He tells himself he is building credibility for the gospel. This passage asks whether he is building the gospel’s credibility or his own, and whether his confidence rests on the Lord’s assessment or on the metrics of human comparison.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at what is before your eyes. Blunt and slightly weary: either a command, face the plain facts, or a diagnosis, you look only at outward appearances (5:12).

If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s. The rival teachers evidently claimed to belong to Christ in some special way, perhaps through links with Jerusalem, perhaps through visions and revelations.

So also are we. Paul does not deny their claim; he simply says that whatever they are, he is too. That is a very controlled response from a man who could have said a great deal more, and it is the meekness of Christ in operation.

Belonging by purchase. What does it mean to be Christ’s? Not to hold a credential or a vision, but to be owned: you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Every believer belongs to Christ in exactly the same way, bought with the same blood, which is why Paul can answer so calmly. Nobody can be more Christ’s than another, and nobody needs a special experience to prove it (1 Corinthians 3:22–23).

For building you up. The parenthesis is a key New Testament sentence about authority in the church. The authority is real: Paul has it from Christ and does not apologise. It is given, not seized, so it is held on someone else’s terms. And it has a stated purpose and limit: construction, not demolition (13:10).

Not for destroying you. The irony is deliberate: four verses of siege warfare, and now his authority is not for destroying. The demolition is aimed at the strongholds, never at the people. He tears down arguments to build up the person who was living behind them.

A simple test. Any Christian with responsibility can apply it, as an elder, a parent, an employer, a husband: after you have exercised authority, is the other person more built up or less? Not, were you right? You may have been entirely right and still used the truth as a wrecking ball. Authority given for building up cannot be used to destroy without ceasing to be what it was given as. A man who crosses that line is no longer exercising the authority Christ gave; he is exercising something else and using Christ’s name for it.

I will not be ashamed. His claim will be vindicated. Paul is content to let the Lord who gave the authority judge how it was used.

What if a church leader is using his authority to destroy people? Then he has stepped outside the authority Christ gave, and it must not be tolerated. Do not stay silent out of misplaced loyalty. Speak to him if it is safe, and then to the other elders or the wider church or denomination, taking a witness (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Where there is abuse of any kind, protect the vulnerable first and report it to the proper authorities; spiritual authority never overrides the law or the safety of the weak. Leaders are to shepherd willingly, not domineering over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:2–3). If a church will not deal with it, you are free to leave and find a faithful one.

For worship. All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to the Lord Jesus (Matthew 28:18), and he uses every ounce of it to build: I will build my church (Matthew 16:18). He tore down the dividing wall, tore the veil of the temple, tore apart the bars of death, all to build a house for God out of living stones. The one with all authority came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Frightening you with my letters. Paul does not want his letters seen as threats from a safe distance. Then he quotes his critics directly, a cruel thing preserved in their own words.

Weighty and strong. The concession is the setup: they grant the letters their force to make the contrast land harder. The letters are still read today, in more languages than his enemies ever heard of.

Bodily presence. He was evidently unimpressive to look at: perhaps small, worn, marked by beatings. A second-century writing outside the Bible describes him as short, balding and bow-legged; it cannot be verified. His speech of no account: literally despised, in a Greek city where public speaking was the highest art. Paul had told them himself that he came in weakness and fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:1–4).

And it worked. The charge, he can write but cannot hold a room, worked because it was partly true (11:6). Paul does not deny it. He quotes it, and moves on to whether the authority is real.

Crucified in weakness. Paul’s deepest answer comes near the end of the letter: Christ was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God, and we too are weak in him (13:4). The weakness the critics despised was the message, written on his body: the death of Jesus carried about, so that the life of Jesus might also be shown (4:10). The Corinthians were looking for a man who looked like power. They were being shown a man who looked like the cross. The Lord whom Paul served had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2). The glory of God came into the world in a body nobody would have picked out of a crowd, and finished his work on a cross where they mocked him as weak.

For the unimpressive. Some people are simply not impressive in the way a room rewards. The voice is wrong, the manner awkward, and the right sentence comes to them in the car afterwards. They have watched someone with half their faithfulness heard twice as attentively, and concluded that God uses other people. Perhaps the most fruitful missionary in the history of the church was despised as a speaker. God did not correct the assessment. He went on using the man, because the treasure was never the jar (4:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not speak well. Acts shows him as a powerful speaker, before crowds, councils and kings. It means he refused the showy techniques the Corinthians admired.

Should churches not want gifted, attractive speakers? Gifts are good, and a preacher should work hard to speak clearly and well; Apollos was eloquent and was a blessing (Acts 18:24–28). The danger is making polish the measure. Choose and judge preachers first by faithfulness to Scripture, godliness of life and love for people (1 Timothy 3:1–7; 2 Timothy 4:2). A plain man who opens the Bible faithfully will feed a church for decades; a brilliant one who does not will starve it while it applauds. And listen to sermons for the word of God in them, not for the performance.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized impressive physical presence and polished oratory.

verseByVerse.quote: Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let such a person understand. The address is singular and slightly cold: probably the ringleader, addressed without being named, which is both a courtesy and a warning.

The same man. The charge was a gap between the written Paul and the present Paul. His answer is that there is none. And he does not promise to be more forceful than they expect; he promises consistency, which is a larger claim. The letters have been gentle as well as firm: he has begged, wept and appealed by the meekness of Christ. All of that will be true in the room as well. He is not warning them that a harsher man is coming; he is telling them the same man is coming, as firm in action as in writing, and as gentle.

Always Yes in him. Paul met this charge before, about his travel plans, and his answer then shows where his consistency comes from: the Son of God was not Yes and No; in him it is always Yes (1:19–20). A man who preaches a Christ with no double-dealing cannot afford to be two men himself. His integrity is borrowed from the faithfulness of his Lord. What Jesus said to the crowds, he said to the Pharisees; what he was on the mountain of transfiguration, he was in the boat with the frightened disciples and on the cross with the dying thief. The Word became flesh, and the flesh was exactly what the Word had said.

Two people. Modern life has industrialised this failure. Almost everyone is now two people: the one who writes and the one who is present. Things are typed that would never be said, in a tone that would collapse if the other person were in the chair opposite. And the respectable version runs the other way: warm and agreeable in person and quietly devastating about the same person elsewhere, a different man in each room.

Undividedness. Integrity means undividedness: being one person. The man who is the same in the letter and in the room can be believed the first time, every time, and no ministry or marriage lasts long without that foundation.

I have already written something I would never say to the person’s face. What now? Go back and put it right. If what you wrote was untrue, unkind or exaggerated, delete it where you can and apologise to the person directly, and to anyone else who read it, without excuses. If it was true but should have been said in person, go and say it in person, gently. If it was about someone rather than to them, stop the conversation it started. Then set yourself a rule for next time: write nothing about anyone that you would not be content for them to read with you sitting beside them. Confession and repair are the way back to being one person.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not that we dare. What is wrong with his rivals is not first their doctrine but their measuring system. He opens with heavy irony, and everyone reading heard the smile in it.

Measuring by one another. They are the ruler and the thing being measured. Nothing external enters the calculation, so the result is always satisfactory: a closed circle of mutual admiration, and, Paul says, without understanding, because it guarantees you will never learn anything true about yourself.

The measure of the stature of Christ. Paul names the true ruler elsewhere: the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13). Beside it every comparison collapses, because nobody comes out ahead of him and everybody comes out needing him. And grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Ephesians 4:7). To resent another believer’s portion is to quarrel with Christ’s distribution.

How comparison works. Here the passage stops being about first-century opponents, because comparison is the water most people swim in. You do not compare yourself with everyone; you select, unconsciously, a group near enough to be relevant and arranged so that you come out somewhere acceptable. The effect is one of two things, both ruinous. Either you come out ahead and are quietly pleased at being better than someone rather than at anything real. Or you come out behind, and something corrosive begins: diminishment, resentment of a person who has done you no harm, the sense that your own work does not count. Neither tells you a single true thing about yourself, because the measurement never touched the real standard.

Where it bites now. A generation ago a person compared himself with the families in his street. Now he does it several times a day with the edited lives of the most photogenic people on earth, and feels a failure at something he was never in a contest about.

How do I actually stop comparing myself with others? You cannot simply stop; you have to change the ruler. Measure yourself by Christ and his word, which humbles you and frees you at once. Remember that your field is assigned by God (vv. 13–14), so another person’s gifts and results are not a verdict on yours. When you notice comparison starting, turn it into prayer: thank God for the other person’s gifts, and ask him for faithfulness in your own task. Limit what feeds it, which for many people means less time scrolling through other people’s edited lives. And rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15); it is the surest cure for envy.

For worship. The Lord Jesus did not come to rank us but to save us. The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other men, or even like the tax collector, who would not lift his eyes and begged for mercy; and it was the tax collector who went home justified (Luke 18:11–14). Before this Saviour there is no top rung to reach and no bottom rung to fear, only a cross where everyone kneels at the same height.

verseByVerse.quote: But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not beyond limits. Having refused the comparison game, Paul says what he measures by instead.

The field God assigned. Area of influence is kanōn: a measuring rod, then the boundary marked out with one, the allotted plot. God gave Paul the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9); he did not pick Corinth from a list. He was given a plot, and he intends to be assessed on that plot and nowhere else.

The size of your field. If God assigns the field, its size is neither your achievement nor your failure. A man given four acres who works them well has done what a man given four hundred has done, and the accounting will be per acre. The small congregation is not a lesser version of the large one. The years given to caring for one dependent relative are not a career that did not happen.

A restraint as well as a comfort. A man who knows his boundary markers does not need a view on every controversy, nor to feel guilty about every good work he is not doing. Many an exhausted Christian is failing at nine things because he was only ever given three.

The work you gave me to do. The Son of God himself kept to an assigned field: sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24), within a small land, leaving the nations to the apostles he would send. And he could say, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). Faithfulness to the given field is the shape of the Saviour’s own obedience.

To reach even to you. Corinth is within that field; Paul is not claiming territory that is not his.

The first to come. He came on from Athens, worked at a bench with Aquila and Priscilla, and stayed eighteen months, founding the church (Acts 18:1–11). The rivals came later, to a church already standing.

How do I know what field God has assigned me? Look at what he has already put in your hands. Your field is made of your relationships, your gifts, your responsibilities and your opportunities: the family you belong to, the church you are a member of, the work you do, the neighbours you have, the needs you can actually meet. Ask what you are uniquely placed to do that no one else is. Listen to mature believers who know you. Pay attention to open doors (1 Corinthians 16:9). Begin there, faithfully, rather than longing for someone else’s field. If God enlarges it later, he will make it plain; for now, the plot you are standing on is the one he gave you.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The labors of others. They had come to a church somebody else planted and taken the credit, like a man moving a boundary stone in the night (Deuteronomy 19:14) and then showing visitors round a field he never cleared.

Not only a first-century problem. A man arrives at a work built over thirty years by someone tired and unfashionable, makes some improvements, and lets it be understood that things really began when he came. It is rarely a lie, only a matter of emphasis, and the person who did the clearing cannot say anything.

As your faith increases. Paul does not ask for a larger field. He asks that their faith grow, and expects his scope to be enlarged as a consequence, because a strong church releases its workers instead of absorbing them. That is the right way round; the usual shape of ambition is a man wanting a bigger platform and hoping his people will supply it.

Lands beyond you. He wants Corinth strong so that he can leave; they are a base, not his destination. He tells the Romans he means to go on to Spain, making it his ambition to preach the gospel not where Christ has already been named (Romans 15:20–24, 28).

Other sheep I must bring. I have other sheep that are not of this fold, Jesus said; I must bring them also (John 10:16). Paul would speak only of what Christ had accomplished through him (Romans 15:18). The pioneer missionary is not ahead of Christ, clearing a way for him. He is following a Shepherd who is already calling his sheep by name where nobody has yet heard the name of Jesus. The lands beyond are not an afterthought; they are the Father’s gift to his Son.

Work already done. The rivals travelled to places where the church was already gathered; Paul travelled to places where nobody had heard of Jesus. Both are moving; only one is advancing. Does a ministry ambition want a share of what already exists, or the gospel to reach somewhere it has not been?

What it does not mean. It does not mean only pioneer work matters. Others water what pioneers plant (1 Corinthians 3:6), and Paul is glad of Apollos. It means no one should take credit for another man’s planting.

What are the lands beyond for an ordinary Christian today? There are still thousands of people groups with little or no access to the gospel, and many neighbourhoods near you where hardly anyone knows a believer. You may not be called to go to Spain, but every Christian can help the gospel move outward. Pray regularly for unreached peoples by name. Give to missionaries and church plants going where Christ is not known. Welcome people from other nations who have come to your town. Consider whether God might send you. And begin with the lands beyond your own circle: the colleague, the neighbour, the family member who has never heard the gospel explained.
verseByVerse.note: Paul hoped to go on to Rome and Spain.

verseByVerse.quote: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boast in the Lord. The chapter ends where the argument has been going, with a quotation Paul had already used in his first letter (1 Corinthians 1:31). It comes from Jeremiah, and he expects his readers to hear the whole: let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practises steadfast love, justice and righteousness in the earth (Jeremiah 9:23–24). All legitimate boasting is in what the Lord is and has done.

Move the object. Brains, strength and money are still the three. Jeremiah does not tell his readers to stop boasting; we are built to admire and to say so. He tells them to move the object, from things that cannot bear the weight. The religious heart has a fourth item it rarely notices: its own goodness, the prayers said, the years of service. That cannot bear the weight either, because our best deeds are like a stained garment (Isaiah 64:6), and the only righteousness worth boasting of is the one Christ gives (Philippians 3:9).

Wisdom, might and riches in one Lord. When Paul first quoted this line to Corinth, he had just said that Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:30–31). Jeremiah’s three objects of pride come home in him: the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the riches of the poor (8:9). Boasting in the Lord is pointing at Jesus Christ and saying that everything worth mentioning in my life is in him.

Approved. The assayer’s word again. A man can commend himself brilliantly and be worthless; he can be despised as a speaker, dismissed by the church he founded, and be approved.

Whom the Lord commends. It is the Lord who judges me; then each one will receive his commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:4–5). If your sense of yourself rests on the assessment of the room, this verse takes it away. If it rests on his, every unfair verdict passed on you is provisional, and the review is scheduled.

In the flow. This also explains the strange boasting that follows: in chapter 11 Paul will speak as a fool, and when he boasts at last, it will be of his weaknesses, where Christ’s power rests (11:30; 12:9).

Is it wrong to accept praise, or to list my achievements in a job application? No. Receive praise graciously with a simple thank you, and quietly give the glory to God in your heart; refusing all thanks can be its own kind of pride. Stating your experience truthfully on a CV is not boasting in the sinful sense; it is giving honest information. What Paul condemns is self-commendation as a way of life: seeking a reputation, inflating your record, needing others to be impressed, and measuring your worth by what people say. Tell the truth about what you have done, never exaggerate it, and keep reminding yourself who gave you every gift you have (1 Corinthians 4:7).

For worship. The commendation Paul is waiting for has already been secured, and not by him. He is approved because he is in Christ, who was made sin for him (5:21). The Father has said of his Son, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased, and in Christ that pleasure rests on us. When everything currently being compared has been forgotten, the only opinion left standing will be his. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this

11.title: The Fool's Speech and the Catalogue of Suffering
11.overview: In this chapter Paul does something he finds distasteful: he boasts. The rival teachers in Corinth commended themselves loudly, with their Jewish pedigree, eloquence, visions and fees, and the Corinthians were impressed. So Paul plays “the fool” for a while, borrowing their method to expose it. He fears for the church as Eve was deceived, defends his free preaching, unmasks the rivals as false apostles, and then lists not his successes but his sufferings, ending in a basket over the Damascus wall. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Jealousy for the Corinthians and the False Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s motive is a godly jealousy for a church promised to Christ as a bride. He answers the charge that preaching free of charge made him inferior, and names his rivals for what they are: false apostles, disguised as Satan disguises himself.
verseByVerse.theology: Calling the false apostles servants of Satan (v. 15) raises the question of how to recognise them, since they come disguised. The letter supplies three tests: the content of the message, the character of the minister, and whether the ministry bears the shape of the cross. Paul’s opponents failed all three.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation is attracted to a visiting teacher who is eloquent, radiantly confident, and preaches a message of spiritual empowerment, prosperity and supernatural experience, all framed in Christian language. The pastor cannot point to an obviously heretical statement. This passage gives him the test: not whether Jesus is mentioned but which Jesus, which spirit, which gospel. The angel-of-light disguise means the most dangerous false teaching often looks impressively spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 11 is Paul’s fool’s speech: he borrows the super-apostles’ boasting to expose it. His motive is a godly jealousy for a bride promised to Christ (vv. 1–6); his refusal of payment marks him off from false apostles disguised as servants of righteousness (vv. 7–15); and his boast is a list of sufferings ending in a basket over the Damascus wall (vv. 16–33). The glory belongs to Christ, and the servant who looks least impressive may look most like him.

A little foolishness. Paul is about to do something he finds distasteful, and he apologises before he starts. “Foolishness” (aphrosynē) is his name for boasting about himself, which he will call speaking not as the Lord would (v. 17). Do bear with me! is the tone of a father who would rather not raise his voice, asking his children to let him say something hard.

A divine jealousy. The reason he is willing to look ridiculous is not wounded pride: he is jealous for them with God’s own jealousy. Jealousy is a vice in most ordinary uses and a divine attribute in Scripture, and the difference is what is being defended. Envy wants what belongs to someone else; this jealousy guards what already belongs to you and is being taken. A husband who feels nothing when his wife is being drawn away does not love her more than a jealous man; he loves her less. So the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Exodus 34:14), and Hosea heard him promise an unfaithful people: I will betroth you to me for ever (Hosea 2:19–20).

Since I betrothed you to one husband. A Jewish betrothal was not a modern engagement. It was legally binding, ended only by divorce, though the wedding and the home-coming came later. Paul, the church’s spiritual father, promised the Corinthians to Christ when they first believed, and regards the promise as his responsibility until the wedding.

The friend of the bridegroom. That is the role Paul claims: the friend of the bridegroom, who in Jewish custom helped arrange the match, watched over the bride through the betrothal, and finally presented her to the husband. John the Baptist described himself the same way, whose whole joy was to hear the bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29). Paul is not the husband, but he is answerable for the bride until the day arrives.

A pure virgin. At Christ’s return, the wedding day, the church will be presented to him (Revelation 19:7–9). This congregation, divided, suspicious, easily impressed by the wrong men, is a bride being kept for a wedding. What does a pure bride mean for a church? Not a congregation with no sinners in it, for no such church exists, but one whose love and trust belong to Christ alone, and whose teaching has not been mixed with another gospel (v. 4). Purity here is faithfulness: a heart kept for one Husband and from every idol (1 John 5:21).

The Husband who paid the bride-price. And the wedding is Christ’s idea from first to last. Paul only made the introduction. It was Christ who loved the church and gave himself up for her, to make her holy, so that he might present the church to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). The bride-price was his own blood. He chose her while she was still unlovely. He is coming for her, and he has never once changed his mind about the arrangement. And on the day the friends of the bridegroom finally hand her over, she will be without spot or wrinkle, not because she kept herself so, but because he washed her, and he will look at her and be satisfied. That is why Paul’s jealousy is not fussiness: the bride being courted by rivals in Corinth belongs to a Husband who died for her, and Paul cannot bear to see her flirt with another Jesus.

Is jealousy ever right for me? Yes, when it guards something that truly belongs to you and to God, and when it is aimed at the danger rather than at the person. A husband or wife may rightly be jealous for the marriage when a third person is drawing one of them away; a parent may rightly be jealous for a child being pulled toward something destructive; a pastor may be jealous for his people. But test it. Godly jealousy wants the other person’s good and faithfulness to Christ; sinful jealousy wants control, suspects without cause, and resents another’s good gifts. The first speaks openly and prays; the second spies, sulks and punishes. If yours looks like the second, it is not God’s jealousy, whatever it calls itself.

Is the church the bride, or am I? Both, in the right order. The bride in Scripture is the whole church, the one people Christ loved and gave himself for (Ephesians 5:25). You are not a separate bride in a crowd of brides; you belong to her, as one member of the body she is. That guards against two mistakes: a sentimental individualism that forgets the rest of the church, and a cold collectivism that forgets that Christ knows each of his own by name. What is true of the bride is true of you because you are in her, and the faithfulness Paul is anxious about is yours too.
verseByVerse.note: In a Jewish betrothal the bride was already bound to her husband-to-be, and her purity was guarded until the wedding; Paul pictures himself in that guardian role.

parallels.desc: I will betroth you to me forever

verseByVerse.quote: But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am afraid. The apostle who has told this church he has complete confidence in them now says he is frightened for them, and the two are not a contradiction: a father can be sure of a child and lie awake about him in the same week.

As the serpent deceived Eve. Once again Paul reaches back to Genesis 3. The serpent, whom Scripture later names as Satan (Revelation 12:9; compare v. 14), deceived Eve with clever words that twisted God’s word. The word Paul uses for his method is panourgia: craftiness, cunning. Deception of this order is patient, plausible, and it works with the grain of what the hearer already half wants to believe.

How the deception worked. Everyone remembers the fruit and forgets the method. The serpent did not arrive denying God. He arrived asking a question: did God actually say? He opened a small gap between what God had said and what God had meant, then offered a better reading of God’s motives, that he was holding something back. By the time he flatly contradicted, saying you will not surely die, the ground was prepared. That is still the pattern. Error rarely begins with a denial. It begins with a question that makes the plain word sound naive. The serpent’s whole strategy was to make God look stingy, and the gospel is God’s answer to that slander: the God who was accused of withholding the fruit did not withhold his own Son.

The Husband who did not stand by. Genesis says her husband was with her (Genesis 3:6). He watched his bride being talked out of God’s word and said nothing. The New Testament calls Christ the last Adam (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:45), and here the contrast is at its sharpest. The first husband stood by while the serpent seduced his bride; the second gave himself up for his bride to make her holy (Ephesians 5:25–26). He does not leave her alone with the serpent’s questions. He answers them, and he holds her. That is what makes the devotion Paul wants simple: it is the plain love of a bride for the Husband who did what Adam would not.

Sincere and pure devotion. The word for led astray means corrupted, seduced, ruined, and the danger comes to the mind through teaching. But what Paul is afraid of losing is not first their orthodoxy, but their devotion. The word behind sincere is haplotēs, the singleness met at 1:12: simplicity, being one thing rather than two. The word behind pure means chastity, the faithfulness of a betrothed bride. Some manuscripts omit and pure, as the ESV’s footnote notes; the meaning is not affected, because both words describe the same undivided heart. The danger is a divided heart, adding something to Christ or quietly replacing him.

The love you had at first. That fear is worth taking personally. The danger to a Christian is rarely that he will one day decide Christianity is false. It is that the plain love of Christ gets crowded, by other loyalties and by a sophistication about the faith that leaves less warmth in it than at the beginning. Nobody renounces anything; the devotion simply stops being single. The Lord said as much to the church at Ephesus, doctrinally sound, hard-working and patient: “you have abandoned the love you had at first” (Revelation 2:4).

What it does not mean. Simple devotion is not simplistic thinking: Paul, one of the most demanding thinkers in the New Testament, means undivided loyalty: a mind that may grow as deep as it likes, so long as it stays fixed on one Lord.

Is Paul saying women are more easily deceived? Not here. In this verse Eve stands for the whole church, men and women alike, and the warning is addressed to every reader in Corinth, most of whose leaders were men. The point of the comparison is the method of deception and the bride’s danger, not the sex of the one deceived. Paul does draw on the order of creation and the fall when he speaks about teaching in the church (1 Timothy 2:13–14), and that passage has its own place, but it is never a licence to treat women as gullible. Adam, standing beside her, was not deceived and sinned anyway, and Scripture lays the fall at his door (Romans 5:12).

How do I keep my devotion simple? By keeping Christ himself at the centre of the means God gives, not merely the activities around him. Read the Gospels regularly, so that you know the Lord’s own face and voice and not only doctrines about him. Pray to him, not only about things. When you sit at the Lord’s Table, remember him rather than yourself. Watch what you allow to compete for the first and last thoughts of your day. And when you notice that the faith has become a complicated arrangement of opinions, projects and causes, go back to the cross and look at what he did there. Love is kept simple by looking at the one you love.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another Jesus. Three things can be counterfeited: a Jesus, a Spirit, a gospel. In every case the counterfeit keeps the word. Nobody arrived in Corinth announcing a new deity; they preached Jesus. Same name, different person. The rivals seem to have preached a Jesus without the cross, perhaps a triumphant wonder-worker whose servants should be impressive, or a Jesus who required law-keeping. Every counterfeit is a smaller Christ: a teacher without a cross, a wonder-worker without wounds, a helper without a throne. The real one is more than all of them together, the eternal Son who took our flesh, bore our curse, broke out of the grave and reigns.

A different spirit. Not a second Holy Spirit; there is only one. Paul means the spirit that animates a false gospel, a spirit of pride, power and spectacle, which enslaves rather than frees (Romans 8:15; Galatians 1:6–7). The Holy Spirit produces humility and love, and his delight is to lift up the crucified Christ, not himself (John 16:14). That is why John says, test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John 4:1).

A different gospel. A message other than the gospel of grace through Christ crucified. Paul told the Galatians that even if an angel from heaven preached such a thing, he should be accursed (Galatians 1:6–9). A gospel is not a different gospel because it uses different words; it is a different gospel because it tells a different story about what is wrong with us and what God has done about it.

So how would you know? The name is unchanged, the vocabulary is unchanged, and the man preaching is impressive. This is the practical question the verse exists to answer, and the whole letter has been supplying the tests. Ask what this Jesus did. The real one was made sin for us and bore the wrath our sin deserved (5:21). A Jesus who is chiefly an example, a teacher, a life-coach or a source of personal power is a different Jesus, however warmly he is spoken of. Ask what this Jesus asks. The real one calls people to die to themselves and no longer live for themselves (5:15). A Jesus who asks nothing that costs anything has been substituted. Ask what the message does with the hearer’s sin. The genuine gospel names it and then deals with it at the cross; a message that never mentions it is not a gentler version of the gospel but a different one, because it leaves the hearer with his actual problem untouched.
