And ask what kind of ministers it produces: does the messenger bear the shape of the cross, or has he been made comfortable, admired and rich by the message he preaches?

You put up with it readily enough. Then the sting, aimed at the Corinthians rather than the teachers. It is irony, you put up with them easily, so put up with me, but it is also the heart of the crisis. The tolerance is the danger. A church that would argue for an hour about the seating plan sat quietly while the identity of its Lord was adjusted.

Where Christians differ: another Jesus. Many groups use the name of Jesus while teaching a different person: a created being, a mere prophet, a spirit brother of Satan, a teacher of self-improvement. This commentary’s view: The true Jesus is the one the apostles proclaimed: eternal Son of God, fully God and fully man, crucified for our sins, risen bodily, Lord of all. Any Jesus who differs from the apostolic Jesus is another Jesus, and any gospel that adds to or subtracts from grace through faith in him is another gospel (Galatians 1:8). Christians must test teachers by Scripture (1 John 4:1–3).

How do I tell a secondary disagreement from another gospel? Ask whether the difference changes who Christ is or how a sinner is put right with God. Believers who love the same Lord differ on the mode and subjects of baptism, on the details of the end times, on church government, on worship styles, and those differences matter, but they do not make another Jesus. Denying that Christ is fully God and fully man, denying his bodily resurrection, denying that his death paid for sin, or teaching that we are justified partly by our own works: these change the person or the gospel, and that is where Paul draws the line. A useful question is this: if the other person is right, would my hope before God be different? If not, it is a family disagreement; if so, it is a different gospel.

What if my church begins preaching another Jesus? Do not simply drift away in silence, and do not stay in silence either. First make sure you have understood correctly: listen carefully, read what is taught, and compare it honestly with Scripture. Then speak to the leaders privately and humbly, asking them to show you from the Bible why they teach what they teach. If the error is real and persistent and touches the person or work of Christ, you have a duty to protect yourself and your family, and you should find a faithful church where the apostolic Jesus is preached. Leave without bitterness, and keep praying for those you leave behind.

How can anyone say that someone else’s Jesus is the wrong one? Not by his own preferences, which would indeed be arrogant. But Paul is not comparing opinions; he is measuring every later account against the Jesus the eyewitnesses proclaimed (v. 4; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Jesus is a real man of history, not a mirror in which each person sees what he likes. To say that a Jesus who did not die for sins or rise from the dead is not the real one is no more arrogant than saying a biography has the wrong man. And humility runs the other way: the proud thing is to remake Jesus to suit ourselves. The Christian claims no credit for knowing the truth; he was blind until God opened his eyes (4:6).

In everyday life. Test what you hear about Jesus, from a pulpit, a podcast or a song, by Scripture. The best protection is not suspicion but knowing the real one well enough that the substitute sounds wrong, as bank clerks, the saying goes, learned forgeries by handling the genuine note.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Super-apostles. The word is probably Paul’s own coinage and it drips: hyperlian apostoloi, literally the extra-super apostles, the more-than-apostles. It is the tone of a man repeating a title other people use with a straight face.

Who were they? Not, on balance, the Jerusalem apostles. Paul has no quarrel with Peter and James here and would not speak of them like this. These are most likely the newcomers in Corinth, the same men he will call false apostles in verse 13, and the title is either their own or the impression they had created: men who claimed a status above Paul’s.

Unskilled in speaking. Then a remarkable concession. The word is idiōtēs: a layman, an amateur, a man without professional training. He is granting the charge of 10:10. In a Greek city, where public speaking was the prestige skill of the age, that was no small thing, and he lets it stand.

I am not so in knowledge. He simply moves the contest to different ground. Not cleverness in general: knowledge of God and of the gospel, the mystery of Christ revealed to him (Ephesians 3:3–4), the thing he has spent ten chapters unfolding.

The knowledge of Christ crucified. And what Paul knows is finally not a subject but a person: the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (4:6). When he first came to Corinth he resolved to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2), and he refused clever rhetoric, he told them, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power (1 Corinthians 1:17). A crucified Saviour sold with technique becomes one more product on the market; preached plainly, he does his own persuading. God has never needed the world’s eloquence. He spoke creation into being with a word and saved the world through a Word made flesh, who had no form or majesty that we should look at him.

Two separate gifts. Speaking well and having something worth saying are different gifts, and they do not always come together. An audience cannot easily tell them apart, which is why an articulate man with a thin message will generally be preferred to a plain man with a deep one, and the preference is called good communication.

Made plain. Whatever he lacked in polish, nobody in Corinth could say they had failed to understand him. That is a better ambition for anyone who teaches, and a harder one. Being admired is easier than being understood, and the two are often confused.

Should I choose a church for its preaching style? Choose it first for what is preached. Ask whether the sermons open the Bible and say what the passage says; whether Christ crucified and risen is at the centre; whether you are being fed, corrected and comforted by God’s word rather than entertained. Style is not nothing: a preacher should work hard to be clear, and a dull sermon is no virtue. But a plain man who handles the Scriptures faithfully will do your soul more good over ten years than a brilliant speaker with little to say. If your pastor is not gifted as an orator, thank God for his faithfulness, and listen for the substance.
verseByVerse.note: “Super-apostles” is Paul’s ironic name for the rival teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted? Now the strangest accusation in the letter: Paul must defend himself for not charging them money. The question is bitter on purpose, the shape of the complaint thrown back at them. Humbling myself means his manual labour as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), a lowly trade in Greek eyes, so that they might be lifted up by the gospel.

How Corinth read it. In a Greek city, teachers of standing were supported, by fees or by a wealthy patron who housed them and gained prestige from the association. Payment was the mark of worth; a man who worked with his hands was a tradesman, and manual labour carried real social contempt. So his refusal was read in two damaging ways: either his teaching was not worth paying for, or, worse in that culture, he was refusing the relationship of obligation a gift creates, holding people at arm’s length.

Because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? Was that a crime (1 Corinthians 9:12–18)? The phrase God’s gospel matters. It was not his to sell. The message that cost God his Son was offered in Corinth without a price tag, and the messenger made sure his own conduct said the same thing.

Humbling myself so that you might be exalted. Paul’s phrase is the gospel in miniature, and he knows it. Christ, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant and humbled himself to death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8); though he was rich, he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (8:9). Paul’s long hours at the workbench, night and day (1 Thessalonians 2:9), were a small, deliberate copy of that descent. Paul preached the Christ who stooped, and stooped himself, so that his hands preached the same sermon as his lips. A minister who insists on being lifted up has told the church what he thinks of a Lord who went down.

I robbed other churches. The word is a military one: to plunder, to strip a defeated enemy. Yes, he says, I took money; I took it from Macedonia and spent it on you. He did not steal; he accepted gifts from poorer churches, desperately poor ones (8:2), so that he could serve the richer Corinthians free.

A right he declined. This was a right he declined, in this city, for a reason. Where money bought influence and created obligation, taking it would have compromised the gospel and given his rivals a way to claim equivalence. He removed the stumbling block (6:3) at real personal cost.

Should my pastor be paid? Yes. Scripture is clear that those who labour in preaching and teaching are worthy of their wages (1 Timothy 5:17–18; Galatians 6:6), and a church that underpays its pastor while expecting all his time is not imitating Paul but disobeying Paul. Some ministers rightly work another job, by necessity or by choice, as Paul did in Corinth and as many church planters and pastors of small congregations do today; that is honourable, not second-class. The point of this passage is the motive and the effect: money must never buy influence over the message, and a minister must be willing to give up his rights when they would hinder the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I did not burden anyone. He was not comfortable: there were times in Corinth when he did not have enough, and still he did not ask. The rare word means to weigh on someone like a dead weight.

Supplied from Macedonia. The money came from Macedonia, most likely Philippi. Silas and Timothy arrived from there while Paul was in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and the Philippians sent to him repeatedly, which he acknowledges warmly (Philippians 4:15–16). The poorest churches in the region were funding the apostle’s work in the richest city he served, so that the rich church would not have to pay and could not say it had.

Not silenced in Achaia. Then the vow, put under oath. He intends to go on refusing their money and to go on saying so (1 Corinthians 9:15). That sounds stubborn until you see what it protects. If Paul once accepted support in Corinth, the distinction between himself and the men who had come for what they could get would collapse, and with it the one visible proof that he was not in this for gain.

The truth of Christ is in me. Look at what Paul swears by. Not heaven or the temple, but the truth of Christ living in him. The one who called himself the truth (John 14:6) has taken up residence in this man; it is no longer Paul who lives, but Christ who lives in him (Galatians 2:20). His honesty rests not on his own reputation but on the Lord who indwells him. That is also why his refusal to be a burden is more than policy. Christ came not to be served but to serve, and the life of Christ in a man shows itself, as it did here, in a servant who would sooner go hungry than lean his weight on the people he came to help.

The cost of an unimpeachable position. Paul’s policy did not make his life easier. It made him poorer and more tired, and it was used against him anyway. He kept it because the gospel’s credibility was worth more to him than his comfort or his reputation. Most such decisions are invisible and unrewarded: the businessman who loses the contract rather than pay what everyone pays, the minister who will not let a major donor into the decision.

Was Paul wrong to swear an oath, when Jesus said do not swear? No. The Lord was forbidding the casual oaths people used to make their ordinary words sound weightier, and the games of swearing by lesser things so that the oath did not really bind (Matthew 5:33–37). He was not forbidding every solemn appeal to God in a serious matter: God himself swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13), and Jesus answered under oath at his trial (Matthew 26:63–64). Paul calls on the truth of Christ in him because his honesty is under attack and the gospel’s honour is at stake. Christians may take a lawful oath when the matter is weighty and the occasion requires it (the Westminster Confession 22.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 23.2), but their everyday yes should be simply yes.

Is it wrong to accept a gift that comes with strings? A gift given freely in love should be received with thanks, and refusing it out of pride is no virtue. But some gifts are not really gifts: they buy access, silence, influence or a favour later. Ask what accepting it would imply to the giver and to others, and whether it would make you less free to do what is right. If it would, decline it graciously and, where you can, explain why. Paul’s rule was simple: whatever would hinder the gospel, he would rather do without.

verseByVerse.quote: And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why? Because I do not love you? He answers the obvious misreading before it can be spoken. Some said Paul refused their money because he did not care about them, and in that culture refusing a gift looked exactly like that: to decline hospitality was to decline a relationship.

God knows I do! His answer is not an argument but a short sentence with God as witness. Some things cannot be demonstrated to people who have decided otherwise, so he states it and moves on.

Love that refused the easy proof. Paul is walking a road his Lord walked first. Christ’s love, too, was read as its opposite. At the cross they mocked him: he saved others; he cannot save himself (Matthew 27:42). He could have silenced every doubter in a moment, and he stayed, because he had come to save them, not himself. Paul’s refusal of Corinthian money is a small shadow of that. He declines the thing that would make him look loving, because accepting it would hurt the people he loves, and he lets God be his witness. Love that copies Christ will sometimes look, for a while, like the absence of love.

To undermine the claim. He will keep preaching free of charge, because the reason for it has not gone away. The rivals took payment and wanted parity. They wanted to be able to say: we operate on exactly the same terms as Paul, so judge us as you judge him. And the one thing that made the comparison impossible was the money. So long as Paul worked for nothing and they took payment, the difference was visible to everybody, and no amount of talking could close it. His empty purse cut the ground from under them: an argument no rival could answer without becoming what he was pretending to be.

What should I do when people I love think the worst of me? Say the truth once, plainly and without heat, as Paul does here. Then stop arguing. Commit your reputation to God, who knows, and go on doing good to the people who misjudge you, which over time is the only answer that persuades. Examine yourself honestly in case some of the criticism is true, and own that part. Do not withdraw your love to punish them, and do not keep a ledger of the injustice. The Lord who was misread more than anyone entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For such men are false apostles. After twelve verses of irony Paul simply says what these men are, in three descriptions, each worse than the last. False apostles, pseudapostoloi, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament, perhaps coined for the occasion.

Deceitful workmen. “Deceitful” (dolioi) means crafty, treacherous, working by trickery. They are workmen: skilled, busy, productive. The problem is not incompetence but craft.

Disguising themselves. The verb means to change one’s outward form, to put on an appearance, to masquerade. They look like apostles, but are not. Paul does not call them sincere men who have gone wrong. They may not know whose servants they finally are (v. 15), but they know they are posing.

An angel of light. No wonder: this is the pattern working as it always has, and it is not what most people imagine. The popular picture of evil is darkness, something obviously repellent, which is precisely why the real thing gets through. Satan’s most effective form is not the monster but the angel of light: the impressive, the luminous, the manifestly spiritual, the thing that looks better than what you already have. His most dangerous tactic is to imitate truth.

Discernment cannot run on instinct. If you are waiting to feel uneasy, you will be caught, because the disguise is designed to produce the opposite feeling. So the test can never be how did it make me feel? It has to be the one Paul gave in verse 4: which Jesus, which Spirit, which gospel. Those are questions of content, which an ordinary Christian with a Bible can answer without any special sensitivity at all.

The light he counterfeits. Whose light is Satan imitating? This letter has already told us. The god of this world blinds unbelievers to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God; and the God who said let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (4:4–6). The true light is Christ’s own glory. So the angel of light is a forger of Christ, and his ministers are forgers of Christ’s apostles. Satan can only borrow light; Christ is the light, and every disguise will be stripped off on the day he appears. And the test of any bright thing is simple. Does it show me the face of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, or does it show me something else that glows?

Does Satan really appear as an angel? The point here is disguise rather than visions: Satan’s usual angel of light is a teacher, a message, a movement that looks holy. But the warning also covers the spectacular. Paul told the Galatians that even an angel from heaven preaching another gospel is to be rejected (Galatians 1:8). So a vision, a voice, a dream or a miracle proves nothing by itself. God’s revelation is complete in Scripture, and every claim to a new word from God must be tested by what he has already said, and refused if it adds to it or contradicts it. Christ’s sheep are not kept safe by experiences; they are kept by his voice in his word.

Can I call someone a false teacher without being harsh? Yes, and you should be careful to. Be sure of the facts, and judge the teaching by Scripture, not by rumour or by a clip taken out of context. Keep the label for what touches the gospel itself. Speak about the teaching more than the person’s motives, which only God sees fully. Warn those who are in danger, because love for them requires it. And pray for the teacher, because he too can be rescued. Paul is severe here because a church is being lost; he is never cruel, and he never enjoys it.

verseByVerse.quote: So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His servants also. If the master appears as light, his servants will appear as righteousness; the disguise runs all the way down. Satan has his ministers, diakonoi, the same word Paul uses of himself and of true servants of Christ. They talk of righteousness, perhaps law-keeping, morality or holiness, but they are his.

Servants of righteousness. Not disguised as scholars or men of power, but as morally serious people. In a religious community that is the most effective camouflage, because a man visibly rigorous about right and wrong is granted enormous latitude.

Severity that looks like holiness. The counterfeit is very often more demanding than the genuine article, not less. The Judaizers in Galatia, teachers who insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, wanted more law, not less. The false teachers of Colossae wanted more self-denial. Some severity is a bid for control: such rules have an appearance of wisdom in self-made religion and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:23).

The righteousness they counterfeit. What are these men imitating? Paul has told the Corinthians that his own work is the ministry of righteousness, which far exceeds in glory the ministry of condemnation (3:9), and he has told them what that righteousness is: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (5:21). The true servant of righteousness hands out a righteousness that is not his own, the righteousness of Christ given to sinners who have none. That gift is justification: the guilty pardoned and accepted as righteous, on no ground in themselves, but because Christ’s obedience and death are reckoned to them and received by faith alone (Romans 4:5; Philippians 3:9). The gift does not make holiness optional, for the same grace that acquits a sinner also makes him new (Romans 6:1–4; Titus 2:11–14). The counterfeit hands out demands. That is the surest way to tell them apart. One leaves you looking at your own performance and wondering whether it is enough; the other leaves you looking at Christ, crucified for you, and knowing that it is.

Their end will correspond to their deeds. First, there is an end, telos: final judgment. The disguise works now and will not work then; everything currently persuasive about these men has a date attached to it (Philippians 3:19; 2 Peter 2:1–3). Second, the correspondence is to deeds, not appearances, the exact reversal of Corinth, where appearance was carrying everything. Behind that one line stands the holiness of God. His eyes are too pure to look on evil (Habakkuk 1:13), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). A disguise can fool a congregation for years; it cannot survive a moment in his presence, where everything is naked and exposed (Hebrews 4:13).

The restraint. He says it in one line and stops, without gloating or threats. The accounts will be settled by a Judge who will do right, and that is what frees a man to speak plainly and then let the matter go.

Can a false teacher repent and be saved? Yes. While a man lives, the door of repentance is open, and Paul himself is the proof: the fiercest enemy of the gospel became its greatest preacher. He tells Timothy to correct opponents with gentleness, in the hope that God may grant them repentance and they may escape from the snare of the devil (2 Timothy 2:25–26). So we warn against the teaching firmly, and we pray for the teacher sincerely. What we may not do is pretend the danger is small, or assume that a man who dies still leading others astray will be excused.

Should I listen to false teachers to understand them? Most Christians do not need to, and many should not. If you are not responsible for answering a teaching, there is little gain in feeding on it, and real danger, because the disguise is designed to work. Pastors and those who must protect others may need to study it carefully, and should do so with prayer, with good guides and with their Bibles open. For everyone else, the best protection is to know the true gospel deeply and to stay close to a faithful church. You do not have to taste every dish to know which one is poisoned.

In everyday life. If you have been hurt by a leader who used righteousness as a weapon, take comfort: their end will correspond to their deeds, and you do not have to arrange it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — The Fool’s Boast and the Catalogue of Sufferings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul boasts under protest, as a fool, because the Corinthians put up with leaders who enslave and strike them. He matches the rivals’ pedigree, then outdoes them as a servant of Christ, not in achievements but in sufferings and in the daily care of the churches. The speech ends in an anticlimax: a basket let down from the wall of Damascus.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of sufferings is Paul’s chief credential. His opponents proved themselves by impressive experiences and social standing; Paul offers a body worn out in service. The one who preaches a crucified Christ must bear in his body the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor has served for 25 years in a declining neighbourhood with little visible breakthrough. When a search committee from a larger church comes to interview him, they ask about his “greatest ministry successes.” He does not know what to say. This passage suggests a different category: faithfulness in hardship and daily care for the congregation are the apostolic credential. The question “what have you built?” is not the only or even the primary question.

verseByVerse.quote: I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I repeat, let no one think me foolish. Three verses of throat-clearing before the fool’s speech proper, and the hesitation is the point. Paul is not really a fool; he is playing a part, and he wants everyone to know it is a part.

Accept me as a fool. Paul adopts the rivals’ style of boasting in order to expose it, and calls it foolishness. In ancient drama the fool could say what others could not, and Paul takes up the role deliberately. If the Corinthians insist on weighing men by their boasts, he will give them a boast to weigh, and they will not like what is in it.

Not as the Lord would. He says it as plainly as it can be said: what follows is not how a Christian should ordinarily talk. Boasting about oneself is not Christlike, and Paul does it under protest. The only person who ever had the right to boast never did it for himself. Christ, the Word who was with God and was God, the maker of the stars, emptied himself and took the lowest place, and the Father boasted of him instead: this is my beloved Son. That candour says something about Scripture: Paul is inspired to record that he is about to do something beneath the gospel.

I too will boast. According to the flesh means about worldly credentials and achievements. The alternative was worse: if Paul stayed silent while impressive men listed their credentials, a church would be lost to a different gospel. So he enters a contest he despises, in order to win people out of it.

Answer a fool according to his folly. There is a genuine pastoral principle here, easily misapplied in both directions. Sometimes the only way to reach people is to meet them briefly on their own ground: to answer, as one of Proverbs’ two facing maxims puts it, a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes (Proverbs 26:5). What keeps Paul’s tactic from becoming worldliness is that he says out loud what he is doing and why. The misapplication is the church that adopts the world’s methods for the world’s reasons and calls it strategy, and is enjoying itself. Paul plainly is not.

Detonated from the inside. He takes the conventions of ancient self-praise, ancestry, achievements, hardships nobly borne, and fills them with floggings, shipwrecks, hunger, and an undignified escape in a basket. He does not win the contest; he blows it apart from the inside.

The road sign. The fool’s speech is built to end somewhere, and Paul has already said where: let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (10:17). The only boast he is truly allowed is Christ, and so he enters the world’s game in order to steer it to the one place it cannot go: the cross, the foolishness of God that is wiser than men (1 Corinthians 1:25). He will boast of the things that show his weakness (v. 30), because his weakness is where the power of Christ shows (12:9).

Is it ever right for me to talk about my achievements? Yes, when there is a real need and the aim is not your glory. A job application, a reference, a report to the people you are accountable to, a testimony of what God has done: all of these may require you to state plainly what you have done. Paul does it here to protect a church. The test is the motive and the manner. Are you saying it because someone needs to know, or because you need to be admired? Do you say it truthfully, without inflation, and give God the credit? And can you stop once the need is met? If you find you are always steering conversations toward your successes, that is the boasting Paul calls foolish.
verseByVerse.note: Paul adopts the rivals’ style of boasting to expose it, calling it foolishness.

verseByVerse.quote: For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being wise yourselves! The irony turns savage, and it is aimed at the congregation. Corinth prided itself on discernment; the earlier letter is full of their confidence about knowledge and wisdom. You are so wise, he says, that you happily put up with fools, and these connoisseurs have been sitting contentedly under men he has just called servants of Satan. Then a list of five things they have put up with in that room.

Makes slaves of you. Someone had taken control: over consciences, over decisions, over what could be questioned. The false apostles were enslaving them, governing their lives in a way Paul had refused to do (1:24).

Or devours you. The word is used of eating something up, and it is about money. These teachers were consuming the church’s resources, demanding payment and living on it. The Lord used the same word of the scribes who devour widows’ houses (Mark 12:40).

Takes advantage, puts on airs. The first verb simply means takes, and here, as in 12:16, it means catching someone out: exploitation dressed up as ministry. Puts on airs is literally lifts himself up: the manner of a man who has let it be known that he is a considerable person, and that you are fortunate to have him.

Or strikes you in the face. And here the list may stop being metaphorical. Someone may have physically hit a member of that congregation, or it may be a figure for public humiliation; either way, it is abusive leadership. That is the whole indictment: a church that would not tolerate an apostle who worked with his hands, and did tolerate a man who slapped them.

Why people submit to it. Why do people submit to domineering leaders and resent gentle ones? Confidence is easily mistaken for authority: a man who behaves as if he has the right to treat you badly creates the impression that he must have it. Being under a strong figure relieves the burden of thinking. And harshness feels like seriousness, so a leader who is hard on people seems more committed to the truth. One man founded the church and refused its money; the others enslaved it, ate it, and struck it, and the Corinthians could not tell which was the apostle.

It shall not be so among you. They should have been able to, because the Lord had settled the question. When his disciples argued about greatness he told them that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and it shall not be so among you; whoever would be great must be your servant, for even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:42–45). Christ’s authority is the most absolute there is, and he used it entirely for the good of those under it. So the measure of a leader is not how firmly he holds people but how closely he resembles the King who gave his life for them.

What does spiritual abuse look like? It is the use of spiritual authority to control, exploit or harm people. Its marks are often the five in this verse. Control: you may not question the leader, and doubting him is treated as doubting God. Exploitation: money, time or bodies are taken for the leader’s benefit. Manipulation: guilt, fear and shame are used to get compliance. Self-exaltation: the leader is beyond correction and surrounded by people who protect him. Humiliation: people are shamed in public, isolated or frightened. Physical harm or sexual misconduct is not spiritual abuse only; it is a crime. A godly leader can be firm, but he will always welcome questions, admit his faults, protect the weak, and point you to Christ rather than himself.

What should I do if I am being abused by a church leader? Tell someone you trust, outside his circle of influence, and do not carry it alone. If you are in danger, or a crime has been committed, go to the police; that is not disloyalty to the church but obedience to God, who appointed the authorities to protect the vulnerable (Romans 13:4). Bring it to the other elders, or to the wider body the church belongs to, and put what has happened in writing. You may need to leave, and it is not a sin to do so. Abuse is never to be tolerated or covered up in the name of peace or forgiveness. Forgiveness does not require you to stay within reach of harm, and Christ is never honoured by a church that protects the wolf instead of the sheep.

Doesn’t the Bible tell me to submit to my leaders? Yes, to leaders who keep watch over your souls as those who will have to give an account (Hebrews 13:17). That submission is real, and a healthy church will gladly follow godly elders without needing everything explained. But it is not unlimited. Elders are commanded not to domineer over those in their charge but to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3). No leader may bind your conscience beyond the word of God (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2), command you to sin, or demand obedience that belongs to Christ alone. The more a leader insists on his own authority, the more carefully you should ask whether he is exercising Christ’s.

For worship. The Lord of the church is the Good Shepherd, and the Good Shepherd is the opposite of the man in this verse. He does not enslave; he sets free. He does not devour; he feeds. He does not take advantage; he lays down his life. He does not lift himself up; he washed his disciples’ feet. He did not strike anyone in the face; he gave his own face to those who struck him and spat on him. Every bruised sheep can run to him, and he will carry it in his arms.

verseByVerse.quote: To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Too weak for that! One line, and among the sharpest in the letter. Paul has just listed five ways the Corinthians have been mistreated, and now, with mock contrition, he apologises for never having managed any of them. Too weak to enslave you, to eat your money, to hit anyone. They had called him weak (10:10); if gentleness is weakness, he admits it.

What makes it defensible here. Scripture contains sarcasm: Elijah suggested Baal might be asleep (1 Kings 18:27). Paul’s is not aimed at the weak but at people in comfortable error who have stopped listening to plain speech. It defends others rather than himself. And it comes after ten chapters of tenderness, so nobody could mistake it for his settled attitude: sarcasm from a habitually gentle man is a shock; from a habitually sharp one it is just his manner.

The weakness of the crucified. Underneath the irony is a real definition of strength, and Paul learned it at the cross. Christ, the letter will say, was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God (13:4). By Corinth’s measure the cross was the weakest moment in history; by God’s it was the strongest, for there the power of sin, death and the devil was broken. Real strength is the capacity to be wronged and not retaliate, to hold power and decline to use it for oneself. When Paul says he was too weak to enslave them, he is confessing that he had been made to resemble his Lord. The Lord Jesus was the strongest man who ever lived, and the gentlest. He had the power to destroy his enemies with a word and used it to heal the ear of a man who came to arrest him.

May I use sarcasm? Rarely, and with great care. Scripture shows it can serve the truth, but James warns how much damage the tongue can do (James 3:5–10), and Paul elsewhere says our speech should always be gracious (Colossians 4:6). Ask the questions Paul’s use passes. Am I defending someone else, or protecting my pride? Is it aimed at comfortable error, or at someone weak or hurting? Would the person know I love them? And is it my habit, or a rare exception? Never use it on your children, your spouse, or anyone who is struggling. If you are known for a sharp tongue, the safest course is to put it away entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they Hebrews? The fool’s speech begins in earnest, and the rhythm is a drumbeat: three questions, three identical answers. So am I. The rivals were Jewish Christians who boasted of their pedigree, and each word carries a different weight. Hebrews is the language and culture claim: not merely Jewish by birth but Hebrew- or Aramaic-speaking, perhaps from Palestine, raised in the tradition rather than assimilated into the Greek world. Paul was entitled to it; he tells the Philippians he was a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), and Luke records him addressing a Jerusalem crowd in Aramaic to their evident surprise (Acts 21:40–22:2).

Are they Israelites? So am I. This is the covenant claim: members of the people God chose, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law (Romans 9:4; 11:1).

Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I. The promise claim: heirs of the man to whom God swore that in him all nations would be blessed. Paul matches them three times without elaborating, and the flatness of the repetition is doing the work. He is refusing to make a speech about it. Whatever they have, he has, and there is nothing more to say.

Why he does not dismantle it here. Elsewhere, when the same credentials were being used to bind Gentile Christians to the law, he took them apart: he listed his pedigree in full and then counted it all as loss, as rubbish, for the sake of Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). Here the rivals are not, as far as we can tell, demanding circumcision; they are trading on prestige. So Paul simply refuses them the advantage and moves on to the ground where the real difference lies.

The offspring of Abraham. Yet the third claim holds more than the rivals meant by it. The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and the offspring, singular, is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Every Hebrew, Israelite and son of Abraham was a branch of a family tree that existed for one Man, and from that family, according to the flesh, came the Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever (Romans 9:5). Everything Israel was meant to be, he was. So a pedigree is worth exactly what it is worth in him. If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29), and if you are not, no ancestry can make you so.

A contest that ends in a tie. A contest of credentials always ends in a tie, because credentials can be matched. Paul is about to show them that the question was never what a man has been given, but what he has been willing to lose. And every heart keeps such a list. The religious one reads: raised in the church, sound in doctrine, faithful in attendance. The irreligious one reads: decent, tolerant, kinder than most. Both are attempts to stand before God on a record, and both fail for the same reason: no record of ours can stand before a holy God, and the only one that can is Christ’s, given to those who trust him (Philippians 3:9).

Does my Christian upbringing count for anything? It counts as a gift, not as a credential. To be raised in a believing home, to have learned the Scriptures early, to have been prayed for by name: these are great mercies, like Timothy’s, who knew the sacred writings from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15). Thank God for them. But they do not make you a Christian, and they give you no standing above someone converted last month from a life of open sin. Each of us stands before God only in Christ. And if you came to faith with no background at all, you have lost nothing that matters: the newest believer is as fully a child of Abraham by faith as the oldest member (Galatians 3:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they servants of Christ? The fourth question breaks the pattern. The first three got so am I; this one gets I am a better one. Here Paul does not merely match them. They claim to serve Christ, and on that ground, the only ground that matters, he will not concede a tie.

Talking like a madman. He immediately interrupts himself. The word means out of one’s mind, stronger than fool: he has moved from foolishness to raving, and he can hear himself. But he does not take it back, because it is true.

Labours, imprisonments, beatings. Everyone in that room expected achievements: churches planted, miracles worked, revelations received. He lists what has been done to him: his proof is not success, but suffering. Imprisonments: at Philippi (Acts 16:23), and others not recorded. Near death: often (1:8–10). Every item carries an intensifier. The beatings were beyond measure; the next verse counts only the official ones, five floggings and three beatings with rods.

The measure of a servant. A diakonos waits at table, and Paul’s claim is that the measure of such a man is not what he has accomplished but what he has absorbed. We measure by output, because output can be counted and photographed; Paul measures by cost. On his accounting, the most useful servant in a congregation may be someone with nothing whatever to show: who has kept turning up, kept forgiving, kept praying for a family member for thirty years, and has been quietly worn down by it.

The shape of the Master. The accounting is the shape of the Master. The Lord’s own ministry, measured by output at the moment it ended, looked like a failure: about three years, a handful of followers, and nearly all of them scattered by Friday morning. What he had was what had been done to him, and it saved the world. That is why Paul can call his scars proof that he serves Christ. They are not his own achievement but a share in his Lord’s sufferings: not in their atoning work, which Christ finished alone, but in the hostility the world still aims at him through his people. As we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, he wrote at the start of this letter, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (1:5). The servant looks like the Master because he is united to him, and the marks of a true servant of Christ are the marks of the cross. Paul’s scars were the marks of his Master, and his Master’s scars are the price of our peace.

Should I seek out suffering to prove my faithfulness? No. Paul never went looking for beatings; he went looking for people to preach to, and the beatings came. Christians are not called to court persecution, to make themselves difficult in order to be opposed, or to treat hardship as a ladder to holiness. We are called to follow Christ wherever he leads, and to accept the cost when it comes rather than trimming the message to avoid it. If you are free from persecution, thank God for it and use the freedom well. The question is not how much you have suffered, but whether you would be willing to.

If my life is fairly easy, am I a lesser Christian? Not because it is easy. God appoints different measures of hardship to different servants, and it is not a competition (John 21:21–22). Many faithful believers live quiet lives without beatings or shipwrecks. But every Christian life has a cost somewhere: the sin you refuse, the opinion of others you give up, the time and money you give away, the patience you keep with a difficult person. Ask whether your faith is costing you anything at all. And use your ease for those whose life is not easy: pray for particular persecuted churches, and give to support them.

verseByVerse.quote: Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty lashes less one. This is the synagogue punishment. The law permitted forty strokes and no more (Deuteronomy 25:3); Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could never break the command. The victim was bound, stripped to the waist and struck with a strap; later Jewish law describes a third of the strokes on the chest and two thirds on the back. Men died of it. Five times: that is 195 strokes. This was the punishment a synagogue administered to its own. To receive it, Paul had to have submitted himself to the synagogue’s jurisdiction, walked in again, knowing what had happened the last four times, because his own people were there and he would not stop going to them first. He accepted their discipline rather than abandon them.

Three times I was beaten with rods. This is the Roman punishment, carried out by officials called lictors, and it was illegal to inflict it on a Roman citizen. Paul was one, and said so at Philippi, after the beating (Acts 16:22–23, 37). Acts records that occasion; the other two are nowhere else in the New Testament.

Once I was stoned. At Lystra. The crowd stoned him and dragged him out of the city supposing he was dead, and he got up and went back into the town (Acts 14:19–20).

Shipwrecked. None of these is the famous shipwreck of Acts 27, which had not happened yet. So there were at least four. And that short clause covers twenty-four hours in the open sea, probably clinging to wreckage, waiting. He who held Paul through a night and a day in the deep is the Lord who walked on the sea and commands the wind and waves.

What Acts leaves out. Acts gives us one beating with rods out of three and none of the five floggings: a book about Paul that leaves out most of what happened to him. The account you have of anyone is partial, and the hardest parts are usually the parts left out. People in your church are carrying things that would not appear in any summary of their lives, and the God who keeps the real record has not mislaid a single stroke of it.

Why are you persecuting me? Before his conversion Paul beat believers in the synagogues (Acts 22:19), and the risen Lord counted every blow on his people as a blow on himself (Acts 9:4); now the same Lord counts these strokes too, for Paul suffers in union with him. (See Acts 22:7 for the fuller answer.)

Why did God let this happen to his best servant? Because he was making Paul like his Son, and making the gospel visible through him. The Lord had said at the start that he would show Paul how much he must suffer for the sake of his name (Acts 9:16). The beatings were not God’s neglect but his appointment, and every one of them was limited: Paul was struck down but not destroyed, carried through each one until his work was done (4:8–10). Through his scars churches were planted, and through his letters written in chains we still read the gospel. God does not waste the suffering of his people. He does not always tell us why, but he always knows, and he never lets go.
verseByVerse.note: The law allowed up to forty lashes; the synagogues gave thirty-nine to be sure of not exceeding it. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment. The shipwrecks were before the one described in Acts 27.

parallels.desc: Paul stoned at Lystra
beaten with rods at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On frequent journeys. Paul travelled perhaps ten thousand miles in the course of his ministry, much of it on foot. Then the word danger eight times in a single sentence: the sound of a man reciting a life.

In danger from rivers, danger from robbers. The ordinary hazards of ancient travel: unbridged rivers deadly in flood, and mountain roads in Asia Minor notorious for bandits.

Danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles. Then the list turns human, and covers everybody. Jewish opponents plotted against him (Acts 9:23; 20:3); Gentile mobs attacked him (Acts 16:19–22; 19:23–41). Then geography: city, wilderness and sea, the three places a person can be. Nowhere was safe.

Danger from false brothers. And then the last one, held to the end because it is the worst. Everything before this could be seen coming: a man knows to watch the river, the road, the mob. What cannot be guarded against is the person inside the fellowship who is not what he appears, who prays with you and is working against you (Galatians 2:4). It goes deeper than persecution, because it comes from inside the family. The psalmist knew it: it was not an enemy who taunted him, which he could have borne, but his companion, his familiar friend, with whom he walked to the house of God (Psalm 55:12–14).

He who ate my bread. And here Paul is walking where his Lord walked first. Jesus took the words of another psalm of betrayal and applied them to Judas at the Last Supper: he who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18; Psalm 41:9). The Son of God chose a false brother into his own circle, washed his feet, handed him the morsel, and was sold by him for silver. So the deepest wound in Paul’s list is one Christ knows from the inside. And the night he was betrayed was the night he gave his body and blood for those who would desert him: the false brother could hand him over; he could not stop him saving his people.

Toil and hardship. Then the list turns from danger to the grinding daily conditions, with nothing dramatic in them. Often without food may mean voluntary fasting, or simply going without. Cold and exposure means lacking clothing and shelter (4:11); years later, in a Roman prison, he would ask Timothy to bring the cloak he had left at Troas (2 Timothy 4:13). This is an ordinary week: tired, hungry and cold. Most Christian faithfulness looks far more like this verse than like the floggings, and it is this sort that wears people out.

What should I do if someone in my church has hurt me? First, take it to the Lord honestly, as the psalmist did; he knows this wound from the inside. Then, if the person is a believer and the matter is serious, follow the path Jesus gave: go to him privately, and if he will not listen, take one or two others, and then the church (Matthew 18:15–17). If it involves abuse or a crime, go to the authorities and to other leaders at once. Forgive from the heart, which means giving up revenge, even if trust takes much longer to rebuild. And do not let one false brother persuade you that the whole family is false. Paul was betrayed, and he never left the church.
verseByVerse.note: Rivers without bridges could be deadly in flood; roads through the mountains were infested with robbers.

verseByVerse.quote: And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And, apart from other things. After the floggings, the stoning, the shipwrecks and the nights in the open, Paul says: apart from all that, here is what actually weighs on me, an inward suffering besides the outward ones.

Daily pressure. The word means something set upon a person, a crowd pressing in, a burden that bears down. And daily: it does not stop when the ship reaches harbour or the bruises heal.

Anxiety for all the churches. The word for what he carries is merimna, care, concern: the word the Lord used when he said do not be anxious about your life (Matthew 6:25), and Paul when he told the Philippians not to be anxious about anything (Philippians 4:6). And its reach is all the churches: every congregation he had planted, scattered across four provinces, most out of contact, several in trouble he could do nothing about from where he was.

Is this anxiety sin? It is worth answering carefully, because a great many faithful people are quietly condemned by the question. The anxiety Scripture forbids is the fretting of a person who does not believe he is provided for: worry about food and clothing and tomorrow, carried by someone who has forgotten he has a Father. What Paul describes here is not about himself at all. It is the weight of caring what becomes of other people. That is not a failure of faith; it is what love feels like when the people you love are at risk and out of reach. The two can be told apart, and the test is what the concern is about and where it goes. Is it fear for yourself, or care for someone else? And does it drive you to God, or round in circles? Paul’s went to God in prayer, and then to a boat: he crossed a sea because he could not bear not knowing (2:13; 7:5–7).

The hidden half of pastoral work. This is invisible by nature and appears in no report. It is the elder awake at two in the morning over a family that is coming apart; the Sunday school teacher who cannot stop thinking about one particular child; the pastor who carries a dozen private sorrows he may not discuss with anyone. Paul lists it as a suffering, alongside the whip and the sea.

The affection of Christ Jesus. Where does such care come from? Paul tells the Philippians: God is his witness how he yearns for them all with the affection of Christ Jesus (Philippians 1:8). It is Christ’s own love for his people beating in a servant’s heart. The churches are not Paul’s; they are Christ’s, bought with his blood, and the Head who loves them shares his care with those who serve them. Paul could only be in one city at a time; Christ walks among all the lampstands. Paul was pressed by care; Christ intercedes, and always lives to do it. That is why the burden is bearable. Paul carries a share of the weight, but the whole of it rests on the Chief Shepherd, and Paul can cast every anxiety on him, because he cares for his people (1 Peter 5:7) far more than any apostle could.

Is my constant worry about my children godly care or sinful anxiety? Usually it is both, tangled together, and the way to untangle it is to pray it. Love for your children is good, and so is concern for their souls and their safety; that is what Paul felt for his churches. But when the concern becomes a sleepless loop of imagined disasters, a need to control every outcome, or a fear that God will not care for them as you would, it has crossed into the anxiety Jesus forbids. Turn each worry into a specific request, give thanks for what God has already done for them, do the next thing you actually can do, and then leave them in his hands, which are far safer than yours. He loves them more than you do.

In everyday life. Pray for your pastor and elders, who carry a daily burden of care you will mostly never see, and tell one of them this week that you are.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is weak, and I am not weak? These two questions explain where Paul’s daily pressure of care for the churches comes from: he keeps no protective distance from his people. When a believer somewhere is struggling, with doubt, with temptation, with a conscience troubled about food offered to idols, Paul does not counsel them from a position of strength. He goes down with them. He feels their weakness with them (1 Corinthians 9:22). He had told this church he would give up meat permanently rather than trip one weak brother (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? The second verb is stronger. “Indignant” is literally I burn, I am set on fire. When someone is tripped up into sin, especially by a false teacher, something in Paul catches fire: grief for the one who has fallen, and anger at whoever caused it.

Tenderness and heat. Together they are the anatomy of a pastor’s heart. Tenderness toward the person who is struggling; heat toward whatever is causing the struggle. Get them the wrong way round and you have Corinth, tolerating men who devoured them and criticising the apostle who would not take their money. Most of us find it easier to be irritated by the struggling person, the one who keeps failing and needing, than by whatever is doing the damage. Paul’s reflexes ran the other way, trained by watching his Lord, who had compassion on the crowds because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36), and kept his woes for the shepherds.

Boasting of weakness. Then the sentence the whole fool’s speech has been climbing toward. Paul has changed the currency. Unlike the rivals, he will boast of weakness, and not as a rhetorical trick: chapter 12 explains that weakness is where the power of Christ rests (12:9–10). The world counts what a man can do. God displays his power at exactly the point where a man can do nothing: in a clay pot, in a beaten apostle, in a crucified Messiah. There has never been a moment when God needed anyone’s strength, and there has never been a weakness he could not fill.

What it does not mean. Weakness is not a virtue in itself: laziness, cowardice and sin are weaknesses too, and Paul never boasts of those.

What does boasting in weakness look like in practice? It means being honest about your limits instead of hiding them, and pointing to Christ when good comes out of them. Admitting you are struggling, when the culture of your church rewards looking fine. Saying, when asked how you got through, that you did not, and God carried you. Telling your testimony with the failures left in. Accepting help rather than insisting on managing alone. Letting your children see you pray because you do not know what to do. It is not running yourself down for sympathy, and it is not false modesty. It is simply refusing to steal the credit for what God has done through a weak instrument.

verseByVerse.quote: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am not lying. Paul swears an oath, and then tells a story about a basket. The catalogue is so far outside what anyone boasts about that it might be read as rhetoric, so he calls God as witness: it happened. And even mid-oath, in one of the most painful passages he ever wrote, the doxology comes out of him almost by reflex: he who is blessed forever.

King Aretas. Then the story, deliberately, almost comically, anticlimactic. This is his first escape as a Christian (Acts 9:23–25). Newly converted, preaching in the synagogues of Damascus that Jesus is the Son of God, he provoked a plot, and the gates were watched. Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus; he ruled from about 9 BC to AD 40, so this escape must have come before about AD 40, which helps to date Paul’s early years (Galatians 1:17–18). Acts says the Jews plotted to kill him; here the governor under Aretas guards the city. The accounts fit naturally: his Jewish opponents could easily have enlisted the governor’s help.

Let down in a basket. The disciples put him in a basket, the word suggests a large woven hamper of the kind used for provisions, and lowered him through a window in the wall at night, like a delivery. Roman soldiers had a crowning honour, the wall crown, given to the first man up the wall of a besieged city. Paul’s wall story is a man going the other way: first down the wall, in a basket, fleeing. That is the joke, and it is a serious one.

How much he must suffer for my name. Of all the incidents he could have ended on, he chose the beginning, and the pattern was Christ’s word before it was Paul’s experience. In that same city, at the very start, the risen Lord had said of him to Ananias: I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name (Acts 9:16). Saul had come to Damascus with letters to arrest the followers of Jesus; he left it in a basket, hunted for preaching that Jesus is the Son of God (Acts 9:20). The man who would carry the gospel across the empire left his first city as freight. The basket was the first instalment of that promise, and the catalogue of this chapter is the rest. So the boast is not finally about Paul at all. It is about the Lord who stopped him on the road, turned the hunter into the hunted, and kept him through every danger until his work was done. The glory belongs to the name he suffered for.

In the flow. The basket is a hinge. Before the story of being caught up to the third heaven (12:1–4), Paul tells the story of being let down, and the order is the argument: whatever he has seen of glory, he boasts of weakness.

When should a Christian flee danger, and when should he stay? Fleeing is often right. Jesus withdrew when his hour had not yet come, Paul left Damascus, Thessalonica and Berea when lives were at risk, and the early church scattered under persecution and spread the gospel as it went (Acts 8:1–4). It is wise to flee when staying would achieve nothing but harm, when others depend on you, or when the door is open elsewhere. It is right to stay when fleeing would mean denying Christ, abandoning those in your care, or running from a duty God has plainly given you. Paul later went to Jerusalem knowing chains awaited him (Acts 20:22–24). Pray, take counsel, and remember that faithfulness, not bravado, is what pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus; he died around AD 40.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me!<sup>2</sup>For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.<sup>3</sup>But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.<sup>4</sup>For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.<sup>5</sup>Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles.<sup>6</sup>Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.<sup>7</sup>Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge?<sup>8</sup>I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.<sup>9</sup>And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way.<sup>10</sup>As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.<sup>11</sup>And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!<sup>12</sup>And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.<sup>13</sup>For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.<sup>14</sup>And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.<sup>15</sup>So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.<sup>16</sup>I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.<sup>17</sup>What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool.<sup>18</sup>Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.<sup>19</sup>For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves!<sup>20</sup>For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.<sup>21</sup>To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!<sup>22</sup>Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.<sup>23</sup>Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.<sup>24</sup>Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one.<sup>25</sup>Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;<sup>26</sup>on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers;<sup>27</sup>in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.<sup>28</sup>And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.<sup>29</sup>Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant?<sup>30</sup>If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.<sup>31</sup>The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.<sup>32</sup>At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me,<sup>33</sup>but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

12.title: The Thorn in the Flesh and Power in Weakness
12.overview:
The rivals in Corinth boasted of visions and revelations. Paul reluctantly matches them, and then turns the boast inside out. He tells, as if about someone else, of being taken up into paradise, but he will not build his reputation on it. He speaks instead of the thorn, the refused prayer, and the Lord’s answer that his grace is enough and his power is made perfect in weakness.

The rest of the chapter returns to the relationship: the Corinthians should have defended him; he is coming a third time, seeking them and not their money; and he fears what he may find when he arrives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Thorn in the Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul plays the rivals’ highest card, a vision of paradise, and then refuses to rest anything on it. What he boasts of is the thorn, and the word of Christ that came with it. This is the heart of the letter.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “power is made perfect in weakness” is the theological summit of the letter. Brought to completion, God’s power reaches its full display in human weakness. Christians are not to cultivate weakness, but neither need they be ashamed when it becomes the place where a power that is clearly not theirs is seen.

The threefold prayer (v. 8) and its refusal show as clearly as anything in the New Testament that God’s answer is sometimes no, with something better given instead: a word of grace and the power of Christ, worth more than the removal would have been.
verseByVerse.examples: A woman with a chronic pain condition has prayed for healing for years. She has been told that her lack of healing shows insufficient faith. This passage speaks directly to her: the greatest apostle prayed three times for the removal of his thorn and was refused. “My grace is sufficient for you” is not a consolation prize; it is a gift that the removal of the thorn would not have given him.

verseByVerse.quote: I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 12 ends the fool’s speech on the rivals’ favourite ground, visions, and turns it into the heart of the letter. Paul was caught up to paradise but will not boast of it (vv. 1–6); he was given a thorn, pleaded three times, and heard: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (vv. 7–10). Then he defends his conduct, seeking not their money but them (vv. 11–18), and fears what he may find when he comes (vv. 19–21).

I must go on boasting. He is still apologising, and now calls it useless too; I must go on carries compulsion. Nobody would guess from the tone that he is about to describe one of the most extraordinary spiritual experiences recorded of any Christian in the New Testament, and that reluctance is the point of the passage.

Nothing to be gained. He does not mean the vision was worthless to him. He means it is worth nothing as an argument. It did not make him a better servant of Christ; the thorn that came with it did rather more, as he is about to explain.

Visions and revelations. The phrase can mean visions and revelations given by the Lord, or visions in which the Lord himself is seen. He raises them because his rivals probably were. In a religious culture fascinated by ecstatic experience, a man who could describe an encounter with the heavenly world had credentials nobody could check and everybody envied. So Paul produces one, and immediately disarms it.

Experiences cannot be checked. Our age prizes spiritual experience as much as Corinth did, and the lesson carries. In any contest of spirituality, the person willing to describe the most remarkable inner life wins, and the claim cannot be tested. Paul refuses to compete on that ground. His credentials in this letter have been things anybody could verify: a church that exists, a body with scars, an empty purse, a life lived in the open.

The revelation he did lead with. Paul had one revelation he spoke of everywhere, and it was not paradise. It was the risen Jesus on the Damascus road. He received his gospel through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12); last of all, Christ appeared also to him (1 Corinthians 15:8). That appearing made him an apostle, and he told it to crowds and to kings (Acts 22; 26). The visions of the Lord he hides; the Lord of the visions he proclaims.

Does God still give visions and revelations like these? Not in the way he gave them to Paul. Paul’s experience belonged to his apostleship, and Scripture is now complete: God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the faith has been once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God may still use dreams, impressions and providences in a believer’s life, and he certainly draws near to his people in deep experiences of his love. But no claimed vision carries authority over others, adds to Scripture, or binds anyone’s conscience. Every such claim must be tested by Scripture and set below it. If you have had a vivid experience, thank God for whatever good it did you, and build your life on his written word. Christians differ here: many brothers and sisters who expect God to speak through dreams or prophecy today also hold Scripture as the final authority, while this commentary takes the view that revelatory gifts belonged to the apostolic foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20); both sides agree that nothing may be set beside the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know a man in Christ. He tells it in the third person and gives himself away in verse 7: it is Paul. The distance is deliberate: a way of describing the experience without standing next to it and taking the credit. In Christ means joined to Christ by faith, so that what is true of Christ counts as true of him (Galatians 2:20). The first thing he says about the man who went to heaven is not that he was special but that he was in Christ, which is the only thing that would ever get anyone there.

Who fourteen years ago. Count back from this letter and it lands around AD 42, in the silent years after Damascus and before the first missionary journey, the long stretch in Tarsus, Syria and Cilicia that Acts passes over in a sentence (Galatians 1:21; Acts 9:30; 11:25–26). Fourteen years of silence: had it been the making of his authority he would have led with it in every city. It appears once, under duress, in a passage he calls foolish. That is a great deal of humility to find in a man who had been to paradise, and it was not his own. It was the humility of the Lord who had been in the glory of the Father before the world existed, the Lord who could have dazzled the crowds with heaven and instead showed them his hands.

Caught up. It is a strong passive verb: seized, snatched. It happened to him. He did not achieve it by technique, which is worth saying in every generation that has a method for arranging such things. The third heaven means the dwelling place of God. Paul uses the simple scheme of his world: the sky of the birds, the sky of the stars, and beyond them God’s dwelling.

God knows. He was there and cannot tell you the mechanics: the one man in Scripture who could have written an authoritative account of the geography of heaven says twice that he does not know what happened to him.

Paradise. The place is given a second name. Paradise is a Persian word for a walled garden or park, used in the Greek Old Testament of Eden, and used by the Lord to the dying thief: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7). It is the same place as the third heaven, the presence of God. The garden that was shut with a flaming sword was opened by the Son of God, who was himself shut out, crucified outside the city, so that a dying thief could hear the words, today you will be with me. Paul has seen it.

Where Christians differ: visits to heaven today. Many popular books claim detailed visits to heaven, and many grieving readers have found them comforting; the apostle’s report, by contrast, is short, reluctant and full of admitted ignorance. This commentary’s view: Paul, an apostle, was taken to paradise and was forbidden to describe what he heard (v. 4). He waited fourteen years to mention it, and then only to rebuke boasting. Claims today to have toured heaven and brought back detailed descriptions do not match Paul’s reticence, add to Scripture, and often contradict it. Scripture is sufficient to tell us what we need to know about heaven (2 Timothy 3:16–17; the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6).

Was Paul dead, or did his soul leave his body? He does not know, and so we do not need to. He allows both possibilities, which tells us that a person can be with God apart from the body, as believers who die are now (5:8; Philippians 1:23), and also that God can take a living man into his presence as he pleases. What this passage does not teach is that Christians should seek out-of-body experiences, or that heaven can be reached by any technique. Paul was caught up; it was done to him. The ordinary way a believer enters paradise is by dying in the Lord, and that is enough.

What will heaven be like, if Paul could not describe it? Scripture tells us what matters most. It is the presence of God and of Christ; we will see his face (Revelation 22:4). There will be no more sin, death, mourning or pain (Revelation 21:4). Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and at his return they will be raised bodily to live in a new heavens and new earth (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; 2 Peter 3:13). Beyond that, what we have is enough to make us long for it. Paul’s silence is not a hint that heaven is vague. It is a hint that it is greater than words.

Caught up together. Paul was caught up once, briefly and alone. The whole church will be caught up together on the last day to meet the Lord, and so we will always be with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). What one apostle glimpsed and could not describe, every child of God will enter and never leave. And the one who will gather us is the Son who came down to a cross and a borrowed grave to open the way into the Father’s presence.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks of himself in the third person. The “third heaven” means the highest heaven, the presence of God; fourteen years before this letter would be in the early 40s AD.

verseByVerse.quote: and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Things that cannot be told. He describes what he heard in two ways. The first means unspeakable, beyond the capacity of language: things too holy for human words.

Which man may not utter. Not permitted, forbidden. Some of it could not be put into words, and some was not allowed to be. That is worth knowing when someone claims a private revelation that must be received on his authority alone. God may give a person something meant for him only, and the mark of the genuine article here is that Paul never traded on it. He built no following on what he could not disclose.

The secret things. God has not told us everything he could have: the Bible is not a transcript of all he knows; it is what he judged his people needed. The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children (Deuteronomy 29:29). Much unhappiness comes from demanding the first half, and much peace from being content with the second.

The Word who could be told. What Paul heard in paradise he could not repeat. What he was sent to tell he repeated everywhere: Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). That is not second best.
