No one has ever seen God; the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known (John 1:18; many early manuscripts read the only God, which most modern Bibles follow). The heaven Paul glimpsed in silence came to earth in a person who ate, taught, wept and died in full view, so that what God most wants us to know of himself could be heard, seen and touched (1 John 1:1). The unspeakable things stayed in paradise. The Son did not.

On behalf of this man. Here is the reason for the third-person device. The man who was caught up to paradise, that man he will boast about, because everything that happened to him was received. It was God’s gift, not his achievement.

On my own behalf. About the man writing the letter, the one with the scars and the tent-maker’s hands, Paul will boast only in what shows how weak he is. What was given to him is God’s to be proud of; what he is, is a clay pot. The times when God has plainly been at work in you are worth speaking of, but they are not your credentials, because you did not produce them.

Should I tell others about my experiences of God? Often, yes, with care. Telling what God has done for you can encourage others and give him glory, as the psalmists do again and again: come and hear, and I will tell what he has done for my soul (Psalm 66:16). But ask why you are telling it. Is it to point to God or to yourself? Will it help the hearer trust Christ, or make them feel they are missing something? Never use an experience to win an argument or to claim authority over someone else. And some experiences are best kept between you and the Lord, as Mary treasured things in her heart (Luke 2:19).

verseByVerse.quote: though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speaking the truth. He is not retracting the vision or hedging it. If he boasted of his revelations, every word would be accurate, unlike the rivals’ exaggerations.

No more than he sees. To refrain is to spare, to hold back. Paul deliberately withholds true information about himself to keep people’s opinion of him accurate. He wants to be judged by what can be seen in his life and heard in his teaching, not by a reputation built on experiences that cannot be checked. All of us manage what people know about us, and the management almost always runs the other way: we put forward what is impressive and leave out the rest.

Not ourselves but Jesus Christ. Why does Paul care so much that no one think too highly of him? Because an inflated apostle would stand in the light where only Christ belongs. He has already said it: what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake (4:5). The light God shone into his heart was the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (4:6), not in the face of Paul. A preacher famous for his visions draws eyes to himself. A preacher known only for what can be seen and heard leaves the hearer looking past him to his Lord. Paul’s reticence is not shyness. It is a window kept clean.

Judge the visible man. What he sees in me or hears from me is an uncomfortable test in an age built on presentation: is the impression people have of you larger than the reality they could observe? The gap is where disappointment lives, and it is why so many admired people are a grief to those who live with them. There is a mercy in Paul’s policy too. A man who has arranged to be overestimated must keep up the estimate, and the work never ends. Paul is exactly what he appears to be, which is why he can admit that he despaired of life and left Damascus in a basket. Christ is the one person whose reputation will never disappoint those who live closest to him. The disciples who saw him tired, hungry and weeping, who watched him at table and on the road for three years, came away worshipping.

Is it dishonest to keep good things about myself hidden? No. Honesty forbids deceiving people, not keeping things private. You are not obliged to tell everyone everything, and Jesus told us to do our giving, praying and fasting in secret (Matthew 6:1–6). What would be dishonest is creating a false impression, making yourself look better than you are, or worse in order to be praised for humility. Paul’s aim is accuracy: he wants people to think of him exactly what is true and visible. That is a good aim for a Christian. Let your reputation be no larger than your life.

verseByVerse.quote: So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The surpassing greatness. Now the thorn. The purpose clause, to keep me from becoming conceited (lifted up above measure), appears at both ends of the sentence, as though the danger of pride were so real it needed saying on both sides of the affliction. Some manuscripts lack the second clause, but most modern Bibles, like the KJV, keep it.

A thorn was given me in the flesh. What was it? The honest answer is that nobody knows, and the guessing has gone on for nineteen centuries. The word skolops means a sharpened stake or a splinter: something driven in. In the flesh suggests the body. The main proposals are a chronic illness, perhaps of the eyes (Galatians 4:13–15; 6:11), or the relentless human opposition that dogged him. The Corinthians probably knew what it was, and Paul did not need to say. But because it is unnamed, no sufferer with a different affliction is shut out of the passage: whatever is driven into your flesh fits the gap. The verb is a divine passive: the giver is God. Satan sent it, but Paul says it was given, and he knows from whose hand.

A messenger of Satan. The harassment is real and it comes from the enemy. Satan meant it for harm. “Harass” (kolaphizō) means to strike with the fist, the very word used when they struck Jesus at his trial (Matthew 26:67). It is in the present tense: an ongoing torment, blow after blow. One event, two agents, two purposes. Satan sends it to wreck a man. God permits it, and appoints it, to save him from something worse. He turns the devil’s fist into his own surgeon’s hand.

Satan’s weapon, God’s purpose. God used Satan’s weapon for Paul’s good. This is the shape of Job, where the accuser is on a leash and the leash is held (Job 1–2); and of Joseph, who told his brothers you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20); and supremely of the cross, where Satan entered Judas and the rulers did their worst, while God was delivering up his Son by his definite plan for the saving of the world (Luke 22:3; Acts 2:23). On the cross Satan struck the Son of God with everything he had, and by that very blow his head was crushed. And God was protecting Paul not from failure or danger but from conceit. So the affliction is not the price of the revelation; it is the provision that made the revelation survivable.

How can both God and Satan be behind the same thing? Because they are doing different things through it. Satan’s aim is to torment and destroy, and he is guilty for it. God’s aim is to humble, protect and strengthen, and he is righteous in it. God does not do evil, tempt anyone to sin, or delight in pain (James 1:13), but nothing happens outside his rule, and he can take what is meant for evil and turn it to good. That is why a Christian can resist the devil and still say of his suffering, this has come to me from my Father’s hand. You do not have to work out where one purpose ends and the other begins. You only need to know which one will win.

What if my thorn is something I brought on myself? Then confess the sin that caused it, and receive God’s forgiveness fully; the guilt is gone in Christ, even if the consequences remain. Paul’s thorn was not the result of his sin, but the promise of verse 9 is not limited to blameless suffering. A recovered addict with a damaged body, a man living with the results of a foolish decision, a woman bearing the scars of a past she regrets: God’s grace is sufficient for them too. He is able to use even the consequences of our sin to humble us, keep us close to him, and make us gentle with others who fall.
verseByVerse.note: No one knows what the thorn was; suggestions include a chronic illness, poor eyesight, or persistent opposition.

parallels.desc: thorns in your sides

verseByVerse.quote: Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this. This line has helped to keep a great many Christians in the faith. Three times: not a passing mention in his devotions, but a repeated, earnest asking. Paul does not draw the comparison, but the number recalls the Lord himself, who prayed three times in Gethsemane about a cup he wanted removed, and submitted to the Father’s will (Mark 14:32–41; Matthew 26:39–44). He is not making a polite request; he is imploring.

With the Lord. The Lord here is almost certainly Jesus, since the answer in verse 9 speaks of the power of Christ. Paul’s prayers are usually addressed to the Father, and it is worth noticing that here he prays directly to the Son, which tells you who he understood him to be.

That it should leave me. He asked for exactly what he wanted, and it was right to ask. And the answer was no.

Every condition was met. Every element that is supposed to guarantee an answered prayer is present here. The man praying is an apostle. The request is not selfish: a healthy Paul could serve more churches. There is no hint of unconfessed sin, no lack of faith, no failure to persevere; he came back three times. And the thorn stayed. That has to be said plainly, because there are believers who have been told that healing is theirs if they can muster the faith for it, and who have concluded, after years, that the fault is in them. Some have stopped praying. Some have stopped believing. This verse was written for them. One of the greatest Christians who ever lived prayed three times for the removal of an affliction and was told no, and the refusal is recorded in Scripture as a mercy rather than a failure.

He stopped at three. Paul did not conclude that persistence was the missing ingredient and press on to three hundred. He asked, he received an answer, and the answer settled it. There is a kind of prayer that will not accept a reply, and it is not greater faith; it is a refusal to let God be God. What changed was not the circumstance but the man, and what changed him was a word, one sentence given in reply, which he carried for the rest of his life and which the church has been living on ever since.

Should I stop praying for healing after three times? Not necessarily. Paul stopped because he received a clear answer, and we do not receive answers in his apostolic way. Jesus also told a parable about praying and not losing heart (Luke 18:1). So keep bringing your need to God for as long as it is on your heart, honestly and without guilt. But let your prayer change as Paul’s did. Ask not only for removal but for grace to bear it, for God to be glorified in it, and for the will to accept his answer, whatever it is. Over time many believers find that the prayer moves from take it away to be with me in it, and that is not defeat. It is the Gethsemane prayer: not my will, but yours.

For worship. The Lord to whom Paul prayed has asked as we ask. In the days of his flesh he offered up prayers with loud cries and tears to the one who was able to save him from death (Hebrews 5:7), and the cup was not taken from him, because if it had passed from him it would have come to us. Now every plea for a thorn to go reaches someone who knows what it is to ask and be refused for a greater good, and when he says no, he does not fall silent.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus too prayed three times in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to me. The summit of the letter. The verb is in the perfect tense: he has said, and it stands. Christ’s answer was not a passing comfort but a permanent word.

My grace is sufficient for you. Begin with the tense. Not will be, when things get worse. Not has been, looking back. It is sufficient: present, continuous, already true in the moment the thorn is still going in. The word sufficient means enough, adequate to the need. It is not a promise of relief but that the supply will not run out before the trouble does. And see what was not said. There is no explanation. The Lord does not tell Paul what the thorn is for beyond the one clause of verse 7, does not say how long, does not promise eventual removal. He gives him himself. That is the whole answer, and the answer is better than the request.

Made perfect in weakness. “Made perfect” is from the root meaning to reach a goal, to be completed, fully displayed. Divine power does not merely cope with human weakness; it comes to its full expression there. Weakness is not the obstacle power has to work around. It is the place power was always heading for. This is the principle of the whole letter: we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (4:7).

All the more gladly. The word to watch is gladly: not I will endure them but I will boast all the more gladly. Something has been so thoroughly reversed in him that the thing he begged to lose has become the thing he is pleased to have.

The power of Christ may rest upon me. “Rest upon” (episkēnoō) means to pitch a tent over, to dwell upon. It is built on the word for the tabernacle, where the glory settled in the wilderness, and it shares its root with John’s the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). Christ’s power settles on the weak, and he does it by his Spirit, the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead, who now dwells in his people (Romans 8:11) and strengthens them with power in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16). The weakness is the ground the tent is pitched on. Where a man is emptied out, the glory of God comes down and settles, and stays. He did not take the thorn away. He came and lived on it.

Where Christians differ: healing and faith. Some teach that it is always God’s will to heal believers who have enough faith, and that remaining sick shows lack of faith. Those who teach it usually want to honour God’s power and compassion, which is right; the question is whether Scripture makes that promise. This commentary’s view: Paul, the great apostle, prayed in faith three times for his thorn to be removed, and the Lord said no. God does heal in answer to prayer, and we should pray for healing (James 5:14–15). But he sometimes chooses not to, for purposes better than healing: humility, dependence, and the display of his power in weakness. Paul left Trophimus sick (2 Timothy 4:20) and advised Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23).

What it does not mean. It is not a call to cultivate weakness, refuse medicine or make a virtue of incapacity; Paul prayed for removal, and was right to. It means that when the weakness does not lift, you have not been shut out of God’s power.

What is grace, in this verse? Here grace is not only God’s pardoning favour, though it is that, but his active help given moment by moment: the strength to keep going, the comfort that holds you up, the patience you did not have, the faith that does not fail. It is not a substance or a feeling but the Lord himself at work in you. That is why it is always sufficient: it is measured not by your need but by his fullness. You will rarely feel it in advance. Most believers find it given for the day, like manna, and only when they look back do they see how much was supplied.

How do I take hold of this grace when I feel nothing? You take hold of it by trusting the word, not by waiting for a feeling. Christ said it is sufficient; believe him and act on it. Pray honestly, even if all you can say is help. Keep using the ordinary means: Scripture, especially the psalms of lament; the Lord’s Supper; the company of believers who will pray with you. Do the next small duty in front of you and leave tomorrow’s for tomorrow. Get the medical and practical help you need, which is one of the ways God gives grace. And tell another believer, so you are not carrying it alone. Grace often arrives through their hands.

Is this not just a pious way of explaining away an unanswered prayer? It would be, if Paul had been left with nothing. But he did not invent a comfort to cover his disappointment. He asked for one thing and was given another he had not thought to ask for: a word from the risen Christ and his presence in the trouble. And the claim can be checked against a life. The man who heard it went on through beatings, shipwreck and prison (11:23–27) and wrote this letter with more joy than his rivals ever showed. Above all, it is the pattern of the cross, where God did his greatest work through what looked like defeat. A comfort invented to soothe us would hardly look like that.

For worship. The voice that said my grace is sufficient for you belongs to a risen man with wounds. He was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God (13:4), so when he speaks of power made perfect in weakness he is describing his own cross before he describes our trouble. There has never been a thorn deeper than his crown, and there is no weakness he will not pitch his tent on. The grace he promises is his own presence, as new each morning as the need it meets, until weakness is swallowed up in glory.

parallels.desc: he gives power to the faint

verseByVerse.quote: For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Content. The Greek word is stronger than the English: it means to take pleasure in, to be well pleased. Not resigned, but glad. It is the word the Father uses at the baptism: with whom I am well pleased (Matthew 3:17). He is pleased with the weak who lean on his Son, because his Son is the one in whom he is well pleased.

Five things he is pleased with. Weaknesses: his own incapacity. Insults: outrages done to him, including the Corinthian talk of him as contemptible. Hardships: the grinding pressure of not enough. Persecutions: being hunted. Calamities: being squeezed into a narrow place with no way out. The qualifier governs the whole sentence: for the sake of Christ. He takes pleasure not in suffering but in what it is for and in who meets him inside it. Take Christ out of the sentence and it becomes unhealthy; leave him in and it is one of the freest sentences in the letter.

For when I am weak, then I am strong. Both halves are literal, and the then is a hinge: not although I am weak, but when I am weak, at that moment, precisely there. The strength is not his own returning; it is Christ’s power resting on the empty ground of verse 9. A self-reliant person can only do what he can do; a person leaning on Christ has a strength beyond his own, and can say with Paul, I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13).

A different account of usefulness. Most of us assume God uses us in proportion to what we bring: the more competent, resourced and spiritually together, the more useful. This verse says the arithmetic runs the other way at exactly the point where our resources fail. Think of the times you have been most useful to another person: it is rarely the season when you were flourishing. It is nearly always when you had been through what they are going through now, and had nothing to offer but that.

Does this mean I should not try to be competent or strong? No. Paul worked hard, planned carefully, argued brilliantly and used every gift God gave him. Competence is a gift, and laziness is not a spiritual weakness to boast of. The point is where your confidence rests. A skilled surgeon, a gifted teacher, a strong father can all be weak in this sense, if they know that every ability is on loan and that nothing of eternal worth will come from them without Christ. The danger is not strength but self-reliance. Use every gift, and then lean on him as though you had none.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — Signs of Apostleship and Pastoral Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fool’s speech is over, and Paul turns to his coming visit. He seeks the Corinthians themselves, as a father provides for his children, and he answers the charge of trickery with a record anyone could check. All of it, he says, was spoken before God for their building up, and he fears finding sin still unrepented when he comes.
verseByVerse.theology: The “signs of a true apostle” (v. 12) are offered not as Paul’s chief credential but as evidence that the Corinthians had already received from him what a true apostle gives. His chief credential, as the whole letter argues, is a ministry shaped like the cross. Making miracles the main test was the super-apostles’ error.
verseByVerse.examples: A church board judges its pastor entirely by attendance, baptisms and giving. This passage suggests a broader test: has the ministry produced changed lives, gospel truth and pastoral care, and has the minister borne the shape of the cross? The absence of spectacular growth does not disqualify; the absence of gospel integrity does.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been a fool! You forced me to it. The fool’s speech ends, and Paul steps out of the character with obvious relief. The Corinthians’ failure to defend Paul forced him to defend himself.

For I ought to have been commended by you. That is the real grievance of the whole four chapters. They should have spoken up for him. He founded that church, was slandered in it by newcomers, and the people who owed him everything sat quietly. Anyone who has been left undefended by people who knew better will recognise the note. It is not the attack that wounds most; it is the silence of the ones who could have spoken and did not.

Even though I am nothing. Both halves are true and neither cancels the other. Measured against the men impressing Corinth, he is not behind by a step. Measured in himself, he is nothing (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). That is not self-hatred but the realism of a man who wrote that our sufficiency is from God (3:5). A Christian can hold a very high view of what God has done through him and a very low view of his own contribution at the same time, and neither is false modesty.

With utmost patience. The signs came wrapped in endurance, staying power under weight, and Paul puts it first because anyone can be impressive for an evening, and only a certain kind of man is still there eighteen months later, making tents.

With signs and wonders and mighty works. Three words for miracles: signs, which point beyond themselves; wonders, which astonish; mighty works, which display power. So the miracles happened in Corinth (Romans 15:19). This is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament that the apostles worked them. But he places the fact: at the end of four chapters of weakness, mentioned once, in a single line, after the beatings and the basket and the thorn.

What Christ accomplished through me. Whose signs were they? Paul answers elsewhere: he will speak only of what Christ has accomplished through him, by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders (Romans 15:18–19). The same three words first marked out Jesus himself, a man attested by God with mighty works and wonders and signs (Acts 2:22). So the signs of an apostle were the risen Lord’s own credentials, carried by the men he had sent, bearing witness that the one who healed in Galilee was alive and still at work (Hebrews 2:3–4). That is why they never pointed to Paul. They pointed back to the one whose sent man he was, which is exactly what the word apostle means. Christ is the great sign and wonder of God, who healed the sick, raised the dead and stilled the storm, and whose greatest mighty work was done in weakness on a cross and in power at an empty tomb.

Where Christians differ: the signs of an apostle today. Some argue that miracles should be normal in every church today. This commentary’s view: Paul calls signs and wonders the signs of an apostle: marks that distinguished true apostles from false. If they were common to all believers, they could not mark out apostles. This supports the view that the miraculous sign gifts were tied to the apostolic foundation of the church (Hebrews 2:3–4; Ephesians 2:20) and are not the norm today. God remains free to do wonders.

Apostles were witnesses. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, brothers and sisters who love the Lord, believe such signs continue. But an apostle in Paul’s sense was a witness of the risen Christ, appointed by him (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), the last of whom saw him (1 Corinthians 15:8), and the apostles were a foundation laid once (Ephesians 2:20). The church today is led by elders and taught by the apostles’ words in Scripture.

What it does not mean. Miracles alone do not prove truth: false prophets can do signs (Matthew 24:24).

If the sign gifts have ceased, should I still pray for miracles? Yes. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped acting; it is the belief that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gifts of working miracles at will, as signs confirming new revelation. God is as powerful as ever and still answers prayer in ways that leave doctors puzzled. So pray boldly for the sick (James 5:14–15), for conversions, for deliverance from danger, and expect God to hear. Give him the glory when he answers. What we should not do is treat miracles as the proof of a ministry, or tell sufferers that their lack of healing shows lack of faith.

How should I treat Christians who believe the gifts continue? As brothers and sisters in Christ. This is an in-house difference among people who love the same Lord and the same gospel, and many charismatic believers put the rest of us to shame by their zeal in prayer and evangelism. Hold your convictions with charity. Discuss the question from Scripture, not from caricatures. Test every claimed word or sign by the Bible, as they themselves should. And reserve your warnings for teaching that adds to Scripture, promises health and wealth, or replaces the gospel with spectacle.

In everyday life. When a pastor, a missionary or a fellow member is criticised unfairly behind their back, say a word in their defence when you next hear it. Silence is not neutral.

verseByVerse.quote: For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in what were you less favoured than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? The irony has one more turn in it. It is bitter and it is funny, and the sarcasm is aimed at an accusation so absurd that stating it plainly is the best refutation available. They received everything other churches did: the gospel, the founding, the teaching, the miracles. The single respect in which Corinth received less than any other church Paul served is that he refused to take their money. Hence the biting mock apology: forgive me this wrong!

Not what is yours but you. This is his third visit (13:1), and the policy has not changed. Here is the line between a shepherd and a hireling. The false teachers wanted what the Corinthians had: their money, their allegiance, their admiration, the standing of leading a well-known church. Paul wanted the Corinthians: not what could be got from them, but them. Run it as a test both ways. Of anyone who ministers to you: does he want you, or something you can supply? And of yourself, wherever you are the stronger party: are you after the person, or the gratitude, loyalty and sense of being needed that they give you?

Parents for their children. Now he speaks not as an apostle but as their spiritual father (1 Corinthians 4:15), and the argument is simply how families work. A father does not present his children with an invoice. Money in a household runs downhill, from those who have it to those who do not, and nobody calls it a transaction. That is exactly the position taken by the Father who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and who has never once sent anyone a bill.

He became poor. Paul did not invent this way of loving a church. He had already told the Corinthians where it came from: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (8:9). In God’s family the wealth runs downhill, from the Son who had everything to children who had nothing. When Paul works nights so as not to be a burden, he is not being eccentric about money. He is preaching 8:9 with his hands.

How do I know whether I want people or what they give me? Watch what happens when they stop giving it. If someone you serve stops thanking you, disagrees with you, or no longer needs you, do you still care for them, or do you lose interest? Do you rejoice when they grow beyond needing you, or feel threatened? Do you pray for them when no one will ever know? A parent who loves a child is glad to see him become independent; a parent who loves being needed resents it. Apply that to your ministry, your friendships and your family, and ask God to purify your love until it seeks them and not what is theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spend and be spent. The first sentence is a great statement of Christian love; the second is a lonely question. The two verbs share a root, active and passive. To spend is to lay out what you have: money, time, energy. To be spent is to be laid out yourself, used up, consumed in the process. Being spent is what happens to people who serve others for a long time. The mother of a disabled child knows it, and so does the man caring for his wife through a long decline, and the pastor in his twenty-fifth year.

Most gladly, for your souls. The adverb is a superlative: not willingly or without complaint, but with delight. And the object is their souls, not their approval or their good opinion; he is spending himself on what will still exist in a thousand years. He learned it from a Lord who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). An apostle used up for the Corinthians is what that love looks like once it has taken hold of a man.

If I love you more, am I to be loved less? Then the question, and Paul lets it stand without answering it. It is heartbreaking. Something has gone wrong that everyone recognises. He has loved them more than any of the newcomers ever will, and it has cost him their affection. The men who exploited them are admired; the man who worked nights so as not to burden them is suspected. The more Paul loved them, the less they seemed to love him in return. Love does not always receive love back. It is a real pain and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But the question does not become a threat or a withdrawal. He asks it, and then goes on loving them and announces he is coming again. Love that stops when it is not returned was something else all along. The one who loved most was loved least, and was spent entirely, and did it gladly, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2), for people who at the time were shouting for his death.

Is it wrong to want to be loved back? No. Paul plainly wanted it, and he says so; he asked them earlier to widen their hearts to him (6:13). Longing for love in return is human and good, and God made us for it. What would be wrong is making your love conditional on it, or punishing people when it does not come. Bring the ache to God honestly, as Paul brings it into the open here. Then go on loving, because your love is first a response to his. If you are pouring yourself out for someone who does not love you back, you are standing where your Lord stood, and he sees it.

How do I keep from burning out while being spent for others? Remember that Paul was spent for souls, not for every demand people made of him. He refused some things, rested at times, accepted help, and was sustained by the churches’ gifts and the company of friends like Titus. Being spent gladly is not the same as being consumed by guilt or by other people’s expectations. Keep a day of rest. Share the load; you are not the only servant God has. Let others care for you. And keep your own soul fed, because you cannot give what you do not receive. The Lord who spent himself also withdrew to lonely places and prayed.

verseByVerse.quote: But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crafty, you say. A new accusation, and the meanest yet. He had never taken a penny from them, so the charge changed shape: he did not take it himself; that was the clever part. The suspicion was most likely that the Jerusalem collection was the real operation, and that the money would be skimmed off through the men he sent.

Unfalsifiable suspicion. The very transparency Paul built, the delegates chosen by the churches and his refusal to handle funds alone (8:20–21), has been turned into evidence of a cleverer fraud. Such suspicion cannot be disproved: honesty becomes proof of cunning.

Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? Paul’s answer is not another protestation. It is a series of questions with names attached, and that is the only thing that works against such a charge. Paul invites them to check the record. Name one.

I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? They knew Titus, and his conduct among them had been spotless.

Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps? Then the two closing questions, and they are quietly conclusive. The word for steps means footprints: walking in the same tracks. Paul and his co-workers behaved identically about money, with the same integrity, and everyone had watched them do it.

In his steps. The charge against Paul was deceit, and the answer was a life that could be watched. That is the pattern Peter saw in Jesus. Christ suffered for you, he wrote, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps; he committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:21–22). Paul and Titus walked in the same footprints because both were walking in his. The only answer to a slander that cannot be disproved is a character that does not need defending.

How should a church handle money so that no one can suspect it? The way Paul did: never let one person handle funds alone. Have at least two unrelated people count every offering and sign for it. Keep clear records and let the members see them. Have the accounts checked by someone independent. Make sure those who decide on spending are accountable to others, and that no leader can quietly benefit. None of this implies that anyone is dishonest; it protects the honest from suspicion and the church from temptation. As Paul put it, we aim at what is honourable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (8:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? Paul stops and reframes the entire four chapters. It is the obvious reading, and he knows it; he has spent four chapters answering charges, matching credentials, listing sufferings and refuting accusations. Anyone would call that a defence. He says it is not, or at least that they are not the court.

In the sight of God. There is the correction. He has not been in the dock before the Corinthians; God is the audience, and they have merely been in the room (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). A man defending himself before people manages an impression. A man speaking before God says what is true and lets the impression fall where it will, which is why these chapters contain so much no advocate would include: that he despaired of life, could not rest at Troas, is unimpressive in person, and left Damascus in a basket. The verdict is not theirs to give. And for those in Christ the only verdict that counts has already been given: they are not on trial before God, because Christ stood trial for them and was condemned in their place. It is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends (10:18).

Speaking in Christ. Paul speaks as a man joined to Christ and answerable to him. Jesus lived his whole ministry before that same court. I do not seek my own glory, he said; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge (John 8:50). Before the council and before Pilate he did not plead for his reputation; he entrusted himself to the Father, and the Father vindicated him. Because Paul is in Christ, he can do the same: say hard and humiliating things, leave his name with God, and spend his words building up the very people who doubt him.

And all for your upbuilding. Every word, the irony, the catalogue of floggings, the fool’s speech he found so distasteful, was construction work on them, not self-protection. It was the authority given for building up and not for destroying (10:8; 13:10).

Beloved. And then, after everything, the last word of the sentence. He has used it only once before in the letter (7:1), and he saves it for people who have doubted him, listened to his enemies, and left him to defend himself alone. That is the tone the whole passage was meant to be heard in. And it is God’s word before it is Paul’s: in his sight they are beloved, the word the Father speaks over all his children for the sake of his Son.

How do I live before God rather than before people? Start by remembering, often, that he is the one you will answer to, and that he already knows everything. Before you speak in a difficult conversation, ask what you would say if God were the only listener; he is the one who matters. When praise comes, give it to him quickly. When criticism comes, ask him whether it is true, rather than first asking how it makes you look. And let the purpose of your words be the good of the hearer, not your own defence. The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25).

verseByVerse.quote: For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I fear. Twice he says I fear, and perhaps guards it: he is dreading a possibility, not predicting. He has not given up on them, and he will not describe their sin as settled before he has seen it.

Not as you wish. If they are unrepentant, he will have to come with severity instead of gentleness, the rod rather than love in a spirit of gentleness (1 Corinthians 4:21). He would far rather not.

Eight sins of a church. Read as a group, these eight are not the sins of a pagan city but of a church. Quarrelling: strife. Jealousy: resentment of another’s good. Anger: outbursts of temper. Hostility: selfish ambition and factions. Slander: speaking against people. Gossip: whisperings. Conceit: puffings-up. Disorder: tumult. Every one is relational, and every one can survive indefinitely in a congregation that would be horrified by anything more obvious. Several of them appear again among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20), and together they are the opposite of the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). Where the Spirit is not followed, this list grows in the space.

My God may humble me. He is afraid he will be brought low in front of them, and my God matters: even the humbling would come from the hand of the God he belongs to.

Humbled by sins not his own. Paul expects to be brought low by other people’s sins, as a father is shamed by his children’s. That is a faint likeness of something far greater. Christ was humbled not by any sin of his own, for he had none, but by ours: he humbled himself to the point of death on a cross (Philippians 2:8), and the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6). Paul could grieve over the impurity in Corinth and discipline it. Christ carried it, so that people who had lived exactly that way could be washed of it (1 Corinthians 6:11).

To mourn. The verb is the strong one: to grieve as at a death (1 Corinthians 5:2). Not to discipline them, though he will; not to be angry, though he might be. To mourn. The apostle of the third heaven, who had been caught up into paradise, is afraid of arriving in a Greek port and finding people he loves unrepentant, and grieving over them as a father grieves.

The old Corinthian sins. The three sins named are the old Corinthian ones, the things the first letter dealt with (1 Corinthians 5–6). The crisis had been resolved and the church had come back to Paul, but some may never have turned.

Corporate repentance is not personal repentance. That is a sober note for any church that has come through a good season. A congregation can be genuinely restored at the level of its relationships and still contain people for whom nothing has changed at all. Repentance is more than regret or a better mood in the church. It is a turning of the mind and the life away from sin to God, which shows itself in deeds (Acts 26:20).

Why does Paul put gossip in the same list as sexual immorality? Because both destroy, and both grieve God. We rank sins by how shocking they look, and gossip and conceit rarely shock anyone. God ranks them differently: Romans 1:29–30 puts gossips and slanderers in the same catalogue as murderers, and Proverbs says a whisperer separates close friends (Proverbs 16:28). Sexual sin defiles the body and breaks covenants; gossip and slander poison a whole church and wreck reputations that took decades to build. Do not excuse the respectable sins because they are common. They are common because we excuse them.

What should I do if I recognise myself in this list? Repent specifically, not generally. Name the sin to God: not I have not been very loving, but I said that about her and it was not true, or not mine to say. Receive his forgiveness, which is complete in Christ (1 John 1:9). Then put it right with people where you can: apologise to the person you slandered, correct the story you spread, make peace with the one you have quarrelled with (Matthew 5:23–24). And starve the habit: stop listening to gossip, as well as spreading it. If sexual sin is involved, tell a mature believer and get help; this is a battle no one wins alone.

In everyday life. Pick the one of these eight most at home in you, very likely the quietest, and ask the Spirit, whose fruit is its opposite, to root it out this week. You will not be free of all eight in this life. Christ never once fell into any of them, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), so you fight them as a forgiven child, not to win his love.

For worship. The Lord of the church mourns before he judges. He wept over Jerusalem, which would not come to him (Luke 19:41), and then went into it to die for sinners. As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). The heart of God toward an unrepentant church is not cold impatience. It is grief, and a door still open to everyone who turns.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.<sup>2</sup>I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows.<sup>3</sup>And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—<sup>4</sup>and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter.<sup>5</sup>On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—<sup>6</sup>though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.<sup>7</sup>So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.<sup>8</sup>Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.<sup>9</sup>But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.<sup>10</sup>For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.<sup>11</sup>I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing.<sup>12</sup>The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.<sup>13</sup>For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong!<sup>14</sup>Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.<sup>15</sup>I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?<sup>16</sup>But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit.<sup>17</sup>Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you?<sup>18</sup>I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?<sup>19</sup>Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.<sup>20</sup>For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder.<sup>21</sup>I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.

13.title: Self-Examination, Final Warnings, and the Grace Benediction
13.overview:
The letter ends with a warning and a blessing. Paul is about to make his third visit, and he will deal with unrepented sin properly, on the evidence of witnesses. The Corinthians have demanded proof that Christ speaks through him, and they will have it, for Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God’s power. But the real test is theirs: whether Christ is in them. He writes now so that he need not be severe when he comes.

Then the tone softens into final appeals, greetings, and the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul announces his third visit and warns that this time he will not spare the unrepentant, though every charge will be properly established. They wanted proof that Christ speaks through him; the answer is the crucified and risen Christ, whose weakness and power Paul shares. Then he turns the test round: they should examine themselves. His authority is for building up, not tearing down.
verseByVerse.theology: Many churches have joined the call to self-examination (v. 5) to the self-examination Paul asks for before the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:28–31). True self-examination is not cultivating doubt but an honest look before God: am I trusting Christ, or my own religious performance? The examination that brings assurance is the one that finds Christ as the ground of hope, not the one that hunts for enough personal righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Before communion a pastor gives the congregation a few minutes for self-examination. This passage makes the goal clear: not to find enough holiness to qualify for the table, but to ask whether Christ is there, whether the faith that receives him is real.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 13 closes the letter with a warning and a blessing. Paul is coming a third time and will not spare the unrepentant; they want proof that Christ speaks through him, and the proof is the crucified and risen Christ, whose power works through Paul’s weakness (vv. 1–4). Then he turns the test round: examine yourselves (vv. 5–10). Brief commands and the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament end the letter (vv. 11–14).

Two or three witnesses. Paul is coming a third time, and he quotes the law (Deuteronomy 19:15), one of the oldest protections in Scripture: no one is to be condemned on one person’s word. The Lord built it into church discipline (Matthew 18:16), and Paul applies it to accusations against elders (1 Timothy 5:19). Many interpreters take the three visits, or Paul’s repeated warnings, as the witnesses themselves; others think Paul means exactly what the law says. Either way, it will be done properly: no acting on rumour; evidence, witnesses and due process. Paul is the injured party, and the first thing he establishes is the procedure that protects the accused. A man who wanted revenge would not begin there.

The trial where the witnesses failed. This protection was denied once, to the one person who least deserved condemnation. At the trial of Jesus many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:56), and the court condemned him anyway, on his own confession that he was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed (Mark 14:61–64). The injustice was men’s; the purpose was God’s. The innocent was condemned by an unjust court so that a just God could acquit the guilty who believe in him (Romans 3:26). Every fair hearing in a church is held in the light of that unfair one.

I warned them. He documents the warning: once on the painful second visit, and now again in this letter. Nobody will be able to say they did not know. That is how God deals with people: warnings come before judgment, in time to be acted on. Nineveh was given forty days (Jonah 3:4).

I will not spare them. The verb is the one he used at 1:23, where he stayed away to spare them. The sparing is over. He had been patient, and they had mistaken patience for inability. Peter had to answer the same mistake about God himself: the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you (2 Peter 3:9). Delay is not weakness but room being given. And behind Paul’s warning stands the holiness of God. Sin in a church is never a private matter, because the church is the temple of the living God (6:16), and the holy God will not leave his temple defiled for ever.

What does church discipline actually involve? It is the church’s loving care for its members, which includes correcting those who fall into serious, unrepented sin. Most of it is quiet and private: a word between friends, a visit from an elder, an honest conversation (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). Only when someone persistently refuses to repent of plain sin does it become public, and in the last resort the church may remove him from membership and the Lord’s Table (1 Corinthians 5:4–5, 13). The aim at every stage is restoration, not humiliation: to win the brother back. When it is done with patience, evidence and tears, as here, it is one of the ways Christ protects his flock and calls his wandering sheep home.

Why insist on witnesses when someone is accused? Because God hates false accusation and injustice, and because a single report, however sincere, can be mistaken, exaggerated or malicious. Requiring confirmation protects the innocent from rumour and the church from being manipulated. It does not mean that a lone victim of abuse should be ignored. Other evidence can confirm a charge, and patterns of behaviour often come to light when one person speaks. Serious allegations, especially of abuse or crime, must be taken seriously at once and reported to the proper authorities; the requirement of witnesses governs the church’s verdict, not whether it listens.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three

verseByVerse.quote: since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Proof that Christ is speaking. Here is the demand behind everything. “Proof” (dokimē) means evidence, the result of a test. They wanted what the super-apostles gave them: presence, force, the manner of a man plainly in charge (11:5–6). Paul, working nights and declining their money, did not have it.

Standing inside the evidence. They were asking for proof from a man who had given them everything. The church itself was the proof (3:2); so were the scars. A wife loved faithfully for thirty years can still ask whether she is loved, because she is looking for a gesture rather than a life. The demand for proof is often a sign that the actual evidence has stopped being looked at.

Not weak but powerful. They asked about Paul; he answers about Christ. Christ himself has shown his power among them: in their conversion, in the gifts, in the miracles. He is the Lord who calmed the sea with a word and raised the dead with a shout, and who now works with the same power through jars of clay.

A domesticated Christ. A church that has learned to disregard a gentle minister can slide into disregarding the Lord who sent him. The messenger’s mildness gets attributed to the message, then to the one who gave it, and a congregation ends up with a tame Christ, endlessly patient in a way that means nothing is at stake. The gentleness is Paul’s; the power belongs to someone else. If your picture of Christ has become someone who never presses, confronts or requires anything, it did not come from the Gospels, where he cleared the temple with a whip and wept over a city that would not come to him (John 2:15; Luke 19:41). He is not weak in dealing with his people. He is patient, which is a different thing entirely.

How does Christ show his power in a church today? Mostly in ways that do not look spectacular. Sinners are converted under ordinary preaching. Hardened people repent. Broken marriages are mended. Believers persevere through cancer, grief and persecution with a peace nobody can explain. Quarrelling members are reconciled. Children raised in the church come to faith. A small, unimpressive congregation keeps going for a hundred years and sends out missionaries. That is resurrection power, as real as any miracle, and it is happening wherever Christ’s word is faithfully preached. Learn to see it, and thank him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crucified in weakness. This is the floor under the whole letter. The crucifixion was not a strategic manoeuvre disguised as defeat; to every eye it was defeat. He was held by nails driven by men he had made, and he died the way the powerless die: publicly, slowly, with nothing to show. The cross looked like utter weakness, yet the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25).

By the power of God. Then the sentence turns, and the turning is the gospel: the same body that hung there is alive. Not a memory kept warm by his followers; alive, by a power that reached into a sealed tomb. The resurrection displayed God’s power (Romans 1:4; Ephesians 1:19–20). Everything in the Christian faith runs through that single fact: the forgiveness, the Spirit, the church, the hope of a body that will not fail.

Weak in him. Paul applies it to himself, and to every servant of Christ since: he shares Christ’s weakness, in suffering and humility. It is not a feature of his temperament but participation in the weakness of a crucified Lord.

We will live with him. And he shares Christ’s resurrection power, which will be seen when he comes to deal with them. The power he will bring to Corinth is not his own recovered strength; it is resurrection power, belonging to Christ, exercised through a man who has none. They had been sorting people into strong and weak and had put Paul in the wrong column. He is telling them the columns do not work, because the one they worship is in both.

Weakness and power at once. For anyone who feels disqualified by frailty: the Christian life is not weakness followed by strength, as though the weakness were a phase to get through. It is weakness and power at the same time, in the same person, as it was in Christ himself: crucified in weakness, but living by the power of God. Both halves are permanently true of him; the risen Lord still bears the wounds.

What does it mean to be weak in him? It means that your frailties, limits and sufferings, borne as a believer, are not outside your union with Christ but part of it. When you are worn out from serving, misunderstood for doing right, sick, grieving or simply ordinary, you are sharing in the pattern of his life on earth, and you are not further from him but closer. It does not mean every weakness is holy; sin is not weakness in him. But it does mean that what makes you feel least like a useful Christian may be exactly where his life is at work in you, and where you will most clearly live with him by the power of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Examine yourselves. They had been examining Paul for months. He turns the instrument round. In the faith means truly believing, united to Christ, and yourselves comes first, emphatic.

Test yourselves. “Test” is the word for assaying metal: is the gold gold? This verse has done a great deal of damage in the hands of people who have used it to manufacture doubt, so it needs handling with care, because the reader most likely to take it seriously is the one who least needs to.

Or do you not realise this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Start with what the test actually is. Paul supplies it in the same breath, and it is a single question. That is the whole examination. Not are you holy enough. Not is your faith strong enough. Not have you felt the right things. Is Christ there? The sign of a true believer is that Christ dwells in him by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27). This does not mean that Christ is a feeling inside you, but that by his Spirit he has joined you to himself, so that his life is at work in yours: a new heart that trusts him, wants him and turns from sin, however weakly (Ezekiel 36:26–27). And the form of the question in Greek expects the answer yes. Paul is not suggesting they will probably fail; he is confident about them.

Fail to meet the test! The failure clause is a sharp afterthought rather than an expectation: adokimos is metal that proves counterfeit. And there is a turn in the argument. If they find Christ is in them, then their faith came through Paul, which proves his apostleship. If not, they have bigger problems than Paul.

Where Christians differ: self-examination and assurance. Some say believers should never doubt their salvation; others make constant introspection the mark of true faith. This commentary’s view: Self-examination is commanded, especially for those whose lives contradict their profession. Assurance rests first on God’s promises in Christ, confirmed by the inner witness of the Spirit and the fruit of a changed life (1 John; the Westminster Confession 18.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2). Self-examination should lead not to endless morbid introspection but to looking at Christ, and to repentance where needed. Those who find Christ in them can rest assured.

How the test is run. Look for Christ, not for your performance. Do you love him at all? Do you want to be free of sin, even where you keep losing? Does the gospel still move you? Do you love his people, including the difficult ones? Is there anything in you that was not there before, that you did not put there? None will find your obedience perfect. The righteousness you stand in is Christ’s, whose perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9). Each question asks only whether he is present. You look inward, find very little to be proud of, and then find Christ there, not because you have kept hold of him but because he has taken up residence and has no intention of leaving.

The dead do not check their pulse. People who are entirely indifferent to Christ do not usually lie awake worrying whether he is in them. The very fear that you might fail this test, when it comes with a longing for Christ and a hatred of sin, is itself a sign of a heart God has made alive: the dead do not check their own pulse. If this verse troubles you in that way, it was written for the comfortable, not for you.

Should I examine myself before the Lord’s Supper? Yes. The church has often applied this verse to the Lord’s Table, where Paul says, let a person examine himself, then, and so eat (1 Corinthians 11:28). The examination is not whether you are worthy enough to come; no one is. It is whether you are trusting Christ and willing to turn from your sin. Confess what you know is wrong, put away any grudge, and come. Those who find Christ in them come to the table; the examination is meant to bring them there, not to keep them away. The Supper is for sinners who need grace, not for saints who think they have outgrown it.

What if I examine myself and honestly do not find Christ? Then do not despair and do not wait. Come to him now. The test is not a final verdict but a summons. Christ invites everyone who is weary and burdened, and promises that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). You do not have to fix yourself first. Confess your sin, trust him as the one who died for sinners, and ask him to make his home in you. Then talk to a pastor or mature Christian who can walk with you. And if you are simply unsure, take the uncertainty to Christ rather than further into yourself. Assurance grows by looking at him.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have not failed the test. Verse 6 returns to the argument: if they examine themselves and find Christ in them, they will discover that the man who brought him to them is genuine after all.

That you may not do wrong. What he wants is not vindication but their holiness.

Though we may seem to have failed. If they repent before he arrives, there will be no showdown, and his critics will go on saying he is all letters and no presence. He prays for exactly that outcome. He would rather be permanently misjudged than have them sin so that he can be proved right.

Numbered with the transgressors. Paul’s prayer has the shape of the cross. Jesus was willing to look like the ultimate failure, rejected by his nation, condemned as a blasphemer and numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12), so that others might be put right with God. And the Father vindicated him in his own time, raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand. Paul is willing to seem to have failed so that the Corinthians may do right. Christ was counted a sinner so that sinners might be counted righteous (5:21). The servant’s small exchange is a copy of his Master’s great one.

How rare that is. Most of us, in a dispute, want two things: for the other person to do right, and for our position to be publicly established. Paul puts their good so far ahead of his reputation that he prays away his own vindication. He can, because the record is not kept by the Corinthians: it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends (10:18). A man who believes that can afford to look like a failure.

What if the person who wronged me changes but never admits I was right? Then thank God, and let it go. Their change is the thing that matters, and it is what you should have been praying for. You may long for an apology, and sometimes it is right to ask for one, especially where a wrong needs to be acknowledged for the sake of others. But do not make your peace depend on being vindicated. God knows who was right, and his opinion is the one that will stand. Holding out for a public admission often keeps a conflict alive long after the real problem is gone. Paul prayed for the outcome in which nobody would ever know he had been right.

verseByVerse.quote: For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only for the truth. The truth means the gospel and God’s will, and his authority is not a possession to use as he likes; it was given for one purpose and does not function for any other. If the Corinthians are doing right, he cannot act against them: not may not, but cannot.

The limits of church authority. A minister’s authority is derived: it comes from the truth of the gospel and extends exactly as far as the gospel does. The moment it is used to defend something the gospel does not teach, or to protect a man rather than serve a people, it has stopped being authority at all. So the test for anyone under a leader is not whether he has authority; very possibly he does. It is what he is using it for. Authority spent on truth is real however gently it is exercised. Authority spent on anything else is a costume.

Nobody can do anything against the truth. There is a larger reading too, and Paul’s wording invites it: not his opponents, not the super-apostles, not the men who have spent months telling this church its founder is a fraud. The truth of God is not fragile. It has outlived better attackers in every century, and it does not depend on the reputation of the people carrying it. So the worst that can happen to a faithful person is to be misunderstood for a while. The truth is not at risk. Gamaliel, of all people, saw it: if this undertaking is of man it will fail, but if it is of God you will not be able to overthrow it (Acts 5:38–39).

The truth before Pilate. The fullest proof of this verse stood in Pilate’s hall. Jesus said that he had been born and had come into the world to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37), and Pilate asked, what is truth? Then the world did everything it could against the one who is the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). It killed him and sealed him in. On the third day the stone was rolled away. That is why Paul can say flatly that nothing can be done against the truth. He knows what happened the one time the whole world tried.

Is it not arrogant to claim to have the truth? That charge would stick if Paul claimed to own it. He claims the opposite: he is under the truth and cannot act against it. The proud position is to make yourself the measure of what is true. A person who says that the truth stands over him, and may judge his own teaching and conduct, has made himself small. And the truth Paul means is not a theory of his own. It is a person, Jesus Christ, who died for those who opposed him and rose again. To believe in that truth is not to look down on anyone. It is to stand under the same truth as the person you speak to, and to point him to the Saviour who has borne with you.

What if my church leaders ask me to do something against Scripture? Then you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), respectfully but firmly. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and no church may bind it to anything contrary to his word (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2). Make sure first that the matter is really one of Scripture and not of your preference; most disagreements with leaders are about wisdom, and there you should be slow to resist and quick to trust. But if you are asked to sin, to keep silent about abuse, to deny what the Bible plainly teaches, or to give a leader the obedience due to Christ, decline graciously, explain why from Scripture, and seek counsel from other mature believers.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Glad when we are weak. Glad means rejoice, not resignation. After four chapters arguing that he is not weak, he says he is delighted to be the weak one, provided they are strong. Their strength is his joy.

That is what a father says. There is no competition in it. A parent who has spent himself raising children does not feel diminished when they outgrow him; the point was to be surpassed. The opposite instinct is common in Christian work and rarely admitted: the counsellor whose people never quite graduate, the leader who cannot delegate, the parent who needs to be needed. It looks like devotion and is a subtle form of self-service, and the sign is whether you are genuinely glad when they no longer require you.

Weak so that you may be strong. Paul’s gladness has a source. The whole letter is built on an exchange: death is at work in us, but life in you (4:12); he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (8:9). That is the shape of Christ’s own work. He went down into weakness so that his people might be made strong, and out of the anguish of his soul he sees the fruit and is satisfied (Isaiah 53:11). A servant who is glad to be the weak one, so long as the church is strong, is wearing his Master’s likeness.

Your restoration is what we pray for. “Restoration” (katartisis) is a rich word: being put right, mended, equipped. Its verb is used of mending nets, as James and John were doing when Jesus called them (Mark 1:19), and by Greek medical writers of setting a broken bone. That is a better picture of what God does with a damaged church, or a damaged Christian, than most we carry: not replacement or papering over, but mending. A mended net still shows where it tore, and it holds fish.

Prayer and command. And it is the same word Paul will use as a command in verse 11: aim for restoration. So he prays for the mending and then tells them to work at it, which is how Scripture almost always handles the relationship between God’s work and ours.

How do I help someone without making them dependent on me? Aim from the start at their growth, not your role. Point them to Christ and to Scripture rather than to yourself. Teach them to pray and to read the Bible for themselves. Connect them to the wider church so that you are not their only support. Give them responsibility as soon as they can carry it, and let them make small mistakes. Celebrate when they no longer need you as much. And watch your own heart: if you feel a pang when someone you helped moves on, take it to God and ask him to make you glad. That gladness is the surest sign your help was love.

For worship. Peter knew what it was to be mended. He had torn himself apart with three denials, and the risen Lord met him by the lake, made him breakfast and restored him with three questions (John 21:9–17). Years later Peter wrote that after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you (1 Peter 5:10), using the very word behind Paul’s prayer here. God does not replace his broken people with better ones; he mends them himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I am away. Paul explains, at the end, why the letter exists. He writes while away so that he will not have to be severe when present: every hard sentence in this letter was written in the hope that it would spare them a harder conversation.

Not severe. “Severe” comes from a verb for cutting off. That reverses the accusation of 10:10. They said he was bold at a distance and feeble in person. In fact he was bold at a distance so that he would not have to be severe in person, which is not cowardice but mercy, and harder than simply arriving and dealing with everyone. There is a lesson for anyone who must confront somebody: say it early, and give the other person room to move before you are face to face. A warning that arrives in time is a kindness; the same words at the confrontation are just a verdict.

For building up. He said it at 10:8, and repeats it at the close because it is the charter of all Christian authority. The Lord gave it, for construction, not destruction. That supplies the plainest test for any exercise of power in a church: not whether the person has the right, but what is being built. Discipline that aims at restoration is building; the same discipline aimed at establishing who is in charge is demolition, though the words may be identical. Paul was building, as his Lord is building, a temple of living stones that the gates of hell will not prevail against.

Not to condemn but to save. The authority is the Lord’s, and so is its purpose. God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). Even Christ’s rebukes serve that end: those whom I love, I reprove and discipline (Revelation 3:19). He spoke his sharpest words to churches he meant to keep, and he warned before he acted, as Paul is doing here.

How should I receive correction? Quickly, humbly and gratefully, even when it hurts. Proverbs says whoever heeds reproof is honoured, and the wise love the one who rebukes them (Proverbs 9:8; 13:18). Listen to the whole of it before defending yourself. Ask whether it is true, even partly, rather than whether it was fairly delivered. Take it to God and ask him to show you what he wants you to learn. Thank the person, since it is rarely easy to say. And then act on it. Paul wrote this letter so that the Corinthians could change before he arrived; correction received in time is one of God’s great mercies.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Final Greetings and the Trinitarian Benediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with brief appeals and the promise that the God of love and peace will be with them, then greetings, and a final blessing that names the Lord Jesus Christ, God the Father and the Holy Spirit together over the whole church.
verseByVerse.theology:
The benediction names the three persons acting distinctly and together, each giving to the believer. The order (Christ, then the Father, then the Spirit) is unusual for Paul, who normally names the Father first, perhaps because this letter has dwelt so much on the grace of Christ (5:21; 8:9).

The fellowship of the Holy Spirit can mean the fellowship the Spirit creates among believers, or our sharing in the Spirit himself, or the Spirit as the one who brings us into fellowship with the Father and the Son. These do not compete; the Spirit does all three, and the life he shares with us shows itself in real love among believers.
verseByVerse.examples: A church has closed every service with this benediction for decades, and it has become a familiar ending. One Sunday the pastor pauses before it and asks what the congregation is about to receive: the grace that flows from Christ’s cross, the love of the Father that sent him, the fellowship the Spirit creates with God and among the people in the room. The benediction is not a farewell but a sending out under the blessing of the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, brothers, rejoice. The tone changes entirely, and the first word is brothers: after a whole letter of defence, irony and warning, that is what he calls them. Then five quick commands, each answering something that had gone wrong there. “Rejoice” was also the ordinary farewell, but here it is a command, said to a quarrelling, suspicious congregation by a man who had been flogged five times.

Aim for restoration. The mending he prayed for in verse 9 he now tells them to work at. Mend the nets. Set the bone.

Comfort one another. Or, as it can also be translated, listen to my appeal. Either way, it is the great word of the letter one last time (1:3–4). The letter that opened with comfort coming down from God closes with comfort moving sideways between believers.

Comfort through Christ. The comfort that is to pass between believers did not start with them. Paul told this church at the outset where it comes from: as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (1:5). Because he suffered, his people are never comforted by someone who does not understand; and because he lives, the comfort never runs dry.

Agree with one another. Literally, think the same thing: be of one mind (Philippians 2:2).
