Not uniformity of opinion, but the shared mind of people pulling in one direction, which is exactly what a church loses first when it starts sorting itself into parties. And live in peace, the plainest of the five and the hardest: end the quarrels (12:20).

And the God of love and peace will be with you. The promise comes last. He does not say God will be with you and then you will manage these things. Obedience does not earn God’s presence, but a church living in mutual comfort and peace is a church where his presence is known and felt, and a quarrelling one is not, whatever is true of it in principle. And the title, found only here in the New Testament, names exactly what that congregation lacked, because the supply was never going to come from inside the room. The God of love and peace is not a distant reward for peaceful people; he is the one who made peace by the blood of his Son’s cross, when we were his enemies.

How can I rejoice when my church is a mess? By rejoicing in the Lord rather than in the church’s condition (Philippians 4:4). Paul commands joy to a church that has broken his heart, because the grounds of joy are not in Corinth: they are in Christ, who has not changed, who is still building his church, and who will present her spotless in the end. Rejoice that the gospel is still preached, that sinners are still forgiven, that God is still patient. Thank him for the people in your church who are faithful. Then do your part in the mending. Joy is not pretending things are fine; it is knowing that the Lord is greater than the mess.

Does agreeing with one another mean I must never disagree? No. It means pulling in the same direction, with the same aim, under the same Lord. Christians will differ on many matters of judgment, and Paul himself disagreed sharply with Barnabas (Acts 15:39). What he forbids is factions, rivalry and the refusal to seek common ground. So disagree honestly and kindly, keep the gospel at the centre, do not let disagreement curdle into contempt, and be willing to give way on what is not essential for the sake of peace. As far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18).

In everyday life. Most church peace is made in small moments: the chair you take next to someone you clashed with, the kind word after a hard meeting, the decision not to replay an old argument on the drive home. All of it is the mending Paul asks for, made possible by the Spirit whose fellowship he pronounces over them in his last sentence (13:14). If there is someone you have not spoken to properly since a disagreement, the first move may be yours.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A holy kiss. Paul gives this instruction in four letters (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26), so it was no throwaway. In that world a kiss on the cheek was the ordinary greeting between family members and close friends, carrying the message: this person is one of mine. In the church it expressed love, reconciliation and family belonging. The word holy is the guard on it: a genuinely family greeting, pure and without any other intent, a caution evidently needed then and now.

Across every line. What makes it worth a command is who was doing it to whom. In a Corinthian gathering the kiss crossed every line the city cared about. A slave greeted his owner, a labourer a householder, a Jew a Greek. And Paul tells this particular church to do it: the one that had sorted itself into factions, taken its members to court and humiliated the poor at the Lord’s Table. It is very hard to greet someone as family in front of the congregation while carrying a grudge against them, which is presumably part of the point.

One in Christ Jesus. Why did those lines fall in that room and nowhere else? Because everyone in it had been received by the same Lord on the same terms. There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28). He himself is our peace, who has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). The holy kiss was not a social experiment. It is what people do when they have all been forgiven by the same blood and adopted into the same family: they greet each other as kin, because in him they are.

All the saints greet you. Paul is most likely writing from Macedonia (7:5; 9:2–4), and he sends greetings from believers the Corinthians have never met: probably the Macedonian churches such as Philippi and Thessalonica, poor and afflicted, whose gifts had supported his work in Corinth (11:9). It reminds a troubled congregation that they are not alone and not the whole story. The church has never been the size of the room you are standing in.

What it does not mean. A literal kiss is not required in every culture; the form is not the command. But the substance is not optional, and it is easily lost. A congregation can hold sound doctrine and never once make warm, public, unembarrassed contact across the lines its society draws, and something the New Testament assumed would be visible every week has quietly disappeared.

What does a holy kiss look like in my church? Whatever form of warm greeting your culture uses between family members, given to fellow believers, especially to those you would not naturally greet. A firm handshake and a real conversation with the visitor nobody knows. An embrace for the widow who sits alone. A greeting for the member of a different class, race or generation. A smile and a word for the person you clashed with at the last meeting. Respect people’s comfort, and keep every gesture appropriate and above reproach, especially with children and between men and women. The holy kiss is family affection made visible; make sure no one leaves your church on a Sunday feeling like a stranger.

For worship. A sinful woman wept over Jesus’ feet and would not stop kissing them, and he sent her away forgiven (Luke 7:38, 45–48). And in the story Jesus told of a lost son coming home, the father saw him a long way off, ran, embraced him and kissed him before the boy could say a word of his rehearsed confession (Luke 15:20). That is the welcome behind every holy kiss in Corinth: a Father who runs to meet the returning, and a Son who received sinners at a cost no one else could pay.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. The letter ends here, and it is the fullest benediction in the New Testament: three persons, three gifts, one sentence. The letter began with a man who had despaired of life itself and found God to be the Father of mercies; it has gone through tears and floggings, a thorn that was never removed, a church that broke his heart and mended, and an apostle lowered out of a window in a basket. It ends with the triune God pronounced over the whole difficult congregation without distinction. Paul closes every letter with grace; here alone he opens the blessing out into all three persons, because every one of the three has been the subject of this letter. Grace was what he was told was sufficient. Love was what he was accused of lacking. Fellowship was what had broken down between him and them. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ is named first, which is unusual; the Father normally comes first in Paul. But grace has been the pressure point of the letter (8:9; 12:9): the free, undeserved favour shown in Christ to people who have earned the opposite, and it is the door everything else comes through. Grace comes first because it is through Christ that we come to know the Father’s love.

And the love of God. The Father’s love, the source of everything (John 3:16; Romans 5:8). It stands behind the grace rather than being produced by it. Christ did not persuade a reluctant Father to love us. The love came first and sent him. John puts it plainly: love does not begin with our loving God but with God loving us and sending his Son as the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). A propitiation is a sacrifice that absorbs the holy anger sin deserves and so removes it, and here the Father himself provided it.

And the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. “Fellowship” (koinōnia) means sharing, communion, having something in common. It means our fellowship with the Spirit, the one who gives us a share in God himself; and the fellowship among believers that the Spirit creates, making a collection of unrelated people into a body. The second was precisely what this church needed.

Be with you all. All of them. The ones who had stayed loyal, and the ones who had listened to his enemies. The man who had insulted him publicly. The people who had let it happen and said nothing. Those who had not yet repented, whom he expected to have to mourn over. Paul has one blessing and he does not divide it.

The Trinity. This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is one of the clearest witnesses to the Trinity in Scripture. Written about twenty-five years after the resurrection, it shows that within a generation Christians were already naming Father, Son and Spirit together as the one source of blessing, the faith the church later set out as one God in three persons. It does not mean three gods, nor one God wearing three masks in turn; it means one God who eternally exists as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God and each truly distinct, into whose one name believers are baptised (Matthew 28:19).

Why does the Trinity matter for ordinary Christians? Because it is the shape of our salvation and of our prayers. The Father planned it and sent the Son in love; the Son accomplished it by his grace, living, dying and rising for us; the Spirit applies it, uniting us to Christ and to one another. If God were not three persons, there would be no one to send and no one to be sent, no Son to stand in our place before the Father, and no Spirit to bring us home. We pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. And because God has always been a fellowship of love within himself, love is not something he needed us for; it is what he is, and what he shares with us freely.

What is a benediction, and does it actually do anything? A benediction is a word of blessing spoken over God’s people in his name, as the priests blessed Israel with the LORD bless you and keep you (Numbers 6:24–26). It is not magic, and it does not work apart from faith. But it is more than a polite wish. It is a declaration of what God gives in Christ, spoken by his word to his people, and God is pleased to use his word. That is why many churches end worship with this verse. When you hear it, do not reach for your coat. Receive it, believe it, and go out under it.

In everyday life. Pray this blessing slowly, one phrase at a time, over someone you find difficult in your church. Paul did not divide the blessing, and neither should you.

For worship. Before there was a world, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit lived in perfect fellowship, needing nothing. This last sentence opens that life to quarrelling, suspicious, half-repentant Corinthians: the grace of the Son that bought them, the love of the Father that sent him, the fellowship of the Spirit that joins them to both and to one another. It closes on you all, because the blessing of God was never rationed to the deserving, and he has not changed.
verseByVerse.note: This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is still widely used to close Christian worship.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>2</sup>I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—<sup>3</sup>since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.<sup>4</sup>For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.<sup>5</sup>Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!<sup>6</sup>I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test.<sup>7</sup>But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.<sup>8</sup>For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.<sup>9</sup>For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.<sup>10</sup>For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.<sup>11</sup>Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.<sup>12</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss.<sup>13</sup>All the saints greet you.<sup>14</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
